Step 2: it sends traffic to 10.20.0.7 in subnet-b. Step 3: both addresses sit in the same VPC, so the route exists automatically. Step 4: a firewall rule permitting port 443 from 10.10.0.0/20 allows the packet through.

Common mistake: assuming a subnet is global, or choosing regional routing for a hybrid link and then finding that on-premises networks are unreachable from the other region after a failover.

Consequence in a running system: if a VPN tunnel in europe-west1 is the only path to the office, and routing is regional, a workload that fails over to us-central1 loses that path silently. Global routing avoids that outage, at the cost of a wider blast radius for route changes.

questions.prompt: A company called Harbor Freight Co-op has a VPC named ledger-net set to regional routing mode. Its Cloud Router link to headquarters (range 172.16.0.0/16) sits in us-east4. Trace one request from a virtual machine in a subnet in europe-west4. Step 1: the VM in the europe-west4 subnet needs to reach 172.16.8.10 at headquarters. Step 2: because routing mode is regional, learned routes such as the headquarters range apply only to subnets in us-east4, where the link sits. Step 3: ______. Step 4: the packet is not delivered and the VM sees a timeout.
choices: The VPC is global by default, so the headquarters route is installed for the europe-west4 subnet and the packet is sent over the link.
A VPC peering connection is created automatically between europe-west4 and us-east4 to carry the packet.
The packet is forwarded to us-east4 and back, which adds latency but still reaches headquarters.
No route to 172.16.0.0/16 exists for the europe-west4 subnet, so the packet has no path and is dropped.
questions.why: In regional mode the learned headquarters route is only installed for subnets in the region of the Cloud Router, so a subnet in europe-west4 has no route and the packet is dropped.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes a subnet in Google Cloud?
choices: A firewall boundary that must be created once for each zone in a region.
A block of IP addresses inside a VPC that belongs to exactly one region.
A global resource that can span every region of the VPC it belongs to.
A separate physical network that lives in a single zone of a region.
questions.why: The teaching text says each subnet is a block of addresses inside a VPC and belongs to exactly one region, so the other options misstate its scope or nature.

questions.prompt: A co-op named Ridgeline Seeds has a VPC called field-net in global routing mode. Its hybrid VPN lands in us-west2, and a reporting workload runs in a subnet in us-east1. Which routing mode lets that workload reach the on-premises network through the us-west2 link?
choices: Global mode, so that learned routes apply to subnets in every region, including us-east1.
Regional mode, because subnets in any region automatically receive routes from every Cloud Router in the VPC.
Regional mode, because the subnet in us-east1 is in a different region from the VPN and so cannot use its routes.
Global mode, but only if the us-east1 subnet was created as a global resource.
questions.why: Global routing mode applies learned routes to subnets in every region, which is what lets a us-east1 subnet use a link terminating in us-west2; the other options misstate how regional mode or subnet scope works.

questions.prompt: A team builds a VPC named orders-net in regional routing mode. Their VPN tunnel to the office is in asia-south1, and their billing service runs in a subnet in asia-northeast1. After a failover the billing service cannot reach the office at all, though its firewall rules allow the traffic. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The office routes were learned by a link in asia-south1 and in regional mode they apply only to subnets in asia-south1, so asia-northeast1 has no route.
The VPN tunnel has exceeded a quota, so the office routes were removed from every region.
Subnets in different regions always need a peering link before any private traffic can pass.
The subnet in asia-northeast1 is missing a global resource flag, so it cannot read VPC routes.
questions.why: In regional mode, routes learned through a Cloud Router apply only to subnets in the region where that connection sits, so a subnet in asia-northeast1 never receives the office routes even when firewall rules allow the traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what is global and what is regional in a Google Cloud VPC network, and name one limit or tradeoff a planner must weigh when choosing the dynamic routing mode.
lessons.modelAnswer: The VPC network itself is global, so one network can hold subnets in many regions, and private traffic between them works without extra links as long as firewall rules allow it. Subnets are regional, each tied to one region and one IP range that must not overlap with other subnets or on-premises ranges. The dynamic routing mode decides where routes learned from a Cloud Router connection apply. Regional mode keeps those routes local to the region, which limits the blast radius of a bad route change but means a failover to another region can lose the on-premises path. Global mode shares learned routes everywhere, which simplifies failover but spreads any route mistake across all regions. Cross-region traffic also adds latency and charges, so I would keep chatty services in one region where I can.
rubricPoints: VPC networks are global while subnets are regional, each with one IP range
Machines in different regions of one VPC can communicate privately if firewall rules allow it
Dynamic routing mode controls whether learned routes apply to one region or all regions
Regional routing limits blast radius but can break hybrid paths during regional failover
Cross-region traffic adds latency and cost, which shapes where workloads are placed

suggested.rationale: A scenario-style design question about region placement and routing mode builds the judgement this objective tests better than a read-only summary, though no existing mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Every network link has a largest packet size it can carry in one piece. That limit is called the MTU, short for maximum transmission unit, and it is measured in bytes. When you connect your office or data center to Google Cloud, traffic travels through a tunnel or a dedicated physical link, and that wrapping can make the usable size smaller than what the cloud network expects. Choosing the MTU means matching the cloud side to the smallest size the whole path can actually carry, so large packets are not silently dropped or chopped up. Get it wrong and small requests work fine while large file transfers or database results quietly stall. This lesson covers how to size it for Cloud Interconnect and HA VPN.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office router sends packets up to 1500 bytes into an encrypted VPN tunnel that reaches a cloud VM. Do you think the VM can receive a 1500-byte packet unchanged after the tunnel adds its own wrapping? Why or why not?
lessons.teach: MTU (maximum transmission unit) is the largest packet, counted in bytes, that a network link will carry without splitting it. A VPC (virtual private cloud, your private network inside Google Cloud) has its own MTU setting, and its subnets and VMs use it. Hybrid links add bytes of their own. HA VPN (High Availability Virtual Private Network, an encrypted tunnel that uses two tunnels for redundancy) wraps each packet in extra headers. Cloud Interconnect (a dedicated or partner physical link between your site and Google) has an MTU set per VLAN attachment, which is the logical circuit on that link. The path MTU is the smallest MTU along the whole route, so it is the real ceiling. Why it matters: when a packet is too big for a hop, the hop either fragments it, which costs time and CPU, or drops it. If the sender sets the Don't Fragment flag, the drop is silent, and the sender only learns the smaller size from an ICMP message. Many firewalls block those messages, so the sender keeps retrying big packets and stalls. Worked example, as an illustration: the on-premises router MTU is 1500 bytes and the tunnel adds about 60 bytes of overhead. Step 1: the usable payload through the tunnel is roughly 1500 minus 60, which is about 1440. Step 2: if the VPC MTU is left at 1460, a full-size VM packet of 1460 bytes cannot pass. Step 3: either lower the VPC or VM MTU to fit, or use MSS (maximum segment size) clamping, which tells TCP to negotiate smaller segments. The real overhead depends on your tunnel and link, so use the documented value for your configuration. Common mistake: sizing only for the cloud side and assuming the default 1460 works everywhere. Consequence: pings and small web pages succeed while large uploads, replication, and backups hang, which looks like a random application bug. The MTU must be sized for the smallest hop on the hybrid path, not for the cloud default.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs reporting workloads in a VPC (virtual private cloud, its private network inside Google Cloud) whose MTU (maximum transmission unit, the largest packet in bytes a link carries without splitting it) is set to 1460. Traffic leaves through a Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment (the logical circuit on a dedicated physical link to Google) with MTU 1500, then crosses a core switch with MTU 1500, then a partner tunnel on the edge firewall that accepts only 1380 bytes. Step 1: list each hop's MTU: attachment 1500, core switch 1500, edge tunnel 1380. Step 2: the path MTU, which is the smallest MTU along the whole route, is 1380. Step 3 is left for you: state what the VPC MTU must be set to, and why, using only the path MTU from Step 2.
choices: The VPC MTU of 1460 is fine because the Interconnect attachment carries 1500 bytes, so the path can handle it.
The VPC MTU can stay at 1460 because the firewall will fragment oversized packets at no real cost to throughput.
The VPC MTU must be lowered to 1380 or below so full-size packets fit the smallest hop on the path.
The VPC MTU must be raised to 1500 to match the Interconnect attachment, since the attachment sets the ceiling.
questions.why: The path MTU is the smallest hop value, here 1380, so any VPC MTU above that lets full-size packets fail or be split on the edge tunnel, and lowering it to 1380 or below is what makes them fit.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines path MTU?
choices: It is the MTU configured on the VPC network only, regardless of the links the traffic crosses.
It is the smallest MTU along the whole route, and it is the real ceiling for packet size.
It is the largest MTU any single hop on the route supports, since that hop sets the limit.
It is the average packet size a sender uses across a route over a day.
questions.why: Path MTU is defined in the teaching text as the smallest MTU along the entire route, which is why it governs the real packet ceiling rather than any single hop or the cloud setting alone.

questions.prompt: A company moves nightly database backups over an HA VPN tunnel (a pair of encrypted tunnels for redundancy). Pings and small web pages work, but large backup transfers stall. The on-premises firewall blocks ICMP (the control messages a router uses to report problems, including a 'packet too big' notice). The sender sets the Don't Fragment flag, meaning routers must not split the packet. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Large packets are silently dropped at a hop with a smaller MTU, and the blocked ICMP notice means the sender never learns to shrink them.
The Cloud Interconnect quota has been exceeded, which only affects traffic that is not encrypted.
The DNS server is returning the wrong address, so the backup connects to the wrong host.
The subnet has too few VM addresses for the backup job to start.
questions.why: With Don't Fragment set, an oversized packet is dropped silently at the smaller hop, and blocking the ICMP message stops the sender from discovering the correct size, which explains why small traffic works while large transfers hang.

questions.prompt: A team's VPC MTU is 1500. Their hybrid path has hops of 1500, 1500, and 1420 bytes, because an overlay adds overhead on one link. Which action best fits the constraint that the smallest hop sets the ceiling?
choices: Keep the VPC MTU at 1500, because the hybrid path includes two hops that support it.
Raise the VPC MTU to 9000 to add headroom, since larger MTUs always reduce packet loss.
Set the VPC or VM MTU at or below 1420, or use MSS clamping (telling TCP to negotiate smaller segments), so packets fit the 1420 hop.
Ignore the 1420 hop because only the cloud side of the path decides MTU for VMs.
questions.why: The path MTU is the smallest value on the route, so sizing must fit the 1420 hop either by lowering the MTU or clamping MSS, and ignoring the on-premises hop is the mistake that causes stalled large transfers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose the MTU for a VPC that connects to on-premises over HA VPN, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by finding the smallest MTU on the whole path, including the on-premises router and the tunnel's encryption overhead, rather than starting from the cloud default of 1460. Then I would set the VPC and VM MTU to fit under that ceiling, or leave the VPC alone and rely on MSS clamping at the gateway so TCP picks smaller segments. The tradeoff is that a lower MTU means more packets for the same data, so throughput and CPU cost go up a little. Lowering it is safer than fragmentation, but it is only as good as the documented overhead I used. If the path changes, for example by moving to Cloud Interconnect with a different attachment MTU, the number has to be checked again.
rubricPoints: MTU is the largest packet a link carries, and the path MTU is the smallest value along the whole route.
Encrypted tunnels such as HA VPN add overhead, so the usable size is smaller than the physical MTU.
Oversized packets are either fragmented or dropped, and dropped ones can stall silently if ICMP messages are blocked.
A fix is to size the VPC or VM MTU to the path, or use MSS clamping, with a tradeoff in packet count.

suggested.rationale: Choosing an MTU is a situational judgment about path limits, so reasoning through a hybrid scenario adds more than reading a single value.

lessons.plain: Some traffic should not go straight from your servers to the outside network. Organizations often want a firewall, an intrusion detector, or another inspection tool to look at it first. Third-party device insertion means placing a software appliance made by someone else into the path that packets already take, so the packets pass through it. You do this with custom routes, which tell the cloud network to send chosen traffic to the appliance instead of its usual exit. When you run several appliances for capacity and safety, a load balancer spreads traffic across them and stops sending to any that fail. Planning this well means knowing where traffic goes out and where replies come back, and what the appliance can and cannot see.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you want every outbound web request from one group of servers to pass through a firewall you run yourself, what two things must you tell the cloud network, and what goes wrong if you only tell it one of them?
lessons.teach: A network virtual appliance is a virtual machine running third-party network software, such as a firewall, intrusion detection system, or router, placed in the traffic path. A route is a rule in a virtual network that says which next hop should receive packets bound for a given destination range. A custom route is one you create yourself, as opposed to the subnet routes and default internet route the network provides. A next hop is the place a packet is handed to next: a gateway, a single instance, or an internal load balancer. A network tag is a label on a virtual machine that a route can match, so the route applies only to tagged machines. Why it works: when several routes match a destination, the most specific prefix wins, and when routes tie, the lower priority number wins. Worked example: web instances carry the tag inspected. You add a custom route for 0.0.0.0/0 with priority 800, scoped to that tag, whose next hop is an internal passthrough load balancer in front of two firewall VMs. The default internet route has priority 1000. Step one: a tagged web instance sends a packet to a public address. Step two: both routes match, and the custom route has the lower number, so it wins. Step three: the load balancer picks one healthy firewall VM for the flow. Step four: that firewall forwards the packet, which requires IP forwarding to be enabled on the VM so it can pass traffic not addressed to itself. Common mistake: forgetting the return path. If replies take a different route, a stateful firewall sees a connection it never started and drops it. Consequence in a running system: outbound calls from the web tier hang while the appliances still report healthy. Another mistake is applying a broad steering route to the appliances' own subnet, which can create a loop. Load balancing gives you several appliances and failover through health checks, but each flow stays pinned to one appliance, so capacity depends on how many long-lived flows land on each box. Plan the return path and the appliances' own routes before you deploy the first custom route.

questions.prompt: Ledgerline Health runs a billing service on VMs tagged billing in subnet 10.40.0.0/24. Its custom route for 10.70.0.0/16 has priority 400 and next hop an internal passthrough load balancer in front of two inspection VMs. Traced step by step: (1) A billing VM sends a packet to 10.70.12.5. (2) The custom route for 10.70.0.0/16 and the default internet route both match, and the custom route wins because its prefix is more specific. (3) The load balancer picks one healthy inspection VM for the flow. (4) The inspection VM forwards the packet to 10.70.12.5, which has IP forwarding enabled on the inspection VM. The reply from 10.70.12.5 is addressed to the billing VM, but nothing has been planned for it yet. Which step is still missing so the reply returns through the same inspection VM?
choices: Add a route on the 10.70.0.0/16 side that sends replies for 10.40.0.0/24 to the same internal load balancer.
Give the inspection VMs the billing tag so the reply matches the custom route.
Raise the priority number of the default internet route to 900 so it loses to the custom route.
Enable Cloud NAT on the billing subnet so the reply is translated before it leaves.
questions.why: A stateful inspection device only accepts replies that travel back through it, so the destination side needs a route that sends replies for the billing subnet to the same load balancer; the other choices change the outbound path or the tags but do not steer the return traffic.

questions.prompt: A subnet 10.9.0.0/16 has a custom route at priority 100 with next hop A, and a second custom route for 10.9.4.0/24 at priority 900 with next hop B. A packet to 10.9.4.7 is sent. Which next hop receives it, and why?
choices: B, because the more specific /24 prefix wins when routes match the same destination, even though its priority number is higher.
Neither, because two custom routes that overlap cause the packet to be dropped.
A and B equally, because the packet is split across both next hops.
A, because the lower priority number always wins regardless of prefix length.
questions.why: Among matching routes the most specific prefix is chosen first, and only when prefixes tie does the lower priority number decide, so the /24 route with next hop B receives the packet.

questions.prompt: A team puts three firewall VMs in subnet 10.30.0.0/24. They add a custom route for 0.0.0.0/0 at priority 500 with next hop the internal load balancer in front of those firewalls, and do not restrict it by tag or scope. Shortly after, the firewalls report high traffic and intermittent stalls. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The firewalls' own outbound traffic matches the broad steering route and can be sent back toward the load balancer, creating a loop.
The load balancer has run out of quota for forwarding rules across all regions.
Network tags on the firewall VMs have overwritten the subnet route for 10.30.0.0/24.
The default internet route has been deleted, so no traffic can reach the internet at all.
questions.why: A broad steering route applied to the appliances' own subnet can match their own traffic, sending it back to the load balancer in a loop, which is the failure case the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: Four inspection VMs sit behind one internal passthrough load balancer. Health checks show all four as healthy, yet one VM is near its bandwidth limit while the other three are mostly idle, and the pattern persists over hours. Which explanation fits the design?
choices: The three idle VMs lack IP forwarding, so the load balancer ignores them for traffic distribution.
The load balancer sends each packet to a random appliance, so the imbalance must be a fault in the health checks.
Each flow stays pinned to one appliance, so a few long-lived flows landing on the same box can overload it while the others sit idle.
Health checks only report on failover, so they cannot show that one appliance is busy.
questions.why: Load balancing across appliances keeps each flow on one appliance, so capacity depends on how many long-lived flows happen to land on each, which is why health being green does not guarantee even load.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would send outbound traffic from an application subnet through a pool of third-party inspection appliances, and name one limit or tradeoff of that design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would place identical appliance VMs behind an internal passthrough load balancer, then add a custom route for the outbound destination range with a lower priority number than the default internet route. I would scope that route with a network tag so only the application tier is steered, and I would make sure the appliance VMs have IP forwarding enabled. The return path has to come back through the same pool, or the stateful firewall will drop replies it never saw start. The tradeoff is that each flow stays on one appliance, so a few long-lived connections can load a single box while others sit idle, and failover only works as well as the health checks behind the load balancer. Before cutover I would run a path trace from a tagged instance, and I would keep the appliances' own subnet off the steering route to avoid loops.
rubricPoints: Names the custom route, its destination range, and its next hop as an internal load balancer or appliance instance, not just 'a firewall'.
Explains how priority and network-tag scoping steer only the chosen traffic.
Covers the need for a symmetric return path through the same stateful appliance.
States the tradeoff that flows stay pinned to one appliance, so capacity and failover depend on flow distribution and health checks.
Mentions IP forwarding on appliances or avoiding loops in the appliances' own routes.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet hop by hop through custom routes and an appliance pool is the core skill here, and the planned path tracer would let the learner check it.

lessons.plain: A hybrid connection is the link that lets computers in your own office or data center talk privately with the systems you run in Google Cloud. Designing one means choosing among a few ways to build that link: a private physical circuit into a shared building, a circuit bought through a telecom partner, an encrypted tunnel sent over the public internet, or a branch device that manages several links. Each choice trades off speed, cost, how much traffic it can carry, how fast it can be set up, and how much security you must add yourself. The right answer depends on where your equipment sits and how much steady traffic you expect.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office has a 1 Gbps internet line and needs to send about 8 Gbps of steady, sensitive data each night to a cloud network. Would you first consider an encrypted tunnel over the internet or a dedicated private circuit, and why?
lessons.teach:
On-premises means equipment you own or rent in your own facilities. Cloud Interconnect is Google's family of private links between that equipment and Google's network. Dedicated Interconnect is a physical circuit you order into a colocation facility, a shared building where Google has equipment, so you must already have racks or a carrier presence there. Its links run at 10 or 100 Gbps and can be bundled together. Partner Interconnect buys a slice of capacity from a service provider that already has that connection, so you can start with much smaller sizes and need no presence in the building. Cloud VPN sends IPsec tunnels, which are encrypted links, across the public internet. HA VPN pairs tunnels across two interfaces for higher availability, but each tunnel has a throughput ceiling and internet paths add variable delay. An SD-WAN appliance is a branch device that chooses among several of these links and sends traffic over whichever is healthy.

Worked example: a branch needs 4 Gbps of steady replication to Google Cloud and must stay private. Step one: 4 Gbps is more than a single VPN tunnel should be relied on to carry, so VPN alone is weak. Step two: the company has no equipment in a colocation facility, so Dedicated Interconnect is out. Step three: a Partner Interconnect attachment sized at 5 Gbps fits the steady load, and an HA VPN link over the internet can serve as a backup path.

Common mistake: assuming a VPN is fine because it is encrypted, without checking throughput or the MTU, which is the largest packet size a link carries. Tunnel headers make the usable MTU smaller than the usual 1500 bytes. If that is ignored, large packets get dropped or fragmented, so small requests succeed while bulk replication stalls.

In a running system this shows up as a link that looks healthy on a status page while the nightly job times out. Choose the link by sustained bandwidth, the privacy you need, and the MTU it leaves for your workloads.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic group needs a steady 2.5 Gbps of private transfers from its records system to Google Cloud. It has no equipment in any colocation facility. Step one: a 2.5 Gbps steady load is more than a single VPN tunnel should be relied on to carry, so VPN alone is weak. Step two: with no colocation presence, Dedicated Interconnect is out. Step three: ____ . Step four: an HA VPN link over the internet is kept as a backup path.
choices: Size a Partner Interconnect attachment near 3 Gbps for the steady load, then confirm the usable MTU across that path is below 1500 bytes and that workloads fit within it
Measure only the status page of the chosen link, since a healthy status means the nightly transfer will finish
Treat the link as safe because the tunnels are encrypted, so packet size does not need checking
Order a 100 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect circuit anyway, since it leaves the most room for growth
questions.why: The missing step is choosing a Partner Interconnect size that carries the steady load and then checking the usable MTU, because tunnel headers shrink the packet size and oversized packets get dropped or fragmented.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits Partner Interconnect?
choices: A physical circuit ordered into a colocation facility where the customer already has racks
An encrypted tunnel carried across the public internet with a per-tunnel throughput ceiling
A branch device that picks among several links and sends traffic over whichever is healthy
A slice of capacity bought from a service provider that already has the connection, usable without equipment in the building
questions.why: Partner Interconnect buys a slice of capacity from a provider that already has the connection, so it allows smaller sizes and needs no presence in the facility.

questions.prompt: A company runs a VPN tunnel to Google Cloud. Small API calls work and pings succeed, but uploads of large backup files stall partway and time out. Which cause best fits this pattern?
choices: The branch SD-WAN appliance has been set to send all traffic over one link
The Dedicated Interconnect bundle has too few 100 Gbps links for backup traffic
The VPN is not encrypted, so the provider is throttling large packets
Large packets exceed the usable MTU left after tunnel headers, so they are dropped or fragmented while small packets pass
questions.why: Tunnel headers reduce the usable MTU below 1500 bytes, so only large packets are affected by drops or fragmentation, which matches small requests working while bulk transfers stall.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer has racks in a colocation facility and needs about 35 Gbps of sustained private capacity to Google Cloud. Which choice best fits the constraints described?
choices: An SD-WAN appliance alone, because it can pick links but does not add capacity
Dedicated Interconnect with multiple 10 Gbps links bundled together, because the company already has presence in the facility
A single Cloud VPN tunnel, because IPsec encryption gives the needed private throughput
Partner Interconnect with a 5 Gbps attachment, because it has the smallest sizes
questions.why: Dedicated Interconnect requires presence in a colocation facility, which the company has, and its 10 or 100 Gbps links can be bundled to reach the needed sustained bandwidth.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Dedicated Interconnect, Partner Interconnect and Cloud VPN for a site that needs steady private bandwidth. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the sustained bandwidth and whether the site can reach a colocation facility. If the company has equipment in a colocation facility and needs tens of Gbps, Dedicated Interconnect is the strongest fit because the circuit is private and dedicated. If the site cannot reach one of those buildings, Partner Interconnect gives private capacity through a provider and can be sized smaller. Cloud VPN is quick to set up and encrypted by default, but it runs over the public internet, so its throughput per tunnel is limited and latency varies. The main tradeoff of Cloud VPN is that you must check MTU, because tunnel headers reduce the usable packet size, and large transfers can fail quietly. I would keep HA VPN as a backup path rather than the primary for steady replication, and I would confirm the encryption needs before choosing the link.
rubricPoints: Chooses based on sustained bandwidth and whether colocation presence exists
Explains that Partner Interconnect provides private capacity without building presence
Names throughput or latency limits of Cloud VPN over the internet
Mentions MTU reduction from tunnel overhead as a risk

suggested.rationale: Choosing a link under bandwidth, privacy and location constraints is best learned by reasoning through a scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers hybrid connectivity directly.

lessons.plain: When some of your systems run in Google Cloud and others run in another cloud provider, you need a private road between the two networks. Cloud VPN builds an encrypted tunnel across the public internet. It is quick and inexpensive to set up, but its speed and delay depend on that shared internet. Cross-Cloud Interconnect is a dedicated link between Google and the other provider, so the traffic does not travel over the open internet. It costs more and takes longer to order, but it gives steadier performance and higher capacity. Choosing between them means weighing cost, bandwidth, and how much variable performance you can accept.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your application runs in Google Cloud and must reach a database in another cloud provider, but both networks use the same address range, 10.0.0.0/16. Before any teaching, what do you think will go wrong, and which connection option would you consider first, an encrypted tunnel or a dedicated link?
lessons.teach: Cloud VPN connects a Google Cloud VPC network to another network over IPsec, an encryption standard for tunnels across an untrusted network such as the internet. HA VPN, the high-availability form, provides two gateway interfaces, each with its own public address, so you can build redundant tunnels. A Cloud Router uses BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, to learn and advertise the routes between the two networks automatically. Cross-Cloud Interconnect is a dedicated, provisioned circuit between Google and another cloud provider, with traffic kept off the public internet and BGP still used for routing. Because both options exchange routes, every address range must be unique across all connected networks. Worked example: Network A uses 10.0.0.0/16 and Network B also uses 10.0.0.0/16. Each side advertises the same prefix over BGP, so routers cannot tell which destination is meant. Renumbering one side to 10.20.0.0/16 removes the conflict before any tunnel is built. Common mistake: assuming a single HA VPN tunnel gives the 99.99 percent availability target. Redundancy needs both interfaces and tunnels, ideally across two gateways, so BGP can move traffic to a surviving path when one fails. Consequence in a running system: with only one tunnel, one failed peer means a full outage between the clouds.

questions.prompt: A team links a VPC in one cloud to an on-premises network over HA VPN. The VPC uses 172.20.0.0/18 and the on-premises side uses 172.20.32.0/19. Work through it. Step 1: list the ranges each side will advertise over BGP: 172.20.0.0/18 and 172.20.32.0/19. Step 2: check for overlap. The /18 covers 172.20.0.0 through 172.20.63.255, so 172.20.32.0/19 sits entirely inside it. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: only after Step 3 is settled, create the two HA VPN gateway interfaces and their tunnels, then let Cloud Router exchange routes.
choices: Raise the BGP priority on the overlapping route so Cloud Router prefers one side.
Add a third tunnel that reuses 172.20.32.0/19 so traffic has a second path.
Move one side to a non-overlapping range and confirm no ranges overlap before any tunnel is built.
Build both tunnels first, then let BGP sort out which overlapping prefix is correct.
questions.why: Because both sides advertise their ranges over BGP, overlapping prefixes must be removed by renumbering one side before tunnels are created, since routers cannot tell which destination is meant.

questions.prompt: Which option provides a dedicated circuit between Google Cloud and another cloud provider, keeping traffic off the public internet while still using BGP for routing?
choices: Cloud Router alone, without a gateway
IPsec tunnel over the public internet
HA VPN with a single gateway interface
Cross-Cloud Interconnect
questions.why: Cross-Cloud Interconnect is the dedicated provisioned circuit described in the text, and it is the option that keeps traffic off the public internet; the other choices either travel over the internet or are not connectivity options at all.

questions.prompt: A team has built one HA VPN tunnel between two clouds and believes it meets a 99.99 percent availability target. Why is that belief wrong?
choices: HA VPN cannot use BGP, so failover never happens automatically.
BGP needs at least four tunnels before any route can be learned.
The availability target only applies to Cross-Cloud Interconnect circuits.
One tunnel means no surviving path if its peer fails, so the link goes fully down. Redundancy needs both gateway interfaces and tunnels, ideally across two gateways.
questions.why: Availability depends on having a second path that BGP can move traffic onto; with a single tunnel, one failed peer causes a full outage between the clouds, so the single tunnel does not deliver the target.

questions.prompt: Two networks both use 192.168.10.0/24 and want to exchange routes over BGP. What must happen before routing can work correctly?
choices: Nothing needs to change, because BGP picks the first advertisement it receives.
Address ranges must be unique across all connected networks, so one side has to be renumbered.
The range must be split into two /25 blocks, one advertised by each side.
Both networks must advertise the prefix with a lower metric so the router chooses one.
questions.why: Because both options exchange routes, every address range must be unique across connected networks; a shared prefix makes the destination ambiguous, so one side must be renumbered.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Cloud VPN and Cross-Cloud Interconnect for a link to another cloud provider, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you rule out.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the requirements. If the traffic is modest, the link is not latency-sensitive, and the team needs it running quickly and cheaply, I would pick Cloud VPN, specifically HA VPN with two tunnels across two gateway interfaces for redundancy. The limit is that the tunnels run over the public internet, so throughput and delay can vary, and each tunnel has a bandwidth ceiling. If the workload needs steady bandwidth, low variance, or large data movement, I would choose Cross-Cloud Interconnect, which is a dedicated link and avoids the internet. Its tradeoff is cost and lead time, since the circuit must be provisioned and paired with the other provider. In either case I would check that address ranges do not overlap, because BGP will advertise duplicates and break routing.
rubricPoints: Cloud VPN runs IPsec tunnels over the public internet, so performance varies.
Cross-Cloud Interconnect is a dedicated link that avoids the internet, with higher cost and lead time.
Address ranges must not overlap across connected networks, because BGP advertises them.
HA VPN needs redundant tunnels and interfaces to reach its availability target.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about the tradeoff and explaining it back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers multicloud connectivity directly.

lessons.plain: Peering is a way to exchange network routes directly with Google so your network can reach Google's public services, such as Google Workspace or public Google APIs, without going over the open internet. Direct Peering means your own network meets Google at one of its physical edge locations and you set up the routing yourself. A Verified Peering Provider is a partner internet company that Google has checked; you buy a link from them instead, which helps when you cannot reach a Google location yourself. Both options are about reaching Google's public addresses, not your private cloud network.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office is in a city with no Google facility nearby, but your staff need fast access to Google Workspace. Would you expect to run a router directly into Google, or to buy a link through a partner? Why?
lessons.teach:
Direct Peering is a connection in which your network exchanges BGP routes directly with Google's network at a physical peering location called an edge point of presence. BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is the routing protocol networks use to tell each other which address ranges they can reach. For Direct Peering you bring your own autonomous system number (ASN, a globally unique number that identifies your network in BGP), your own router, and your own public IP addresses, and you must meet Google's eligibility requirements. A Verified Peering Provider is the alternative: a service provider that Google has verified connects to Google on your behalf, so you buy a circuit from that partner instead of meeting Google in a facility yourself.

Both paths carry traffic to Google's public services over a private link rather than the public internet. Neither gives your VPC subnets a private route into Google Cloud. For that you need Cloud Interconnect or Cloud VPN, which carry your private RFC 1918 address ranges.

Worked example: a company has an office in a city with a Google edge location. Step 1: its network engineer confirms the company has an ASN and a router that can run BGP. Step 2: it orders a link to that facility and establishes a BGP session. Step 3: Google advertises routes for its public services, and the company advertises its own public prefixes. Step 4: staff traffic to Workspace now takes the direct path. For a branch office with no nearby facility, the same company would order a link from a Verified Peering Provider, which carries the BGP session onward to Google.

Common mistake: choosing peering to reach private database addresses inside a VPC. Peering does not connect private VPC subnets, so that traffic never reaches them.

Consequence: a peering link is a single physical path from your site. If it fails, staff lose access to those public services until it returns, so teams usually plan a second path.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dairy Co-op runs a warehouse in a rural town with no Google edge facility within reach. It wants staff traffic to Google Workspace to use a dedicated link instead of the public internet. Its network team works through the path. Step 1: they choose a Verified Peering Provider that Google has verified to connect on their behalf. Step 2: they order a circuit from that provider to the warehouse. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: staff traffic to Workspace now takes the dedicated link. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Enable Cloud NAT on the warehouse subnets so private RFC 1918 ranges can reach Google
Purchase a Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment so the warehouse can reach VPC private subnets
Ask Google to install its own router at the warehouse so the BGP session runs there
Establish a BGP session through the provider, which carries it onward to Google, and advertise the co-op's own public prefixes
questions.why: The provider carries the BGP session onward to Google, and the co-op advertises its own public prefixes so routes can be exchanged for the public services.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic group has its own ASN and public IP addresses and wants Direct Peering. Which statement about what Direct Peering asks of the clinic group is accurate?
choices: The group must bring its own router that can run BGP and meet Google's eligibility requirements
The group must buy a circuit from a Verified Peering Provider, because that is the only way to meet Google
The group must host its servers inside a Google-run facility so Google can route on their behalf
The group must lease private RFC 1918 address ranges from Google to use for its VPC subnets
questions.why: Direct Peering requires you to bring your own ASN, router, and public IP addresses, and to meet Google's eligibility requirements.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has on-premises servers and a VM in a VPC subnet with private address 10.20.4.15. It has a Direct Peering link to Google. Its staff want the servers to reach that VM's private address over the link. What is the correct understanding?
choices: The servers reach the VM once the firm adds its public IP addresses to the VM's network interface
Direct Peering routes private addresses only when Cloud NAT is enabled on the VM's subnet
Peering does not connect private VPC subnets, so the servers need Cloud Interconnect or Cloud VPN to reach it
Direct Peering lets the servers reach the VM's private address as long as the BGP session stays up
questions.why: Peering only carries traffic to Google's public services and does not give VPC subnets a private route, so Cloud Interconnect or Cloud VPN is needed for private RFC 1918 ranges.

questions.prompt: A retail chain runs one Direct Peering link to a Google edge facility so staff can reach public Google services. What is the main operational risk, and the sensible response?
choices: Only Cloud Interconnect has this risk, so Direct Peering links cannot fail in a way that matters
The BGP session protects the link, so a failure only slows traffic and needs no response
Google reroutes the traffic into the VPC private subnets automatically, so no plan is needed
The link is a single physical path, so a failure cuts staff access until it returns, and teams usually plan a second path
questions.why: A peering link is one physical path from the site, so its failure removes access to the public services until repaired, which is why a second path is usually planned.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague asks why we are ordering a Verified Peering Provider link instead of Direct Peering for the new branch office, and whether it can reach our Cloud SQL instances over private addresses. Explain the choice in your own words, naming one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: We are using a Verified Peering Provider because the branch office is not in a city with a Google edge location where we could install our own router, and Direct Peering requires us to meet Google at such a facility. The partner carries our BGP session to Google, so we still exchange routes and reach Google public services such as Workspace. The tradeoff is that we depend on the partner's link and their network, and we do not control the path end to end. It will not reach our Cloud SQL private addresses, though. Peering only carries Google public addresses, so private access to Cloud SQL needs a different construct, such as Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect, which carry our private ranges into the VPC. I would confirm that with the branch team before we build anything.
rubricPoints: Direct Peering means meeting Google at a physical edge location with your own ASN, router, and BGP session
A Verified Peering Provider is a verified partner that carries the connection when you cannot meet Google directly
Peering reaches Google public services, not private VPC subnets
Private access to VPC addresses needs Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect instead
A single peering link is a single failure path that may need a backup

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about which path fits a site and explaining the public-versus-private limit, which no listed mission covers.

lessons.plain: When a network has to keep working even if one city, data centre or cloud region has a bad day, it must be connected in more than one place. High availability means the network stays up when a single link or device fails. Disaster recovery means that if a whole region is lost, the network can still be reached or rebuilt somewhere else within a time you have agreed. For a cloud network, your office or another cloud needs at least two independent paths into it, and those paths should sit in different regions so one regional outage does not cut everything off. The hard part is not buying two links. It is making sure traffic moves to the backup path automatically, and that the backup has the routes, firewall rules and capacity it needs when it is used.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office connects to a cloud network through one encrypted tunnel into a single region, and that region has a power outage. Before reading on, what would you add to keep the office connected, and what must be true about the second path for it to take over without a person switching it on?
lessons.teach:
A region is a geographic area in which your cloud resources run. A VPC network (a virtual private cloud, your own private software-defined network) is global in Google Cloud, but each subnet (a range of IP addresses inside it) is regional. A Cloud Router is the component that exchanges routes with your other network using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the routing protocol that tells each side which address ranges sit behind which connection). HA VPN is an encrypted tunnel service that gives you two interfaces per gateway, so you can run redundant tunnels.

Why it works: a route only stays in the routing table while its BGP session is up. When a tunnel or a whole region fails, its session drops, its routes are withdrawn, and traffic uses whatever routes remain. You control which path is preferred with route priority or with MED (multi-exit discriminator, a number attached to each advertised route where a lower value is preferred). For a router in one region to learn subnets in another region, the VPC's dynamic routing mode must be global. In regional mode, a Cloud Router advertises only its own region's subnets.

Worked example: a data centre connects to a global VPC with subnets in region A and region B. You create a gateway in each region with two tunnels to the data centre. Step 1: region A advertises the subnets with MED 100 and region B with MED 200. Step 2: traffic prefers A. Step 3: A's tunnels fail, its BGP sessions drop, and its routes are withdrawn. Step 4: the route through B remains, so traffic moves to B once BGP detects the failure.

Common mistake: giving both paths equal preference, so traffic splits and a failure looks like a slowdown instead of an outage. Another is never testing that the backup region has matching firewall rules, routes and replicated data.

Consequence in a running system: if the return path differs from the forward path, a stateful firewall may drop replies it never saw requested, so failover can look successful while sessions still break.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Clinic runs a global VPC with subnets in two regions and links its office network to both regions with HA VPN, which is an encrypted tunnel service with two tunnels per gateway. Each region has a Cloud Router, the component that exchanges routes with the office over BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the protocol that announces which address ranges sit behind which connection). The primary region advertises the office route with route priority 100 and the backup region with priority 300, where a lower number wins. Step 1: both regions advertise their subnets to the office over BGP. Step 2: office-bound traffic uses the priority 100 route through the primary region. Step 3: the primary region's tunnels are taken down for maintenance, and its BGP sessions drop. Step 4 is missing. What should the learner conclude happens next?
choices: Office-bound traffic keeps using the priority 100 route until someone manually resets the BGP session.
The priority 100 routes are withdrawn from the routing table, so the priority 300 route through the backup region becomes the only path and traffic moves there.
Office-bound traffic splits evenly between the two regions because both routes are still advertised.
The backup region's routes are ignored because priority 300 is too high to be used during a failure.
questions.why: A route stays in the routing table only while its BGP session is up, so once the primary sessions drop, the remaining priority 300 route is the one traffic uses.

questions.prompt: A VPC is set to regional dynamic routing mode. A Cloud Router in region X advertises routes to an on-premises network. Which statement is true?
choices: The Cloud Router advertises subnets only if the on-premises network sends it routes first.
The Cloud Router advertises subnets in all regions, but only those that have a running virtual machine.
The Cloud Router advertises only the subnets in its own region, so a router in region Y will not learn them.
The Cloud Router advertises subnets from every region in the VPC, because the VPC itself is global.
questions.why: In regional mode a Cloud Router advertises only its own region's subnets, which is why global mode is needed for one region to learn another region's subnets.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight Co. has two HA VPN gateways to its warehouse network, one in each of two regions. It wants the second region to carry traffic only when the first region's path is gone. Which setup achieves this?
choices: Remove the BGP sessions in the backup region so it never advertises any routes.
Give the primary region a lower MED than the backup region, so the primary is preferred and the backup takes over only after the primary's routes are withdrawn.
Give both regions the same MED value so traffic is balanced evenly across both.
Set the backup region's MED lower than the primary's so the backup is always preferred.
questions.why: Lower MED is preferred, so a lower value on the primary makes it the normal path, and the backup's higher-value route takes over once the primary's BGP routes disappear.

questions.prompt: A team gives both regions equal preference for routes to an on-premises network. The primary region's tunnels fail in one of their two tunnels but the BGP session stays up. Which symptom is the team most likely to see?
choices: No change at all, because equal preference automatically pins traffic to the first region that answered.
A clean outage, with every request failing immediately and an error message naming the failed region.
The on-premises network stops receiving any routes and the backup region is never used.
Traffic is split across both regions, so the problem looks like a general slowdown rather than an obvious outage.
questions.why: With equal preference traffic splits across both paths, so a partial failure shows up as slower responses instead of a clean outage, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect an office to a cloud network so it survives the loss of one cloud region. Name the routing setting that lets both regions share routes, how the backup path is chosen, and one limit or tradeoff of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would build a gateway in each of two regions, and give each gateway at least two tunnels to the office so one tunnel failing does not matter. The VPC needs global dynamic routing so each region's Cloud Router can learn subnets from the other region. The office sees the same subnets from both regions, but region A is advertised with a lower MED, so it is preferred. If region A fails, its BGP sessions drop, its routes are withdrawn, and traffic moves to region B automatically. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: two regions mean double the tunnels and charges, and region B must have matching firewall rules, routes and data, or failover will work on paper but break applications. I would test the failover on a schedule rather than trust it.
rubricPoints: Uses at least two gateways or connections spread across different regions, not just two links in one place
Names global dynamic routing mode as the setting that lets routes cross regions
Explains that preference comes from route priority or MED, and that failed paths are withdrawn by BGP
States a real limit, such as cost, duplicated configuration, or the need to test the backup region

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner reason through regional failure scenarios and recovery timing, which this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: When one organisation runs several separate private networks in the cloud, and an office or data centre needs to reach them, the question is how to connect everything without a tangle of links. Think of a campus of buildings. You can make one large shared building that everyone uses, let separate buildings open direct doors to each other, or run a central lobby that every building connects to. Each approach sets different rules for who can reach whom, and each has a limit you need to know before choosing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose three teams each have their own private cloud network, and your office must reach all three. Before reading on, which would you expect to be harder to manage as the company grows: one shared network that all teams plug into, or three networks that each link directly to one another? Say why in a sentence.
lessons.teach:
A VPC network is a private, isolated network inside Google Cloud, with its own IP address ranges (subnets) and firewall rules. Shared VPC lets one project, called the host project, own a single VPC network, while other projects, called service projects, attach to it and create resources on its subnets. Central network staff manage the routes, firewalls and any link to the office from one place. VPC Network Peering is a direct private connection between two separate VPC networks. Each side must set it up, and the two networks exchange their subnet routes so resources can talk over private addresses. Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A still cannot reach C through B. Network Connectivity Center, often shortened to NCC, is a hub that connects spokes. A spoke can be a VPN tunnel, an Interconnect attachment, a router appliance or a VPC network. Spokes can be grouped into a mesh, where they exchange routes with each other, or a star, where they route through a central group.

Worked example: an office reaches VPC-A through one Cloud VPN tunnel. VPC-A is peered with VPC-B. Step 1: the office sends traffic to VPC-A over the tunnel and succeeds. Step 2: the office sends traffic meant for VPC-B. Step 3: VPC-B is reachable from VPC-A through peering, but the office's traffic is not carried onward across the peering, so the packet is dropped. Peering does not let one network use another network's hybrid link as a transit path. Two fixes: give VPC-B its own link to the office, or make both VPC-A and VPC-B spokes on an NCC hub.

The common mistake is assuming that peering chains. Students often draw lines between networks and assume every line carries traffic end to end. A second constraint is IP overlap: peered networks cannot have overlapping subnet ranges, so plan address space before linking anything. In a running system, the symptom of a missing transit path is a timeout from the office to one project only, while the others work, which looks like a firewall fault but is a routing design gap.

questions.prompt: Lumen Clinic has a host project named clinic-net-host that owns a Shared VPC network called clinic-shared, with one subnet 10.40.0.0/20 in europe-west1. Its records-app service project needs virtual machines on that subnet, and those machines must reach the clinic's on-premises database over the office VPN. Work through the setup. Step 1: enable Shared VPC on clinic-net-host and attach records-app as a service project. Step 2: the records-app engineer creates a virtual machine on clinic-shared using the 10.40.0.0/20 subnet. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the machine reaches the database over the office VPN, which central network staff already manage. Which action correctly fills step 3?
choices: The records-app team sets up a second Cloud VPN tunnel from its own project to the office.
The team widens the subnet to 10.40.0.0/16 so it covers the database addresses.
The central network staff add a firewall rule on the host network that allows the application port from the subnet range.
The records-app team creates a VPC Network Peering link between clinic-shared and a new VPC in its own project.
questions.why: In Shared VPC the host project owns the firewall rules, routes and office links, so the central network staff must add the firewall rule on the shared network, not the service project.

questions.prompt: Northwind has VPC network north-core with subnet 10.20.0.0/22 and VPC network north-edge with subnet 10.20.2.0/24. A colleague proposes VPC Network Peering between them so their resources can use private addresses. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Peering works because the subnets are in different networks, so their addresses do not conflict.
Peering can be set up, but the peered networks will then route only the smaller subnet.
Peering is not possible because the two subnet ranges overlap, so the networks must be re-addressed first.
Peering works only if both networks are first converted into Shared VPC networks.
questions.why: Peered networks cannot have overlapping subnet ranges, and 10.20.2.0/24 sits inside 10.20.0.0/22, so address planning must come first.

questions.prompt: A team has VPC network Blue peered with VPC network Green, and Green is peered with VPC network Red. Blue's servers time out when connecting to a database in Red, while Blue reaches Green without trouble. What best explains this, and what is a sound fix?
choices: Red's database has a bad route, so the fix is to restart the database instance.
Peering does not carry traffic onward, so Blue cannot reach Red through Green; fix it with a direct peering to Red or by making both networks spokes on an NCC hub.
A firewall rule in Blue blocks Red, so the fix is to open the port in Blue's firewall.
Blue and Green have overlapping subnets, so the fix is to renumber Green only.
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so traffic cannot pass from Blue through Green to Red, and the design needs a direct path or a shared hub.

questions.prompt: A company has four VPC networks and a VPN tunnel to its office. It wants every network to exchange routes directly with every other network, with no central group carrying traffic between them. Which Network Connectivity Center (NCC, a hub that connects spokes) layout fits this requirement?
choices: A single peering link between the two busiest networks.
A Shared VPC host project that owns all four networks.
A star, where spokes route through a central group.
A mesh, where spokes exchange routes with each other.
questions.why: In an NCC mesh the spokes exchange routes with each other directly, which matches the requirement, while a star routes through a central group.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes connecting our office to three project networks by peering each project network to the others and giving the office one VPN into the first. Explain to them, in your own words, what breaks in that design, which construct you would recommend instead among Shared VPC, peering and a Network Connectivity Center hub, and name one tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: The design breaks because peering is not transitive. The office reaches the first network over its VPN, but the other two networks are only peered to that first network, so office traffic meant for them is not carried across the peering and gets dropped. Peering also needs non-overlapping subnet ranges, so the address plan has to be checked first. I would recommend a Network Connectivity Center hub. The office VPN becomes a spoke, and each project network becomes a spoke too, so routes are exchanged through one central point. If the three projects belong to one organisation and should share one network team and one set of firewall rules, Shared VPC would be a better fit instead. The tradeoff with the hub is more moving parts to monitor and some cost for the central routing, in exchange for a clear, single place to see and change every path.
rubricPoints: Peering is not transitive, so traffic from the office cannot cross the first peering to reach the other networks.
Peering requires non-overlapping subnet IP ranges, which must be planned in advance.
A Network Connectivity Center hub with spokes provides a central routing point for multiple networks and links.
Shared VPC suits one organisation that wants central network administration and a single shared network.
The answer names a concrete tradeoff, such as operational complexity, cost, or loss of per-team autonomy.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet's path hop by hop across peerings and hub spokes would make the transitive-routing limit visible in a way reading alone does not.

lessons.plain: Your company's data center often needs to call Google services such as file storage or a data warehouse. Doing that over the public internet means exposing traffic and relying on public addresses. Private access means the on-premises servers reach those services through the private connection your company already has to Google Cloud, using Google's internal addresses. Getting this right takes two things working together: the name of the service must resolve to the right private addresses, and the network must send traffic for those addresses down the private link. Think of it as a private road you have to both sign for on the map and actually build a route onto.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server in your company's data center calls a Google storage service by its normal name. Without any changes, does that traffic go over your private connection to Google, or over the public internet? What would you need to change to make it take the private path?
lessons.teach: A Google API is a service endpoint, such as object storage or a data warehouse, that your code calls over the network. Private access to these APIs means the calls travel over Google's internal network using private virtual IP addresses that Google provides, instead of public internet addresses. Two parts must work together. First, DNS, the system that turns a name such as storage.googleapis.com into an address, must return one of those private virtual IP ranges. The two common ranges are restricted.googleapis.com and private.googleapis.com, each a small fixed block of addresses. Second, routing must send traffic for that block into your hybrid link, which is Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect. Cloud Router is the component that exchanges routes with your on-premises routers using BGP, the standard protocol routers use to share reachability, and it can advertise that block to the data center as a custom route. Worked example: a server in the data center resolves storage.googleapis.com. Your private DNS zone answers with an address inside the restricted block, for example 199.36.153.4. The server sends the request toward its default gateway. Its router has a route for that block learned from Cloud Router, so the packet enters the VPN tunnel. Google receives it on the private virtual IP and delivers it to the service. Common mistake: configuring the DNS override but not advertising the route, or advertising the route while public DNS still answers for some clients. The consequence is that the service appears reachable from some hosts and not others, and the failure depends on which resolver each client uses, which makes it hard to diagnose. The Private Google Access setting on a cloud subnet covers virtual machines without external addresses inside the cloud; it does not by itself cover traffic originating from on-premises hosts.

questions.prompt: Lantern Freight runs a batch reporting server in its own data center, and the server calls bigquery.googleapis.com over a Cloud Interconnect. The path works like this. (1) The data center DNS resolver answers bigquery.googleapis.com with an address inside the restricted block. (2) [MISSING STEP] (3) The server's router has a route for that block and forwards the packet into the interconnect. (4) Google receives the packet on the private virtual IP and delivers it to BigQuery. Which choice correctly fills step 2?
choices: Add a cloud firewall rule that allows outbound traffic to every address
Cloud Router advertises the restricted block to the data center over BGP as a custom route
Point the server's default gateway at the public internet router so Google's public address is used
Enable Private Google Access on the reporting server's subnet so its traffic counts as internal
questions.why: Cloud Router must advertise the restricted block to the on-premises routers over BGP, because the router only has a route for that block (step 3) if it learned it from Cloud Router.

questions.prompt: In this teaching, which hosts does the Private Google Access setting on a cloud subnet cover?
choices: Hosts in the data center that connect through a Cloud VPN tunnel
All traffic leaving on-premises routers toward the public internet
Virtual machines inside the cloud subnet that have no external address
Any host, wherever it is, whose DNS returns the restricted block
questions.why: The text says the setting covers virtual machines without external addresses inside the cloud and does not by itself cover traffic from on-premises hosts.

questions.prompt: A team has set DNS so clients receive a private-range answer for storage.googleapis.com, and Cloud Router advertises the matching route. Some lab hosts fail while others work, and the only difference is which DNS resolver each host uses. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The failing hosts' resolver still returns a public address, so their traffic bypasses the private path
Private Google Access must be enabled inside each lab host's operating system
The route is advertised, so DNS cannot be the cause and the Cloud Router autonomous system number is wrong
The Cloud Router has been configured with too few BGP sessions to serve the lab hosts
questions.why: A resolver that returns a public address sends traffic outside the private path even though the route exists, which explains why behaviour depends on the resolver each client uses.

questions.prompt: For an on-premises host to reach Google APIs privately over a hybrid link, which two things must both be in place?
choices: Private Google Access enabled on a cloud subnet, plus a public firewall rule for port 443
DNS returns a private range, and each host is given an external address in the cloud
DNS returns a private virtual range, and routing sends that range into the hybrid link
A public IP address on each host, plus a default route to the internet gateway
questions.why: The text names two parts that must work together: DNS must return a private virtual range, and routing must send that range into Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an on-premises server reaches a Google API privately, naming the two parts that must both be configured and one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: The on-premises server has to get two things right. First, DNS for the API name must return one of Google's private virtual IP ranges, such as restricted.googleapis.com, instead of public addresses. Second, the routing must send that range into the hybrid link, which means Cloud Router advertises the range to our routers over BGP, and the route has to be in place before the traffic leaves the data center. If only one part is done, some hosts take the private path and others fall back to the internet, which is the hardest kind of failure to diagnose. The tradeoff is that the restricted range only covers the services Google marks as supported for that path, and the DNS override applies to every host that uses our resolver, so we need to check what else depends on those names before changing them.
rubricPoints: Names the two required parts: DNS resolving to a private virtual IP range and routing that sends that range over the hybrid link.
Identifies Cloud Router advertising the range to on-premises routers via BGP as the routing mechanism.
Explains that partial configuration causes inconsistent behavior across hosts.
States a real limit, such as supported-service coverage or the DNS override affecting all clients using that resolver.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is walking the DNS-then-route path and explaining the failure modes back, which no listed mission or planned engine directly practices.

lessons.plain: Companies often need their cloud applications to use a managed service, such as a hosted database or a cache, without sending that traffic across the public internet. Google Cloud offers two common ways to do this privately. One connects two separate private networks so their machines can talk using internal addresses. The other gives your network a private internal address that leads to one specific service. Both keep traffic off the public internet, but they differ in how much they expose and what can break. Choosing between them is a design decision with real limits, and this lesson explains those limits in plain terms.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your application network and a managed database run in two different private networks, and both use the same range of internal addresses. Which approach would you expect to have trouble connecting them, and why?
lessons.teach:
A VPC network is a private virtual network you create in the cloud to hold your subnets, routes and firewall rules. VPC Network Peering is a connection between two separate VPC networks. Once it is set up on both sides, machines in each network can reach the other using internal addresses, and the traffic stays on Google's network. Because routing is shared between the two networks, their subnet ranges must not overlap. Peering is also not transitive: if network A peers with B, and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B.

Private Service Connect, often shortened to PSC, works differently. You create an endpoint, which is a private internal IP address inside your own VPC. That endpoint forwards traffic to one specific target, such as a Google API or a service another team publishes. You see only the endpoint address, not the provider's network, so overlapping ranges are not a blocker, and the connection is narrow and one-directional.

Worked example: your app VPC uses 10.0.0.0/16, and the managed database's network also uses 10.0.0.0/16. Peering cannot be set up, because the ranges overlap. With PSC, you create an endpoint at 10.0.1.5 inside one of your subnets and attach it to the database service. Step one: the app sends a request to 10.0.1.5. Step two: the endpoint forwards it to the attached service. Step three: the reply returns along the same path.

Common mistake: assuming a hub network that peers with several spokes gives every spoke access to every other spoke. Consequence: traffic silently fails because no route exists, and the team loses time chasing a firewall problem that is really a missing peering path.

Peering suits broad, trusted connectivity between networks you control, while PSC suits narrow access to a single service, even when address ranges collide.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's analytics VPC uses 172.31.0.0/20, and a partner's reporting VPC uses 172.31.8.0/22, so the two ranges overlap and VPC Network Peering is ruled out. The team uses Private Service Connect instead. The steps so far are: (1) reserve endpoint address 172.31.2.15 in an analytics subnet; (2) attach that endpoint to the partner's published reporting service; (3) MISSING STEP; (4) replies return along the same path to the analytics machine. Which action completes step 3?
choices: Create a peering in the reverse direction so the partner's range becomes visible to the analytics VPC.
Point the analytics application's requests at 172.31.2.15 instead of the reporting service's public hostname.
Remove the egress firewall rule that blocks traffic to the partner's range.
Give the endpoint a public IP address so the partner service can send replies.
questions.why: The endpoint only forwards traffic that is actually addressed to it, so the application must send its requests to the endpoint's internal address.

questions.prompt: A platform team needs one internal address inside its own VPC that reaches a single partner service, and the partner's network uses address ranges that collide with the team's ranges. Which construct fits best?
choices: Copying the partner's subnet ranges into the team's VPC so the routes match.
A Private Service Connect endpoint in one of the team's subnets, attached to the partner service.
A firewall rule that allows traffic from the partner's address range.
A second VPC Network Peering with a different name between the same two networks.
questions.why: Private Service Connect gives a narrow endpoint inside your own VPC and works even when address ranges overlap, which peering cannot handle.

questions.prompt: A hub network H peers with spoke S1 and with spoke S2. A virtual machine in S1 tries to reach a virtual machine in S2 using internal addresses, and the connection fails. What is the most likely cause, and what fixes it?
choices: Peering is not transitive, so S1 cannot reach S2 through H; S1 needs its own direct peering to S2 with non-overlapping ranges.
The connection works only when both spokes are in the same region, so the fix is to move one spoke.
The hub must export its routes to S2 by name, so the fix is to rename the hub network.
The hub relays traffic between all peered spokes automatically, so the firewall in H must be blocking S2's range.
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so a route through the hub does not exist, and the spokes need a direct peering between them.

questions.prompt: A team's VPC uses 10.20.0.0/18, and a managed cache's network uses 10.20.32.0/19. The team wants its application to call the cache over internal addresses. Which approach is correct?
choices: Open a firewall rule that allows traffic to 10.20.32.0/19 and leave the networks as they are.
Add a static route that sends 10.20.32.0/19 to the cache's network through a peering.
Peer the two networks and rely on route propagation to resolve the overlap.
Create a Private Service Connect endpoint inside the team's own subnet and attach it to the cache service.
questions.why: The ranges overlap, which blocks peering, so a Private Service Connect endpoint in the team's own subnet is the way to reach the single service.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick VPC Network Peering over Private Service Connect for reaching a managed service, and name one limit of the option you did not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use VPC Network Peering when two networks I control need broad, trusted reach to each other and their subnet ranges are planned so they never overlap. Peering exposes routes between the whole networks, so it is powerful but wide. The main limit is that it is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A still cannot reach C through B, so a hub-and-spoke design built only from peering will fail silently. I would pick Private Service Connect when I want to reach one managed service privately, especially when its address range overlaps with mine, because I get a single internal endpoint address and see only that service. Its limit is that it only gives access to the one target I attach, so I cannot use it for general network-to-network traffic.
rubricPoints: Peering joins whole VPC networks, so their subnet ranges must not overlap
Peering is not transitive, so reach does not pass through a middle network
Private Service Connect gives an internal endpoint to a single service
Private Service Connect works even when address ranges overlap, and is narrow in scope

suggested.rationale: Choosing between peering and endpoints is an exam-style design situation, and reasoning through overlapping ranges and transitivity adds the most here, though no listed mission or engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Every network has addresses, a bit like house numbers. When you connect an office network to a cloud network, or two cloud networks to each other, their address numbers must not collide. If two places both claim the same block of numbers, traffic meant for one can be delivered to the other. Designing address space means choosing, before you build, which blocks each environment uses, leaving room to grow, and checking that none of them share numbers. This is cheap to do on paper and expensive to fix later, because moving a running network to new addresses means changing every server that uses them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office network already uses 10.0.0.0/16 for its computers. You are about to create a cloud network and want to give its production subnet 10.0.0.0/20. Before any teaching, what would you expect to happen the first time the office and the cloud network try to talk to each other?
lessons.teach:
Start with the core terms. An IP address is a numeric label for one network interface.
