questions.prompt: A company has a custom-mode network retail-vpc with an existing subnet 10.90.8.0/22. An engineer reserves 10.90.0.0/20 as the address range for private services access in the same network so a managed database can be reached privately. Which problem does this configuration create?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because private services access ranges are allowed to sit inside existing subnets
The reserved range overlaps the existing subnet, which the rules forbid, so the reservation must be changed
The managed database cannot be reached, because private services access only works in auto-mode networks
The reserved range is too large, because a /20 always exceeds the limit for private services access
questions.why: The reserved private services access range must not overlap any subnet in the VPC, and 10.90.0.0/20 contains the subnet 10.90.8.0/22, so the reservation needs a non-overlapping block.

questions.prompt: A subnet is given the range 10.70.16.0/21. How many internal IP addresses does this subnet contain?
questions.why: In a /21 the first 21 bits are fixed and 11 bits remain free, and 2 to the power of 11 is 2048 addresses.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to open a database port for their app and proposes one firewall rule that applies to the whole network. Explain to them what a firewall rule targets, what the priority does, and one limit of relying on a broad rule. Name the setting you would check first.
lessons.modelAnswer: A firewall rule in a VPC network does not protect a subnet as a whole. It protects the instances in that network that match its target, which can be every instance, instances with a given network tag, or instances running a given service account. The priority sets the order: Google checks rules from the lowest number upward and applies the first match, so a deny with a smaller number can override an allow. Traffic that matches nothing falls through to the implied deny-ingress rule. The limit of a broad rule is that it opens the port to every matching instance, including instances added later. I would narrow the source range and the target tag to the app's clients and the database instances, then confirm with a test connection from an allowed machine and a blocked one. The first setting I would check is the target, because a wrong target is the most common reason a rule seems to do nothing.
rubricPoints: A firewall rule applies to instances in the network that match its target, not to a whole subnet.
Priority is numeric, lower numbers are checked first, and the first match decides the outcome.
Implied deny-ingress applies to anything no rule allows.
A broad source or target exposes the port to more instances or sources than intended.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a near-miss firewall or subnet setup in an exam-style situation adds the most, because the skill is spotting the wrong setting.

lessons.plain: VPC network peering is a private link between two separate virtual networks in the cloud, so a machine in one network can reach a machine in the other using internal addresses, without going over the public internet and without a gateway in between. Think of two office buildings agreeing to open a connecting corridor. Each building's owner has to agree to open its side, and the corridor only works if the room numbers do not clash. A virtual network here is an isolated group of addresses and rules that you control. Peering joins two of them, but it does not let traffic pass through a third network, and it does not open any doors, because each network's own rules still decide what is allowed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two company networks each use the address range 10.0.0.0/16. Do you think a peering link between them can be created as-is, and why might that matter for a machine on one side trying to reach a machine on the other?
lessons.teach:
VPC network peering links two Virtual Private Cloud networks, which are isolated networks of internal IP addresses, so that resources in each can talk over private internal addresses. A VPC network is the container; a subnet is a slice of its address range inside a region. Peering is configured as two matching halves: one network creates a peering that points at the other, and the other network creates its matching peering back. The link only becomes active when both halves exist and agree. Until then the status shows inactive. Each side can choose whether to import and export custom routes, meaning routes you created by hand or learned dynamically, while subnet routes are always exchanged.

Worked example. Network A has subnet 10.0.0.0/24 and network B has subnet 10.1.0.0/24. Step 1: create the peering on A pointing at B; status is inactive. Step 2: create the peering on B pointing at A; status becomes active. Step 3: a VM at 10.0.0.5 in A can now reach 10.1.0.7 in B, provided firewall rules in B allow the traffic. Peering does not open ports on its own.

Common mistake: assuming peering is transitive. If A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Each pair that needs to talk needs its own peering. The consequence in a running system is that a service can appear reachable in the console but time out for clients on a network that is only indirectly connected.

questions.prompt: A small logistics company has two VPC networks: shipping-core, which holds a subnet at 172.16.0.0/20, and warehouse-edge, which holds a subnet at 192.168.10.0/24. A VPC network is the isolated container of internal addresses, and a subnet is a slice of that address range inside one region. An engineer works through the peering setup. Step 1: on shipping-core, create a peering that points at warehouse-edge. The console shows the link as inactive. Step 2: [missing step left for you to supply]. Step 3: the link shows active, and a VM at 172.16.2.9 can reach 192.168.10.20 over internal addresses, provided firewall rules on warehouse-edge allow the traffic. Which action fills in Step 2?
choices: Wait for the inactive status to clear on its own after a few minutes
Add a hand-made static route on shipping-core for 192.168.10.0/24
Create the matching peering on warehouse-edge that points back at shipping-core
Create a second peering on shipping-core that also points at warehouse-edge
questions.why: A peering link only becomes active when both halves exist and agree, so the missing half is the matching peering created on the other network pointing back.

questions.prompt: An engineer creates a peering on network ledger-prod that points at network ledger-dr, but the status stays inactive. Which explanation best fits?
choices: The matching peering on ledger-dr that points back at ledger-prod has not been created yet
Subnet routes must be added by hand before the status can change from inactive
The status stays inactive until a VM on either side sends traffic across the link
Firewall rules on ledger-dr are blocking the link, which stops the status from changing
questions.why: The link is active only when both matching halves exist and agree, so a missing reverse peering keeps the status inactive regardless of firewalls or traffic.

questions.prompt: Network sensor-hub has subnet 10.40.0.0/16 and a hand-made static route for 172.20.0.0/16. It peers with network sensor-lab. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both 10.40.0.0/16 and 172.20.0.0/16 reach sensor-lab automatically because peering exchanges every route
10.40.0.0/16 arrives on sensor-lab automatically, while 172.20.0.0/16 arrives only if custom route export is enabled on sensor-hub and custom route import is enabled on sensor-lab
Only 172.20.0.0/16 is exchanged, because subnet routes are never shared through peering
Neither route is exchanged unless a firewall rule on sensor-lab allows the traffic first
questions.why: Subnet routes are always exchanged, but custom routes are exchanged only when the exporting side's export setting and the importing side's import setting are both enabled.

questions.prompt: Network orders-api peers with network billing, and billing peers with network fraud-check. Can a VM in orders-api reach an internal address in fraud-check?
choices: Yes, provided both peerings show active in the console
Yes, because billing forwards traffic between its two peerings automatically once both are active
Yes, as long as billing exports its custom routes to orders-api
No, unless fraud-check is also given a peering of its own with orders-api, since peering is not transitive
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so orders-api cannot reach fraud-check through billing and needs its own direct peering with fraud-check.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says their application in network A cannot reach a database in network B, even though the peering shows Active. Explain to them what peering does, what it does not do, and one limit or check they must make before blaming the peering.
lessons.modelAnswer: Peering is a private connection between two networks, and once it is active, internal addresses in one network can route to the other. It is not a permission system and it does not open ports, so each network's firewall rules still decide which traffic is allowed. The first thing to check is whether the destination network's firewall rules allow the source's address range on the database port. Also check that the subnet ranges on both sides do not overlap, because overlapping ranges block the link. Finally, remember peering is not transitive, so if the application is actually reaching the database through a third network, a direct peering between the two is required.
rubricPoints: Peering creates a private route between two networks, and both sides must create their half of the link.
Peering does not replace or open firewall rules; each network's rules still apply.
Subnet address ranges must not overlap between peered networks.
Peering is not transitive: traffic does not pass through a third peered network.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine walks through peering setup, so reading the configuration steps and limits is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: A Shared VPC network is one private network that a central team builds and owns, and other teams' projects are allowed to plug into it. Picture a company that builds one office network with a single set of doors and locks, then gives each department a desk on that network without letting every department run its own wiring. In Google Cloud, a project is the container that holds resources and their bill. With a shared network, one project owns the network and its subnets (smaller address ranges carved out of the network), and other projects use those subnets to run their machines. The platform team controls addressing and firewall rules in one place, while application teams keep their own projects, budgets and access.
lessons.guessPrompt: If three application teams each have their own project and their machines need to talk privately to each other, what problems would you expect if every team built its own separate network with its own address ranges and firewall rules, and how might one central network help?
lessons.teach:
Definition. A Shared VPC is a setup where one project, called the host project, owns a VPC network (a virtual private network: a set of IP address ranges, subnets and firewall rules inside Google Cloud). One or more other projects, called service projects, are attached to that host project. Service projects do not own the network. Their machines, such as VMs or GKE nodes, are created inside subnets that the host project shares with them. Enabling a project as a host needs the organization-level Shared VPC Admin role, which is a permission to manage this setup across the company.

Why it works. Network decisions such as IP ranges, routes and firewall rules are made once, by the central network team, in the host project. Application teams keep their own projects for billing, quotas and access, but their resources land on the same network, so they can reach each other over private internal addresses without building peering or VPN links between their projects.

Worked example. A platform project named net-host becomes a host project. The network admin creates the network prod-vpc with a subnet prod-subnet-eu in region europe-west1 using range 10.10.0.0/20. They attach the service project app-orders to net-host. Then they grant the app-orders team the Network User role (the permission that lets someone create resources on a shared subnet) on prod-subnet-eu only. A developer in app-orders creates a VM and picks that subnet. The VM gets an address from 10.10.0.0/20 and is governed by the firewall rules of net-host. If they pick a subnet they have no Network User role on, the creation fails.

Common mistake. Creating the VPC inside a service project and calling it shared. A network is only shared if it lives in the host project. Another frequent error is granting Network User on the whole host project or organization when only one subnet should be used.

Consequence. Because firewall rules live in the host project, a rule change there immediately affects every attached service project's machines, so those changes should go through the network team.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a host project named logistics-host and a service project named ticket-api. The network admin has already done two things. First, a person with the organization-level Shared VPC Admin role enabled logistics-host as a host project. Second, the admin created a VPC named sales-core inside logistics-host, with a subnet named core-west in region us-central1 using range 172.16.4.0/22. The admin then attached ticket-api to logistics-host. The step that is missing is this: the admin has not yet granted the Network User role on core-west to the ticket-api developer group. Without that grant, a developer in ticket-api who tries to create a VM on core-west gets a creation failure. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Create a second VPC named sales-core inside the ticket-api project
Grant the Shared VPC Admin role to the ticket-api developer group
Grant Network User on core-west only, to the ticket-api developer group
Grant Network User on the whole logistics-host project so every subnet is available to ticket-api
questions.why: Network User must be granted on the specific subnet the team should use, and granting it on the whole host project or giving Shared VPC Admin is either too broad or the wrong role, while a VPC created in a service project is not shared at all.

questions.prompt: In a Shared VPC setup, which project owns the VPC network and its firewall rules?
choices: The service project whose VMs are created first
The organization node that holds the billing account
The host project
Every attached service project together, by majority vote
questions.why: The host project is the one project that owns the network, and service projects only use subnets shared from it.

questions.prompt: A project called retail-host is the host project, and a project called mobile-bff is attached to it as a service project. A developer in mobile-bff wants to create a GKE node pool on the subnet bff-subnet in the shared network, but no one has granted them Network User on that subnet. What happens?
choices: The creation succeeds, because the project is attached to the host
The creation fails, because Network User on that subnet is required and attachment alone does not give it
The creation fails only if a firewall rule in mobile-bff blocks it
The creation succeeds, because the developer's project has its own quota
questions.why: Attaching a service project lets it use the shared network, but creating resources on a specific shared subnet still needs the Network User role on that subnet.

questions.prompt: A web team creates a VPC named edge-net inside their service project web-front and then tells other teams that edge-net is a shared network. Which statement describes the problem?
choices: Network User must be granted on the organization for the network to be shared
A network is only shared if it lives in the host project, so edge-net is not shared
Service projects may not hold any VPC, so the team must delete edge-net and rename it
The name edge-net is not allowed for shared networks and must be changed
questions.why: Sharing only happens when the VPC is created inside the host project, so a network created in a service project is not shared with anyone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Shared VPC is set up, what a service project can and cannot do with the network, and name one limit or tradeoff of centralising network control this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Shared VPC has a host project that owns the network and its subnets, and service projects attached to it. The network must be created in the host project, because a network created in a service project is not shared. Once the host is enabled and a service project is attached, we grant the service project's users the Network User role on specific subnets, so they can create VMs there but cannot change the network itself. The tradeoff is control: the central network team owns IP ranges, routes and firewall rules, so a change in the host project affects every attached service project at once. Application teams gain independence over billing and access, but they must request network changes from the platform team and plan address ranges carefully, because a subnet's range is shared across teams.
rubricPoints: The host project owns the VPC and its subnets; service projects attach to it and use shared subnets.
The network must be created in the host project, not in a service project.
Access is granted per subnet with the Network User role, not by giving broad rights over the whole network.
A stated tradeoff: central control of firewall rules and IP ranges means changes affect all attached projects.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration steps and settings to recall, which the course can cover through reading and console-step reference rather than an existing or planned hands-on engine.

lessons.plain: Shared VPC lets one project, called the host project, own a computer network and share pieces of it, called subnets, with other projects, called service projects. Those other teams can then start machines inside a shared piece without owning the network itself. Sharing alone does not let anyone use it, though. You still have to hand the right permission to the right person or robot account, and only enough of it. This objective is about choosing who gets permission to use a shared subnet, where to grant it, and which level of permission is the smallest one that does the job. Think of it like giving someone a key to one office rather than a master key to the whole building.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team in a service project needs to create virtual machines in one subnet that lives in the host project. Should you give them broad admin rights over the host project's network, or only the ability to use that one subnet? Which is safer, and why?
lessons.teach: Shared VPC has three roles to keep apart. The host project owns the network and its subnets. A service project is attached to the host, and its users create resources such as virtual machines that plug into a host subnet. Identity and Access Management, usually called IAM, decides who can do what. A role is a named bundle of permissions. A binding attaches a role to a principal, which is a user, a group, or a service account. To let a service project use a shared subnet, grant the principal the Compute Network User role, written roles/compute.networkUser. It lets someone attach resources to a subnet and use it, but not change the network, its firewall rules, or its routes. Grant it on the individual subnet when you want the narrowest scope. Granting it at host project level reaches every subnet there, which is usually broader than needed. Worked example: the payments team's service project needs VMs in subnet sub-payments of host project net-host. Step 1: name the principal, the payments group. Step 2: open the IAM policy of subnet sub-payments. Step 3: add a binding for that group with Compute Network User. Step 4: the team creates a VM in that subnet and it succeeds, while the same group is still refused on subnet sub-finance, which shows the grant was scoped. Common mistake: giving a service project team Compute Network Admin or Editor on the host project. Creation works, but the team can now change shared firewall rules and routes for every service project. Another mistake is granting the role on the service project itself, which does nothing for a subnet owned by the host. The consequence in a running system: if the service project's Kubernetes Engine service agent lacks Compute Network User on the host, cluster creation fails with a permission error even though the projects look set up correctly. Least privilege on the subnet is the correct default.

questions.prompt: The clinic's service project lumen-web needs VMs in subnet sub-web, which belongs to host project lumen-host. This trace covers a different case from the teaching text. Step 1: the principal is the service account lumen-deployer, which will create the VMs. Step 2: the grant is placed on subnet sub-web, because only that subnet is needed. Step 3: this step is missing. Step 4: a VM created in sub-web succeeds, while the same account is refused when it tries to create a VM in sub-backend, which shows the grant was scoped to one subnet.
choices: Grant Compute Network Admin on the lumen-web service project so the account can manage its own networking.
Grant Owner on lumen-host so the account can add its own subnet bindings.
Grant Compute Network User on the lumen-host project so every subnet there is reachable.
Add a binding on subnet sub-web that gives lumen-deployer the Compute Network User role.
questions.why: The binding on sub-web with Compute Network User is the missing step that lets the account attach VMs to that subnet while keeping the grant narrow; the other choices are either broader than needed or placed where they do not apply.

questions.prompt: A principal holds Compute Network User on subnet sub-orders only. Which action is it allowed to take?
choices: Adding a new subnet to the host project
Creating a VM in sub-orders and attaching it to that subnet
Editing the firewall rules that apply to sub-orders
Changing the routes in the host project's network
questions.why: Compute Network User lets a principal attach resources to a subnet and use it, but it does not allow changing the network, its firewall rules, or its routes.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Bakery gave its developers Compute Network Admin on host project kestrel-net so they could fix one subnet. What is the main risk?
choices: They can only see the subnet they were told about, so there is no risk.
They can change shared firewall rules and routes for every attached service project.
Their VMs will fail to start because the role blocks compute instances.
Their access expires automatically once they have used one subnet.
questions.why: Compute Network Admin is broader than the Compute Network User role and reaches the shared network settings that every attached service project depends on, which is the common mistake this objective warns about.

questions.prompt: Ridgeline Labs has service project rl-data and host project rl-host, which owns subnet sub-data. An admin grants Compute Network User on the service project rl-data, not on sub-data. The team then tries to create a VM in sub-data. What happens?
choices: It succeeds only after the team restarts the service project.
It fails, and the fix is to give the team Owner on the service project.
It fails, because a grant on the service project does nothing for a subnet owned by the host.
It succeeds, because a grant on the service project reaches all of its subnets.
questions.why: Shared VPC subnets belong to the host project, so the role has to be granted on the subnet itself or at host level; a grant on the service project does not cover them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would let a service project's team use one shared subnet, where you would grant the permission, and what you would deliberately avoid granting. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would grant the team's group the Compute Network User role on that one subnet, in the host project, rather than on the whole host project. That lets them create VMs or other resources attached to the subnet, and it does not let them edit shared firewall rules, routes, or other subnets. I would avoid Network Admin or Editor on the host, because those let them change networking that other service projects depend on. The tradeoff is maintenance: subnet-level grants are narrow and safe, but each new subnet needs its own binding, so the team has to track them. Also, a service agent such as the one used by GKE may need the same role separately, or cluster creation fails even though the people have access.
rubricPoints: Grant Compute Network User on the specific subnet in the host project, not on the service project.
Explain that the role allows use of the subnet but not changes to firewall rules or routes.
Name the risk of broad admin or Editor roles on the host project.
State a real tradeoff, such as per-subnet bindings needing upkeep.
Mention that service agents, such as for GKE, may need the same role.

suggested.rationale: The planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test which principals can use which subnet, reinforcing scope-by-role reasoning.

lessons.plain: Some machines in a cloud network have only a private address inside that network and no public one. They still need to reach Google services such as file storage and databases. This lesson covers two ways to handle that. One is a subnet setting that lets private-only machines reach Google's services over Google's own network. The other is giving a machine a public address so it can reach the wider internet. Think of an office building with an internal mail room that can deliver to partner offices without using the public post office.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine has only an internal IP address and no public IP address. By default, can it upload a file to a Google Cloud Storage bucket, and which single setting would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A VPC network is the private virtual network you build in the cloud. A subnet is a range of internal addresses inside that network, and each virtual machine in the subnet gets an internal IP address from that range. An external IP address is a public address that lets a machine be reached from the internet and reach the internet itself. Private Google Access is a setting on each subnet. When it is on, machines in that subnet that have only internal addresses can reach Google's public APIs and managed services, such as Cloud Storage, using Google's network instead of their own public address. It does not make a machine public, and it does not give access to ordinary websites on the internet.

Why it works: the VPC keeps a default route, which sends traffic that matches no other route to the default internet gateway, the standard exit point. Private Google Access lets traffic bound for Google's service addresses use that route and stay on Google's network, so the machine never needs an external IP.

Worked example: a VM at 10.0.1.5 in subnet app-subnet has no external IP and runs an upload to a bucket. Step 1: the request names the storage service, which resolves to a Google service address. Step 2: the VPC finds the default route, which leads to the default internet gateway. Step 3: because app-subnet has Private Google Access on, Google's service address is reachable from the subnet and the upload succeeds. Step 4: with the setting off, the same request times out.

Common mistake: deleting the default route to tidy up, or assuming the setting gives full public internet access. Removing the default route breaks Private Google Access for Google service addresses unless a custom route to those addresses exists. Egress firewall rules must also allow the traffic.

Consequence in a running system: private machines that suddenly cannot reach their storage after a routing cleanup look like an application bug, but the cause is a network routing change.

questions.prompt: A batch job runs on a VM at 192.168.20.7 in analytics-subnet, which has no external IP. The job publishes messages to Pub/Sub, a Google-managed messaging service. Step 1: the request names Pub/Sub, which resolves to a Google service address. Step 2: the VPC finds the default route, which leads to the default internet gateway. Step 3: [missing step; choose the correct completion]. Step 4: the publish is delivered and the job continues.
choices: The VPC removes the default route so the publish goes straight from inside the subnet to the topic.
Traffic to Pub/Sub is sent over a VPN tunnel, because a private range never uses the default route.
The VM's internal address is swapped for a public one, so the publish leaves through the internet gateway as public traffic and reaches the topic.
analytics-subnet has Private Google Access on, so the topic's service address is reachable over Google's network using the default route.
questions.why: Private Google Access on the subnet is what lets a VM with only an internal address reach a Google service address, and the default route carries that traffic on Google's network.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Private Google Access?
choices: It gives every VM in a subnet a public address so the internet can reach it.
It opens access to ordinary websites on the internet for machines that have no external address.
It is a firewall rule that allows inbound traffic from Google's data centers into the VPC.
It is a subnet setting that lets machines with only internal addresses reach Google's public APIs and managed services over Google's network.
questions.why: Private Google Access is a per-subnet setting that lets internal-only machines reach Google service addresses without making them public or opening general internet access.

questions.prompt: A VM at 10.8.2.14 in reporting-subnet has only an internal IP. Private Google Access is off on reporting-subnet, and the VM cannot read objects from Cloud Storage. The team wants the VM to keep no external IP. Which change fixes this?
choices: Give the VM an external IP so it can reach the internet gateway.
Turn on Private Google Access on reporting-subnet.
Add an inbound firewall rule allowing Cloud Storage to reach the VM.
Remove the default route so Google service traffic uses a custom path.
questions.why: The missing piece is the subnet setting itself; turning it on lets the internal-only VM reach Google service addresses without adding a public address or touching routes.

questions.prompt: A team deletes the default route in their VPC to tidy up. Afterwards, private VMs in subnets with Private Google Access on can no longer reach Cloud Storage, and ordinary websites are also unreachable. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Storage service addresses are no longer reachable because nothing routes them, unless a custom route covers those addresses.
Private Google Access only works with the default route removed, so removing it should not matter.
Private Google Access gives full public internet access, so deleting the route only affects websites.
The VMs became public when the route was removed, so the firewall now blocks them.
questions.why: Private Google Access depends on a route existing for Google service addresses, and removing the default route leaves those addresses without a path unless a custom route is added.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between giving a VM an external IP address and turning on Private Google Access for its subnet. Name one limit of Private Google Access.
lessons.modelAnswer: An external IP address is a public address attached to one VM. It lets that VM send and receive traffic from the internet, and it works for any destination, including websites and other public services. Private Google Access is a subnet-level setting. It lets VMs that have only internal addresses reach Google APIs and managed services such as Cloud Storage over Google's network. It does not give those VMs general internet access, and it does not make them reachable from outside. One limit: it only covers Google service addresses, so a VM that needs to call an external vendor's API still needs a path out, such as Cloud NAT or an external IP. Also, the default route to the default internet gateway must still exist for the traffic to flow.
rubricPoints: An external IP is a per-VM public address with general internet access.
Private Google Access is a per-subnet setting that reaches Google APIs and services only.
Private Google Access does not make a VM public or give general internet access.
A limit: traffic to non-Google external destinations still needs another path, and the default route must remain.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path a request takes from a private VM to a Google service would make the default route and the subnet setting visible as steps.

lessons.plain: A subnet is a slice of a cloud network with its own block of IP addresses, the numbered labels machines use to find each other. Sometimes that block turns out too small: the slice fills up and new machines cannot get an address. Expanding a subnet's range means making the block bigger after it has been created, so more addresses become available. You can make it bigger but never smaller, and the new block must still contain the old one. Existing machines keep their addresses; the change adds room for new ones.
lessons.guessPrompt: A subnet uses 10.0.1.0/24 and is almost full. Which of these would be a valid expansion, and why: 10.0.0.0/20 or 10.0.2.0/23?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A VPC network is your private virtual network in the cloud. A subnet is a regional piece of that network, and its primary IPv4 range is the block of addresses the subnet hands out to machines. That block is written in CIDR notation, where the number after the slash, the prefix length, says how many leading bits are fixed. A smaller prefix number means a bigger block: a /24 holds 256 addresses, while a /20 holds 4,096.

Why expansion works: because the addresses are defined by a prefix, you can widen the block by lowering the prefix length, as long as the new block fully contains the old one. The platform keeps existing addresses valid and makes the rest of the larger block available. Expansion is one-way. You cannot shrink a range, and you cannot move it to a different starting address.

Worked example. A subnet called app-subnet has primary range 10.0.1.0/24. Its 256 addresses are nearly used up. Step 1: choose a candidate, 10.0.0.0/20, which spans 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.15.255. Step 2: check that it contains the old block. The old block, 10.0.1.0 through 10.0.1.255, falls inside that span, so it passes. Step 3: check that it does not overlap any other subnet in the same VPC. If another subnet uses 10.0.8.0/24, that address sits inside the candidate, so the expansion is refused and you need a different plan.

Common mistake: choosing a range that looks plausible but does not contain the original, such as 10.0.2.0/23. It covers different addresses, so it is not an expansion at all and is rejected. A second mistake is expanding far beyond real need. Because you cannot shrink the range, the extra space is locked in and may later clash with networks you connect to.

Consequence in a running system: existing virtual machines keep their addresses during the change. New machines draw from the enlarged block, so a subnet that cannot start new instances can recover without being rebuilt.

questions.prompt: A team runs a subnet named batch-subnet in a separate project with primary range 10.20.64.0/22, which holds 1,024 addresses from 10.20.64.0 through 10.20.67.255. They want more room and choose candidate 10.20.64.0/21, which spans 10.20.64.0 through 10.20.71.255. Step 1 is done: the candidate is 10.20.64.0/21. Step 2 is left for you to complete and is the only step missing. Step 3: another subnet in the same VPC, 10.20.72.0/22, spans 10.20.72.0 through 10.20.75.255, which lies outside the candidate, so no overlap exists and that check passes. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Confirm that the candidate's prefix length is longer than /22 so that the block gets smaller and the subnet keeps its current size.
Confirm that the candidate fully contains the old block 10.20.64.0 through 10.20.67.255, which it does because it spans 10.20.64.0 through 10.20.71.255.
Confirm that the candidate starts at 10.20.0.0 so that it aligns with the start of the VPC's address space.
Delete the subnet and recreate it with the candidate range so that existing machines are assigned new addresses inside the larger block.
questions.why: An expansion is only valid when the new block fully contains the old one, and 10.20.64.0/21 does contain 10.20.64.0/22, so step 2 is the containment check.

questions.prompt: Which statement about expanding a subnet's primary IPv4 range is true?
choices: Raising the prefix length, such as moving from /20 to /22, is the standard way to make room for new machines.
Expansion can move the range to a new starting address as long as the size stays the same.
Lowering the prefix length, such as moving from /22 to /20, widens the block while keeping the existing addresses valid.
Changing a /22 to a /20 shrinks the subnet to a quarter of its former size.
questions.why: A smaller prefix number means a bigger block, so lowering the prefix length widens the range while existing addresses remain in use.

questions.prompt: A subnet has primary range 172.20.128.0/21. An engineer asks to expand it to 172.20.136.0/21 because the new block looks like the next one along. Why will the platform refuse this change?
choices: Any range that begins with 172.20 is reserved and cannot be used for a subnet's primary range.
The platform refuses any expansion that touches a range already used by a virtual machine.
The prefix length is the same, and the platform only accepts expansions that change the prefix length.
The new block 172.20.136.0/21 starts at a different address and does not contain the original block, so it is a move rather than an expansion.
questions.why: An expansion must fully contain the original block, and 172.20.136.0/21 covers different addresses from 172.20.128.0/21, so it is not an expansion at all.

questions.prompt: A subnet uses 10.50.0.0/22, which holds 1,024 addresses. Another subnet in the same VPC uses 10.50.8.0/24. The team wants more room without moving the other subnet. Which target range can be applied?
questions.why: 10.50.0.0/21 contains the original /22 and ends at 10.50.7.255, so it does not overlap 10.50.8.0/24, while 10.50.0.0/20 would cover that subnet and 10.50.0.0/23 would shrink the range.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can just grow the subnet from /24 to /28 to get more room. Explain to them what expansion actually allows, the limit they are missing, and one tradeoff of choosing a very large range.
lessons.modelAnswer: Expanding a subnet means lowering its prefix length so the block gets bigger. Going from /24 to /28 would make the block smaller, which is not an expansion, and the platform does not allow it, because a range can only grow. The new range must fully contain the current one and must not overlap any other subnet in the VPC. We also need to check networks we might connect to later, since a range that clashes with them causes trouble when we connect. Existing machines keep their addresses, so the change is safe for running workloads, but it cannot be undone. The tradeoff is that a very large range gives headroom now while locking in space we may never use and that may collide with a future network. We should size it to a realistic forecast.
rubricPoints: Expansion only increases the range by lowering the prefix length; a smaller prefix number is a bigger block.
The new range must fully contain the original range.
The new range must not overlap other subnets in the VPC or networks we connect to.
The change is one-way; a range cannot be shrunk.
Existing machines keep their addresses while new ones draw from the larger block.

suggested.rationale: A scenario with a near-miss range choice tests the exact setting and the reason a candidate is refused, which no listed mission covers.

lessons.plain: A service perimeter is a fence drawn around a group of your cloud projects and the managed services they use, such as storage and databases. Its job is to stop data from being copied out to places you do not control, even by someone who has a valid login. Requests that cross the fence from outside are refused, while requests inside it keep working. You can open small, deliberate gaps for known partners or trusted office locations. Learning to draw this fence, and to test it safely before turning it on, is what keeps a leaked credential from becoming a data leak.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an engineer with the correct IAM roles runs a copy command from a personal laptop on a home network to a storage bucket in your company's project. What single control would you add to block that copy while still letting staff at the office work normally, and why would IAM alone not be enough?
lessons.teach:
A service perimeter is a boundary, configured in Google Cloud's VPC Service Controls, that wraps a set of projects and a set of restricted services. Restricted services are managed APIs such as object storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub. Generically, the perimeter is a data-exfiltration fence. Inside the perimeter, calls between protected resources are allowed. A call that arrives from outside, or that tries to send data from inside to a project outside the perimeter, is denied even when the caller holds a valid IAM role. IAM answers who may do something; the perimeter answers from where, and to where data may flow.

Why it works: the check happens at the API front door of each restricted service, so a stolen key used from an unknown network still hits the fence. Exceptions are written as access levels, which describe trusted conditions such as a corporate IP range or a managed device, and as ingress and egress rules, which name specific identities or projects allowed across the boundary.

Worked example: a perimeter holds an analytics project and BigQuery. Step 1: a job inside the analytics project reads a table. Both caller and resource are inside, so the call is allowed. Step 2: a laptop on a home network with valid credentials calls the same API. It is outside the perimeter and no access level matches, so it is denied. Step 3: the office IP range is added as an access level and attached through an ingress rule. The same call from the office is now allowed.

Common mistake: enforcing a new perimeter immediately. Use dry-run mode first, which logs what would have been blocked without blocking it. Review those logs for legitimate callers such as build systems, scheduled jobs, or partner pipelines before enforcing.

Consequence: a missing rule can break a running pipeline at 2 a.m. The job fails with a permission-style error that looks like an IAM problem, so responders may waste time changing roles when the real fix is an ingress rule.

A perimeter does not replace IAM, encryption, or firewall rules. It is an additional layer that controls where requests may come from and where data may go.

questions.prompt: A research lab keeps a project called lab-ingest. A perimeter wraps that project and includes a Pub/Sub topic and a storage bucket. A nightly job runs from a separate partner project outside the perimeter, using a valid service account that has write permission to the bucket. Step 1: the partner job's call to the bucket is denied, because the caller is outside the perimeter and no access level matches it. Step 2: the team checks the logs and confirms the caller is the legitimate nightly job, not an intruder. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the team reruns the job, and the call succeeds from the partner's fixed IP range. Which choice completes step 3?
choices: Create an access level describing the partner's fixed IP range and attach it to an ingress rule on the perimeter that names the partner service account.
Add a firewall rule on the partner project's virtual machines that allows outbound traffic to the bucket.
Remove the bucket from the perimeter so the partner job can reach it without any rule.
Grant the partner service account the Storage Admin role at the organisation level, so its IAM role covers the bucket.
questions.why: The perimeter denial comes from the location of the caller, so the fix is an access level for the trusted source attached through an ingress rule that names the identity, not a change to IAM roles or firewalls.

questions.prompt: A service account holds the correct IAM role on a BigQuery dataset inside a perimeter. A call made with that account's valid key from a laptop outside the perimeter is denied. What best explains the denial?
choices: The key has silently expired, which always produces a denial from any network.
The perimeter checks where the request comes from, no access level matches the laptop, so the call is denied even though the role is valid.
The IAM role is too narrow, so the account needs the Owner role.
The dataset lacks encryption, and the perimeter refuses unencrypted resources.
questions.why: A perimeter adds a location and data-flow check on top of IAM, so a valid role does not help when the caller is outside and no access level or ingress rule admits it.

questions.prompt: A data export job runs inside a perimeter and tries to copy a table to a storage bucket in a project outside that perimeter. It fails with a permission-style error. Which explanation is most likely?
choices: Data is trying to leave the perimeter, and no egress rule allows that destination, so the perimeter blocks it.
The export job is missing the Viewer role on its own project.
The table is too large for the storage bucket's default size limit.
The bucket's region differs from the job's region, which always blocks copies.
questions.why: Egress rules control data leaving the perimeter toward a project outside it, so a missing egress rule produces a denial that looks like an IAM problem.

questions.prompt: A team creates a new perimeter and turns on dry-run mode. What happens to a call that the perimeter would block?
choices: The call is blocked and the team receives an alert email.
The call is held in a queue until an access level is approved.
The call is logged as one that would have been blocked, but it is still allowed to go through.
The call is blocked, but the owner's IAM role is automatically upgraded.
questions.why: Dry-run mode records what enforcement would have blocked without actually blocking it, which lets the team review legitimate callers before switching to enforcement.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because our engineers already have the right IAM roles, a VPC Service Controls perimeter is redundant. Explain to them in your own words what the perimeter adds, and name one limit or tradeoff of turning it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: IAM decides whether a particular identity may perform an action, such as reading a bucket. It does not care where the request comes from, so a valid key used from an unknown network still succeeds. A service perimeter adds the second question: is this request coming from an allowed place, and is the data going somewhere allowed? It wraps projects and managed services, and it refuses calls that cross the boundary unless an access level or an ingress or egress rule allows them. The tradeoff is operational. Every legitimate caller from outside, such as a CI runner, a partner, or a remote analyst, needs an explicit exception, and a missed one fails with a permission-style error that looks like an IAM problem. That is why I would run it in dry-run mode first and review the logs before enforcing.
rubricPoints: IAM controls who may act, while the perimeter also controls where requests come from and where data may flow.
A perimeter wraps projects and restricted managed services and denies boundary-crossing calls by default.
Exceptions are made with access levels and ingress or egress rules, not by loosening IAM.
A tradeoff is that missing exceptions break legitimate callers, so dry-run mode is used before enforcement.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style situation about who is blocked, why, and which exception is needed adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers perimeters directly.

lessons.plain: Think of your cloud network as a town with its own roads. A route is a road sign that tells traffic which way to go for a given address range. Your VPC, which is your private virtual network in Google Cloud, needs signs for places outside it, such as an office data center or another cloud. You can write those signs by hand. That is a static route: it stays exactly as you left it until someone changes it. Or the two sides can talk automatically and announce which address ranges they can reach. That conversation is dynamic routing, and a managed service called Cloud Router runs it for you. This lesson covers when to use each and how the network picks between competing paths.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office and your cloud network are linked by two encrypted tunnels. Would you rather type every office address range into the cloud network by hand, or let the two sides announce their ranges to each other? Which option handles a tunnel failure better, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A route is an entry saying that traffic for a destination address range should be sent to a next hop, the next device or gateway on the way. A static route is one you create and maintain yourself. A dynamic route is one learned from a peer through BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, the standard way networks announce which address ranges they can reach. Cloud Router is the regional Google Cloud service that speaks BGP for your VPC. It forms a BGP session with a router on the other side, such as the far end of an HA VPN tunnel (high-availability VPN, a pair of encrypted tunnels between your VPC and an outside network), and exchanges routes with it. MED, the multi-exit discriminator, is a BGP attribute a peer can set to influence which of its paths is preferred. When two routes match the same destination, the lower priority number wins.

Why it works. Static routes are simple and predictable, but they do not react to failures. A BGP session notices when its peer goes away and withdraws the routes it had learned, so traffic moves to a backup path without anyone editing anything. Cloud Router also advertises your subnet ranges, or a custom list you choose, to the peer so the far side knows how to reply.

Worked example. Your VPC has subnet 10.0.1.0/24. The office range 10.20.0.0/16 is reachable through two HA VPN tunnels. Step one: Cloud Router learns the office range on each tunnel from its BGP peer. Step two: the peer sets a lower MED on the primary tunnel, so that route gets the better priority. Step three: traffic to 10.20.5.9 uses the primary tunnel. Step four: if the primary session drops, its learned route is withdrawn and the backup route carries the traffic.

Common mistake. Adding a static route for the office range and leaving BGP running for the same range. The static route does not disappear when BGP fails over, so traffic can keep pointing at a dead next hop while the two sources disagree. Choose one method per destination.

Consequence. A stale static route to a failed tunnel can black-hole traffic for hours while the tunnel looks merely unhealthy. Dynamic routing through Cloud Router is what gives you automatic failover.

questions.prompt: A team runs a regional Cloud Router in europe-west2 with two HA VPN tunnels to a supplier network at 172.30.0.0/20. Both tunnels' BGP sessions learn that range. The supplier sets a lower MED on tunnel A, so tunnel A's learned route is preferred. Trace traffic to 172.30.3.14. Step 1: Cloud Router learns 172.30.0.0/20 on tunnel A and on tunnel B. Step 2: the route learned on tunnel A has the better preference, so traffic to 172.30.3.14 uses tunnel A. Step 3: ____. Step 4: traffic to 172.30.3.14 moves to tunnel B without anyone editing a route.
choices: The supplier raises its MED on tunnel A to match tunnel B, which makes both routes equal and keeps traffic on tunnel A
Cloud Router stops advertising subnet 10.50.2.0/24 to the supplier so the supplier chooses tunnel B on its own
Tunnel A's BGP session drops, its learned route is withdrawn, and the route learned on tunnel B carries the traffic
An administrator adds a static route for 172.30.0.0/20 with priority 1000 pointing at tunnel B so failover is preserved
questions.why: When a BGP session drops, Cloud Router withdraws the routes it learned on that session, leaving the route on the other tunnel to carry traffic, which is the automatic failover step that Step 4 depends on.

questions.prompt: A network engineer in asia-southeast1 has two routes to 10.200.0.0/18 in the same VPC: one learned by Cloud Router over BGP with priority 100, and one static route to the same range with priority 500. Which statement is correct?
choices: The routes cancel each other out, so no traffic reaches 10.200.0.0/18 until one of them is deleted
The static route wins because a higher priority number is preferred in Google Cloud routing
Both routes are used at the same time for every packet, splitting traffic evenly between them
The BGP-learned route wins because the lower priority number is preferred when two routes match the same destination
questions.why: When two routes match the same destination, the lower priority number wins, so the priority 100 route is chosen over the priority 500 static route.

questions.prompt: A team in a company called Harbor Freight Lab has a static route for 198.51.100.0/24 pointing at an HA VPN tunnel, and their Cloud Router also learns 198.51.100.0/24 over BGP on that same tunnel. The tunnel's BGP session goes down. What happens to traffic sent to 198.51.100.40?
choices: Traffic is dropped only if the subnet 198.51.100.0/24 is also attached to the VPC, otherwise it keeps working
The BGP session failure automatically removes the static route, so traffic falls back to the default internet gateway
Cloud Router immediately creates a new static route to the backup tunnel and sends traffic there
The static route stays in place, so traffic can keep pointing at the dead next hop while BGP has withdrawn its copy
questions.why: A static route is not removed when a BGP session fails, so it can keep sending traffic to a dead next hop while the BGP-learned copy disappears, which is why the two methods should not be mixed for one destination.

questions.prompt: A company's VPC uses subnet 10.70.0.0/20 and must reach a partner network at 10.200.0.0/18 through two HA VPN tunnels managed by a regional Cloud Router. The partner should be reachable with automatic failover if one tunnel fails. Which configuration meets that goal?
choices: Create a static route for 10.200.0.0/18 to the primary tunnel only and let BGP handle nothing for that range
Let Cloud Router learn 10.200.0.0/18 over BGP on both tunnels and add no static route for that range
Create a static route for 10.200.0.0/18 to each tunnel, then add a second static route for 10.70.0.0/20 to the backup tunnel
Create one static route for 10.200.0.0/18 to each tunnel with the same priority and disable BGP on both tunnels
questions.why: Relying on BGP-learned routes for the partner range lets Cloud Router withdraw a failed tunnel's route automatically, whereas static routes would not react to the failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use a static route instead of dynamic routing through Cloud Router, and name one limit or tradeoff of the static approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a static route when the destination is small, stable, and reached through one fixed next hop, such as a single appliance or a lab network that never changes. It is easy to read and needs no BGP session. The tradeoff is that it does not react to failures. If the next hop or tunnel fails, a static route keeps pointing at it until someone notices and changes it. For an office or another cloud reached over redundant links, I would use Cloud Router. Its BGP session withdraws routes when a peer disappears, and the peer's preferences decide which path wins. The cost is more setup: you must configure the BGP peers and manage which ranges get advertised, so a wrong advertisement can send traffic the wrong way.
rubricPoints: A static route is manually set and stays until changed, with no automatic reaction to failures.
Cloud Router uses BGP to learn and advertise routes dynamically with an outside peer.
BGP withdraws learned routes when a session fails, enabling automatic failover.
Mixing a static route and a BGP route for the same destination can leave stale paths in use.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration facts and route-selection rules that a reading and console walkthrough covers best, and no listed mission or planned engine targets BGP or Cloud Router.

lessons.plain: A virtual network in a cloud account is a private network you build in software. Some of its routes are not typed in by hand. They are learned automatically from another network, such as an office or another cloud, through a router service that trades route information. The routing mode is a setting on the whole network that decides how far those learned routes travel. In regional mode, a learned route only works in the region where its router lives. In global mode, the learned route is shared with every region the network spans. Think of a postal network. In regional mode each local branch knows only the addresses on its own street. In global mode the branches share their address books. The choice is about reach, not speed, and it sits on the network itself.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company network is connected to a cloud network through a router in one city. A server in a different city inside the same cloud network cannot reach the company network, but the server next door can. Without any further detail, what single network-level setting would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A VPC network is a private network you define in a cloud project. It is split into subnets, and each subnet lives in one region, a geographic area with its own data centres. A Cloud Router is a managed service that exchanges routes with an outside network, such as an on-premises office, using a dynamic routing protocol. A route is simply a rule saying which destination range goes to which next hop. Dynamic routing means the router learns these rules from its peer instead of you typing them in. The routing mode is a property of the VPC network that controls the scope of the routes that Cloud Routers learn and advertise. Regional mode limits learned routes to the region of the router that learned them. Global mode makes them available in all regions of the network.

Worked example. A VPC has subnets in us-central1 and europe-west1. A Cloud Router in us-central1 learns the prefix 10.20.0.0/16 from an office. Step 1: in regional mode, that route is programmed only for us-central1 subnets. Step 2: a virtual machine in europe-west1 sending traffic to 10.20.0.5 matches no learned route, so it falls to a default route or is dropped. Step 3: switch the network to global mode and the same prefix is now programmed for europe-west1 too, so the traffic reaches the office through the us-central1 router.

Common mistake: assuming the router's region only decides where the router sits, and not realising that regional mode quietly hides its routes from other regions. Another mistake is expecting a mode change to have no effect on existing traffic paths.

Consequence in a running system: when the mode is regional, failures appear only in the regions without the route, so they look intermittent and region-specific. In global mode, if two routers advertise the same prefix, one path is preferred, so traffic can take an unexpected route across regions.

The routing mode is the setting that decides whether a learned route serves one region or the whole VPC network.

questions.prompt: A VPC network called ledger-prod has subnets in asia-southeast1 and australia-southeast1 and is set to regional routing mode. A Cloud Router in asia-southeast1 learns the prefix 172.16.40.0/22 from a partner data centre. Step 1: the route is programmed only for asia-southeast1 subnets, because regional mode limits learned routes to the router's region. Step 2: a virtual machine in australia-southeast1 sending traffic to 172.16.40.9 matches no learned route. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the same prefix now serves australia-southeast1 as well, and that VM reaches the partner through the asia-southeast1 router. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: Add a second subnet in asia-southeast1 so the learned prefix has a local subnet to attach to.
Restart the virtual machine in australia-southeast1 so it reloads its routing table at boot.
Move the Cloud Router to australia-southeast1 while keeping the network in regional mode.
Change the network's routing mode from regional to global so learned routes apply across all regions.
questions.why: Switching the VPC from regional to global mode is the setting that makes the learned route available in every region, which is what step 4 depends on.

questions.prompt: In a VPC network, what does the routing mode control?
choices: The scope of the routes that Cloud Routers learn and advertise, either one region or the whole network.
The IP address ranges that subnets are allowed to use.
The protocol a Cloud Router uses to talk to its on-premises peer.
The region in which a Cloud Router physically runs.
questions.why: The routing mode is defined in the teaching text as the network property that decides whether learned routes serve one region or the whole VPC.

questions.prompt: A VPC is in regional mode. A Cloud Router in southamerica-east1 learns 192.168.77.0/24 from a branch office. A virtual machine in northamerica-northeast1 cannot reach 192.168.77.10, while a virtual machine in southamerica-east1 can. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The Cloud Router must be restarted so it advertises the prefix to every region.
The learned route is programmed only for the router's own region, so the other region has no route to the prefix.
The subnet in northamerica-northeast1 is too small to hold a route to 192.168.77.0/24.
The branch office has blocked traffic from northamerica-northeast1 at its edge.
questions.why: In regional mode a learned route is limited to the region of the router that learned it, so failures appear only in other regions.

questions.prompt: An engineer switches a VPC from regional to global mode and expects existing traffic paths to stay exactly the same. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Nothing changes, because the mode only affects newly created subnets.
Existing paths can change, because learned routes now apply in all regions and a preferred path may be chosen across regions.
Only Cloud Routers that were created after the change will be affected.
Traffic is blocked until every region receives a fresh copy of the routes.
questions.why: Global mode makes learned routes available in all regions, so traffic that previously fell to a default route or was dropped can now take a learned path, and a preferred path can change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the difference between regional and global dynamic routing is on a VPC network, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing global routing.
lessons.modelAnswer: Regional dynamic routing means routes learned by a Cloud Router only apply to subnets in that router's region. Global dynamic routing means those learned routes are programmed for every region in the VPC network, so a router in one region can serve workloads in another. The tradeoff is that global mode makes reach wider but also makes path selection more complex. If two routers in different regions advertise the same destination, one route wins based on priority and metric, so traffic may leave through a region you did not expect. Before switching a network to global mode, I would check which routers advertise which prefixes and confirm that the preferred path is the one we intend.
rubricPoints: Regional mode limits learned routes to the router's own region
Global mode shares learned routes with all regions of the VPC network
Global mode can cause traffic to take a path in another region if several routers advertise the same prefix
Changing the mode affects existing traffic paths, so check advertised routes first

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine exercises VPC routing modes, so reading the setting and its effects is the best available route.

lessons.plain: When a packet leaves a virtual machine, the network must choose one entry from its routing table to send it along. Usually there is one obvious answer, but sometimes you want a particular group of machines to take a different path, such as sending only some servers through a security inspection appliance. Network tags are short labels attached to machines, and a route can be limited so it applies only to machines carrying a matching label. Route priority is a number that breaks ties when two routes cover the same destination, and the lower number wins. Together they let you steer one group of machines differently without changing everyone else.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine has two routes for all internet-bound traffic: one at priority 1000 and one at priority 900. Which route does it use, and what is your reasoning?
lessons.teach:
A route is a rule in a network's routing table that says packets for a given destination range should be handed to a given next hop. The next hop is the first place the packet goes, such as a virtual appliance machine, a gateway, or an internal load balancer. A network tag is a label you attach to a virtual machine. A route can also carry network tags. When it does, it applies only to machines that have at least one matching tag; a route with no tags applies to every machine in the network. Priority is a whole number from 0 to 65535 where a lower value wins. Custom routes default to 1000 if you do not set one.

The network first prefers the most specific destination range. If several applicable routes cover the same range, the one with the lowest priority number wins. If two applicable routes tie on both range and priority, traffic is shared between them.

Worked example: the network has a default route, 0.0.0.0/0, sending to the default internet gateway at priority 1000, applying to all machines. You add a second route, 0.0.0.0/0, pointing at an inspection appliance at priority 900, tagged inspect. Step one: a machine with the tag inspect sees two matching routes, one at 900 and one at 1000. Step two: 900 is lower, so it wins and traffic goes to the appliance. Step three: a machine without the tag sees only the 1000 route, so it still goes to the internet gateway.

Common mistake: assuming a higher priority number means more important. It is the reverse, so a route at priority 1100 would lose to the default and never take effect. Another mistake is forgetting the tag, since a tagged route applies to nobody if no machine carries that tag.

Consequence: if the inspect tag is removed from a machine, its outbound traffic falls back to the default route and skips inspection without any error being raised.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental runs a VPC with two routes for the same machines. Route A is 10.50.0.0/16 sending to a VPN gateway at priority 1000, applying to all machines. Route B is 0.0.0.0/0 sending to an egress proxy at priority 500, tagged egress-proxy. A machine tagged egress-proxy has a packet for 10.50.3.9. Step one: both routes match that destination, since 10.50.3.9 falls inside 10.50.0.0/16 and inside 0.0.0.0/0. Step three: the packet goes to the VPN gateway. What is the missing step two?
choices: The network prefers the more specific range 10.50.0.0/16, so the VPN route is chosen before priority is compared.
The two routes tie on priority, so the packet is split evenly between the VPN gateway and the proxy.
The tag egress-proxy makes the proxy route ignore the destination range, so the VPN route is chosen by default.
The network compares priority first, so the 500 route wins and the packet goes to the egress proxy.
questions.why: The network first narrows to the most specific destination range, and 10.50.0.0/16 is more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, so priority only matters among routes that cover the same range.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does attaching a network tag to a route do?
choices: It sets the destination range the route covers to the tag's value.
It makes the route apply to every machine in the network, including untagged ones.
It raises the route's priority so it is checked before other routes.
It limits the route so it applies only to machines carrying at least one matching tag.
questions.why: A tagged route applies only to machines that have at least one matching tag, while an untagged route applies to every machine in the network.

questions.prompt: A team creates a route for 172.16.0.0/12 at priority 1200 to a firewall appliance, tagged dmz. They expect it to override the default route at priority 1000. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: The route is rejected at creation because priorities above 1000 are not allowed.
The route never takes effect for traffic it could otherwise handle, because the default route at 1000 would win over it when both apply.
The route overrides the default because a larger priority number means a more important route.
The route takes effect only for machines with no tags at all.
questions.why: Lower priority numbers win, so a route at 1200 loses to a competing route at 1000 for the same range and never overrides it.

questions.prompt: Two routes both cover 192.168.40.0/24, both are applicable to the same machine, and both have priority 800. One goes to a NAT gateway and the other to a VPN tunnel. What happens to the machine's traffic to that range?
choices: The network picks whichever route was created first and ignores the other.
The network sends all traffic to the NAT gateway because it is listed first alphabetically.
The network shares the traffic between the two routes, since they tie on both range and priority.
The network drops the traffic because the routes conflict.
questions.why: When two applicable routes tie on both destination range and priority, the network splits traffic between them rather than choosing one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how network tags and route priority together decide which route a given virtual machine uses, and name one limit or tradeoff of steering traffic with tags.
lessons.modelAnswer: A route can be scoped with network tags, so it only applies to machines carrying a matching tag. If no tags are set, the route applies to every machine in the network. When several applicable routes cover the same destination range, the network picks the one with the lowest priority number, where lower means more preferred and the default is 1000. So a tagged route at 900 overrides an untagged default at 1000 for tagged machines only, while everything else keeps the default. The main limit is that the steering depends entirely on tags being correct and present, so a removed or misspelled tag quietly moves traffic back to the default path. Tags also are not a security boundary by themselves, so they should be combined with firewall rules and review of who can change machine tags.
rubricPoints: A route with network tags applies only to machines that carry a matching tag; untagged routes apply to all machines.
Among routes with the same destination, the lowest priority number wins, and the default for custom routes is 1000.
A higher priority number is less preferred, the opposite of the intuition many beginners have.
Changing or removing a tag silently changes which route a machine uses, which is a real operational risk.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which route a packet takes from a given machine under different tags and priorities is the core skill, and the planned path tracer would make that practice concrete.

lessons.plain: When a cloud network has more than one possible path to the same destination, something has to decide which path traffic takes. That decision is what this objective covers. Each route in the network's table is a rule saying where to send traffic for a range of addresses, and each route carries a priority number. Some routes are typed in by hand, some are learned automatically from a neighbouring network, and some are chosen by matching the kind of traffic. Global dynamic routing means routes learned in one region can be used across the whole network, not just nearby. Knowing how priority works lets you predict which path wins before something breaks, and set up a backup path that only takes over when the main one disappears.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two routes lead to the same destination: one has priority 100 and the other has priority 200. Which one would you expect the network to use, and what would change your answer if one of the routes pointed to a narrower range of addresses?
lessons.teach:
A route is a rule that tells the network where to send traffic for a range of destination addresses, written as a prefix such as 10.20.0.0/16. Routes come from three places. Static routes are entered by an engineer. Dynamic routes are learned over BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the standard way networks exchange reachability information) through a Cloud Router, which is the managed component that speaks BGP for a VPC. Policy-based routes match traffic by attributes such as source address or protocol, then send the matched traffic to a chosen next hop.

When several routes could handle a packet, the network first prefers the most specific prefix, meaning the longest match, so a /24 beats a /16. Only when the prefixes are equal does priority decide. A route priority is a number where a lower value wins. A static route defaults to 1000. A dynamic route takes its priority from the MED (multi-exit discriminator), a BGP value the on-premises router sets to signal preference. If two routes tie on priority, traffic is shared between them.

Global dynamic routing is a VPC setting that lets a Cloud Router advertise and learn routes across every region of the VPC, so a route learned in one region can be used by workloads in another. In regional mode, learned routes stay within the Cloud Router's own region.

Worked example: a VPC learns 10.20.0.0/16 over two links. Link A advertises MED 100 and link B advertises MED 200. Step one: both routes have the same prefix, so priority is compared. Step two: 100 is lower, so link A wins and matching traffic uses it. Step three: link A fails, its route is withdrawn, and link B's route is the only one left, so it carries the traffic.

Common mistake: assuming a higher number means a more preferred route, or expecting a priority setting to override a more specific prefix that also matches.

Consequence: if the backup link has less capacity than the primary, failover can silently saturate it.

questions.prompt: A VPC in global dynamic routing mode has two routes that could carry traffic to 192.168.40.9. Route X is a static route for 192.168.0.0/16 with priority 100, pointing to a firewall appliance. Route Y is a dynamic route for 192.168.40.0/24 learned over BGP from an on-premises router that sets MED 50, so its priority is 50. Step one: both prefixes contain 192.168.40.9, so both routes match. Step two: the network compares prefix length first, and /24 is more specific than /16, so priority is not compared at all between these two routes. Step three is missing: which route carries the packet, and why does the priority number not matter here?
choices: Route X, because 100 is a higher priority than 50 and so is preferred
Route Y, because its priority number is lower, so it beats route X's number
Route X, because a static route always beats a dynamic route
Route Y, because its prefix is longer, so it wins before priority is compared
questions.why: Prefix length is checked before priority, so the longer /24 wins even though its priority number is not the deciding factor and route X has a numerically higher priority number.

questions.prompt: In a VPC with global dynamic routing, two routes both cover exactly 10.50.0.0/20. One has priority 300 and the other has priority 250, and both are up. Which one carries the traffic?
choices: Both routes, split evenly, because their priorities differ
Whichever route was learned first, because priority is ignored
The priority 300 route, because a higher number is treated as more preferred
The priority 250 route, because a lower number wins
questions.why: When prefixes are equal, the route with the lower priority number wins, so the 250 route is used.

questions.prompt: A team adds a static route for 10.80.0.0/12 at priority 10 to send traffic to a backup appliance. The VPC also learns 10.80.4.0/22 dynamically from an on-premises router. Which statement about traffic to 10.80.4.20 is correct?
choices: The dynamic route is ignored because the static route was entered by an engineer
The dynamic /22 route is used because it is the more specific match, so the priority 10 static route does not override it
The static route at priority 10 is used because a low priority number always overrides everything
Traffic is split between the two routes because the priorities are close
questions.why: The longest matching prefix is chosen before priority, and /22 is more specific than /12, so the learned route carries the traffic despite the static route's low priority number.

questions.prompt: A VPC is in regional mode. A Cloud Router in europe-west1 learns 172.30.0.0/16 over BGP. A virtual machine in us-central1, in the same VPC, sends traffic to 172.30.5.10. What happens?
choices: The VM has no route to that prefix in its region, so it does not use the learned route
The VM uses the learned route, because the VPC spans all regions
The traffic is passed to the Cloud Router in europe-west1, which forwards it onward
The VM uses the learned route at the default priority of 1000
questions.why: In regional mode learned routes stay within the Cloud Router's own region, so the us-central1 workload cannot use the route learned in europe-west1.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how route priority decides which path traffic takes when the same destination is learned over two links, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on priority for failover.
lessons.modelAnswer: When two routes cover the same destination prefix, the network compares their priority numbers and uses the lower one. For routes learned dynamically through a Cloud Router, that number comes from the MED the on-premises router advertises, so the on-premises side effectively chooses the preferred link. If the preferred route is withdrawn because its link fails, the remaining route takes over automatically. The limit is that priority only compares routes with the same prefix; a more specific prefix wins regardless of priority, so a leaked narrow route can pull traffic away unexpectedly.
