The tradeoff is that a backup link with lower priority may have less capacity, so failover can overload it. Checking prefix length, priority and capacity together is what prevents surprises.
rubricPoints: Lower priority number wins when prefixes are equal
Longest prefix match is considered before priority
Dynamic route priority comes from the advertised MED
Failover happens when the preferred route is withdrawn, and capacity on the backup link matters

suggested.rationale: A path tracer that shows which route a packet selects and why lets learners see prefix length and priority decide the outcome, which reading alone does not give them.

lessons.plain: Normally a cloud network sends traffic straight to its destination. Sometimes you want certain traffic, such as everything headed for one range of addresses, to pass first through a group of machines that share the work, like firewalls or inspection boxes. A route is a rule that says where to send packets for a destination range. Here the route's next hop, the next stop, is not a single machine but a balancer that spreads traffic across a pool of healthy backend machines. The balancer is reached through a private address inside your own network, so the traffic never leaves that private network. Think of a receptionist who hands each visitor to whichever clerk is free and skips clerks who have gone home.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you point a route for one range of addresses at a balancer instead of a single machine, what do you think happens when one of the backend machines behind that balancer stops responding?
lessons.teach:
A route is a rule in a virtual network that matches a destination address range and names a next hop, the place a packet goes next. When several routes match a packet, the most specific range wins, and among equal ranges the lowest priority number wins. A route whose next hop is an internal load balancer sends matching packets to that balancer's private forwarding address. A forwarding rule is the entry that gives the balancer its address and protocol handling. A backend is a machine in the balancer's pool. A health check is a periodic probe that decides which backends are healthy enough to receive traffic. Because a backend receives packets addressed to some other destination, it must have IP forwarding turned on, meaning it is allowed to pass along traffic it is not the final target of.

Worked example: a subnet 10.0.0.0/24 holds a client VM at 10.0.0.5. You add a route for 10.50.0.0/16 with next hop the balancer's forwarding address 10.0.0.10 and priority 100. Step 1: the client wants to reach 10.50.4.7. Step 2: no subnet covers that address, so the route for 10.50.0.0/16 matches. Step 3: the packet goes to 10.0.0.10. Step 4: the balancer picks a healthy backend, say 10.0.0.20. Step 5: that backend forwards the packet onward toward 10.50.4.7.

Common mistake: leaving IP forwarding off on the backends. They drop the packets, and the client sees silent timeouts while the balancer looks healthy.

Consequence: if every backend fails its health check, traffic for that range has no healthy next hop and is dropped, so the balancer and its backends become a single point of failure for that range.

Subnet routes for a subnet's own range always take precedence over custom routes, so you cannot use this to redirect traffic that stays inside a subnet.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics has a subnet 192.168.20.0/24. Two custom routes point at internal load balancers in that subnet. Route A covers 10.90.0.0/15, has priority 100, and uses forwarding address 192.168.20.50. Route B covers 10.90.32.0/20, has priority 500, and uses forwarding address 192.168.20.70. A client VM at 192.168.20.12 sends a packet to 10.90.33.9. Step 1: the client addresses the packet to 10.90.33.9. Step 2: both route A and route B match that address. Step 3 is not shown; choose what happens next. Step 4: the chosen balancer picks a healthy backend, 192.168.20.81. Step 5: that backend, with IP forwarding on, passes the packet onward toward 10.90.33.9.
choices: Route B wins because its range 10.90.32.0/20 is more specific, so the packet goes to 192.168.20.70.
Route A wins because its priority number 100 is lower, so the packet goes to 192.168.20.50.
The packet is dropped because two custom routes match the same destination.
Both routes are used in turn, so the packets alternate between 192.168.20.50 and 192.168.20.70.
questions.why: The most specific matching range wins before priority is considered, so the /20 route is chosen and its balancer receives the packet.

questions.prompt: In a route whose next hop is an internal load balancer, what does the forwarding rule do?
choices: It runs the periodic probe that decides which backends are healthy.
It turns on IP forwarding on every backend in the pool.
It gives the balancer its private address and sets how it handles the protocol.
It sets the route's priority number against other matching routes.
questions.why: A forwarding rule is the entry that gives the balancer its address and protocol handling, as described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A route for 172.20.0.0/16 uses an internal load balancer as its next hop. All three backends in the pool are failing their health checks. What happens to a packet that matches this route?
choices: It waits in a queue until a backend passes its health check again.
It is dropped, because the range has no healthy next hop.
It is delivered straight to its destination, skipping the balancer.
It is sent to the network's default gateway instead.
questions.why: With no healthy backend, the balancer has no next hop to offer for that range, so matching traffic is dropped.

questions.prompt: A subnet 10.40.1.0/24 has a custom route for 10.40.1.128/25 whose next hop is an internal load balancer. A VM at 10.40.1.9 sends a packet to 10.40.1.200. Does the custom route redirect this packet to the balancer?
choices: No, the subnet's own route takes precedence, so the packet is not redirected to the balancer.
Yes, but only if the balancer's backends have IP forwarding turned on.
Yes, the /25 is more specific than the /24, so the packet is redirected.
No, the packet is dropped because two routes conflict.
questions.why: Subnet routes for a subnet's own range always win over custom routes, so custom routes cannot redirect traffic that stays inside the subnet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a packet reaches a destination when a custom route's next hop is an internal load balancer, and name one limit or tradeoff of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a VM sends a packet, its network picks the most specific matching route. If that route's next hop is an internal load balancer, the packet goes to the balancer's private forwarding address. The balancer chooses a healthy backend from its pool, and that backend receives the packet even though it is not the final destination. It must have IP forwarding turned on, so it can pass the packet along using its own routing. The backend then sends the packet on toward the real destination. The main tradeoff is that the route depends on the pool's health. If health checks fail on every backend, traffic for that range is dropped, so you must size the pool and monitor its health. You also cannot use this pattern to redirect traffic inside a subnet's own range, because subnet routes always win.
rubricPoints: Explains that a route matching the destination sends packets to the balancer's forwarding address as the next hop
Notes that a healthy backend is chosen and must have IP forwarding enabled to pass on packets not addressed to it
Names the limit that if no backend is healthy the traffic is dropped, making the pool a single point of failure
Mentions that subnet routes for a subnet's own range take precedence over custom routes

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet hop by hop through routes and a balancer to its backend is the skill this objective needs, and the planned path tracer would practice it directly.

lessons.plain: A cloud network is split into separate virtual networks, and sometimes two of them need to reach each other's routes. Routes are the signposts that tell traffic where to go. Some routes are added by hand or learned from a router, and these are called custom routes. Connecting two networks does not automatically share these custom routes. This lesson covers the settings that decide which custom routes cross the connection, both for a direct peering between two networks and for a central hub that links many networks together. Getting these settings right is what lets traffic reach the far side.
lessons.guessPrompt: If network A has a hand-made route to an on-premises address range and then peers with network B, should B automatically know how to reach that range? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Subnet routes describe the subnets inside a virtual network. Custom routes are everything else: static routes you type in, and dynamic routes learned from on-premises equipment through a router called Cloud Router. Subnet routes are exchanged over a peering by default. Custom routes are not, because the network owner may not want a peer to see them. VPC Network Peering is a direct link between two virtual networks, and it has two separate settings on each side: import custom routes and export custom routes. Export means this network offers its custom routes to the peer. Import means this network accepts the custom routes the peer offers. A custom route reaches the other side only when one side exports and the other side imports. Network Connectivity Center is a hub that links many networks, called spokes, and it applies the same idea: each spoke controls what it sends into the hub and what it accepts from the hub.

Worked example. Network app-vpc has a static route for 10.50.0.0/16 that points to a VPN gateway, and it peers with data-vpc. Step 1: on app-vpc's side of the peering, turn on export of custom routes. Step 2: on data-vpc's side, turn on import of custom routes. Step 3: data-vpc now has a route for 10.50.0.0/16 whose next hop is the peering. If step 2 is skipped, data-vpc never learns the route, so its traffic to 10.50.0.0/16 falls back to a default route or is dropped.

Common mistake: turning on export on one side and assuming the route is now shared. In a running system this causes traffic to take a different path or disappear, while the peering still shows as active, so the cause is easy to misdiagnose as a firewall problem. Check the import and export flags on both sides first.

questions.prompt: A retail company has warehouse-vpc and reporting-vpc, both spokes of one Network Connectivity Center hub. warehouse-vpc has a static route for 10.80.0.0/20 that points to a VPN tunnel, and the reporting team needs to reach it. Step 1: On the warehouse spoke, turn on export of custom routes into the hub. Step 2: This step is missing and is the one you must supply. Step 3: Check that reporting-vpc's routing table lists 10.80.0.0/20 with the hub as the next hop.
choices: Turn on subnet route export on the warehouse spoke so the static route is included automatically
Turn on import on the warehouse spoke so it accepts reporting-vpc's routes as well
Add a firewall rule on reporting-vpc allowing traffic to 10.80.0.0/20 from any source
On the reporting spoke, turn on import of custom routes so it accepts routes from the hub
questions.why: A custom route reaches a spoke only when the sending side exports it into the hub and the receiving spoke imports it from the hub, so the missing step is the reporting spoke's import setting.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a custom route as this course uses the term?
choices: A route that only the peer network can create, and which the local network can only read
A route for a subnet that exists inside the virtual network and is exchanged over every peering by default
A route that is created automatically by the hub the moment a new spoke joins
A route that is not a subnet route, such as a static route you type in or a dynamic route learned from on-premises equipment, and which a peering does not exchange by default
questions.why: The teaching text defines custom routes as everything other than subnet routes, including static and dynamic routes, and states that they are not exchanged over a peering by default.

questions.prompt: Network north has a custom route 172.30.0.0/16 and turns on export over its peering with network south. South has not turned on import. What happens?
choices: South learns the route because the peering is active
South must enable export on its own side before the route can flow to north
South learns the route, but only for the subnet 172.30.0.0/16 itself
South never learns the route, so its traffic to 172.30.0.0/16 falls back to a default route or is dropped
questions.why: A custom route reaches the other side only when one side exports and the other side imports, so with no import on south the route never reaches south's routing table.

questions.prompt: A peering between two VPCs shows as active, but traffic to a remote custom route fails. Which check should come first?
choices: Check the import and export flags on both sides of the peering
Increase the size of the subnets on both networks
Add a higher-priority firewall rule to each network
Rebuild the peering as a Network Connectivity Center spoke
questions.why: The teaching text explains that a peering can look healthy while custom routes are missing because one of the import or export flags is off, so the flags on both sides are checked first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a custom route from one peered VPC network is not automatically visible in the other, which two settings must line up, and one limit or tradeoff of exchanging custom routes.
lessons.modelAnswer: Subnet routes are shared over a peering by default, but custom routes such as static routes or routes learned through Cloud Router are not, because the owner may want to keep them private. Each side of the peering has its own import and export switches. The network that owns the route must turn on export, and the network that needs the route must turn on import, so both settings have to line up. The tradeoff is that every custom route you export is visible to the peer, so you should export only the ranges the peer actually needs. Also, the peering does not carry routes through to a third network, so a route that is exported over one peering will not reach a network further along the chain. When traffic misbehaves, check both sides' flags before looking at firewalls.
rubricPoints: Custom routes are not exchanged over peering by default, unlike subnet routes.
Export on the owning network and import on the receiving network must both be enabled.
Exporting shares every custom route, so only needed ranges should be exported.
Peering does not pass routes through to a third network.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which route a packet actually takes between peered networks is the skill this objective tests, and the planned virtual network path tracer would practise it directly.

lessons.plain: Normally a cloud network decides where to send each packet by looking mainly at its destination, using a routing table. Policy-based routing adds rules that look at more than the destination, so you can send some traffic a different way based on where it comes from, which protocol it uses, or where it is going. For example, traffic from one group of servers can be sent through a particular inspection appliance first, while everything else follows the usual path. Think of a mail room that sends one department's letters through a scanner before normal delivery, but leaves all other mail alone.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your routing table sends all internet-bound traffic out through the default gateway, but the security team needs traffic from one application subnet to pass through a firewall appliance first. Could a normal destination-based route do this alone, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Policy-based routing means making forwarding decisions that look at more than the destination address. A normal route says that packets for a destination range go to a next hop, which is the device or address the packet is handed to next. A policy-based route adds matching conditions: if a packet's source range, destination range, and protocol fit the pattern, the packet goes to a chosen next hop, such as an internal load balancer that fronts a group of appliances. Each policy rule has a priority number, so when several rules could match, the network uses the one that ranks first.

Why it works: the network checks policy-based routes before it consults the ordinary routing table. If a packet matches a policy rule, that rule decides the next hop and the table is not used for that packet. If nothing matches, the normal table applies, so a policy route only changes the traffic it names.

Worked example: an application subnet 10.10.1.0/24 must send TCP traffic to any destination through an inspection appliance behind an internal load balancer at 10.20.0.100. Step 1: a packet from 10.10.1.5 to 203.0.113.9 on TCP port 443 reaches the decision point. Step 2: the source range matches 10.10.1.0/24, the protocol matches TCP, so the rule matches. Step 3: the next hop 10.20.0.100 is chosen, and the packet goes there instead of the default route. A UDP packet from the same subnet does not match, so it follows the normal table.

Common mistake: assuming that a rule matching outbound traffic also handles the replies. The return path is a separate decision and must be matched too, or the connection becomes asymmetric and breaks. A second mistake is giving a broad rule a higher priority than a specific one, so the broad rule captures traffic the specific rule was meant to handle.

Consequence: a misordered or overly broad rule silently sends production traffic through the appliance, adding latency or dropping sessions, and it often looks like an application outage rather than a routing change. Policy routes are a narrow override, so keep them specific, ordered, and checked in both directions.

questions.prompt: An office network uses subnet 192.168.40.0/24 for staff laptops. DNS queries (UDP port 53) from that subnet must go through a DNS filter behind an internal load balancer at 10.50.0.20, while all other traffic uses the normal routes. Work through one packet. Step 1: a packet from 192.168.40.77 to 198.51.100.4 on UDP port 53 reaches the decision point. Step 2: the source range matches 192.168.40.0/24 and the protocol matches UDP, so the policy rule matches. Step 3: [missing]. Which completion is correct?
choices: The routing table is checked first, and the policy rule is applied only if the default route fails.
The reply packet is matched by the same rule automatically, so no second step is needed.
The packet is sent to 10.50.0.20 instead of following the default route.
The packet is dropped, because a policy rule that names a next hop cannot handle public destinations.
questions.why: When a policy rule matches, it sets the next hop and the ordinary routing table is not consulted for that packet, so the packet goes to 10.50.0.20.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a policy-based route?
choices: A static route that stays in the table permanently and never needs a next hop.
A route that looks only at the destination address and hands every matching packet to the default gateway.
A rule that replaces the subnet ranges of a VPC so that all traffic is inspected.
A rule that matches on source range, destination range, and protocol, and sends matching packets to a chosen next hop.
questions.why: A policy-based route adds matching conditions beyond the destination address and directs matching packets to a chosen next hop, which is the description in the fourth choice.

questions.prompt: A network has two policy rules. Rule A is broad: it matches all traffic from 10.30.0.0/16 to any destination and is ranked first. Rule B is specific: it matches TCP port 8080 from 10.30.5.0/24 to an inspection appliance and is ranked second. A TCP packet from 10.30.5.9 to port 8080 arrives. What happens?
choices: Rule B matches because it is more specific, so the packet goes to the appliance regardless of ranking.
Rule A matches first and sends the packet to its next hop, so the specific Rule B never applies to it.
Neither rule matches because the packet has a port number, so the normal table decides.
Both rules apply, and the packet is sent to both next hops in turn.
questions.why: Rules are checked in ranking order and the first match decides the next hop, so a broad rule ranked above a specific one captures the traffic the specific rule was meant to handle.

questions.prompt: A team configures a policy rule that sends outbound TCP traffic from 10.70.2.0/24 through an appliance behind an internal load balancer, but adds no rule for the replies. What is the most likely result?
choices: Increasing the priority of the outbound rule makes it cover the replies as well.
Replies may take a different path than the outbound packets, so the connection becomes asymmetric and can break.
Nothing breaks, because replies always follow the same policy rule as the outbound packets.
Replies always use the default route, so the connection works but the appliance is bypassed for inspection only.
questions.why: The return path is a separate forwarding decision, so unless it is matched too, the replies can leave by a different route and the session fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use policy-based routing instead of an ordinary route, and name one limit or tradeoff you would warn them about.
lessons.modelAnswer: Use policy-based routing when the destination alone cannot express what should happen, for example when traffic from one source range must pass through an inspection appliance while other traffic from the same network leaves normally. The rule matches on source range, destination range, and protocol, and it sends matching packets to a chosen next hop, such as an internal load balancer in front of the appliances. The tradeoff is that policy routes are checked ahead of the ordinary routing table, so they are easy to overuse and hard to notice when something breaks. A broad rule with a high priority can quietly capture traffic you did not intend. Before shipping one, I would confirm which rule a sample packet actually hits, check that the return path is handled, and test a flow from both sides.
rubricPoints: Policy-based routes match on more than destination, such as source range, destination range, and protocol.
They are checked before the ordinary routing table, and only the traffic they match is affected.
Each rule has a priority, and a broad rule can shadow a more specific one.
Return traffic needs its own handling, or connections become asymmetric and fail.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which rule a sample packet hits is the fastest way to build the ordering intuition this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A Network Connectivity Center hub is a central place where you plug in different networks so they can exchange routes with each other. Each network you plug in is called a spoke. There are three kinds. A VPC spoke is one of your own cloud networks. A hybrid spoke is a link to a network outside Google Cloud, such as an office or another data center. A producer spoke is a network run by a service provider, often Google itself, that your networks need to reach. Knowing which kind you are looking at tells you who owns the network, how it connects, and what routes it is allowed to share.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has a cloud network, an office network, and a network that a vendor runs for a managed database. All three plug into one hub. Which of these would you expect to be owned and operated by someone other than your team, and what might that change about how you connect to it?
lessons.teach:
A Network Connectivity Center hub is a central routing point. Each network attached to it is a spoke, and the hub shares routes among spokes so they can reach one another. The spoke type tells you what kind of network sits on the other end.

A VPC spoke is a Google Cloud VPC network, which can sit in your project or in another project in your organization. Routes between VPC spokes flow through the hub, so a hub is often used to join many VPCs without building a full mesh of pairwise links.

A hybrid spoke is a link to a network outside Google Cloud. In practice this means a Cloud VPN tunnel, a Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment, or a router appliance. Routes are learned over these links with dynamic routing, so the on-premises side advertises its prefixes and the hub learns them.

A producer spoke attaches a network owned by a service producer, such as the VPC behind a managed service, that your workloads need to reach. You usually do not own that network, so you treat it as a destination you consume rather than a place you deploy.

Worked example: a team has VPC A, VPC B, and an office connected by VPN. They add all three as spokes to one hub. Step one: label each spoke by type, so A and B are VPC spokes and the office is a hybrid spoke. Step two: confirm the routes the hub exchanges, so A should learn B's subnet routes and the office should learn both VPC subnets. Step three: test traffic from A to the office and check that it follows a learned route.

Common mistake: treating every spoke as interchangeable and assuming a hybrid link will automatically carry traffic to a producer network. Each spoke type exchanges routes differently, and the hub's routing settings decide what traffic actually flows.

Consequence: if a route is missing from the hub's table, traffic to that subnet fails even when both endpoints look healthy. The spoke type is the first clue for where to look.

questions.prompt: A retailer has a storefront VPC in project shop-prod and a warehouse VPC in project wh-prod, both in one organization. Its warehouse site connects to Google Cloud through a Cloud Interconnect VLAN attachment. A managed analytics database runs in a producer network the retailer consumes but does not own. All four networks are added as spokes to one hub. Step one: label each spoke by type, so the two project VPCs are VPC spokes, the warehouse site is a hybrid spoke, and the analytics network is a producer spoke. Step two: [missing]. Step three: test traffic from the storefront VPC to the warehouse site and confirm it follows a route the hub learned.
choices: Delete the producer spoke, since a producer network can only be reached directly and never through the hub.
Confirm the hub has learned the warehouse prefixes over the Interconnect attachment and that the two VPCs learn each other's subnet routes.
Relabel the warehouse Interconnect link as a VPC spoke, because Interconnect runs inside Google's network.
Assume the hybrid spoke will carry storefront traffic to the analytics database automatically, so no route check is needed.
questions.why: Step two is the route check: the hub must show the learned prefixes from the hybrid link and the VPC routes it shares, because routes decide what flows.

questions.prompt: Which spoke type fits a network owned by a service producer that your application must reach but that you never deploy into?
choices: A producer spoke
A hybrid spoke carried over a VPN tunnel
A VPC spoke you build and manage yourself
A VPC spoke in another project in your organization
questions.why: A producer spoke is the type for a producer-owned network you consume as a destination rather than deploy into.

questions.prompt: A company has an on-premises data center linked by Cloud VPN and two VPCs, dev-vpc and test-vpc, each in its own project. It adds all three to one hub. The data center team says its prefixes were advertised, but traffic from dev-vpc fails. Which check best fits the spoke-type clue?
choices: Relabel the data center as a producer spoke so the hub will route to it.
Check that the hub learned the data center prefixes over dynamic routing on the VPN link, since the data center is a hybrid spoke.
Confirm dev-vpc has a static route to every data center subnet and skip the hub entirely.
Delete test-vpc, because two VPC spokes in the same hub block traffic from each other.
questions.why: The data center is a hybrid spoke that learns routes dynamically, so the hub's learned routes for those prefixes are the first thing to verify.

questions.prompt: A team adds a managed service's producer network as a spoke and assumes the existing hybrid VPN spoke will carry its traffic. Traffic to that service fails even though both endpoints look healthy. What is the most useful first step?
choices: Rename the producer spoke to match the VPC naming pattern.
Look at the hub's routing table for a route to the producer network's destination, since a missing route makes traffic fail even when endpoints look healthy.
Add a second VPN tunnel so the hybrid spoke has more capacity.
Recreate the hybrid spoke as a VPC spoke so that routes flow through the hub.
questions.why: Since each spoke type exchanges routes differently and a missing hub route causes this failure, the hub's routing table is the place to check first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a VPC spoke, a hybrid spoke, and a producer spoke. Then name one limit or tradeoff you would check before attaching a producer spoke to a hub.
lessons.modelAnswer: A hub is a shared routing point, and each spoke is a network attached to it. A VPC spoke is one of our own VPC networks, so we control its subnets and routes and can share them through the hub. A hybrid spoke is a link to a network outside Google Cloud, like a VPN tunnel or Interconnect attachment, and its routes are learned dynamically over that link, so a failed link or a missing advertised prefix removes those routes. A producer spoke is a network owned by a service provider that we consume rather than manage. Before attaching one, I would check which routes the producer network is allowed to share and which of our subnets can reach it, since we do not control the producer side and a missing or filtered route will silently break access.
rubricPoints: VPC spoke is one of our own VPC networks whose subnet routes can be shared through the hub
Hybrid spoke is a link to an outside network, such as VPN or Interconnect, with routes learned dynamically
Producer spoke is a network owned by a service provider that we consume rather than control
A limit or tradeoff: route sharing and reachability for a producer spoke depend on settings we do not fully control

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right spoke type for a mixed-network scenario is an exam-style reasoning task that benefits most from working through a situation.

lessons.plain: A VPC network is your private, isolated network inside Google Cloud. Teams often need several of them to talk to each other, and the pattern of links between them is called the topology. A mesh links every network directly to every other network, so each pair has its own link. A star, also called hub-and-spoke, picks one central network as the hub and connects each other network, called a spoke, to that hub. A mesh is easy to picture, but the number of links grows quickly as you add networks. A hub has fewer links and one place to manage routing and security, but everything depends on that hub. Choosing between them is mostly a tradeoff between how many links you maintain and where traffic is forced to flow.
lessons.guessPrompt: Four offices each have their own network, and you want every office to reach every other office. Would you connect each pair directly or route everything through one central network, and what do you expect to become harder as you add a fifth office?
lessons.teach:
A topology is the pattern of links between networks. A full mesh connects every pair of networks directly, so with n networks you need n times (n minus 1) divided by 2 links. A hub-and-spoke, also called a star, connects each spoke only to one central hub, so you need n minus 1 links. VPC Network Peering is a direct private link between two VPC networks. Its key rule is that it is not transitive, meaning a route learned through one peering does not carry onward to a third network. Network Connectivity Center, often shortened to NCC, is a managed hub: you attach VPC networks to it as spokes, and it exchanges routes so spokes can reach each other through the hub.

Why it works: routing only follows links that exist. A peering gives routes between its two ends and nothing beyond them. A hub that passes traffic between spokes must be built to relay routes, and that relaying is the job of the hub service.

Worked example. Take four networks A, B, C and D. A full mesh built from peerings needs 6 peerings (4 times 3 divided by 2). A star built from peerings makes A the hub and peers B, C and D to A, which is 3 peerings. Now trace B sending to C. B sends to A over its peering. A knows a route to C, but the peering from B does not pass A's routes onward for B's traffic, so the packet is dropped. Rebuild the same four networks on a hub that relays routes between spokes: each network attaches once, and B to C works through the hub.

Common mistake: assuming a hub built from peerings gives full spoke-to-spoke reachability. The consequence in a running system is that connections simply time out with no clear error, and teams often check firewall rules first when the real gap is missing transitive routing.

A mesh gives direct paths with no central dependency but many links to maintain. A hub gives fewer links and one place for routing and policy, but the hub becomes a shared dependency for all cross-network traffic.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has seven VPC networks named Ledger, Depot, Route, Yard, Crane, Fleet and Port. Step 1: a full mesh built from peerings needs 7 times 6 divided by 2, which is 21 peerings. Step 2: a star built from peerings with Ledger as the hub needs 6 peerings, one from Ledger to each other network. Step 3: Fleet sends traffic to Port through the Ledger hub. Ledger knows a route to Port, but the peering from Fleet does not pass Ledger's routes onward, so the traffic is dropped. Missing step: state what the firm must change so that Fleet reaches Port through the hub, and name one thing it should not rely on as the fix.
choices: Attach all seven networks to Network Connectivity Center as spokes of one hub, so the hub relays routes between spokes. Do not rely on firewall rules as the fix.
Enable Private Google Access on Port so that Fleet can reach it over the peering.
Add a firewall rule allowing Fleet to reach Port, since the routing is already correct.
Keep the peerings and raise the priority of Ledger's routes, since the route to Port already exists in Ledger.
questions.why: A peering does not relay routes beyond its two ends, so the hub must be a managed relay such as Network Connectivity Center where each network attaches once as a spoke, and the firewall and route-priority options do not address the missing transitive routing.

questions.prompt: A campus has nine VPC networks and uses one hub-and-spoke layout where each network connects only to a central hub. How many links does this star layout need, counting each link once?
questions.why: A star connects each spoke only to the hub, so with nine networks there is one hub and eight spokes, giving n minus 1 equals 8 links.

questions.prompt: A team built a hub from VPC peerings. Two spoke networks cannot reach each other, and connections time out without an error message. The team has already confirmed the firewall rules allow the traffic. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The spoke networks use overlapping subnet ranges that must be renamed.
The hub has too many peerings and has hit a quota limit that drops packets silently.
The peerings are not transitive, so a spoke's routes are not carried through the hub to another spoke.
The peerings lack a route to the hub's public address range.
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so routes learned through one peering do not pass onward, and this produces silent timeouts even when firewall rules are correct.

questions.prompt: A company is choosing between a full mesh of direct links among its networks and a central hub that relays traffic between them. Which statement correctly describes the trade-off?
choices: A mesh needs fewer links to maintain, but every cross-network path depends on a single hub.
A hub removes the need for any routing, so spokes never need route exchange.
A mesh gives direct paths with no central dependency, but it requires many more links to maintain.
A hub gives direct paths between every pair of networks, so it always has more links than a mesh.
questions.why: A mesh gives direct paths without a central dependency but many links to maintain, while a hub gives fewer links and one place for routing and policy at the cost of being a shared dependency for cross-network traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a hub built only from VPC peerings does not let two spoke networks reach each other, and name one tradeoff between a full mesh and a hub-and-spoke design.
lessons.modelAnswer: VPC peering is a direct link between exactly two networks, and it is not transitive. If spoke B peers with hub A and spoke C peers with hub A, A can see both, but B's traffic does not get relayed through A to C, so B and C cannot reach each other over those peerings. To get spoke-to-spoke reachability you need a hub that actually relays routes between attachments, such as NCC with VPC spokes, or you need direct peerings between every pair of spokes, which is a mesh. The tradeoff is that a full mesh has direct paths and no central dependency, but the number of links grows with n times (n minus 1) over 2 and each one needs its own configuration. A hub has far fewer links and one place to manage routing and policy, but it becomes a shared point that all cross-network traffic depends on.
rubricPoints: Peering is a direct link between two networks and is not transitive, so routes do not pass through a hub
A hub that relays routes between spokes, such as NCC, is needed for spoke-to-spoke reachability
A full mesh needs n times (n minus 1) over 2 links and grows quickly
A hub-and-spoke design has fewer links but makes the hub a shared dependency

suggested.rationale: No listed mission builds a VPC topology, and explaining the non-transitive peering rule and its tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Private NAT lets a cloud network reach private destinations, such as machines in an office data center or another private network, while presenting a chosen set of internal addresses in place of the real ones. Private Service Connect gives your network a private address inside your own network that leads to a service, so the traffic never has to cross the public internet. Configuring either one well means two things: the addresses involved must be reachable from the other side, and the routing system must be told to share them. Think of a building with a private side entrance. The door exists, but other networks only find it if the directions are passed on to them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your on-premises data center needs to call a service that you reach through a private address inside your cloud network. Besides the service existing and the address being assigned, what do you think must be true before the data center's routers can send packets to that address?
lessons.teach:
Private NAT is a form of network address translation, which means rewriting the source address of packets as they pass through a gateway, so the receiving side sees a different address from the real one. In the private form, the translation happens between private networks rather than out to the internet. You give it a dedicated range of addresses, and those addresses are what the far side sees as the source. Private Service Connect, often shortened to PSC, creates an endpoint: a private IP address in your network that forwards traffic to a published service, whether a Google API or a service owned by another team or company.

Why it works: a private address only helps if the routers on both sides know how to reach it. The endpoint address is a route, and routes are shared through a routing protocol or a configured export list. Propagation means that route being advertised to other networks. If the export is not configured, the endpoint works from inside your own network but remains invisible to the on-premises side.

Worked example. An on-premises network uses 10.50.0.0/16. A PSC endpoint in your VPC has the address 10.10.5.7. Step 1: the endpoint is created and the service connection is accepted. Step 2: the Cloud Router that connects to the on-premises network is configured to advertise the endpoint address, usually as a single /32 route. Step 3: the on-premises router learns 10.10.5.7 and sends traffic toward it. Step 4: if Private NAT is also used, the source addresses from 10.50.0.0/16 are translated into the NAT range before reaching the service, so the service's replies return to that range.

Common mistake: assuming that because the endpoint works inside the VPC, the on-premises side can already reach it. Consequence in a running system: packets leave the data center, reach nothing that knows how to answer, and time out, which often looks like a firewall problem when the real fault is a missing route advertisement.

questions.prompt: A payments firm runs an on-premises network on 172.20.0.0/16. It needs to call a partner's reporting service through a Private Service Connect endpoint with the private address 10.40.7.3 in its VPC. The steps are: (1) the endpoint is created and the partner accepts the service connection; (2) Private NAT rewrites on-premises sources from 172.20.0.0/16 into the dedicated range 192.168.50.0/28 before they reach the partner; (3) Step missing here; (4) the on-premises router learns 10.40.7.3 and sends traffic toward it. What belongs in step 3?
choices: Configure the Cloud Router to advertise the endpoint address 10.40.7.3/32 to the on-premises network.
Peer the firm's VPC directly with the partner's VPC so the endpoint becomes a shared subnet.
Increase the NAT range to a /24 so the partner's replies have more addresses to return to.
Add a firewall rule on the partner side allowing 172.20.0.0/16 on port 443.
questions.why: The on-premises router can only learn the endpoint if the Cloud Router advertises the endpoint's /32 route to it, which is the propagation step that is missing.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does Private NAT do to the source address of a packet that passes through it between private networks?
choices: It rewrites the source address into a dedicated range so the far side sees that range instead of the real address.
It hides the destination address so that the receiving service cannot see which client sent the request.
It copies the source address into a log entry and then forwards the packet unchanged.
It assigns a public internet address to each on-premises host so that the service can reply over the internet.
questions.why: Private NAT rewrites the source address to an address from its own dedicated range, which is what the receiving side sees.

questions.prompt: A team's VM in the VPC reaches a Private Service Connect endpoint without trouble. An on-premises application to the same endpoint times out. The endpoint is healthy and the service connection is accepted. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The VM's subnet is too large and the endpoint is rejecting its traffic for that reason.
The NAT range was set to a public address, which the service blocks by design.
The on-premises application is using the wrong port number on its outgoing requests.
The endpoint's /32 route was never advertised to the on-premises network, so the on-premises side does not know how to reach it.
questions.why: The endpoint works inside the VPC but stays invisible to the on-premises side until its route is advertised, so the on-premises traffic has nowhere to go and times out.

questions.prompt: A company wants a managed service to reply to on-premises clients without renumbering its on-premises network. Which configuration achieves this?
choices: Advertise the on-premises range to the service's network through a public internet gateway.
Disable route advertisement and rely on the VM's internal address being copied into the service's logs.
Change the on-premises addresses to match the endpoint range so that no translation is needed at all.
Keep the on-premises subnet unchanged and configure Private NAT with a dedicated range so the service sees that range as the source.
questions.why: Private NAT lets the on-premises addresses stay as they are, because the service only ever sees the dedicated NAT range as the source and replies return there.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Private NAT differs from a Private Service Connect endpoint, and what must be configured so that an on-premises network can actually use a PSC endpoint address. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you describe.
lessons.modelAnswer: Private NAT rewrites source addresses when traffic crosses between private networks, so the far side sees a chosen NAT range instead of the real internal addresses. A PSC endpoint is different: it is a private address in our own network that leads to a service, and it is a route that other networks only learn if we export it. So for on-premises systems to reach the endpoint, the Cloud Router that connects them must advertise the endpoint address, and the on-premises routers must accept it. The tradeoff is that NAT hides the original source addresses, so the service's logs show only the translated range, and we must size that range to handle the number of connections we expect.
rubricPoints: Private NAT translates source addresses between private networks using a dedicated range.
A PSC endpoint is a private address that reaches a service and is a route that must be shared.
Propagation requires explicitly advertising or exporting the endpoint route to the other network.
Tradeoff: NAT hides original source addresses and needs enough translated addresses for the traffic.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path from an on-premises source to a PSC endpoint address would show directly whether the route was propagated and where packets stop.

lessons.plain: A hub is a central place that connects several private networks, and each network attached to it is called a spoke. When the hub shares routes between spokes, it can share everything or only selected address ranges. An IP/CIDR range filter is a list of address blocks you write down. Only routes that fall inside the list are passed along, and everything else is held back. Think of a receptionist who forwards calls only to departments on an approved list. Getting the list right decides which networks can reach which. A list that is too narrow silently cuts off traffic, and one that is too wide exposes networks that should stay separate.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your hub's filter allows only the block 10.10.0.0/24. A spoke advertises 10.10.0.0/16, which is a larger block that contains that /24. Do you expect the /16 to be shared? Explain your reasoning.
lessons.teach:
Network Connectivity Center, often shortened to NCC, is the Google Cloud service that acts as a hub. Each network or connection attached to it is a spoke. Two spoke types you will meet are VPC spokes, which are Google Cloud virtual networks, and hybrid spokes, which link to networks outside Google Cloud. A route is an entry that tells a network which destination it should send traffic to. A CIDR block is an address range written as a starting address and a prefix length, such as 10.10.0.0/16. A larger prefix length means a smaller block, so /24 is smaller than /16. An IP/CIDR range filter is a list of these blocks that the hub uses to decide which routes it accepts or shares.

Why it works: a route passes the filter when its block sits inside an allowed block. The /24 sits inside the /16, so an allowed /16 would cover it. But a /16 does not sit inside a /24, so an allowed /24 never lets a /16 through.

Worked example: spoke A advertises 10.10.0.0/16 and 10.20.0.0/16. The hub filter allows only 10.10.0.0/16. Step 1: check 10.10.0.0/16 against the list. It is an exact match, so it is shared with spoke B. Step 2: check 10.20.0.0/16. It is not inside any allowed block, so it is held back. Spoke B learns only the first range.

Common mistake: writing a narrow list, such as one /24 taken from a larger subnet, and expecting the whole subnet to be reachable. Consequence: traffic to the unlisted addresses has no matching route on the receiving side, so it fails, or it follows a default route to an unexpected place. A filter that looks right on paper can still break traffic, so the route table on the receiving spoke is the real proof that the change worked.

questions.prompt: A company has a hub whose filter allows only 192.168.0.0/22. Spoke C advertises three ranges: 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24, and 192.168.0.0/21. Step 1: 192.168.1.0/24 lies entirely inside the allowed /22, so it is shared. Step 2: 192.168.2.0/24 also lies entirely inside the allowed /22, so it is shared. Step 3, which you complete: decide whether 192.168.0.0/21 is shared or held back.
choices: Held back, because a /21 is larger than the allowed /22 and cannot lie inside it
Held back, because a hub filter only accepts /24 blocks or smaller
Shared, because the filter only checks the first address of each advertised block
Shared, because it starts at 192.168.0.0, the same first address as the allowed block
questions.why: A route passes only when its whole block lies inside an allowed block, and the /21 covers twice the addresses of the /22, so it cannot fit inside it.

questions.prompt: In a Network Connectivity Center hub filter, what must be true for an advertised route to be shared with another spoke?
choices: Its starting address appears somewhere in the filter list
Its prefix length matches the prefix length of some allowed block
The spoke that advertised it is named in the filter list
Its whole block lies inside one allowed block in the filter
questions.why: The filter test is containment: the route's entire address block must sit inside a single allowed block, not merely share a starting address or prefix length.

questions.prompt: The hub filter allows only 172.20.4.0/23. Spoke D advertises 172.20.4.0/24, 172.20.5.0/24, and 172.20.6.0/24. How many of these routes are shared with other spokes?
choices: Three, because all three routes share the 172.20 prefix
Zero, because a /23 filter cannot match any /24 route
One, because only the first listed route is checked
questions.why: The /23 covers 172.20.4.0 through 172.20.5.255, so the first two /24 routes fit inside it while 172.20.6.0/24 falls outside and is held back.

questions.prompt: A team has just edited the hub filter on a live network. Which check is the best proof that traffic will now flow as intended?
choices: Confirming that the filter change saved without an error message
Pinging an address from the hub itself
Looking at the route table on the receiving spoke to see which routes it now has
Confirming that the filter list has the same number of entries as before
questions.why: The receiving spoke's route table shows what it actually learned, which is the real result of the filter, whereas a saved file or a hub-side test does not prove the routes arrived.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an IP/CIDR range filter on a Network Connectivity Center spoke controls, and name one limit or tradeoff of making the filter too narrow and one of making it too broad.
lessons.modelAnswer: An IP/CIDR range filter is a list of address blocks that decides which routes a spoke's network exchanges through the hub. A route is passed only if its block sits inside one of the allowed blocks, so the filter controls which networks can reach which. The main tradeoff is between safety and reachability. If the list is too narrow, some subnets are never shared, traffic to them has no route, and the failure can look like a firewall or application fault even though the filter is the cause. If the list is too broad, networks that should be isolated can learn routes to each other, which weakens separation. Before trusting a change, I check the receiving spoke's route table, because the filter is only correct if the expected routes actually appear there.
rubricPoints: Defines the filter as a list of CIDR blocks that decides which routes pass through the hub
Explains that a route passes only when it sits inside an allowed block
Names the narrow-list tradeoff: unreachable subnets and silent route gaps
Names the broad-list tradeoff: unintended reachability between networks that should stay separate
Says to verify the result in the receiving route table

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises hub route filters directly, so the learner should read the configuration steps and fields for the spoke type first.

lessons.plain: Network Connectivity Center is a way to keep track of the many private networks a company links together, such as its cloud networks, its office networks, and networks run by other providers, all from one central place. Think of it as a traffic control room for a city: each connection is a road, and the room can see which roads are open, which routes traffic is taking, and where a jam is forming. Monitoring means watching those connections over time. Troubleshooting means working out why two machines on different networks cannot reach each other and which link in the chain is at fault.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose one of your company's cloud networks and one of its office networks can no longer talk to each other, but both still reach the internet normally. Before we teach anything, list three things you would check first to find which link in the chain broke, and say briefly why each would help.
lessons.teach: A hub is the central object in Network Connectivity Center. A spoke is a network connection attached to that hub. A VPC spoke wraps a cloud network, a hybrid spoke wraps a link to an on-premises or other-cloud network, and a producer spoke wraps a network that a managed service provider runs for you. The hub shares routes between spokes, so a machine in one spoke can learn a path to a subnet in another. Routes a spoke has learned appear in the hub's route table, and each entry records which spoke it came from and whether it was accepted. Two things can block a path even when the spoke looks healthy: the far side never advertised the route, or an import or export filter dropped it. Monitoring shows the spoke state and route counts over time. A connectivity test is a path analysis tool that simulates a packet between two endpoints and reports where it is delivered or dropped. Worked example: a hybrid spoke to an office network shows ACTIVE, but a VM in a VPC spoke cannot reach 10.20.0.0/16 in the office. Step one, check the spoke state: ACTIVE, so the attachment is up. Step two, look in the hub route table for 10.20.0.0/16: it is missing, so the link is up but no route arrived. Step three, check whether the office router advertises that range and whether the spoke's import filter excludes it: the filter's range is too narrow, so the route is dropped. Widening the filter restores the route, and a connectivity test from the VM then reports delivery. Common mistake: treating ACTIVE as proof of reachability. An active spoke only means the attachment works; it says nothing about which routes arrived. Consequence: traffic to a missing route either fails outright or falls back to a default path such as the internet, which can leak data or cause timeouts that look like application bugs. Confirm that the routes arrived before blaming the application.

questions.prompt: A retail company has a VPC spoke with subnet 10.40.0.0/20 and a hybrid spoke to its warehouse network, which owns 172.16.8.0/22. A VM in the VPC spoke cannot reach 172.16.8.10. Step one: the warehouse hybrid spoke shows ACTIVE, so the attachment is up. Step two: the hub route table has no entry for 172.16.8.0/22, so no route arrived from that spoke. Step three is missing. Step four: after the warehouse side is corrected, the route appears in the hub table and a connectivity test from the VM reports delivery. What is the missing step three?
choices: Widen the spoke's import filter to include the range
Check whether the warehouse side advertises 172.16.8.0/22
Recreate the VM so it picks up new routes
Check the VM's machine type for network limits
questions.why: A route that never arrived cannot have been dropped by a filter, so the next check is whether the far side advertises the range at all.

questions.prompt: What does a route entry in a hub's route table record?
choices: The IP address of the VM that will use the route
Which spoke it came from and whether it was accepted
The monitoring graph on which the route's count is shown
Only the destination range it covers, with nothing about its origin
questions.why: Each hub route table entry records the spoke it was learned from and whether it was accepted, which is what makes it useful for diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A hybrid spoke shows ACTIVE, but monitoring shows its route count has been zero since it was created. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The far side never advertised routes, or a filter dropped them
The hub is out of quota for VPC networks
The VM's operating system is out of date
The spoke is not attached to the hub
questions.why: ACTIVE only shows the attachment works; zero routes points to the far side not advertising or an import or export filter dropping them.

questions.prompt: A team says connectivity is fine because every spoke is ACTIVE and the route-count graphs look flat. An app in one VPC spoke times out reaching a subnet in another VPC spoke. What should they check first?
choices: Whether the monitoring dashboard refresh interval is short
Whether the VM can be rebooted safely
Whether the app's connection pool size is large enough
Whether the destination subnet's route appears in the hub route table
questions.why: Since an active spoke says nothing about which routes arrived, confirming the destination route is in the hub route table is the first diagnostic step before blaming the application.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a hybrid spoke is broken or whether a route is simply missing, and name one limit of the check you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by separating two questions: is the attachment up, and did the routes I need arrive. The spoke state tells me the attachment is up, but it does not tell me the routes are there. So I check the hub's route table for the destination range and see whether it was learned from that spoke. If it is missing, I look at the other side: is the on-premises router actually advertising that range, and does an import or export filter on the spoke drop it? If the route is present, I run a connectivity test from the source to the destination, which shows where the packet stops. One limit: a route table and a connectivity test describe the network path, not the firewall rules on the destination or the application listening there, so a passing test does not prove the service works.
rubricPoints: Spoke state shows the attachment is up but says nothing about which routes arrived.
Check the hub route table for the destination range and which spoke it was learned from.
Check whether the far side advertises the range and whether an import or export filter drops it.
Use a connectivity test to see where a packet is delivered or dropped.
Name the limit: path tests do not prove firewall rules or the application are correct.

suggested.rationale: The planned virtual network path tracer would let the learner walk a path hop by hop, which is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: When you run containers on Google's managed Kubernetes service, each small group of containers, called a pod, needs its own network address. A VPC-native cluster takes those pod addresses from ranges you reserved inside your virtual private network, the same way a machine takes an address from its subnet. Other machines in that network can then reach a pod directly, without translation tricks or hand-made routes. The trade-off is that you must plan how many addresses you reserve before you build the cluster.
lessons.guessPrompt: If every pod needs its own IP address, should those addresses come from the same block as the machines' addresses, or from a separate reserved block, and why could that choice run out with 500 machines?
lessons.teach:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your private network in Google Cloud. A subnet is a block of addresses inside one region of that network. A CIDR block is shorthand for an address range: /24 means 256 addresses, /14 means 262,144. A subnet can have a primary range, which its machines use, and named secondary ranges, which are extra blocks reserved for other uses. A node is a virtual machine that runs pods. A pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, holding one or more containers. An alias IP is an extra address attached to a node's network interface, so the node can answer for more than one address. A Service range holds the virtual addresses Kubernetes uses to load-balance traffic to pods.

Why it works: in a VPC-native cluster, each node's interface receives alias IPs from the pod secondary range. The VPC already knows that those addresses sit behind that node, so traffic routes without extra custom routes.

Worked example. Suppose the subnet's primary range is 10.0.0.0/20 for nodes, the pod secondary range is 10.4.0.0/14, and the Service range is 10.8.0.0/20. Step 1: a node joins and gets 10.0.0.5 from the primary range. Step 2: the cluster gives that node a /24 slice of the pod range, 10.4.0.0/24, which holds 256 addresses, enough for the default limit of 110 pods per node. Step 3: the next node gets 10.4.1.0/24. Step 4: a pod on the first node gets 10.4.0.7 as an alias IP. The /14 pod range holds 1,024 slices of /24, so it supports about 1,024 nodes.

Common mistake: sizing the pod range for pods alone and forgetting that each node consumes a whole /24 slice, or choosing a range that overlaps another subnet or a peered network.

Consequence: when the pod range runs out, new nodes cannot receive a pod slice, and pending pods stay unscheduled until you add a range or resize the cluster.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a VPC-native GKE cluster. Its node subnet has primary range 10.20.0.0/22, and its pod secondary range is 10.60.0.0/16. Step 1: the first node joins and takes 10.20.0.4 from the primary range. Step 2: the cluster reserves 10.60.0.0/24 for that node's pods. Step 3: the next node receives 10.60.1.0/24. Step 4: the cluster keeps assigning one /24 slice per node in the same way. What is the largest number of nodes the pod range can support before it runs out?
choices: 65,536 nodes, one for each address in the /16
256 nodes, because a /16 holds 256 slices of /24
110 nodes, the default pod limit per node
254 nodes, because the first and last slice are reserved
questions.why: A /16 holds 65,536 addresses, and each node consumes a whole /24 slice of 256 addresses, so the range yields 256 slices and therefore supports 256 nodes.

questions.prompt: In a VPC-native GKE cluster, what does a node actually consume from the pod secondary range?
choices: The same addresses as its primary range, mirrored
One address per container inside each pod
A single /24 slice that the node's pods draw their alias IPs from
One alias IP for each pod it will ever run
questions.why: Each node is given a whole /24 slice from the pod range, and its pods receive alias IPs from that slice, so the node consumes the slice rather than individual addresses.

questions.prompt: A team has a pod secondary range of 172.16.0.0/20 and wants to run 30 nodes. What is the result?
choices: The cluster automatically splits the /20 into smaller slices so all 30 fit
Only 110 nodes can join, because of the default pod limit
All 30 nodes fit, because the /20 holds 4,096 addresses
The range holds only 16 /24 slices, so nodes beyond the sixteenth cannot get a pod slice and their pods stay unscheduled
questions.why: A /20 contains sixteen /24 slices, and each node needs one whole slice, so the range supports 16 nodes and pending pods appear once it is exhausted.

questions.prompt: A team's node subnet is 10.30.0.0/20 and its peered network uses 192.168.0.0/16. Which candidate pod secondary range is the mistake?
questions.why: 10.30.8.0/21 falls inside the node subnet 10.30.0.0/20, and overlapping another subnet is the common mistake in choosing a pod range, while the other three do not overlap either network.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the pod range and the Service range are in a VPC-native GKE cluster, and name one limit or tradeoff you must plan for before creating the cluster.
lessons.modelAnswer: In a VPC-native GKE cluster, pods and Services get addresses from named secondary ranges on the subnet, not from a separate overlay. The pod range is split so that each node gets a slice, usually a /24 with room for about 110 pods, and each pod's address is an alias IP on its node's interface, so the VPC routes pod traffic without custom routes. The Service range holds virtual addresses for load balancing. The main tradeoff is planning size up front: the pod range must hold one /24 slice per node you expect, so a /14 supports about 1,024 nodes. If you undersize it or overlap it with another network, new nodes cannot get pod addresses and pods stay pending.
rubricPoints: Pods and Services take addresses from secondary ranges on the subnet.
Each node gets a slice of the pod range, usually a /24, and pod IPs are alias IPs on the node.
Because the VPC knows these routes, pod traffic is routable without custom routes.
The pod range must be sized for the maximum node count, and overlaps with other networks cause failures.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers Kubernetes networking, and explaining range sizing and its tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill for this objective.

lessons.plain: A GKE cluster is a group of machines that runs containers for you, and GKE is Google's managed Kubernetes service that runs the cluster's control part for you. Shared VPC lets one project, the host, own a private network and lend its subnets to other projects, called service projects. Setting up a GKE cluster with Shared VPC means the cluster lives in a team's own project but is plugged into a network that a central networking team owns and controls. Most of the real work is not the cluster command itself. It is getting the permissions and the address ranges right so the cluster can use that shared network.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a product team needs a Kubernetes cluster, but a central networking team must own every IP address range, which project should the cluster be created in, and what could go wrong if the networking team's permissions are missing?
lessons.teach: Three terms first. A host project owns the Virtual Private Cloud network, which is a private network made of subnets, and it is where Shared VPC is switched on. A service project is attached to that host and may use some of its subnets. A GKE cluster has a control plane that makes decisions and nodes that run your workloads. Each Pod is a small group of containers that gets its own IP address, and each Service is a stable address in front of Pods. Pod and Service addresses come from secondary IP ranges, which are extra address blocks attached to a subnet and given names. The sequence works like this. The network administrator enables the host project and attaches the service project. Both projects enable the Kubernetes API. The subnet in the host gets two named secondary ranges, one for Pods and one for Services. The administrator then grants the service project's GKE service agent, which is the Google-managed identity that builds the cluster, the Kubernetes Host Service Agent User role on the host project, and grants network use on the shared subnet to that agent and to the project's Google APIs service account. Finally the cluster is created in the service project, pointing at the host network, the shared subnet, and the names of the Pod and Service ranges. Worked example: service project pay-svc, host net-host, subnet gke-subnet with primary range 10.20.0.0/20, Pod range named pods at 10.40.0.0/14, Service range named services at 10.44.0.0/20. Nodes take addresses from 10.20.0.0/20, and Pods take addresses from pods. Common mistake: skipping the service agent grant, so cluster creation fails with a permission error even though the subnet looks right. Consequence in a running system: if the shared subnet's primary range runs out, new nodes cannot start and autoscaling stalls, so address planning is part of the setup. Shared VPC keeps network control in one place, and the service project's cluster can only use what the host has granted.

questions.prompt: A retail team has a host project named shop-net-host and a service project named checkout-svc. The administrator has already enabled Shared VPC on the host and attached checkout-svc to it. Both projects have the Kubernetes API enabled. The subnet orders-subnet in the host has primary range 172.16.8.0/22, with two secondary ranges added: order-pods at 172.20.0.0/16 and order-svcs at 172.24.0.0/20. Next, the administrator grants the Kubernetes Host Service Agent User role on shop-net-host to the GKE service agent of checkout-svc. One step is still missing before the cluster is created in checkout-svc. Which step is it?
choices: Grant network use on orders-subnet to the GKE service agent and to the project's Google APIs service account
Move the Pod range into the primary range 172.16.8.0/22 so nodes and Pods share one block
Create the cluster in shop-net-host so the host can own its nodes
Rename orders-subnet so its name matches the service project
questions.why: The sequence requires network use on the shared subnet to be granted to both the GKE service agent and the project's Google APIs service account, and that grant has not yet been made in this scenario.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a secondary IP range in a GKE Shared VPC setup?
choices: A second subnet created in a different region for backup traffic
An extra named address block attached to a subnet and used for Pod or Service addresses
A firewall rule that permits Pod-to-Pod traffic inside the cluster
A public IP address reserved for a load balancer in front of the cluster
questions.why: A secondary range is an additional address block attached to a subnet and given a name, which GKE then uses for Pod or Service addresses.

questions.prompt: A team creates a GKE cluster in service project ledger-svc on a shared subnet ledger-subnet. Node scale-up stalls, and the logs show that new nodes cannot get an address, while the Pod secondary range still has many free addresses. Which range should the administrator check first?
choices: The Pod secondary range, because a full range always blocks nodes
The Service secondary range, because it controls node startup
The host project's firewall rules, because they block new nodes
The subnet's primary range, because nodes take their addresses from it
questions.why: Nodes take addresses from the subnet's primary range, so when that range runs out new nodes cannot start even if the Pod range still has room.

questions.prompt: The host project northwind-host owns a subnet app-subnet with primary range 10.60.0.0/22, and a service project app-svc will host a GKE cluster on it. Which setup correctly gives Pods their own addresses from the shared subnet?
choices: Set the cluster's Pod range to the primary range 10.60.0.0/22 so nodes and Pods share it
Add a secondary range to app-subnet for Pods, then name that range when creating the cluster in app-svc
Skip secondary ranges and rely on the Service agent to hand out Pod addresses automatically
Create the cluster in northwind-host and let the host assign Pod addresses from its own project
questions.why: Pods draw addresses from a named secondary range attached to the shared subnet, and that name must be given when the cluster is created in the service project.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a GKE cluster in a service project gets its network from a host project, naming the Pod and Service ranges and one limit or tradeoff of this setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: The host project owns the VPC and its subnets, and the service project is attached to it so its cluster can use those subnets. When we create the cluster in the service project, we point it at the host network and the shared subnet, and we name the secondary ranges that hold Pod and Service addresses. Before that works, the host admin has to grant the GKE service agent and the project's Google APIs service account network access on that subnet, and the Kubernetes Host Service Agent User role on the host project. The tradeoff is that the networking team controls the address space, so if the subnet or secondary ranges run short, teams cannot grow their clusters until the network owner expands them. That is why I plan the ranges before creating any cluster.
rubricPoints: The cluster is created in the service project but uses a network and subnet owned by the host project.
Pod and Service addresses come from named secondary ranges on the shared subnet.
The GKE service agent and Google APIs service account need network and host-role permissions before creation succeeds.
A tradeoff exists: central control of address space can block cluster growth if ranges run out.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers GKE networking, and explaining the split of host and service project responsibilities is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: A private GKE cluster is a Kubernetes cluster where the machines that run your containers, called nodes, have no public addresses, so the open internet cannot reach them directly. Kubernetes also has a managing part called the control plane, which accepts commands like deploy this app. A private control plane endpoint means that managing part can be reached only through private network addresses rather than from anywhere on the internet. Think of an office building with no public front door: people inside can still do their work, but outsiders need an approved entrance. The aim is to shrink what the internet can touch while the cluster keeps working.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a cluster's worker machines have no public IP addresses. Why might they still need some outbound path to the internet, and what would you expect to fail if they had none?
lessons.teach:
A private GKE cluster is a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster whose nodes, the virtual machines that run your containers, have only internal IP addresses. Its control plane, the component that schedules workloads and answers kubectl commands, runs in a Google-managed network. A private endpoint is the address you use to reach that control plane, and it is internal, so only traffic inside your VPC network, or networks connected to it, can reach it. The link between your VPC and Google's control plane network is VPC Network Peering, and it needs a reserved block of addresses, a /28 range such as 172.16.0.0/28, that must not overlap any subnet you own.

Why it works: nodes without public IPs cannot be contacted from the internet, but they still need outbound access. Private Google Access lets them reach Google APIs, such as the registry that stores container images, over Google's network. Cloud NAT, a managed network address translation gateway, gives them outbound access to other internet hosts.

Worked example: your VPC has subnet 10.0.0.0/20 for nodes, and you reserve 172.16.0.0/28 for the control plane peering. You create the cluster with private nodes on, enable Private Google Access on the subnet, and attach a Cloud NAT gateway to a Cloud Router in the same region. A bastion VM in the same VPC can then run kubectl against the private endpoint.

Common mistake: choosing a control plane range that overlaps a subnet, or turning off the public endpoint before a working private path exists. You then lose the only way to manage the cluster.

Consequence: without outbound access, Pods stall in ImagePullBackOff because nodes cannot fetch images, and kubectl from a laptop times out.

A private cluster is only as reachable as the private paths you design for it.

questions.prompt: A retail company, Lumen Retail, builds a private GKE cluster in a VPC it owns. Their notes so far: step 1, create subnet 10.40.0.0/21 for the nodes. Step 2, reserve 172.20.5.0/28 as the control plane peering range, after confirming it overlaps no subnet. Step 3, create the cluster with private nodes turned on and the public endpoint still on for now. Step 4 is missing from the notes. Their nodes have no public IP addresses, and Pods are stuck pulling container images from Google's registry. Which step belongs in the missing slot?
choices: Turn off the public endpoint on the control plane
Widen the 172.20.5.0/28 range to a /24
Give every node a public IP address so it can reach the registry
Enable Private Google Access on subnet 10.40.0.0/21
questions.why: Private Google Access lets nodes without public IPs reach Google APIs such as the image registry over Google's network, which is the gap that causes the image pull stall here.

questions.prompt: A team's nodes have no public IP addresses, and they need to pull images from Google's container registry. Which setting lets those nodes reach Google APIs over Google's own network?
choices: Cloud NAT, used on its own with no Cloud Router in the region
Assigning a public IP address to each node
Private Google Access enabled on the node subnet
VPC Network Peering to the control plane range
questions.why: Private Google Access on the node subnet is the setting that gives private nodes a path to Google APIs without public addresses; the other options either add public exposure or do not serve Google APIs.

questions.prompt: An engineer picks 10.40.0.0/28 as the control plane peering range, but the VPC already has subnet 10.40.0.0/21 for nodes. What is wrong with this choice?
choices: A /28 range is too small to hold a control plane
The range overlaps a subnet the team owns, so the peering cannot be built correctly
Nothing is wrong, since the control plane range is kept separate from node subnets
The control plane range has to be a public address block
questions.why: The peering range must not overlap any subnet you own, and 10.40.0.0/28 sits inside 10.40.0.0/21, so the configuration fails on that rule rather than on size or visibility.

questions.prompt: A team turns off the public endpoint on their private cluster before any private path, such as a bastion VM in the VPC or a VPN, exists. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Nodes lose their outbound internet access and cannot run any workloads
The control plane is moved onto a public network automatically
Pods are evicted from every node immediately
The team loses the only way to run kubectl against the cluster until a private path is built
questions.why: With the public endpoint off and no private route in place, nothing can reach the control plane to manage it, which is the lockout the teaching text warns about.
