lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes a GKE cluster private, covering where the nodes and the control plane endpoint can be reached from, and name one tradeoff of turning off the public endpoint.
lessons.modelAnswer: A private GKE cluster gives its nodes internal IP addresses only, so they are not reachable from the internet. The control plane endpoint can be made private too, which means it is reached over the VPC network through a peering link to a Google-managed network. That link uses a reserved /28 block that must not overlap any of our subnets. Nodes still need outbound access, so we rely on Private Google Access for Google APIs and Cloud NAT for other internet hosts. The tradeoff of turning off the public endpoint is that engineers can no longer run kubectl from outside the network. They must come in through a bastion host, VPN, or Interconnect, so access depends on that private path working.
rubricPoints: Nodes have only internal IPs, so they are not directly reachable from the internet.
The control plane private endpoint is reached through VPC peering using a reserved non-overlapping /28 range.
Nodes need outbound access via Private Google Access and/or Cloud NAT to pull images and reach other services.
Turning off the public endpoint removes access from outside the private network, so a private path such as a bastion, VPN, or Interconnect is required.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which setting is wrong on a near-miss private cluster design builds the reasoning this objective needs more than a catalogue read would.

lessons.plain: A GKE cluster (Google's managed Kubernetes service, which runs containers across a group of machines) has a control plane, the front door where tools like kubectl send their requests. Its address is the control plane endpoint. Authorized networks is a short list of IP address ranges that you allow to reach that door. Anyone outside the list is refused before they can even try to log in. Think of it as a guest list checked at the building entrance, before the badge check, so a stolen key is less useful when it is used from an address you never allowed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's CI runner (an automated build machine) starts timing out when it runs kubectl against a cluster that worked yesterday. The only recent change is that someone added a list of allowed IP ranges to the cluster. Before any teaching, what would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
The control plane is the set of components that accepts API requests and decides what the cluster does. For a GKE cluster it is reachable at a control plane endpoint, a single IP address. An authorized network is a named IPv4 CIDR range, a block of addresses written like 203.0.113.0/24 where the number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed. When the feature is enabled, the endpoint accepts connections only when the source address falls inside one of the listed ranges.

Why it works: the check happens at the edge of the control plane, before authentication. A request from an unlisted address is refused, so someone holding a stolen credential still cannot reach the API from an unlisted network. Authorized networks narrows who can reach the door. It does not replace authentication, which still decides who you are once a request arrives.

Worked example. Your office egress address is 198.51.100.7. Step 1: you enter 198.51.100.7/32, which means exactly one address. Step 2: a laptop on home Wi-Fi, with a different address, is refused. Step 3: the office router later moves to the block 198.51.100.0/29, which includes .7 plus neighbours. Colleagues on the new addresses are now refused by the single /32, so you replace it with the whole block and schedule a review whenever the network changes.

Common mistake: adding only your own /32 to a shared pipeline. CI runners often leave through a shared NAT address or a cloud range, so the pipeline times out while your laptop still works. Whether this matters also depends on whether the endpoint is public or private, which is a separate setting you must check.

Consequence: a list that is too narrow breaks every automated client quietly. Deployments and dashboards stop reaching the API, and the failure looks like a network outage rather than a permissions problem.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs a GKE cluster whose control plane endpoint is set to public. Their office egress range is 192.0.2.64/26, which covers 64 addresses from 192.0.2.64 to 192.0.2.127. Step 1: the engineer enters 192.0.2.64/26 as an authorized network. Step 2: a contractor connecting from 192.0.2.200 is refused, which is expected because that address is outside the block. Step 3 is not shown. Which step completes the change?
choices: Remove the old authentication setting, because the authorized network list now replaces it
Add 0.0.0.0/0 so the endpoint accepts every address during testing
Restart every node pool so the new list is read at boot
Confirm the cluster's control plane endpoint is public, because the list is the access check that applies to it, and check that the endpoint setting matches what the team expects
questions.why: The teaching text says whether the list matters depends on whether the endpoint is public or private, which is a separate setting to check, and authorized networks only controls access to a public endpoint of this kind; the other choices either open access too widely, touch unrelated nodes, or wrongly treat the list as replacing authentication.

questions.prompt: In a CIDR block such as 203.0.113.0/27, what does the number after the slash tell you?
choices: The number of client machines allowed to connect at one time
The count of authentication tokens issued to that range
How many leading bits are fixed, so a larger number means a smaller range of addresses
The port number the control plane endpoint listens on
questions.why: The teaching text defines the number after the slash as how many leading bits are fixed, and a larger fixed count leaves fewer free bits and so a smaller block.

questions.prompt: An authorized network entry of 203.0.113.0/27 is the only entry on a GKE control plane endpoint. Which source address is refused?
questions.why: The /27 block covers 203.0.113.0 through 203.0.113.31, so 203.0.113.32 falls outside it and is refused at the endpoint, while the other three addresses fall inside the block or in a different range.

questions.prompt: A data team adds only one engineer's workstation /32 to the authorized networks of a public GKE control plane endpoint. Their scheduled deployment runners, which leave through a shared cloud NAT address in a different range, start timing out while the engineer's laptop still works. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The deployment runners' source addresses are outside the list, so the endpoint refuses them before authentication is checked
A Kubernetes RBAC binding expired, which blocks the runners from reading cluster objects
The runners lack an IAM role, so the API rejects them after the connection is made
The authorized network list only applies to pods running inside the cluster, not to outside clients
questions.why: Authorized networks is checked at the edge of the control plane before authentication, so clients from unlisted addresses fail as network timeouts, and the other choices describe permission or scope problems the teaching text does not connect to this failure.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says authorized networks is just a password for the cluster, so we can drop our IAM setup. Explain to them, in your own words, what authorized networks does, what it does not do, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Authorized networks is an allowlist of source IP ranges that may reach the cluster's control plane endpoint. If a request comes from outside those ranges, it is refused before any login is checked, which cuts off exposure from everywhere else. It is not a password. It does not say who the caller is, so IAM and Kubernetes authentication still decide what an allowed client can do, and we keep both. The tradeoff is that the list is only as accurate as our knowledge of where traffic really comes from. Shared NAT addresses, changing office networks, and CI runners can all fall outside it, and then legitimate automation fails in a way that looks like a network outage. So we keep the ranges as narrow as the real sources allow, record who owns each one, and review them whenever our network changes.
rubricPoints: Authorized networks is an allowlist of source IP ranges for the control plane endpoint.
It filters by network source before authentication; it does not replace IAM or Kubernetes authentication.
A tradeoff is that a list that is too narrow silently breaks legitimate clients such as CI runners.
Ranges must be maintained as networks change, with the owner and the reason for each recorded.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a near-miss situation, such as a too-narrow /32 on a shared pipeline, adds the most to recognising the wrong setting, and no listed mission covers GKE.

lessons.plain: Every Kubernetes cluster on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) has a control plane, the management part that receives commands such as deploy this or scale that. Your tools reach it through an address called an endpoint. Traditionally that endpoint is a plain IP address, which can be awkward to allow through firewalls and to keep stable. A DNS-based endpoint gives the control plane a stable name instead, so people and tools connect by name and the network resolves that name to the right place. Access is still decided by who you are and what permissions you hold, not only by where you connect from. It is like calling a company by its published name instead of a changing extension number.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your laptop connects to a cluster by a name rather than a raw IP address, what do you think changes about how the cluster can move or be reached, and what still has to be checked before you are allowed in?
lessons.teach:
The control plane is the management layer of a GKE cluster. It runs the API server, which accepts requests from kubectl, the command-line tool, and from automation. An endpoint is the address a client uses to open a connection to that API server. A DNS name is a human-readable name, such as a hostname, that a DNS resolver turns into an IP address when a client asks for it. A DNS-based endpoint means the cluster's control plane is reached through such a name, and that name is kept stable even if the underlying address changes.

Why it works: the client stores the name in its kubeconfig file. Each time it connects, it resolves the name, opens a secure connection to the returned address, and then proves its identity. Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) checks whether that identity holds a permission on the cluster. The name is a way to find the service, not a way to grant access.

Worked example. A cluster has a DNS-based endpoint enabled. An engineer runs kubectl get pods. Step 1: kubectl reads the endpoint name from the kubeconfig. Step 2: the laptop's resolver turns the name into an address. Step 3: the request reaches the control plane over an encrypted connection. Step 4: IAM checks the engineer's credentials and role. Step 5: the API server answers with the pod list.

Common mistake: assuming the DNS name by itself secures the cluster, or assuming it is the same thing as a private cluster. The name only changes how the endpoint is found. Access still depends on IAM roles and on any other access controls you configure.

Consequence: if the client's DNS resolver cannot resolve the name, every command fails with a name resolution error even though the cluster is healthy. Check name resolution first when kubectl fails with an unknown host message.

questions.prompt: Redwater Logistics runs a build job that calls kubectl rollout status deployment/tracker against its cluster dispatch-east, which has a DNS-based endpoint. The job's steps are: 1) the job reads the endpoint name from the kubeconfig file its pipeline provided. 2) The build runner's DNS resolver turns that name into the control plane address. 3) [one step is missing here]. 4) The API server returns the rollout status to the job. Which step correctly fills the gap at step 3?
choices: The connection is encrypted, and then IAM checks whether the job's service account holds a permission on dispatch-east.
The kubeconfig file is rewritten with the new address before the request is sent.
The DNS name itself grants the job rollout rights, so no permission check happens.
The runner caches the resolved address and skips opening a connection to the control plane.
questions.why: After the secure connection opens, IAM checks the identity presented by the job against its permissions on the cluster, because the DNS name only helps find the service and does not grant access.

questions.prompt: A platform team at Kestrel Analytics changes the public IP address of their GKE control plane. Their DNS-based endpoint is enabled and their engineers' kubeconfig files were never edited. What happens to their kubectl commands?
choices: Commands keep working because the stored name still resolves to the current address.
Commands fail permanently because a DNS name cannot survive an address change.
Commands work only for the platform team, because the name is tied to their accounts.
Every command fails until each engineer rewrites the kubeconfig with the new IP address.
questions.why: A DNS-based endpoint keeps a stable name that a resolver maps to whatever address is current, so clients with an unchanged kubeconfig keep connecting.

questions.prompt: An engineer at Marlow Dental runs kubectl get nodes against the cluster smile-core and gets the message that the host is unknown. A colleague on a different network runs the same command successfully against the same healthy cluster. Which check should the engineer make first?
choices: Whether the cluster's node pool has enough CPU for the request.
Whether the engineer's IAM role was recently removed from the project.
Whether the API server has returned an error for this specific pod list.
Whether the engineer's own machine can resolve the endpoint name to an address.
questions.why: An unknown host message means the client could not turn the name into an address, so checking name resolution on the failing machine is the first step, and that is the choice with the correct logic here.

questions.prompt: A junior engineer at Tidewell Insurance tells the team that enabling a DNS-based endpoint on their cluster means anyone who knows the name cannot reach the API server without a valid identity. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Naming the endpoint in kubeconfig hides the cluster from unauthenticated users by default.
The DNS-based endpoint makes the cluster private, so only machines on the internal network can reach it.
The DNS name only changes how the endpoint is found, and IAM roles and other access controls still decide who may act.
The DNS name encrypts every request, so IAM checks are unnecessary for anyone who has the kubeconfig.
questions.why: The name is a way to find the service and not a way to grant access, so IAM and related controls still decide permissions, while the name by itself neither makes a cluster private nor secures it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a DNS-based endpoint for a GKE control plane changes compared with a traditional IP endpoint. Name one limit or tradeoff they should check before relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A traditional GKE endpoint is an IP address stored in the kubeconfig, so clients connect straight to that address. With a DNS-based endpoint, the kubeconfig holds a stable name, and the client resolves that name to reach the control plane. The benefit is that the name stays the same even if the underlying address changes, and tools do not need to be updated. The important tradeoff is that the name must resolve from wherever people connect. If a laptop, CI runner, or network has a resolver that cannot look up the name, commands fail even though the cluster is fine. Also, the name does not replace authentication: IAM permissions still decide who can do what. Before relying on it, I would check name resolution from each client location and confirm the IAM roles, not just the endpoint type.
rubricPoints: A DNS-based endpoint gives the control plane a stable name that clients resolve, instead of a fixed IP address.
The name only helps find the endpoint; IAM still controls which identities can access the cluster.
The name must resolve from every client network, or connections fail with name resolution errors.
It is distinct from a private cluster, which concerns where the control plane is reachable from.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console settings and endpoint facts that are best read first, and none of the listed missions or planned engines covers GKE access.

lessons.plain: GKE is Google's managed service for running containers, which are packaged apps that each get a small slice of a machine. Inside a GKE cluster, each container group, called a pod, gets its own network address and needs to reach other pods. Dataplane V2 is the part of the cluster that actually moves that traffic and decides which connections are allowed. You choose it when you build the cluster, and it gives you a modern traffic engine that also enforces the rules you write about which pods may talk to which. Think of it as the cluster's internal traffic officer, chosen at the start rather than swapped in later.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you build a cluster where pods are supposed to talk only to specific other pods, and you write the rules but never check which networking engine the cluster was built with, what do you think could happen to the rules?
lessons.teach:
Dataplane V2 is the networking engine inside a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. It forwards traffic between pods and services, and it enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects, which are rules saying which pods may connect to which. It is built on eBPF, a technique that lets small, verified programs run inside the Linux kernel so packets are handled efficiently. A node is one virtual machine in the cluster. A pod is one or more containers scheduled together on a node, and each pod gets an address from a range you assign.

Why it works: instead of relying on older per-node packet rules, Dataplane V2 handles service routing and policy enforcement in one data path. Every allowed or denied connection passes through the same place, so you can see both. It also expects a VPC-native cluster, meaning pods and services draw addresses from secondary ranges on a subnet of your VPC using alias IPs.

Worked example. You create a Standard cluster for a checkout service. Step 1: choose a VPC-native cluster and set a pod range and a service range. Step 2: enable Dataplane V2 in the cluster creation form. Step 3: create a NetworkPolicy that allows only pods labelled frontend to reach the payment pods on port 8080. Step 4: deploy everything. The engine checks each connection against the policy, so a test pod without the frontend label is refused.

Common mistake: treating Dataplane V2 as a switch you flip later on a running cluster, or turning on the older Calico network policy add-on alongside it. Dataplane V2 is chosen at creation and provides policy enforcement itself, so the two approaches conflict.

Consequence: on a cluster built without Dataplane V2 and without another enforcement method, NetworkPolicy objects are accepted but not enforced. Traffic that should be blocked flows freely, and nobody notices until an audit or an incident.

Dataplane V2 is a creation-time decision that determines how a GKE cluster forwards and filters pod traffic.

questions.prompt: A media company is building a GKE cluster for video transcoding. The platform engineer works through the setup in this order. Step 1: create a VPC-native cluster with pod range 10.40.0.0/16 and service range 10.80.0.0/20. Step 3: create a NetworkPolicy that allows only pods labelled role=encoder to reach the storage pods on port 9000. Step 4: deploy, then confirm that a test pod labelled role=batch is refused. Step 2 is missing from the notes. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Enable Dataplane V2 in the cluster creation form, before the cluster exists
Assign each pod an address from the node's own subnet instead of the pod range
Switch Dataplane V2 on later through the settings of the already running cluster
Turn on the Calico network policy add-on alongside the cluster so that it enforces the policy
questions.why: Dataplane V2 is chosen at creation time and is the engine that enforces NetworkPolicy, so Step 2 must enable it in the creation form, while the other three options either conflict with it, are done too late, or confuse pod addresses with node addresses.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy object do in a GKE cluster?
choices: It sets rules that decide which pods may connect to which
It sets the CPU limit that each pod is allowed to use
It assigns each node its external IP address
It stores the container images the cluster pulls at startup
questions.why: The teaching text defines a NetworkPolicy as a rule saying which pods may connect to which, so it is a connection rule, not an address, resource limit, or image store.

questions.prompt: A team builds a GKE cluster without Dataplane V2 and without any other enforcement method, then applies several NetworkPolicy objects. What is the most likely result?
choices: Dataplane V2 switches on automatically the first time a policy is saved
The policies are accepted but not enforced, so traffic that should be blocked still flows
The cluster refuses to start until the policies are removed
The policies are enforced only for pods on the first node in the cluster
questions.why: The teaching text states that without Dataplane V2 or another enforcement method, NetworkPolicy objects are accepted but not enforced, so blocked traffic flows freely.

questions.prompt: A platform engineer has a running GKE cluster built without Dataplane V2 and now needs pod traffic to be filtered by NetworkPolicy. Which approach fits the teaching text?
choices: Turn on the Calico add-on next to the existing setup so that both enforce the policies
Switch Dataplane V2 on in the settings page of the running cluster
Create a new cluster with Dataplane V2 enabled at creation and move the workloads to it
Edit the node pool labels so that the networking engine starts on the existing nodes
questions.why: Dataplane V2 is a creation-time decision and cannot be flipped on later, and combining it with Calico conflicts, so a new cluster built with Dataplane V2 is the correct route.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Dataplane V2 does for a GKE cluster, why it has to be chosen when the cluster is created, and one limit or tradeoff of choosing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Dataplane V2 is the networking engine for a GKE cluster. It forwards traffic between pods and services and enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules, using eBPF inside the Linux kernel. It is set when the cluster is created because the traffic path is built into the cluster from the start, so we cannot switch an existing cluster over with a simple toggle. We would build a new cluster and move workloads to it. The tradeoff is that it expects a VPC-native cluster, so we need to plan pod and service address ranges up front, and we should not run the older Calico network policy add-on at the same time. If we get the choice wrong, policies can look configured while nothing enforces them, so we check the cluster's setting before trusting the rules.
rubricPoints: Dataplane V2 is the GKE cluster's networking engine that forwards pod and service traffic and enforces NetworkPolicy rules.
It is chosen when the cluster is created and is not simply toggled later on a running cluster.
It expects a VPC-native cluster, so pod and service address ranges must be planned in advance.
Combining it with the Calico network policy add-on conflicts, and a cluster without enforcement silently ignores policies.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which cluster setting meets a policy requirement adds the most, since no listed mission builds a GKE cluster.

lessons.plain: When a program running inside a container in a Kubernetes cluster sends a message to a machine outside the cluster, the message carries the container's private address as its return address. That private address often means nothing outside the cluster. Source network address translation, usually called SNAT, is the trick of swapping that return address for the address of a machine the outside world can reach, the node the container runs on. IP masquerade is the common name for doing this automatically. This objective is about deciding which destinations get that swap and which keep the original address.
lessons.guessPrompt: A container with a private address inside a cluster sends a request to a server on your company's office network. Should the office server see the container's private address, or the address of the machine the container is running on? Why might the answer matter for the office firewall?
lessons.teach:
A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs; it wraps one or more containers and gets its own IP address, taken from a block called the Pod range. A node is a virtual machine in the cluster that hosts Pods. SNAT means rewriting the source address of a packet as it leaves a machine. IP masquerade is SNAT done automatically for outbound traffic, so the rest of the network sees the node's address instead of the Pod's. The reason this works is that a Pod address is usually meaningful only inside the cluster's network. A reply can only find its way back if the destination knows where to send it, and the node is the address the outside world already knows how to reach.

On GKE, the rules that decide which destinations are masqueraded are typically held in a cluster-level configuration object named ip-masq-agent in the kube-system namespace. Its key setting is a list of destination blocks, called nonMasqueradeCIDRs, that should keep the original Pod source address. Traffic to any destination not on that list is masqueraded.

Worked example. A Pod has address 10.8.0.5 and runs on node 10.0.0.3. It calls a database at 192.168.50.10 on the office network. Step one: the packet leaves the Pod with source 10.8.0.5. Step two: the agent checks the destination against the list. Step three: suppose 192.168.0.0/16 is on the list. The source stays 10.8.0.5, so the office firewall must allow the Pod range. If the block were not on the list, the source would be rewritten to 10.0.0.3, and the office firewall would need to allow the node instead.

Common mistake: editing the list and assuming the change is instant, or adding a destination without making sure the receiving firewall and routes accept the Pod range. The consequence in a running system is that a service can break silently. Requests succeed in one direction but replies are dropped or rules keyed on Pod addresses stop matching.

Masquerading is a per-destination decision, and the non-masquerade list is the control that sets it.

questions.prompt: A cluster gives Pods addresses from 172.20.0.0/14 and runs its nodes at 10.40.1.7 and 10.40.1.8. A Pod at 172.20.4.9 calls a partner API at 203.0.113.25. The cluster's non-masquerade list contains only 10.0.0.0/8, so 203.0.113.25 is not on it. Step one: the packet leaves the Pod with source 172.20.4.9. Step two: the agent sees that the destination is not on the list, so the source is rewritten. Step three: the partner's firewall must allow the source address it actually sees, which is ____. Fill in the missing step.
choices: 172.20.0.0/14, the whole Pod range
172.20.4.9, the Pod's own address
203.0.113.25, the partner's own address
10.40.1.7, the node the Pod runs on
questions.why: Because the destination is not on the non-masquerade list, the source is rewritten to the address of the node the Pod runs on, so that is the source the partner's firewall must allow.

questions.prompt: What does IP masquerade mean on GKE?
choices: Assigning a new Pod range to each node when it starts
Encrypting traffic between Pods on the same node
Hiding Pods from the cluster's internal DNS names
Rewriting the source address of outbound traffic to the node's address so the outside network sees the node
questions.why: IP masquerade is SNAT applied automatically to outbound traffic, so the outside network sees the node's address instead of the Pod's.

questions.prompt: A cluster's non-masquerade list does not include 198.51.100.0/24. A Pod calls a partner in that block, and the partner's firewall allows only the Pod range 172.20.0.0/14. What most likely happens?
choices: The cluster rejects the Pod's address at its edge before the packet leaves
The request keeps the Pod source address and is accepted because the Pod range is allowed
The request is masqueraded, the partner sees the node address, and the firewall drops it because the node address is not allowed
The partner replies directly to the Pod without any address rewrite
questions.why: A destination not on the non-masquerade list is masqueraded, so the partner sees the node address, which its firewall does not allow.

questions.prompt: Where are the rules that decide which destinations are masqueraded typically held on GKE?
choices: In a cluster-level configuration object named ip-masq-agent in the kube-system namespace
In environment variables set inside each Pod
In a route that points at the Pod range
In a firewall rule attached to each subnet
questions.why: The masquerade rules are typically held in the cluster-level ip-masq-agent configuration object in the kube-system namespace, as the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what SNAT and IP masquerading do for traffic leaving a GKE cluster, and name one tradeoff of keeping the Pod source address for a particular destination.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a Pod sends traffic outside the cluster, its source address is its private Pod IP, which the destination usually cannot route back to. IP masquerade rewrites that source to the node's address, so replies come back to the node, which then delivers them to the Pod. The cluster's ip-masq-agent configuration decides which destinations get this rewrite. The tradeoff of excluding a destination, so the Pod address is kept, is that the receiving side now sees real Pod addresses. That means its firewall and routes must accept the Pod range, and any rule that expects the node address will stop matching. Adding a destination to the list is cheap, but it moves responsibility to the far side's network rules.
rubricPoints: Defines SNAT as rewriting the source address and masquerade as doing it automatically
Explains why a Pod address often cannot be replied to from outside the cluster
Identifies the non-masquerade destination list as the per-destination control
States the tradeoff: keeping Pod addresses requires the receiver to accept the Pod range

suggested.rationale: A scenario where the learner decides which destinations keep the Pod address adds the most, since the skill is reasoning about the far side's firewall.

lessons.plain: A GKE network policy is a set of rules that controls which pods inside a Kubernetes cluster may talk to which other pods. GKE is Google Kubernetes Engine, the managed service that runs clusters of containers. A pod is the smallest unit a cluster runs, roughly one small running program with its own network address. By default, pods in a cluster can reach each other freely. A network policy picks out a group of pods using their labels, which are short tags attached to each pod, and then states which incoming and outgoing connections are allowed. It works like an internal firewall placed around a chosen group of pods, not around the whole network.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a web frontend and a database each run as pods in the same cluster, and you add a policy saying only the frontend pods may connect to the database pods. Before reading on, what do you think happens when an unrelated pod in that cluster tries to connect to the database?
lessons.teach:
A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is an object that selects pods and restricts their network traffic. A label is a key-value tag on a pod, and a selector is the part of the policy that matches pods by those labels. Ingress means traffic coming into the selected pods, and egress means traffic leaving them. Once any policy selects a pod for a direction, that pod is isolated in that direction: only connections matching an allow rule from some policy are permitted. Unselected pods remain open. Multiple policies that select the same pod combine as a union of allowed traffic; no policy can remove what another policy allows. Enforcement depends on the cluster's dataplane, the software layer that actually moves packets, so the cluster must support network policy, for example through GKE Dataplane V2.

Worked example: database pods carry the label role=db and a policy selects them for ingress. The rule allows traffic from pods labeled role=frontend on TCP port 5432. Step 1: a database pod is selected, so incoming traffic to it is now isolated. Step 2: a frontend pod opens a connection on port 5432, which matches the rule, so it is allowed. Step 3: an unrelated pod opens the same connection, matches no rule, and is dropped.

Common mistake: assuming a policy on the database also restricts what the database may send out. It does not, because the policy only lists ingress, and the database's egress stays open unless another policy selects it for egress.

In a running system, an ingress policy with no allow rules on a selected group cuts off all incoming traffic to those pods, which can take a service down at once.

questions.prompt: A team in a retail company's shop namespace runs cache pods labeled tier=cache. They apply one NetworkPolicy that selects those pods for ingress only, with one allow rule: traffic from pods labeled tier=api on TCP port 6379. Step 1: the cache pods are selected for ingress, so incoming connections to them are isolated and only matching allowed connections pass. Step 2: an api pod opens a connection to a cache pod on port 6379, which matches the rule, so it is allowed. Step 3: a cache pod then opens an outbound connection to a logging pod on port 514. What happens to that outbound connection, and why?
choices: It is allowed, because no policy selects the cache pods for egress, so their outbound direction is not isolated.
It is dropped, because the cache pod is isolated and every connection it makes must match an allow rule.
It is dropped, because the single allow rule covers all traffic on the cache pods regardless of direction.
It is allowed only if the logging pod carries the label tier=api, because labels control both directions.
questions.why: A pod is isolated only in the directions that some policy selects, and this policy selects only ingress, so the cache pod's egress stays open.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean for a pod to be isolated in one direction under a NetworkPolicy?
choices: The pod is moved to a separate node so that its traffic never shares a dataplane with other pods.
The pod's labels are hidden from other policies, so they cannot be used in selectors.
The pod cannot be reached by any pod in the cluster, in either direction, until a policy names it.
Only connections matching an allow rule from some policy that selects that pod in that direction are permitted.
questions.why: Isolation in a direction means that once a policy selects the pod for that direction, only traffic matching an allow rule from some selecting policy gets through.

questions.prompt: A ledger pod is selected for ingress by two different policies. Policy A allows ingress from pods labeled tier=web on TCP port 8080. Policy B allows ingress from pods labeled tier=monitor on TCP port 9100. A pod labeled tier=web opens a connection to the ledger pod on TCP port 9100. What happens?
choices: It is allowed, because a pod already allowed by one policy can use any port on that pod.
It is dropped, because the presence of two policies cancels out the allow rules of both.
It is allowed, because the two policies merge into one rule that accepts either label on either port.
It is dropped, because no single allow rule permits a tier=web pod on port 9100.
questions.why: Policies combine as a union, and each allow rule requires both the matching source label and the matching port, so the web pod on port 9100 matches neither rule.

questions.prompt: A team creates a NetworkPolicy that selects pods labeled app=reports for ingress and includes no allow rules. The cluster supports network policy. Which outcome is correct?
choices: Only traffic arriving from outside the cluster is cut off; traffic between pods is unaffected.
Nothing changes, because a policy with no rules is ignored by the dataplane.
Outbound traffic from the reports pods is cut off as well, because the policy isolates the whole pod.
All incoming traffic to the reports pods is dropped, while their outgoing traffic is unaffected.
questions.why: A selected pod is isolated for ingress, and with no allow rules nothing is permitted into it, while the policy says nothing about egress, which stays open.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a GKE network policy decides whether one pod can reach another, and name one limit or tradeoff of using network policies.
lessons.modelAnswer: A network policy selects pods by their labels and sets rules for incoming or outgoing traffic. If a pod is selected for ingress, only connections that match an allow rule from some policy get through; pods that no policy selects stay open by default. When several policies select the same pod, their allowed traffic is combined, so you cannot use a second policy to take away what the first one permits. The main limit is that the policy only works when the cluster's dataplane enforces it, such as GKE Dataplane V2. On a cluster without that support, the objects can be created and accepted yet do nothing, so a team can believe a database is protected when it is not. A tradeoff is that a rushed deny-all policy can break a service, so you should test the allowed paths before applying it to production pods.
rubricPoints: Pods are selected by labels, and selected pods become isolated for the directions the policy covers
Unselected pods stay open by default, and multiple policies combine as a union of allowed traffic
Enforcement requires a dataplane that supports network policy, so the cluster setup must be checked
A policy covers only the directions it lists, so ingress and egress must be considered separately

suggested.rationale: Choosing which pods a policy selects and predicting what a connection does is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, since no current OpsForge mission covers this.

lessons.plain: When you run containers on Google Cloud with GKE, each container group gets its own network address, and each service that groups them gets a stable address too. This objective is about setting aside two separate blocks of addresses inside your network for those two jobs, one for the groups that run the containers and one for the stable service addresses. If the blocks are too small or overlap each other or other networks, the cluster cannot grow or traffic goes to the wrong place. Think of it like planning house numbers on a street before the houses are built.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your cluster will run about 200 nodes, and each node can run up to 110 Pods by default. Roughly how big should the Pod address block be, and what goes wrong if you make it too small?
lessons.teach:
A VPC-native GKE cluster gives Pods IP addresses taken from your VPC, so they can talk to other VPC resources directly. This uses alias IP ranges, which are extra IPv4 ranges attached to a subnet. A subnet used by a cluster carries three kinds of range. The primary range gives addresses to the nodes, which are the virtual machines that run your containers. The Pod range is a secondary range for Pods, the smallest units that hold containers. The Service range is another secondary range for Services, the stable virtual addresses that front groups of Pods. The Pod range and Service range are separate pools. They must not overlap each other, the subnet primary range, or any other network you connect to.

Why it works: GKE gives each node a fixed block of Pod addresses, sized from the maximum number of Pods per node, which defaults to 110. A node that runs 110 Pods needs a /24 block of 256 addresses, so each node takes one /24 from the Pod range. The Pod range therefore sets the ceiling on how many nodes you can have. Service addresses are not handed out per node. The Service range only needs room for the Services you plan to create.

Worked example: you plan 200 nodes at the default of 110 Pods per node. Step 1: each node needs one /24. Step 2: 200 nodes need 200 blocks of /24. Step 3: a /16 range holds 256 blocks of /24, so a /16 Pod range fits. Step 4: a /24 Pod range holds only one block, so the second node could not get Pod addresses.

Common mistake: sizing the Pod range for the Pods you expect instead of the nodes you expect, or letting the Service range overlap the Pod range. Consequence: once the Pod range runs out, new nodes cannot get Pod blocks, new Pods stay pending, and the cluster stops growing even though CPU and memory are free.

A Pod range and a Service range are separate pools, and the Pod range must be sized for nodes times the per-node block.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm plans a VPC-native GKE cluster with 60 nodes at the default of 110 Pods per node. Each node takes one /24 block (a range of 256 addresses) from the Pod range. Step 1: each node needs one /24 block. Step 2: 60 nodes need 60 blocks. Step 3 is missing. Which completion finishes the sizing?
choices: Choose a /24 Pod range, because 60 is less than 256 so one block covers the nodes.
Choose a /18 Pod range, which holds 64 blocks of /24, enough for 60 nodes.
Choose a /20 Pod range, which holds 60 blocks of /24.
Choose a /19 Pod range, because 60 is close to 64, and a /19 holds 60 blocks.
questions.why: The smallest Pod range that holds 60 blocks of /24 is a /18, since a /18 contains 64 such blocks, while a /20 holds only 16 and a /19 holds only 32.

questions.prompt: In a VPC-native GKE cluster, which secondary range holds the stable virtual addresses that front groups of Pods?
choices: The Pod range
The Service range
The node range
The subnet primary range
questions.why: The Service range is the secondary range reserved for Services, which are the stable virtual addresses that front groups of Pods, while the Pod range holds Pod addresses and the primary range holds node addresses.

questions.prompt: A retail firm uses a subnet with a Pod range of 10.4.0.0/21 and plans 30 nodes at the default 110 Pods per node. Each node needs one /24 block, and a /21 holds 8 such blocks. What is the problem?
choices: The Service range is too small for 30 nodes.
Nothing is wrong, because a /21 has 2048 addresses, which covers 30 nodes times 110 Pods.
The primary range must match the Pod range exactly.
The Pod range is too small: a /21 holds only 8 blocks of /24, but 30 nodes need 30 blocks.
questions.why: The Pod range must hold one /24 block per node, so 30 nodes need 30 blocks, and a /21 holds only 8; counting total addresses instead of blocks is the near-miss that hides this shortfall.

questions.prompt: A healthcare group sets a Pod range of 172.16.0.0/16 and wants a Service range of 172.16.128.0/20 in the same VPC. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is allowed, as long as the Service range is smaller than the Pod range.
It is not allowed, because the Pod range and Service range must not overlap, and 172.16.128.0/20 sits inside 172.16.0.0/16.
It is allowed, because Services use no per-node blocks so they can share the Pod range.
It is allowed, as long as the subnet primary range is different from both.
questions.why: The Pod range and Service range are separate pools that must not overlap, and the /20 lies entirely within the /16, so the configuration is invalid regardless of size or the primary range.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the Pod range and the Service range are for, how you would size the Pod range before creating a cluster, and one limit or tradeoff you would have to plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Pod range is the pool of addresses GKE hands out to Pods. Each node takes a fixed block from it, sized by the maximum Pods per node. With the default of 110 Pods per node, each node uses a /24, so the Pod range limits how many nodes the cluster can ever have. Before creating the cluster, I would multiply the number of nodes I expect by the block size and pick a range that holds that with room to spare. The Service range is separate. It holds the stable virtual addresses for Services and only needs to fit the Services I plan to create. The tradeoff is that both ranges must be chosen up front and must not overlap the subnet primary range or any network we peer with. A range that is too small is hard to fix later without disruption, so I would rather size generously now than watch the cluster stall at its node limit.
rubricPoints: Pod range and Service range are separate secondary ranges on the subnet, and neither can overlap the primary range or other connected networks.
Each node takes a fixed Pod block based on max Pods per node, so the Pod range caps the node count.
Service range is sized by how many Services are needed, not by node count.
A too-small Pod range stalls scaling: new nodes cannot get Pod addresses and Pods stay pending.

suggested.rationale: Sizing and separating address ranges is best learned by reasoning through a planning scenario, and no listed mission covers VPC address planning yet.

lessons.plain: A Kubernetes cluster runs your containers in small units called Pods, and each Pod needs its own network address. On Google Cloud, those addresses come from a block of addresses reserved on your network. Over time a cluster can grow past the block it started with, or you may want a separate block for a group of machines. Deploying an additional Pod range means reserving another block of addresses and giving the cluster access to it, so new machines can host Pods without running out of room. Think of it like adding a new street of house numbers when the old street is full.
lessons.guessPrompt: A cluster is planned for 300 nodes, but its only Pod range holds enough slices for 256 nodes. Before any teaching, what do you expect happens to Pods on the 257th node, and why might that node's spare CPU and memory not help?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A node is a virtual machine that runs Pods. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules. A VPC-native cluster gives each Pod a real IP address from the network, using alias IPs, so Pod addresses come from secondary IP ranges attached to a subnet. A secondary range is an extra block of addresses on a subnet, separate from the block the nodes use. A CIDR block is a range written with a slash, such as 10.4.0.0/16, where the number after the slash says how many leading bits are fixed. A smaller number means a bigger block.

Why it works. The cluster does not hand out single Pod addresses one at a time. Each node receives a slice of the Pod range sized for the maximum number of Pods that node can run. With the common default of 110 Pods per node, each node takes a /24, which is 256 addresses.

Worked example. A subnet has a Pod secondary range of 10.4.0.0/16, which holds 65,536 addresses. Each node takes a /24, so this range supports 256 nodes. The cluster now needs 300 nodes. Step one: check how many slices of the current range are still unclaimed. Step two: reserve a second secondary range on the subnet that does not overlap anything, such as 10.5.0.0/16. Step three: attach that range to the cluster as an additional Pod range. Step four: create a node pool that draws its Pod addresses from the new range. The cluster now has room for 512 nodes across two ranges.

Common mistake. Choosing a range that overlaps another subnet, a peered network, or an on-premises network. The new block then conflicts with routes elsewhere, and it is hard to undo once nodes depend on it.

Consequence. When the range is full, new nodes cannot receive Pod slices, so new Pods stay in Pending even though the machines have idle CPU and memory. Existing Pods keep running, but the cluster cannot scale out until a new range is added.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a GKE cluster, which is Google's managed Kubernetes service. Its Pod secondary range is 172.24.0.0/22, a block of 1,024 addresses. A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes schedules, and a node is a virtual machine that runs Pods. The nodes are set to 64 Pods each, so each node takes a /25 of 128 addresses, and the range supports 8 nodes. The firm needs 12 nodes. Its on-premises network reaches the cloud over a VPN route covering 172.24.8.0/21. Step one: the existing range has room for 8 nodes, so 4 more are needed. Step two: a second range of 1,024 addresses would support 8 more nodes, which is enough. Step three is missing: choose the second range that fits the rules and reserve it on the subnet. Which completion of step three is correct?
choices: Reserve 172.25.0.0/22, which overlaps neither the existing range, the subnet's own blocks, nor the on-premises 172.24.8.0/21 route.
Reserve 172.24.4.0/23 and attach it, since any block adjacent to the existing range avoids conflicts.
Raise the existing range's limit to 128 Pods per node so the current /22 holds more nodes without adding a range.
Reserve 172.24.8.0/22, since it sits right after the existing range and the VPN route only covers its upper part.
questions.why: 172.25.0.0/22 has enough addresses for 8 more nodes and does not overlap any existing or on-premises route, while 172.24.8.0/22 falls inside the on-premises 172.24.8.0/21 route and 172.24.4.0/23 is too small.

questions.prompt: A team gives its cluster a secondary Pod range of 10.90.0.0/19. Roughly how many addresses does that range hold?
questions.why: A /19 fixes 19 leading bits, leaving 13 bits free, and 2 to the power of 13 is 8,192 addresses.

questions.prompt: A clinic's cluster allows 32 Pods per node, so each node takes a /26 of 64 addresses. Its current Pod range is 10.70.0.0/20, which holds 64 nodes. The clinic must reach 80 nodes. What is the smallest second secondary range that gives enough room?
questions.why: Sixteen more nodes need 16 slices of 64 addresses, or 1,024 addresses, which is exactly a /22; a /24 gives only 4 nodes.

questions.prompt: A cluster's nodes show idle CPU and memory, yet new Pods stay in Pending. Existing Pods keep running. Which cause best fits this symptom?
choices: Firewall rules block new Pods from reaching the control plane, so they are never scheduled.
The node pool lacks a network tag, which stops Pods from being assigned any address.
The cluster's Pod secondary range is fully claimed, so new nodes receive no Pod slice and their Pods cannot start.
The nodes' CPU is saturated, so the scheduler cannot place any new Pods on them.
questions.why: When the Pod range is full, new nodes cannot get Pod slices, and idle machines with running Pods behind them match that failure rather than a CPU shortage or firewall block.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a GKE cluster can run out of Pod addresses even when its nodes have spare CPU and memory, and what adding another Pod range fixes and does not fix. Name one limit or tradeoff of planning the new range.
lessons.modelAnswer: Pod addresses come from a fixed block, and each node takes a slice of that block sized for its maximum Pod count. If the block has no unclaimed slices left, the cluster cannot give a new node a Pod range, so new Pods wait in Pending even when the machines have idle CPU and memory. Adding another secondary range on the subnet and a node pool that uses it gives new nodes fresh slices, so the cluster can keep growing. The tradeoff is that the new range must not overlap any other subnet, peered network, or on-premises network, and it is hard to resize or remove once nodes depend on it. Existing nodes keep their original slices, so the fix adds new capacity rather than reshuffling old nodes.
rubricPoints: Pod addresses come from a fixed secondary range, and each node takes a slice sized for its maximum Pod count
Running out of slices blocks new nodes or Pods even when CPU and memory are free
Adding a non-overlapping secondary range and a node pool that uses it adds capacity without moving existing nodes
The new range must not overlap other subnets, peered, or on-premises networks, and is hard to undo

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a scale-out scenario where Pods stay Pending adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission or planned engine covers GKE Pod addressing directly.

lessons.plain: A Kubernetes cluster runs many small workloads that constantly need to look up names, such as finding the address of another service by its name. The cluster needs a phone book for those names. The setup decisions are which phone book answers the lookups, whether answers are cached close to the workloads so they come back faster, and whether names can come only from inside the cluster or from the wider private network. Getting these wrong makes applications slow, makes some names fail to resolve, or lets names resolve that should stay private.
lessons.guessPrompt: A pod in your cluster asks for the address of a service called orders by name. Before reading anything, what would you expect to happen between the pod asking and getting an address back, and where might a delay come from if the same question is asked again a second later?
lessons.teach: DNS is the system that turns a name into an address. In Kubernetes, a pod is the smallest unit that runs your containers and gets its own address, and a service is a stable name that points at a group of pods. kube-dns is the built-in DNS service that runs as pods inside the cluster and answers service names. Cloud DNS for GKE is Google's managed DNS, which replaces the in-cluster DNS pods with a service run by Google; its scope decides whether it answers only cluster-internal names or names across the whole VPC network. NodeLocal DNSCache is a small cache agent that runs on every node, so pods ask a nearby cache first. The cache exists because most lookups repeat, and a nearby answer is faster and reduces load on the central DNS service. Each answer carries a TTL, the number of seconds it may be reused. Worked example: a pod asks for orders. The node cache has no entry, so it forwards the question to the cluster DNS. The DNS returns the service address with a TTL of 30 seconds. The cache stores it. For the next 30 seconds, lookups for orders are answered on the node without leaving it. Common mistake: assuming a DNS change takes effect instantly. Cached answers keep the old address until their TTL expires, so some pods can still reach the previous address for that long. In a running system, this shows up as intermittent failures right after a service moves. Check which DNS provider and scope a cluster uses before diagnosing any name problem.

questions.prompt: A team runs a service called ledger in a cluster that has the node-local cache turned on. The cache is a small agent on each node that stores answers so pods can reuse them. At 09:00:00 a pod asks for ledger, and the cluster DNS returns 10.8.4.20 with a TTL (time to live, the number of seconds the answer may be reused) of 90 seconds. The cache stores that answer. At 09:00:20 the team moves ledger to 10.8.7.55, and the cluster DNS starts returning the new address right away. Step 1: the cache entry was stored at 09:00:00 and is valid for 90 seconds. Step 2: the entry stays valid until 09:01:30. Step 3: a pod on the same node asks for ledger at 09:01:00, which is before 09:01:30, so the cache answers without asking the cluster DNS. Missing step: the address the pod receives is what?
choices: 10.8.4.20 only if the pod is scheduled on a different node
10.8.7.55, because the cluster DNS was updated at 09:00:20
10.8.4.20, the old address, because the cached answer has not yet expired
No answer, because the cache must wait for a fresh query before replying
questions.why: The cache answers from its stored copy until the TTL runs out at 09:01:30, so the pod gets the old address 10.8.4.20 even though the cluster DNS already has the new one.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a TTL (time to live, a number of seconds) on a DNS answer tell a cache?
choices: The number of pods that may ask for the same name at once
The number of nodes in the cluster that hold a copy of the answer
The number of seconds the answer may be reused before it must be looked up again
The time a new pod needs before it can resolve any name
questions.why: A TTL is the number of seconds an answer may be reused, after which the cache must ask again.

questions.prompt: A cluster uses Cloud DNS for GKE (Google's managed DNS for cluster names). A pod needs to resolve the name db-vm, which is a plain virtual machine in the same VPC network but not a Kubernetes service. Which scope must the managed DNS use for this lookup to succeed?
choices: Node scope, which answers only names held by the local node cache
Pod scope, which answers only names of pods with a fixed address
VPC scope, which answers names across the whole VPC network
Cluster scope, which answers only names of services inside the cluster
questions.why: Scope decides whether the DNS answers only cluster-internal names or names across the whole VPC network, and db-vm is a VPC name outside the cluster, so VPC scope is required.

questions.prompt: Right after a service moved to a new address, a few pods in a cluster intermittently fail to connect. What should you check first before diagnosing the name problem?
choices: Delete and recreate the service to clear every cache
Assume the change is instant and check the firewall rules
Restart application pods, since DNS changes only apply to new pods
Check the DNS provider and scope, then allow for cached answers within their TTL
questions.why: The text says to confirm which DNS provider and scope the cluster uses first, and cached answers keep the old address until their TTL expires, which explains intermittent failures after a move.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a pod's name lookup reaches an answer in a GKE cluster. Name the difference between kube-dns and Cloud DNS for GKE, and name one limit or tradeoff of caching DNS answers on each node.
lessons.modelAnswer: A pod sends its lookup to the DNS endpoint configured for the cluster. If NodeLocal DNSCache is enabled, the node-level cache answers from memory when it holds a fresh entry; otherwise it forwards the query upstream. Upstream is either kube-dns, which runs as pods inside the cluster, or Cloud DNS for GKE, which is a managed service whose scope decides whether it serves only cluster names or names across the VPC. The main tradeoff of caching is speed against freshness. A cached answer can outlive a change until its TTL expires, so a moved service may still be reached at its old address for a short window. Teammates should check the provider, the scope, and whether the cache is enabled before assuming a lookup is broken.
rubricPoints: Describes the lookup path from pod to node cache to upstream DNS provider
Distinguishes kube-dns (in-cluster pods) from Cloud DNS for GKE (managed, with scope)
Explains that NodeLocal DNSCache answers from a per-node cache and why that reduces latency
Names the tradeoff: cached answers can be stale until the TTL expires

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine walks through DNS provider and cache configuration, so the learner should read the settings and facts directly.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic director that sits in front of several copies of a service and hands each incoming request to one of them, so no single copy gets overwhelmed and a broken copy can be skipped. Choosing one means answering three everyday questions: who is allowed to reach it, how widely its traffic is spread across places, and how much of each request it reads. A website open to the whole internet needs a different director than an internal reporting service used only inside a company's private network. The right answer comes from the requirement, not from the name of the most popular option.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website must serve users in Europe and Asia, understand URL paths such as /shop and /images, and be reachable from the public internet. Before reading on, which of these three choices would you pick first: public or private, one region or several, or simple packet forwarding or reading the URL?
lessons.teach:
Three choices narrow the field. First, exposure: an external balancer has a public address that clients on the internet can reach, while an internal balancer has only a private address reachable from inside your network or networks connected to it. Second, scope: a regional balancer and its backends live in one region, while a global balancer uses one anycast address (a single address announced from many places, so each user's traffic enters at the nearest point) and sends users to healthy backends in several regions. Third, layer: a layer 7 application balancer reads HTTP details such as host name and URL path and opens its own connection to the backend. A layer 4 proxy balancer ends TCP or SSL connections without reading HTTP. A layer 4 passthrough balancer forwards packets unchanged, so the backend sees the original client address and handles the connection itself.

Why it matters: the more a balancer reads and rewrites, the more routing choices it offers, but it adds processing and must hold connection state. Passthrough is the simplest and keeps packets intact, which suits non-HTTP protocols or appliances that need the true source address.

Worked example: a public shop with URL-based routing, used worldwide. Step 1: the users are on the internet, so external. Step 2: they are worldwide and should reach the nearest healthy region, so global. Step 3: routing depends on the URL path, which only a layer 7 application balancer can read. Result: an external, global, application load balancer.

Common mistake: picking a passthrough balancer for a web app because it sounds simpler, then finding it cannot route by URL path or terminate TLS for HTTP.

Consequence: a regional-only entry point fails completely when its region has an outage, while a global frontend can shift users to healthy regions. Pick the scope and layer from the requirement before you pick the product.

questions.prompt: A company runs an internal order-status API that only its own backend services call. All callers and backends sit in the europe-west1 region, and no client outside the company network ever reaches the API. The API routes requests by URL path, so the team needs a balancer that reads HTTP. Step 1: the callers are inside the company's private network, so the balancer must be internal, with only a private address. Step 2: the missing step is the scope. Choose the scope that fits the requirement and state it. Step 3: routing depends on the URL path, which only a layer 7 application balancer can read. Result: an internal, scope-chosen, application balancer.
choices: Global, because a global balancer is always the safer default for internal APIs
External, because the API must be reachable from anywhere on the internet
Regional, because all callers and backends live in one region and no traffic needs to enter from elsewhere
Passthrough at layer 4, because the API should receive packets without modification
questions.why: Since every caller and backend is in one region, a regional scope matches the requirement, and a global scope would add reach the API does not need.

questions.prompt: A video game company needs to forward raw UDP game traffic from players on the internet to its game servers in one region. The servers need the real player address and must not have the packets altered. Which balancer fits?
choices: Internal, global, layer 4 passthrough balancer
External, regional, layer 4 passthrough balancer
External, global, layer 7 application balancer
Internal, regional, layer 4 proxy balancer
questions.why: Players are on the internet so the balancer must be external, one region means regional, and a passthrough balancer keeps packets intact so the servers see the true player address.

questions.prompt: A team runs a network appliance that filters traffic based on the original source address of each connection. They put it behind an external, regional, layer 4 proxy balancer and find the filtering rules no longer match real clients. What best explains this?
choices: The appliance needs a global balancer, because regional balancers always hide source addresses
Proxy balancers only work with HTTP, so the appliance receives malformed requests
Proxy balancers cannot be external, so the rules are applied to the wrong balancer
The proxy ends the TCP connection and opens its own, so the appliance does not see the original client address that a passthrough balancer would preserve
questions.why: A layer 4 proxy terminates the client connection and starts a new one, so the backend loses the original source address, which a passthrough balancer would have kept.

questions.prompt: A mobile app backend has users in Asia and Europe. Requests are routed by host name, and each user should reach the nearest healthy region. Which balancer should the team choose?
choices: External, regional, layer 4 proxy balancer
Internal, global, layer 7 application balancer
External, global, layer 7 application balancer
Internal, regional, layer 4 passthrough balancer
questions.why: Users are on the internet so it must be external, users are spread across regions so it must be global, and routing by host name requires a layer 7 application balancer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between an external and an internal load balancer, a regional and a global one, and an application balancer versus a passthrough balancer. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not choose first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with exposure: if clients come from the public internet, the balancer needs a public address, so it is external; if callers are only inside our private network, it is internal. Next I ask about scope. A global balancer gives one entry address that sends users to healthy backends in several regions, which helps users spread across the world and survives a regional outage, but it costs more and needs backends in more than one region to be useful. Then I look at layer. If we need routing by host or URL path, or TLS handled at the edge, I use an application balancer. The tradeoff is that it terminates connections and adds processing, so it sees HTTP and not arbitrary protocols. A passthrough balancer is simpler and keeps the original client address, but it cannot route on URL paths, so I would only choose it when the protocol is not HTTP or the backend needs the raw packets.
rubricPoints: Exposure decides external versus internal, based on where the clients are.
Scope decides regional versus global, based on where users and backends are and how much regional failure matters.
Layer decides application versus proxy versus passthrough, based on whether routing needs HTTP details.
Names a real tradeoff, such as cost or processing overhead for global and application balancers, or lost URL routing for passthrough.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among load balancer types is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios with competing requirements, and no current mission covers network traffic delivery.

lessons.plain: Think of a load balancer as a receptionist who sends each visitor to one of several desks. A backend service is the list of those desks, along with the rules for checking whether each desk is open. A network endpoint group is a labelled list of the addresses and ports where the work actually runs. A managed instance group is a set of identical virtual machines that the cloud creates, replaces, and adds or removes as demand changes. This objective is about choosing between these ways of grouping backends, and setting up how a group grows and shrinks.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website runs on three identical servers behind a traffic splitter. On a busy afternoon the servers become slow. Which would you rather have: a fixed set of three servers you add to by hand, or a group that adds identical servers on its own when they are busy and removes them when they are idle? Explain your choice in two sentences.
lessons.teach:
A backend service is the part of a load balancer that owns a set of backends, a health check that decides which backends may receive traffic, and the settings for spreading traffic among them. A backend is one group attached to that service. A managed instance group, or MIG, is a set of identical virtual machines created from one instance template, and the cloud can resize it automatically. A network endpoint group, or NEG, is a list of endpoints: an IP address and port of a machine, a container, a service outside Google Cloud, or a serverless service. Use a MIG when the cloud should create and scale identical machines for you. Use a NEG when the receivers are not simply VMs in a MIG, such as containers, serverless services, or machines outside Google Cloud. Autoscaling is the rule that changes a MIG's size. You set a minimum and maximum number of instances and a signal, such as average CPU utilization or the load balancer's serving capacity. The autoscaler adds instances when the signal is above its target and removes them when it is below.

Worked example: a MIG with a minimum of 2, a maximum of 10, and a CPU target of 60 percent. Traffic doubles and average CPU rises to 90 percent. The autoscaler estimates that 2 instances at 90 percent need about 3 instances to run near 60 percent, so it adds one and waits for it to boot. Only after the new instance passes its health check does the balancer send it traffic. If the estimate is still too high, it keeps adding instances up to the maximum of 10.

Common mistake: treating autoscaling as instant, or leaving out a health check so that a new instance still booting receives requests and fails them. Consequence: during a surge, users see errors even though the group reports that capacity was added.

A MIG and a NEG are chosen by what receives the traffic, and autoscaling only ever changes the size of a MIG.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs a managed instance group with a minimum of 3 and a maximum of 12 instances, and a CPU target of 70 percent. Its 3 instances currently average 105 percent CPU. Worked so far: total load is 3 x 105 = 315 units, and at the 70 percent target each instance should carry 70 units, so 315 / 70 = 4.5 instances are needed. The one step left is turning that 4.5 into a whole-number size that the group can be set to, staying within the minimum and maximum. What size does the autoscaler set the group to?
choices: 5, because the estimate is rounded up to a whole instance and checked against the minimum and maximum
4.5 instances, because the group can run fractional machines
12, because any overload should jump straight to the maximum
4, because 4.5 is rounded down to the nearest whole instance
questions.why: Instances are whole machines, so the estimate is rounded up to 5, which lies between the minimum of 3 and the maximum of 12.

questions.prompt: A team runs its web front end as containers on a managed container platform, and its background API as a serverless service. Which backend type fits when the load balancer must reach these receivers?
choices: A managed instance group, with the containers installed as software on each VM
A managed instance group built from an instance template, because any compute workload runs on VMs
A network endpoint group, because the receivers are containers and serverless services rather than identical VMs in a managed instance group
One shared health check, since the health check decides which receiver type is used
questions.why: A network endpoint group lists endpoints such as containers and serverless services, while a managed instance group only holds identical VMs created from one template.

questions.prompt: A managed instance group autoscales on average CPU with a target of 50 percent. During a sudden surge, a newly added instance is still booting, and users receive errors for several minutes even though the group reports added capacity. Which setting most directly stops requests from reaching instances that are not ready?
choices: A health check that a new instance must pass before the balancer sends it traffic
Raising the maximum instance count
Switching the signal to a higher CPU target
Removing the minimum instance count
questions.why: A health check gates which backends may receive traffic, so a booting instance gets no requests until it passes; changing the maximum or the target does not prevent this.

questions.prompt: A team lists three on-premises servers in a network endpoint group behind a load balancer and turns on autoscaling for that backend, expecting the cloud to add more on-premises servers when load rises. What is the correct understanding?
choices: The cloud will create new on-premises servers, since network endpoint groups can scale like any backend
It works if the three servers are placed into an instance template
It works once the group's health check is set to a higher CPU target
Autoscaling only changes the size of a managed instance group, so the cloud does not add endpoints to this group and the team must manage them
questions.why: Autoscaling only ever changes the size of a managed instance group, so endpoints in a network endpoint group must be added or removed by the team.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose a network endpoint group instead of a managed instance group for a backend, and name one limit of autoscaling that they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would choose a network endpoint group when the receivers are not just identical VMs that the cloud can create for me. Examples are containers, a serverless service, or machines in another environment. A NEG lists the endpoints directly, so the balancer routes to them without needing a MIG behind them. A managed instance group fits when I want the platform to build identical machines from a template and resize them. The key limit to plan for is delay. Autoscaling reacts to a signal such as CPU, and new instances need time to boot and pass health checks before they take traffic. So during a sudden spike, capacity arrives late. We should keep the minimum size high enough to absorb the first minutes of a surge, and test that the health check is strict enough to keep half-started instances out of rotation.
rubricPoints: A NEG lists endpoints directly and suits containers, serverless services, or machines outside a MIG
A MIG is a set of identical VMs from one template that the cloud can resize
Autoscaling reacts to a signal, so new capacity arrives after a delay
A health check keeps instances that are still booting out of traffic
Set the minimum instance count to absorb the delay during a sudden spike

suggested.rationale: The planned autoscale engine would let the learner work through scaling signals, minimum and maximum sizes, and the lag before new capacity serves traffic.

lessons.plain: Imagine a busy restaurant with one host at the door who sends each arriving guest to the right table. In a Kubernetes cluster on Google Cloud, your app runs as many small copies, and something has to receive outside web requests and spread them across those copies. This lesson covers three pieces that do that job: the Ingress controller and the Gateway controller, which turn written routing rules into a real Google Cloud load balancer, and network endpoint groups, which are lists of the actual addresses the load balancer sends traffic to. Knowing which piece to use for a given situation is the skill being tested.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs as forty identical containers spread across a cluster, and you want one public address that sends /api requests to one set of them and /images requests to another. Before reading on, what would you need to write down to describe that routing, and who on a team would normally own that description?
lessons.teach:
A Kubernetes cluster runs your app as Pods, which are small units that each hold one or more containers. Pods come and go and receive new addresses, so nothing outside the cluster should point at one directly. A load balancer is a managed Google Cloud component that takes traffic at one stable address and spreads it across healthy backends. In GKE, the piece that builds these load balancers from your Kubernetes configuration is a controller: a program that watches cluster objects and makes the outside world match what they describe.

Two controllers do this job. The GKE Ingress controller reads Ingress resources, a single object that combines the front door, the routing rules and the backend mapping. The GKE Gateway controller implements the newer Gateway API, which splits the job in two. A Gateway, usually owned by a platform team, defines listeners and the load balancer itself. Routes such as HTTPRoute, usually owned by app teams, define path and header matches. That split lets app teams change routing without touching shared infrastructure, and it supports richer traffic rules. Kubernetes now recommends Gateway API for new designs.

Network endpoint groups, called NEGs, are the list of endpoints a backend service sends traffic to. With container-native NEGs, each entry is a Pod IP and port, so the load balancer reaches Pods directly instead of hopping through a node port first. That removes an extra network hop and lets health checks see individual Pods.

Worked example: a team wants shop.example.com/cart served by the cart Service. They create a Gateway for the public load balancer, then an HTTPRoute that matches the path /cart and forwards to the cart Service. GKE creates a NEG holding the cart Pod addresses. The load balancer health-checks those Pods and sends requests only to the healthy ones.

Common mistake: assuming that creating an Ingress or Gateway object is enough on its own. If the Service is not wired for container-native NEGs, traffic can take the node-port path and lose the direct Pod route.

The load balancer only ever sends traffic to the Pods that its NEG currently lists as healthy.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs its status page as a Service named status-api on port 8080. The platform team has already created a Gateway named public-edge with an HTTPS listener on port 443. Step 1: the platform team creates the Gateway, which defines the listener and the load balancer at one stable address. Step 2: ___ . Step 3: the GKE Gateway controller sees the new route and builds the load balancer's backend with a NEG that lists the status-api Pod addresses. Step 4: the load balancer health-checks those Pods and sends requests only to the healthy ones.
