choices: The app team deletes the Gateway and recreates it with the path rules placed inside its listener.
The platform team edits the Gateway to add the /status path rule, since only the Gateway defines path matches.
The team creates an Ingress object alongside the Gateway so that both controllers handle the same path.
The app team writes an HTTPRoute that matches the path /status and forwards to the status-api Service on port 8080.
questions.why: In the Gateway API, the app team's HTTPRoute holds the path and header matches and forwards to a Service, so writing that route is the missing step that connects the listener to the status-api backend.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a network endpoint group (NEG) in GKE?
choices: A DNS zone that maps a company's domain names to the cluster's public address.
A Kubernetes namespace that groups all Services belonging to one application team.
The list of endpoints a backend service sends traffic to, which with container-native NEGs holds Pod IPs and ports.
A firewall rule that lists which IP ranges may reach a Kubernetes namespace.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a NEG as the list of endpoints a backend service sends traffic to, and with container-native NEGs those endpoints are Pod addresses and ports.

questions.prompt: A payments team created a Gateway and an HTTPRoute, yet their load balancer still sends traffic to node ports first and the health checks report node-level results. Which explanation fits the teaching text best?
choices: The load balancer needs a second Gateway per node pool before it can reach any Pod.
Health checks always run against nodes, so the Pod route can never be used in GKE.
The Service is not wired for container-native NEGs, so the traffic takes the node-port path and loses the direct Pod route.
The Gateway controller only works with Ingress resources, so the HTTPRoute is ignored entirely.
questions.why: The teaching text's common mistake says that when the Service is not set up for container-native NEGs, traffic can fall back to the node-port path, which removes the direct route to Pods.

questions.prompt: A Pod sits in a load balancer's NEG, but it begins failing its health checks. What does the load balancer do with requests, according to the teaching text?
choices: It stops sending requests to that Pod, because it only sends traffic to Pods its NEG lists as healthy.
It sends requests to the node port of the Pod's node instead, so the failing Pod still gets traffic.
It deletes the Pod from the cluster and then waits for the Ingress to be recreated.
It keeps sending requests to every listed Pod in turn, since the NEG cannot be changed while running.
questions.why: The teaching text states that the load balancer only sends traffic to the Pods its NEG currently lists as healthy, so an unhealthy Pod stops receiving requests.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick the GKE Gateway controller over the GKE Ingress controller for a new service, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a new service I would pick the Gateway controller. Ingress puts the front door, the routing and the backend in one object, which is quick for a small app but means everyone who edits it touches the same file. Gateway splits that into a Gateway owned by the platform team and HTTPRoutes owned by the app team, so an app team can change its path rules without editing shared listeners. It also offers more expressive routing, such as weighted traffic splitting. The tradeoff is more objects to learn and set up, and someone has to create and maintain the Gateway and its GatewayClass. Either way, the backend should be reached through container-native NEGs, so traffic goes straight to Pods and health checks see each one. If the team already runs many Ingress resources, I would keep them working and migrate deliberately rather than rewriting everything at once.
rubricPoints: Gateway separates platform-owned infrastructure from app-owned routes, while Ingress keeps everything in one object
Gateway supports richer routing features, and Kubernetes recommends it for new designs
Gateway adds setup and ownership overhead, a real tradeoff for small apps
NEGs let the load balancer send traffic directly to Pod IPs and health-check each Pod
Existing Ingress resources should be migrated deliberately, not all at once

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these controllers in a scenario adds the most, and no listed mission or planned engine covers Kubernetes load balancing yet.

lessons.plain: A load balancer sits in front of several copies of an application and decides which copy handles each incoming request. An application load balancer works at the level of web requests, so it can look at the path, the host name, and the headers before choosing. This objective covers three extra controls on top of that routing. Traffic splitting sends a chosen share of requests to one group of servers and the rest to another, which is how you try a new version on a small slice of users. Traffic mirroring sends a copy of requests to a second group for observation, while users still get answers only from the main group. URL rewrites change the path or host name of a request before it reaches the servers, so the backend does not need to match the public address.
lessons.guessPrompt: You want 5 percent of your website's visitors to try a new version of the checkout service, and the rest to keep using the old one. Without looking anything up, how would you split the traffic, and where in the request path would the split happen?
lessons.teach:
Each rule in a URL map, which is the set of routing rules attached to a load balancer, can send matching requests to one or more backend services. A backend service is a named group of servers or endpoints that do the actual work. Traffic splitting, also called weighted routing, gives each backend service a weight, and the balancer picks a backend for each request in proportion to those weights. Weights are relative, so 9 and 1 behave the same as 90 and 10. It works because the choice is made per request by the balancer, so a 10 percent share of requests reaches the new version without changing DNS or restarting anything.

Worked example: a rule for the path prefix /api sends weight 90 to a stable backend service and weight 10 to a new version. Step one: a request for /api/orders arrives. Step two: the balancer makes a weighted choice across the total weight of 100. Step three: if the choice falls in the first 90 units, the stable group answers; otherwise the new group answers. Across a thousand requests, about 100 reach the new group, though any single request is not guaranteed to.

Traffic mirroring copies each matching request to a second backend service. The copy is sent for observation only. The mirror's response is discarded, and the user is answered only by the primary backend.

URL rewrite changes part of a request before it is forwarded. A rule can strip a public prefix so that a request to /shop/items/42 reaches the backend as /items/42, or it can change the host name the backend sees.

Common mistake: assuming mirroring is harmless. Errors from the mirror never reach users, but its load and its side effects do. A mirrored POST that creates an order can create a second order if the mirror writes to the same database.

In a running system, a mirror that is overloaded adds cost and load without changing what users see, so mirror traffic should go to a read-only or isolated copy of the service.

questions.prompt: A video company runs a URL map rule for the path prefix /thumbs. The rule gives weight 5 to a backend service called resize-v2 and weight 15 to resize-v1. A request for /thumbs/cat.jpg arrives. Step one: the balancer adds the weights to get a total of 20. Step two: the balancer picks a number from 0 to 19. Step three: [missing]. Which sentence correctly completes step three?
choices: If the number is below 5, resize-v2 answers; otherwise resize-v1 answers, so about 25 percent of requests reach v2.
The balancer sends 5 percent of requests to resize-v2 because 5 is 5 percent of 100.
resize-v2 answers every fifth request in a fixed rotation, regardless of weight.
The balancer asks DNS to return resize-v2's address to 5 percent of clients.
questions.why: The balancer compares the chosen number with the weights out of the total of 20, so resize-v2 takes 5 of 20 slots, which is about 25 percent.

questions.prompt: A URL map rule on a shopping site sends /reports to a primary backend and mirrors every matching request to a second backend. The second backend returns a 500 error for one request. What does the user see?
choices: The request is retried against the primary until the mirror returns a successful response.
A 500 error page, because the mirror's failure replaces the primary's answer.
A 503 response for the whole /reports path until the mirror recovers.
The primary backend's response, because the mirror's response is discarded and only the primary answers the user.
questions.why: Mirroring sends a copy for observation only, so the user is answered only by the primary backend and the mirror's response is thrown away.

questions.prompt: A travel booking site has a rule for the path /search with weight 3 for a current backend and weight 7 for a new backend. Roughly what share of requests reaches the new backend?
choices: 3 percent, because the weight of the current backend is the share sent to the new one.
70 percent, because the new backend has the larger weight.
43 percent, because 3 divided by 7 gives the share for the new backend.
30 percent, because 7 out of a total of 10 is the share for the new backend.
questions.why: Weights are relative, so the new backend gets 7 out of a total of 10, which is about 70 percent, and the choice above that reads the share backwards.

questions.prompt: An ecommerce app mirrors every POST to /orders to a copy of the backend that writes to the same live orders database. A customer places one order. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The primary backend stops receiving the POST, so the order is never created at all.
Customers see charges twice only when the mirror is slower than the primary backend.
The mirror can write the same order a second time, creating a duplicate order.
Nothing changes, because the mirror's response is discarded and its writes are ignored by the system.
questions.why: A mirror's response is discarded, but its side effects still happen, so writing to the same live database can create a second order.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between traffic splitting and traffic mirroring on an application load balancer, and name one limit or risk of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Traffic splitting decides which backend answers a real user request. You give each backend service a weight, and the balancer picks one per request in proportion to those weights, so a 10 to 90 split sends about one request in ten to the new version. The user gets the answer from whichever backend was chosen, so a bad new version affects the users it receives. The limit is that the split is per request, not per user, so one user can bounce between versions across requests unless you add session affinity. Mirroring is different. The balancer copies each matching request to a second backend and throws away that backend's response, so users only see the primary's answer. It is useful for testing a new version against real traffic. The risk is that the mirror still does real work, so any writes or charges it performs are duplicated.
rubricPoints: Traffic splitting sends real user responses from weighted backends, proportional to the weights.
Traffic mirroring copies requests and discards the mirror's response, so users see only the primary.
Splitting is per request, so one user may hit different versions unless session affinity is set.
Mirrored requests still cause load and side effects such as duplicate writes.

suggested.rationale: Weighted canary traffic is a deployment strategy, so the planned deployment-strategies engine would let the learner practise choosing and reasoning about split weights.

lessons.plain: Cloud CDN is a content delivery network feature. It keeps copies of responses in storage locations close to the people asking for them, so repeat requests are answered from a nearby copy instead of travelling all the way back to the original server. That original server is called the origin. In Google Cloud, Cloud CDN sits in front of a load balancer, and the origin can be a group of virtual machines, a storage bucket holding files, or a container-based web service. Think of a local newsagent keeping copies of a popular magazine so customers do not each need a trip to the publisher. Your job is to pick the origin type that fits the content and decide how long copies stay valid.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website serves the same product photos to thousands of visitors every hour from a single server in one region. Without changing the app itself, what would you put in front of that server to reduce its load, and what kind of content would be safe to keep copies of?
lessons.teach:
A cache is a store of copies kept so that repeated requests can be answered without redoing the work. A CDN (content delivery network) is a set of caches spread across many locations. Cloud CDN is the Google Cloud feature that turns this caching on for traffic passing through an external Application Load Balancer. The load balancer is the front door, and the origin is whatever sits behind it.

Each supported origin attaches differently. A managed instance group (MIG), which is a set of identical virtual machines that scale together, attaches as a backend service. A Cloud Storage bucket attaches as a backend bucket, a special backend type. Cloud Run, the managed container platform, attaches through a serverless network endpoint group (NEG), a backend that points at a serverless service rather than at IP addresses. Caching must be switched on for each attached backend.

Why it works: the first request for a URL misses the cache, goes to the origin, and the response is stored with a time-to-live (TTL), meaning how long that copy may be served. Later requests inside that window hit the cache and never reach the origin. The cache mode decides what is stored. CACHE_ALL_STATIC caches common static file types by default and respects the origin's no-cache instructions. USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS caches only what the origin marks as cacheable. FORCE_CACHE_ALL caches everything regardless of headers.

Worked example: a bucket holds logo.png with a one-hour max age. Visitor A asks for it, which is a miss, so the copy is fetched from the bucket and stored. Visitor B asks a minute later from the same region, which is a hit, so the copy is served from cache and the bucket sees nothing. After an hour the copy expires and the next request refreshes it.

Common mistake: choosing FORCE_CACHE_ALL for a page that shows per-user data. The cache then hands one user's response to another visitor. Personal responses belong outside shared caches.

Consequence: a cached response is only as fresh as its TTL. If a price changes, the old figure can keep appearing for the full window, so set TTLs to match how quickly the content really changes.

questions.prompt: A small publisher, Harbor Notes, serves its daily digest API from a Cloud Run service named digest-api. The team wants repeated reads answered from a cache at the edge, and they set it up in this order. Step 1: create a serverless network endpoint group (NEG) that points at the digest-api Cloud Run service. Step 2: create a backend service that uses that serverless NEG as its backend. Step 3 is missing from their runbook and must be filled in. Step 4: choose CACHE_ALL_STATIC as the cache mode, then attach the backend service to an external Application Load Balancer. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Switch Cloud CDN caching on for that backend service, because caching has to be enabled on each attached backend.
Replace the serverless NEG with a backend bucket, since Cloud Run content is stored in buckets.
Set the TTL to zero on the backend so the cache never keeps a copy.
Point the Cloud Run service's URL straight into the public DNS record, bypassing the load balancer entirely.
questions.why: Caching must be switched on for each attached backend, so Step 3 is enabling Cloud CDN on the backend service, and a serverless NEG (not a backend bucket) is the correct attachment for Cloud Run.

questions.prompt: In the context of Cloud CDN, what is a serverless network endpoint group (NEG)?
choices: A set of identical virtual machines that scale together behind a load balancer.
A DNS record that maps a domain name to a cache location.
A special backend type that stores static files inside the load balancer itself.
A backend that points at a serverless service such as Cloud Run instead of at IP addresses.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a serverless NEG as a backend that points at a serverless service rather than at IP addresses, which is the Cloud Run attachment method.

questions.prompt: A news site sets its article pages to cache with a 24-hour TTL. Editors correct headlines several times a day. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The load balancer will refuse to serve the pages until the TTL expires.
Readers will always see the newest headline because the cache checks the origin on every request.
The cache will automatically shorten the TTL whenever the content changes.
Corrected headlines may keep showing the old text for up to the full 24-hour window.
questions.why: The teaching text says a cached response is only as fresh as its TTL, so an old headline can keep appearing for the full window after a change.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs a managed instance group of identical web servers that generate a product listing page, and wants Cloud CDN in front of it. Which attachment is correct?
choices: Attach the managed instance group as a serverless NEG.
Attach the managed instance group directly to the DNS record with no load balancer.
Attach the managed instance group as a backend bucket.
Attach the managed instance group as a backend service.
questions.why: A managed instance group attaches to an external Application Load Balancer as a backend service, while backend buckets are for Cloud Storage and serverless NEGs are for Cloud Run.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should not simply turn on CDN caching for every route on the site. Explain which content suits Cloud CDN caching, how the three supported origin types differ in how they attach, and one tradeoff they should accept or watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud CDN suits content that is the same for every visitor and changes slowly, such as images, scripts and downloadable files. Per-user pages should stay uncached, because a shared copy could show one person's data to someone else. The three supported origins attach in different ways. A managed instance group attaches as a backend service, a Cloud Storage bucket attaches as a backend bucket, and Cloud Run attaches through a serverless network endpoint group. The main tradeoff is freshness. Every cached response can be stale for up to its time-to-live, so a short TTL keeps content current but sends more traffic to the origin, while a long TTL saves origin load but can show old content for longer.
rubricPoints: Names cacheable content as shared, mostly static content, and excludes per-user responses
Identifies the attachment method for each origin: backend service for MIGs, backend bucket for buckets, serverless NEG for Cloud Run
Explains the TTL tradeoff between origin load and content freshness

suggested.rationale: Choosing an origin, cache mode and TTL for a stated requirement is a scenario to reason through, and no listed mission covers CDN.

lessons.plain: A content delivery network, or CDN, is a set of servers spread around the world that keep copies of files a website or app serves often. When a visitor asks for a file, a nearby copy can answer instead of the original server, which is faster for the visitor and lighter on the original. That original is called the origin, and it is the real source of the content. On Google Cloud, Cloud CDN is switched on in front of a load balancer. This lesson covers the case where the origin is not a Google service: your own web servers reached over the internet, or object storage run by another provider. The central question is how the cache decides what to keep and for how long.
lessons.guessPrompt: A visitor in Tokyo and a visitor in Paris both request the same logo image from your server in Virginia, and nothing caches it along the way. How many trips to Virginia happen for those two requests, and what would you expect a cache placed near each visitor to change?
lessons.teach:
Terms first. An origin is the server or storage bucket that holds the real copy of your content. A cache is a nearby store of copies. A cache hit is a request answered from that store. A cache miss means the request goes back to the origin, and the answer may then be stored for next time. Cloud CDN is Google's cache, attached to an external Application Load Balancer, which is the front door that receives visitor traffic and routes it to a backend service. A backend can be a managed instance group, a Cloud Storage bucket, Cloud Run, or a network endpoint group, usually shortened to NEG, which is a list of addresses or hostnames the load balancer can send traffic to. For origins outside Google, you use an internet NEG, which points at a hostname and port on the public internet. That is how third-party object storage or any external web server joins the setup.

Why it works: the cache keeps a copy keyed by the full URL by default, and it stores only responses it considers cacheable. Cacheability comes from the cache mode you choose and from the origin's Cache-Control headers, which say how long a copy may live (the max-age value). A response marked private, or one with no caching signal under a mode that requires one, is not stored.

Worked example: a logo at example.com/logo.png, where the origin sends max-age=3600. Visitor A requests it at 09:00. That is a miss, so the origin answers and the CDN stores the copy for an hour. Visitor B asks at 09:10 and gets a hit from the nearby cache, so the origin sees no request. At 10:01 the copy has expired, the next request is a miss, and the cycle restarts.

Common mistake: assuming the CDN caches everything. An API response marked private, or one that varies per user through a cookie, is generally not shared, so the hit rate stays near zero and the origin handles every request.

Consequence: a changed file can keep reaching visitors in its old form until its lifetime ends, so lifetimes are a deployment decision, not an afterthought.

questions.prompt: Harbor Books serves product catalogue PDFs from a third-party object store at files.partner-host.net on port 443. They attach it to an external Application Load Balancer through an internet NEG (a list of hostnames and ports the load balancer can send traffic to, here pointing at a server on the public internet), with Cloud CDN enabled. The store sends Cache-Control: max-age=600, so each copy lives 10 minutes. Visitor 1 requests catalogue.pdf at 14:00. Nothing is stored yet, so this is a cache miss, the store answers, and the CDN keeps a copy until 14:10. Visitor 2 requests it at 14:04 and gets a cache hit, so the store sees no request. Visitor 3 requests it at 14:12. Which outcome is correct for Visitor 3?
choices: The copy is still fresh, so it is a cache hit and the store receives no request.
The copy expired at 14:10, so this is a cache miss and the request goes back to the store, which may then store a new copy.
Cloud CDN caches all responses regardless of headers, so the 14:00 copy never expires.
The internet NEG bypasses the cache entirely, so every request goes straight to the store.
questions.why: A copy with max-age=600 stored at 14:00 is only valid until 14:10, so a request at 14:12 finds it expired, which is a miss that goes back to the origin.

questions.prompt: In Cloud CDN setups, what is an internet NEG used for?
choices: Setting how long a cached copy may live, measured in seconds.
Routing visitor traffic between two managed instance groups in the same region.
Pointing the load balancer at a hostname and port on the public internet, so an origin outside Google can be a backend.
Storing a permanent backup of the origin's files inside the load balancer.
questions.why: An internet NEG lists a hostname and port on the public internet, which is how an origin outside Google joins the load balancer as a backend.

questions.prompt: A team runs a customer account API. Its responses carry Cache-Control: private, and each response depends on the logged-in user. The team expects Cloud CDN to reduce origin load. What is the most likely result?
choices: Hit rate climbs to nearly 100 percent because the CDN shares responses across users.
The load balancer rewrites the private header so the responses become cacheable for one hour.
The CDN stores the responses but serves them to every visitor, including other users.
The responses are generally not stored for sharing, so the hit rate stays near zero and the origin handles almost every request.
questions.why: A response marked private is not shared through the cache, so the hit rate stays near zero and the origin answers each request.

questions.prompt: A supplier's storage bucket serves a price list with Cache-Control: max-age=86400 behind Cloud CDN. The supplier overwrites the file at 08:00 with new prices, and a visitor who loaded the old copy at 07:30 returns at 09:00. What does the visitor most likely see?
choices: The new prices, because overwriting a file automatically clears every cached copy worldwide.
An error, because the cache refuses to serve a file whose contents changed.
The new prices, because the CDN checks the origin on every request regardless of max-age.
The old prices, because the cached copy stays valid until its max-age lifetime ends, which is a full day after it was stored.
questions.why: The cached copy keeps being served until its max-age lifetime expires, so changed files can reach visitors in their old form until then, which makes lifetimes a deployment decision.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can put Cloud CDN in front of our third-party object storage bucket and everything will just get faster. In your own words, explain what has to be true for that to work, and name one limit or tradeoff they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cloud CDN only sits in front of a load balancer, so the third-party bucket has to be reached through an external Application Load Balancer backend, usually via an internet NEG that points at the storage provider's hostname. The cache only helps if the responses are cacheable: the storage must return sensible Cache-Control headers, and signed or per-user URLs will often be treated as unique, so the hit rate stays low. The main tradeoff is that copies live until they expire, so an updated file can be served stale for the length of its lifetime. There is also a cost angle: every miss fetches from the provider, so a low hit rate can cost money as well as speed. After turning it on, we should check the hit ratio and origin traffic rather than assume it is faster.
rubricPoints: The third-party origin must be reached through an external load balancer backend, typically an internet NEG pointing at its hostname.
Caching depends on the origin's Cache-Control headers and the cache mode, and private or per-user responses are generally not stored.
Copies live until they expire, so updated content can be served stale for the length of its lifetime.
Misses fetch from the origin each time, so a low hit rate raises origin load and cost, and the hit ratio should be measured.

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying an origin type and its cache behaviour is best learned by explaining the reasoning back, since no listed mission covers CDN configuration.

lessons.plain: Cloud CDN is a content delivery network: Google keeps copies of your web responses on servers spread around the world, so people fetch them from a nearby copy instead of from your origin server. Each copy stays for a set time, called the time to live, and then expires. Cache invalidation means throwing away copies early, before that timer runs out, for example after you publish a fix to a page that was wrong. It is a fast but blunt tool, so it is worth knowing when to use it and when a better approach exists.
lessons.guessPrompt: You fixed a typo on a product page that is cached worldwide with a one-hour lifetime. Ten minutes later, some visitors still see the typo. What do you think is happening, and what could you do to make the corrected page show up sooner?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. An origin is the server or storage bucket that holds the real content. A cache is a stored copy of a response kept closer to the people asking for it. Cloud CDN, Google's content delivery service, keeps those copies at edge locations, which are points of presence spread around the world. Each cached object has a cache key, the identifier the edge uses to decide whether a request matches a stored copy. It is usually built from the host and path, and sometimes the query string. A time to live, or TTL, says how long a copy may be served before it is treated as stale and fetched again from the origin.

Invalidation tells the edges to discard copies whose path matches a pattern now, without waiting for the TTL. A pattern names one exact path, or a prefix ending in a wildcard, such as a folder followed by an asterisk. The next time someone asks, the edge fetches a fresh copy from the origin. Invalidation is not instant. The removal has to reach every edge, so a short delay of a few minutes is normal.

Worked example. A site caches its product pages with a one-hour TTL. You change a page at 09:00 and invalidate the pattern for that folder at 09:02. Until the removal reaches a given edge, that edge may still serve the old copy. Once it has propagated, the next request at each edge misses the cache, goes to the origin, and stores the new version for another hour.

Common mistake: writing a pattern that does not match the cache key, for example invalidating the bare page URL when the cached copies include a query string, so no stored copy matches. Another is invalidating on every release. Broad or frequent invalidations send many requests back to the origin at once.

Consequence: during a traffic spike, a mass invalidation can overload the origin, so invalidate narrowly and only when content must change before its TTL ends.

questions.prompt: Harbor Kitchen runs a recipe site whose ingredient files sit in a storage bucket behind Cloud CDN, with a 20-minute TTL on everything under /lists/. At 11:15 the team saves a corrected /lists/soups.json at the origin. At 11:16 they invalidate the exact path /lists/soups.json. Step 1 is the corrected file being saved at the origin at 11:15. Step 3 is that the next request for soups.json at each edge fetches the corrected copy from the origin. What fills Step 2?
choices: The 20-minute TTL is shortened to zero, and the edges wait for it to run out before fetching again.
The origin restarts so that its cache key for soups.json changes at every edge.
Each edge immediately rewrites its stored copy with the corrected file, so no origin fetch is needed.
Each edge discards its stored copy of that path as the removal reaches it, typically within a few minutes.
questions.why: Invalidation removes the matching stored copies at each edge once the removal reaches it, which is what makes the next request miss the cache and go to the origin.

questions.prompt: A media company caches thumbnails under /thumbs/2024/ with a 6-hour TTL. It replaces one image, /thumbs/2024/cover-17.jpg, and wants to remove only that cached copy. Which invalidation pattern does this?
choices: /thumbs/2024/*
/thumbs/2024/cover-1*
/thumbs/*
/thumbs/2024/cover-17.jpg
questions.why: A pattern naming one exact path removes only copies of that path, while a wildcard prefix would also remove other files in the folder or beyond.

questions.prompt: A shop team invalidates /shop/* after every small deployment, across about 40 folders, including during a flash sale. What is the most serious risk of this habit?
choices: The cache key is rebuilt, so the edges can no longer match any request.
The origin files are deleted when the invalidation reaches the edges.
A broad mass removal sends many requests to the origin at once, which can overload it during a traffic spike.
Pages stay stale for the full TTL, so customers never see the change.
questions.why: Broad or frequent invalidations force many edges to fetch from the origin together, which can overload it at peak traffic.

questions.prompt: A team invalidates a path at 15:00. At 15:02 a user in one region still sees the old copy. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The origin ignored the invalidation because it only applies to edges in one region.
The invalidation failed permanently and must be recreated from scratch.
The removal has not yet reached that edge, and a delay of a few minutes is normal.
The TTL must be reset to zero before any edge will honour the removal.
questions.why: Invalidation is not instant because the removal must reach every edge, so a short lag before a given edge drops its old copy is expected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what cache invalidation does in Cloud CDN, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it instead of letting content expire naturally or versioning file names.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cache invalidation tells Cloud CDN to discard cached copies of matching paths before their time to live runs out, so the next request goes back to the origin and stores fresh content. I would explain that it is not instant, because the removal has to reach edge locations around the world, so a few minutes of old content can still appear. The main tradeoff is cost and load: each invalidation sends traffic back to the origin, and frequent or broad invalidations during a surge can overload it. For content that changes with each release, I would prefer versioned file names, since a new name is a new cache key and nothing needs invalidating. I would reserve invalidation for urgent corrections to content whose URL cannot change, such as a page showing wrong prices.
rubricPoints: Defines cache invalidation as discarding cached copies before the TTL expires
Notes that invalidation propagates across edges and is not instant
Names a tradeoff such as origin load or cost from broad or frequent invalidation
Mentions versioned file names as an alternative that avoids invalidation

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers CDN cache invalidation, so reading the concept and its tradeoffs is the best fit.

lessons.plain: A DNS zone is the part of the internet's address book that one team is responsible for, such as everything under example.com. Records are the individual entries inside that zone: this name points to that address, this name is an alias for another name, and this mail server handles mail for the domain. Managing a zone means creating it, adding, changing and removing these entries, and deciding how long other computers may remember each answer. Get this right and visitors reach the right service. Get it wrong and a working site can disappear for people whose computers still hold an old answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website moves to a new server with a new IP address, and you update the DNS entry at 9:00. At 9:30, some visitors still reach the old server while others already reach the new one. Which setting on the old record controls how long that mixed period lasts, and why?
lessons.teach:
A DNS zone is the portion of the domain name system that one party manages, such as everything under example.com. A zone can be public, answering anyone on the internet, or private, answering only inside networks you choose. Inside a zone sit record sets. Each record set has a name, a record type, and one or more values. The common types are A (a name to an IPv4 address), AAAA (a name to an IPv6 address), CNAME (a name that is an alias for another name), MX (the mail servers for a domain), TXT (free text, often used to prove ownership), and NS (the name servers responsible for a delegated part of the namespace). Every record set also carries a TTL, meaning time to live: the number of seconds that resolvers elsewhere may keep the answer in a cache before asking again. A resolver is the server that looks up names on behalf of a user's device.

Why it works: resolvers do not ask the authoritative zone every time. They remember answers for the TTL. So a change does not land everywhere at once. It lands as each cached copy expires. Lowering the TTL well before a planned change shortens that window. Raising it reduces lookup load but makes changes slower to take effect.

Worked example: www.example.com has an A record with value 203.0.113.10 and TTL 3600. Step 1: lower the TTL to 300 and wait at least the old 3600 seconds, so every cache holds the short value. Step 2: replace the value with 198.51.100.7. Step 3: within about five minutes, new lookups return the new address. Step 4: raise the TTL again once the move is stable.

Common mistake: editing a record and assuming the change is instant, then calling the migration broken when old answers persist. A second mistake is placing a CNAME on a name that also has other record types, which DNS does not allow.

Consequence: a record with a long TTL that points at a retired address keeps sending users to a dead server until caches expire, even though the zone already holds the correct answer.

questions.prompt: A small veterinary clinic runs its booking site at book.harbourvet.example. The name currently has an A record with value 192.0.2.44 and TTL 1800 seconds. The team plans to move the site to 192.0.2.91 at 14:00 on Friday, and they follow this sequence. Step 1: at 12:00, lower the TTL to 300 seconds. Step 2: wait at least 1800 seconds so that every cached copy holds the short TTL. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: once the new address has been stable for a day, raise the TTL back to 1800 seconds. Which action belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: Raise the TTL to 86400 seconds so that caches hold the new address longer
Delete the whole harbourvet.example zone and recreate it with the new address
Change the A record's value from 192.0.2.44 to 192.0.2.91 in the zone
Add a CNAME record on book.harbourvet.example that points to 192.0.2.91
questions.why: Step 3 is the edit itself: replacing the record's value in the zone, which then spreads to resolvers as their short-TTL caches expire.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a TXT record in a DNS zone?
choices: It holds free text and is often used to prove ownership of a domain
It maps a name to an IPv6 address so that dual-stack clients can connect
It makes one name an alias for another name that is looked up instead
It lists the mail servers that accept messages for the domain
questions.why: The teaching text defines TXT as free text, often used to prove ownership, which is the only option that matches that description.

questions.prompt: A bakery changed the A record for orders.sunridgebakes.example from an old server address to a new one at 16:00. The record's TTL is 86400 seconds. At 17:00, some customers still reach the old server. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The zone's authoritative server has not saved the change, so it still returns the old address
The record type was wrong, so DNS ignores the new value until the type is corrected
Resolvers elsewhere may still hold the old answer in cache until its TTL runs out
The bakery's customers are using IPv6, which always reads a different A record
questions.why: Resolvers cache answers for the TTL, so a long TTL means cached copies of the old address can persist for up to a day even though the zone already holds the new one.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a name, track.bluefin-freight.example, that is set up as a CNAME pointing to a hosted tracking service. An engineer wants to add a TXT record on that same name to prove domain ownership to a third-party tool. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: It cannot be done on that name, because a CNAME name may not also carry other record types
It works, but only if the TXT value is written in IPv6 form
It works only if the TTL of the CNAME is set below 300 seconds
It works, because TXT records are free text and do not count as record types
questions.why: The teaching text states that DNS does not allow a CNAME on a name that also has other record types, so the TXT record cannot sit on that name.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that to move a website to a new server you only need to change the DNS record, and the change will be live everywhere immediately. Explain to them what actually happens, and name one limit or tradeoff of the TTL setting that you would weigh before a planned change.
lessons.modelAnswer: Changing the record only updates the answer held in the authoritative zone. Other resolvers, such as those run by internet providers or office networks, keep the old answer in their cache until its TTL runs out. During that window, some users reach the old server and others reach the new one. Before the change, lower the TTL well ahead of time, wait at least the old TTL so the short value is everywhere, switch the value, and raise the TTL again once the move is stable. The tradeoff is that a very short TTL means more lookups hitting your name servers, which adds load and cost. A long TTL makes the cutover slow and hard to reverse quickly. So the right value depends on how fast you need to be able to roll back.
rubricPoints: Changing a record updates the authoritative zone, but cached copies elsewhere keep the old answer.
Caches expire on the TTL, so the switch is gradual and users can see old and new answers at the same time.
Lowering the TTL before a change shortens the transition window, while long TTLs slow cutovers.
A short TTL trades faster change for more lookup traffic on the name servers.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises DNS zone or record management, so reading the record types and TTL rules is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Migrating to Cloud DNS means moving the job of answering questions like 'what address does www.example.com point to?' from your current DNS provider to Google Cloud's managed DNS service. DNS works like the internet's phone book, and the servers that hold a domain's records are its authoritative servers. Moving them safely is less like flipping a switch and more like moving house: you copy everything into the new place, check that it works, and only then update the address the rest of the world uses to find it. If you do this in the wrong order, people looking up your names can get no answer for a while.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's website name is currently answered by a DNS provider you plan to leave. If you change the domain's nameserver setting at the registrar before copying the records into the new service, what might visitors see, and why?
lessons.teach:
A DNS zone is the set of records a domain owns, such as A records (name to IPv4 address), MX records (mail servers) and TXT records (text used for verification). A managed zone is a zone hosted for you by a managed service instead of on a server you run yourself. Delegation is the step where the parent of your domain, changed through your domain registrar, lists which nameservers are authoritative for your zone. Each record carries a TTL, the number of seconds resolvers may keep an answer in their cache.

Why the order matters: resolvers ask the nameservers the registrar currently lists. Only after delegation changes do the new nameservers become the source of answers. So the records must already exist in the new zone, and must be verified, before delegation moves.

Worked example. The domain example.com has an A record for www with TTL 3600 pointing to 203.0.113.10. Step 1: lower the TTL to 300 at the old provider and wait at least one old TTL so cached copies expire. Step 2: create a public managed zone for example.com in Cloud DNS. Step 3: recreate or import every record, including www A 203.0.113.10 and the mail records. Step 4: query the new zone's nameservers directly and confirm every answer matches the old zone. Step 5: change the nameservers at the registrar to the new ones. Step 6: keep the old zone live until caches have expired, then retire it.

Common mistake: changing delegation before every record is imported, so web and mail names return no answer for anyone whose resolver has refreshed. A missing answer can also be cached for a period, so the mistake can persist after the fix. Lowering TTLs in advance limits how long old answers linger. Verify first, delegate second, and retire the old zone last.

questions.prompt: A team runs harbourtools.net and wants to hand the subdomain shop.harbourtools.net to a new Cloud DNS managed zone. The parent zone at the current provider holds NS records for shop that must point at the new nameservers. Their plan: Step 1, create a public managed zone for shop.harbourtools.net in Cloud DNS. Step 2, import the A record shop 198.51.100.7 and its TXT verification records. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, change the NS records for shop in the parent zone to the new nameservers. Step 5, keep the old shop records live until caches expire. Which action belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: Query the new zone's nameservers directly and confirm each answer matches the old zone before changing the NS records.
Wait for the registrar to send a confirmation email before doing anything else.
Set the shop A record TTL to 86400 so cached copies last longer during the switch.
Delete the shop records from the old zone so that only one copy of each answer exists.
questions.why: Resolvers begin using the new zone only after the parent's NS records change, so the records must be checked against the new nameservers before delegation moves.

questions.prompt: What is a managed zone in this context?
choices: A record type that lists the mail servers that accept email for a domain, used by senders to find where to deliver messages.
A zone hosted for you by a managed service, instead of on a server you run yourself, which holds the records a domain owns and answers queries for them.
A list kept by the domain registrar of the nameservers that the parent of your domain says are authoritative for your zone.
A text record used to prove to a verifier that you control a domain, commonly added during setup of a new hosting service.
questions.why: A managed zone is a DNS zone hosted by a managed service rather than a server you operate, which is the definition the text gives; the other options describe MX records, TXT records, and delegation.

questions.prompt: A team at mydocs-lab.org changes the nameservers at their registrar to the new Cloud DNS zone, but they never imported the MX records for mail. Which outcome is most likely, and why?
choices: Mail keeps working with no problem, because mail servers are looked up from a global directory and never from the zone the registrar points to, so the missing records are irrelevant to delivery.
Only web visitors are affected, because mail routing always uses the old zone's cache, which never expires once delegation has moved.
Mail is delivered to the old provider until someone changes the registrar back, because the registrar keeps a copy of the previous MX records.
Resolvers that have refreshed receive no mail server answer from the new nameservers, and that missing answer can persist in caches even after the records are added.
questions.why: Delegation sends resolvers to the new nameservers, so records absent there return no answer, and a cached missing answer can prolong the outage after the fix.

questions.prompt: The api.harbourtools.net A record has a TTL of 14400 seconds, and a team wants to move the domain to a new Cloud DNS zone within ten minutes. Which first step does the teaching text's ordering support?
choices: Retire the old zone immediately so that stale cached answers stop being served by anyone who asks.
Raise the TTL to 86400 so the record is cached less often by resolvers during the transition period.
Lower the record's TTL at the current provider and wait at least one old TTL, four hours, so cached copies expire before delegation moves.
Change the nameservers at the registrar now, since the 14400 second TTL only affects resolvers that have not yet fetched the record.
questions.why: Lowering the TTL in advance and waiting at least one old TTL lets cached copies expire before the nameservers change, which the text recommends over changing delegation immediately.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we cannot just point the domain at Cloud DNS and fix the records afterwards. Explain the migration order to them in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of lowering TTLs before the move.
lessons.modelAnswer: Delegation is what makes the world use the new zone. Once the registrar points to the new nameservers, resolvers start asking them, and if the records are not there yet, names quietly stop resolving for anyone who refreshes. So we first copy every record into a managed zone, check that its answers match the old ones, and only then change the registrar's nameservers. Lowering TTLs before the move means cached old answers expire quickly, so a mistake is corrected fast. The tradeoff is that low TTLs send more queries to the authoritative servers and cache less, so we raise the TTLs again once the migration is stable. We also keep the old zone running until the old TTL has passed, because some resolvers still hold the previous delegation.
rubricPoints: Records must be copied and verified in the new zone before delegation changes.
Delegation at the registrar is the switch that sends resolvers to the new nameservers.
Lowering TTLs before the move shortens how long old answers stay cached.
The old zone stays live until cached answers have expired, then it is retired.
Low TTLs add query load, so TTLs are raised again once the move is stable.

suggested.rationale: The migration is a sequence of facts and console steps that no listed mission practises, so reading the procedure is the best fit.

lessons.plain: A DNS record normally gives every asker the same answer. A routing policy lets the DNS service choose the answer based on who is asking or whether a destination is still working. Geolocation routing answers with a server near the asker's region, so users in one part of the world can be sent to a different copy of a site than users somewhere else. Failover routing answers with a main server while it passes health checks, and switches to a backup when it does not. Both are attached to one name, so users keep typing the same address and nothing changes on their side.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one website name is served from two data centers, and you want users in Europe to reach the European one while the rest of the world uses the other, what would you change in the DNS setup, and what would you need to know to know when the European one is down?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A DNS zone is the set of names one domain manages in Cloud DNS, Google's managed DNS service. A record set is the group of answers for one name and one record type, such as the IP addresses behind www.example.com. A routing policy replaces the plain answer list with rules that Cloud DNS evaluates each time a lookup arrives. A geolocation policy maps regions to their own answers. Cloud DNS infers where a request comes from using the location of the querying network, so the answer reflects where the request appears to originate, not the exact user. A failover policy holds a primary answer set and a backup answer set. Cloud DNS runs a health check, a probe that asks each target whether it is alive, against the primary targets. While they pass, the primary answers. When they fail, the backup answers.

Why it works: the decision happens inside DNS, so clients keep the same name and need no code change. Answers are cached for their time to live (TTL), so a switch is not instant. Clients may hold an old answer until its TTL expires.

Worked example. www.example.com has a failover policy with primary 203.0.113.10 and backup 198.51.100.10, health-checked over HTTPS. Step 1: a client asks for www.example.com. Step 2: Cloud DNS looks at the health state of 203.0.113.10. Step 3: the probes pass, so the primary address is returned. Step 4: the primary stops answering, and enough probes fail to mark it unhealthy. Step 5: new lookups now receive 198.51.100.10. Clients holding a cached answer switch once their TTL runs out.

Common mistake: assuming a failover policy without a working health check will ever switch, or setting a long TTL and expecting an instant switch.

Consequence: during an outage, some users keep receiving the dead address until caches expire, so the TTL is part of your recovery time.

questions.prompt: A media company runs stream.example.net with a failover policy. The primary answer is 192.0.2.44 and the backup is 192.0.2.88. The health check is HTTP and the TTL is 300 seconds. Step 1: the primary origin servers start failing their probes. Step 2: the probes keep failing until the policy marks 192.0.2.44 unhealthy. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: a viewer whose device cached the old answer just before the failure looks up the name again 6 minutes later and receives 192.0.2.88. Which completion fills step 3?
choices: Cloud DNS keeps returning 192.0.2.44 until someone edits the record set by hand.
Cloud DNS sends the viewer a redirect so the switch happens at the connection level, not in DNS.
New lookups now receive 192.0.2.88, while devices holding the old answer keep it until its 300-second TTL expires.
The TTL drops to zero, so every device switches to 192.0.2.88 at the moment of the failure.
questions.why: Once the primary is marked unhealthy, new lookups receive the backup, and cached copies of the old answer only change when their TTL runs out.

questions.prompt: In Cloud DNS, what does a geolocation routing policy do?
choices: It checks each target's health and switches between a primary and a backup answer set.
It maps regions to their own answers, inferred from the querying network.
It sends every lookup to the nearest data centre by measuring each user's exact location.
It replaces the TTL so that clients never cache an answer.
questions.why: A geolocation policy gives region-specific answers, and the region is inferred from where the querying network appears to be, not from the exact user.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants visitors in one part of the world to receive a server address near them and visitors elsewhere to receive a different address, all through DNS with no code change. Which setting fits?
choices: A failover policy with a health check, which switches between primary and backup answers.
A geolocation policy, returning answers by querying-network region.
A single record set listing both addresses, so each client picks the nearer one itself.
A longer TTL on a plain record set, so answers stay the same for longer.
questions.why: Only a geolocation policy returns different answers based on where the querying network appears to be, and it does this inside DNS so clients keep the same name.

questions.prompt: A team set up a failover policy for app.example.io with a primary and a backup address but never attached a health check. The primary server then crashes. What happens to new lookups?
choices: They return the backup only after the TTL runs out.
They are refused until the team adds a health check.
They switch to the backup at once, because the policy assumes failure when no probe exists.
They keep returning the primary, since without a health check the policy never sees it fail.
questions.why: A failover policy only switches when its health check marks the primary unhealthy, so without a working health check the primary keeps being returned.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a geolocation routing policy and a failover routing policy on the same service name, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on DNS for failover.
lessons.modelAnswer: Geolocation routing decides the answer by where the request seems to come from. Each region gets its own set of addresses, so European users might get a European server and others get a different one. Failover routing decides the answer by whether the primary is healthy. It returns the primary addresses while health checks pass and returns the backup when they fail. The two can be combined on the same name, but you need to be clear which rule you are relying on. The main limit is caching. DNS answers are held by resolvers and clients for their TTL, so a failover is not immediate, and a long TTL means some users keep hitting a dead address for a while. A shorter TTL speeds switching but increases query volume. Another tradeoff is that health checks only see what they probe, so a check that passes while the real application is broken will keep users on a bad server.
rubricPoints: Geolocation chooses the answer by the requester's location, with one answer set per region.
Failover chooses the primary while health checks pass and the backup when they fail.
The health check defines what counts as healthy, so a weak check can keep users on a broken target.
TTL caching delays switches, so recovery time depends on how long answers are cached.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is choosing between geolocation and failover and explaining their limits, which is best practiced by articulating the tradeoffs rather than by a console-only or mission-based exercise.

lessons.plain: DNSSEC is a way to prove that the answers a domain name gives out are genuine. When someone looks up the address for a website, their computer normally trusts whatever answer comes back, and a clever attacker can slip in a fake one that sends people to the wrong place. DNSSEC attaches a digital signature to the records, made with a secret key that only the domain owner holds. Anyone checking the answer can use the matching public key to confirm that the owner signed it and that nothing was changed on the way. Turning it on is a choice you make for each domain zone, and it only works fully when the trust chain is also published with the domain's parent.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an attacker could sneak a fake IP address into a resolver's cache for your domain, what extra piece of information would let a resolver tell the fake answer from the real one, and where would that information need to come from?
lessons.teach: A DNS zone is the set of records that one party controls for a domain, such as the address records for www.example.com. A resolver is the server that asks questions on a client's behalf and caches the answers. DNSSEC, the DNS Security Extensions, adds signatures to DNS answers so a resolver can check that the data came from the zone owner and was not altered. The signing works with a pair of keys. The zone signing key signs each record set and produces an RRSIG record, which is the signature stored alongside the data. The key signing key signs the set of public keys itself, which lives in DNSKEY records. The key signing key is also hashed into a DS record, the delegation signer, which the domain's parent zone publishes. That link is the chain of trust: a validating resolver checks the record signature against the zone's public key, then checks that key against the DS record in the parent, and so on up to the root. Worked example: the zone example.com is signed, so the www record and its RRSIG are returned together. The resolver verifies the RRSIG using the DNSKEY, then hashes the key signing key and compares it to the DS record published under the .com zone. If all three match, the answer is accepted. Common mistake: enabling signing in the zone but never copying the DS record to the registrar, or moving DNS hosting and leaving the old DS record in place. Validating resolvers then reject the answers and return a failure, so the site appears down for those users while unvalidating resolvers still work, which makes the fault hard to spot. DNSSEC protects answer integrity, not confidentiality, and it only helps when every link in the chain is kept in step.

questions.prompt: The team at lab.example.ac signs its zone. A validating resolver asks for portal.lab.example.ac and receives the address record together with its RRSIG. The team's sequence for making the chain complete is: (1) enable signing in the zone, which creates a zone signing key and a key signing key; (2) publish the DNSKEY records for both keys in the zone; (3) [missing step]; (4) confirm that a validating resolver accepts the answer. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Give the zone signing key's DNSKEY to the resolver operator by email
Hash the key signing key into a DS record and submit it to the parent zone's registrar
Delete the RRSIG record so resolvers stop comparing signatures
Set the portal host's record to a shorter cache lifetime
questions.why: The parent zone can only vouch for the key signing key once a DS record made from that key is published there, so without this step the resolver has no link from the parent to the zone's keys.

questions.prompt: In a signed zone, which key signs the set of public keys that is stored in the DNSKEY records?
choices: The DS record held by the parent zone
The resolver's cache key
The key signing key
The zone signing key
questions.why: The key signing key signs the DNSKEY set, and it is also the key that gets hashed into the DS record the parent publishes.

questions.prompt: The owner of example-gear.store moves DNS hosting to a new provider and turns on signing there, but the registrar still holds the DS record for the old key. What happens to validating resolvers when they ask for the zone's answers?
choices: They ignore DNSSEC and serve the answers without checking
They serve the answers but mark the connection as encrypted
They reject the answers and return a failure, while non-validating resolvers still work
They automatically fetch a new DS record from the zone itself
questions.why: A validating resolver checks the chain up to the parent, and a DS record that no longer matches the zone's key breaks that chain, so answers are rejected even though non-validating resolvers still get them.

questions.prompt: A team enables DNSSEC for a booking zone and asks whether it also hides the record contents from anyone watching the network. Which statement is correct?
choices: Yes, but only for the address record type
No, it only hides the zone's key signing key from the public
Yes, signed answers are encrypted in transit
No, it adds signatures so answers can be checked for origin and alteration, not secrecy
questions.why: DNSSEC provides integrity and origin checking through signatures, but it does not encrypt or hide the record data, so confidentiality is not part of what it provides.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should not just enable DNSSEC on the zone and call it done. Explain to them what DNSSEC protects, what it does not protect, and the operational tradeoff we accept by turning it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: DNSSEC lets resolvers verify that a DNS answer was signed by the zone owner and was not changed in transit, so cache poisoning and spoofed answers can be detected. It does not encrypt the lookup, so anyone on the path can still see which names are queried, and it does not stop the domain owner from publishing a wrong record. The tradeoff is operational: the zone signs its records and keys have to be rotated, and the DS record in the parent must match the current key signing key. If that chain breaks, for example after a DNS provider change or a missed key rollover, validating resolvers fail the lookup and the site looks down to some users. So enabling it is only finished when the DS record is published, verified, and monitored through key changes.
rubricPoints: DNSSEC proves that answers came from the zone owner and were not altered, which defends against spoofing and cache poisoning.
DNSSEC does not encrypt queries or hide which names are looked up.
The chain of trust needs the DS record published at the parent, so enabling signing alone is incomplete.
A broken chain, such as after a provider change or key rollover, causes validating resolvers to fail, so the change must be managed and monitored.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic failure where signing is on but validation fails adds more than reading facts, because it tests how the chain of trust links the zone to its parent.

lessons.plain: Many organisations run their own DNS servers, the phone book that turns names such as billing.corp.example into network addresses, and they also run systems in the cloud. Self-hosted DNS integration means making those phone books work together, so a name kept on your own servers can be found from the cloud and a private cloud name can be found from your data centre. Forwarding is the rule that says 'for this part of the naming tree, ask that other server instead of answering yourself.' A DNS server policy is the cloud network setting that decides which resolvers its machines use and whether outside systems may ask the cloud for names.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your data centre runs its own DNS server that is the authority for corp.example, and a virtual machine in the cloud needs to reach billing.corp.example. With no DNS setup at all, which server would the cloud machine ask first, and why would it probably fail to get an answer?
lessons.teach:
DNS (the Domain Name System) turns names into addresses. A resolver is the server that receives a question and works out the answer. An authoritative server is the one that actually holds the records for a domain. Cloud DNS is Google Cloud's managed DNS service. A forwarding zone is a Cloud DNS zone that holds no records of its own; instead it lists target servers and says, for one domain, send every question to them. A DNS server policy is a setting on a VPC network (a virtual, private network in the cloud) that controls the resolvers its machines use and can enable an inbound forwarding endpoint, an address inside the VPC that on-premises resolvers can query to reach Cloud DNS private zones.

Why it works: a resolver that does not own a domain can pass the question to a server that does, and the answer comes back to the original asker. Worked example: a cloud VM asks for billing.corp.example. Step 1: the query goes to the VPC's resolver. Step 2: the resolver finds no record for corp.example, but finds a forwarding zone for that domain listing 10.20.0.5. Step 3: it forwards the question to 10.20.0.5 over the VPC's routing, which goes through the VPN or interconnect. Step 4: the on-premises server answers 10.30.4.12 and the answer returns to the VM.

Common mistake: pointing a forwarding zone at a server that forwards the same domain back to the cloud. The two resolvers then pass the question between them until it times out. In a running system, that loop or an unreachable target makes every lookup for that domain slow or failing, so services report name-resolution errors even though the records exist.

The same logic runs the other way: on-premises resolvers can only reach private cloud zones if an inbound forwarding endpoint exists and the network path allows the query.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, Harbor Lane, runs warehouse software on a VM inside a VPC and keeps its internal names under depot.harbor.test. Its office DNS server is 172.16.8.20. The VM asks for scanner1.depot.harbor.test. Step 1: the query reaches the VPC's resolver. Step 2: the resolver finds no local record, but finds a forwarding zone for depot.harbor.test listing 172.16.8.20. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the office server answers 172.16.9.31 and the answer returns to the VM. Which sentence correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: The VM sends the question straight to a public root server, bypassing the VPC's resolver.
The resolver copies the scanner record from the office server into a new private zone before answering.
The resolver sends the question to 172.16.8.20 over the VPC's routing, which crosses the VPN tunnel to the office.
The resolver replies NXDOMAIN at once, because a forwarding zone never sends questions anywhere.
questions.why: A forwarding zone passes the question to its listed target over the VPC's routing, which here runs through the VPN to the office, so the correct step is the forward to 172.16.8.20.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a forwarding zone in Cloud DNS?
choices: A full mirror of an office server's record set, kept in sync by Cloud DNS automatically
A zone with no records that forwards one domain's questions to listed targets
A VPC setting that selects the resolvers its machines use and also copies office records over
An inbound endpoint address inside the VPC that on-premises servers query for private zones
questions.why: A forwarding zone holds no records of its own; it names target servers and sends every question for one domain to them.

questions.prompt: The Bluefin Dental office resolvers, at 10.50.0.2, need to look up names in a private Cloud DNS zone called clinic.bluefin.test. Which setup meets that need?
choices: Set the office resolver to query public internet root servers for the zone name and trust whatever comes back
Enable an inbound forwarding endpoint with a DNS server policy and allow the query path
Add a forwarding zone in the VPC that sends clinic.bluefin.test back to the office resolver 10.50.0.2 for every lookup it receives
Copy the private zone's records into a text file on the office server and reload that file by hand each night
questions.why: On-premises resolvers reach private Cloud DNS zones through an inbound forwarding endpoint enabled by a DNS server policy, provided the network path permits the query.

questions.prompt: Quarry Labs set up a forwarding zone for lab.quarry.test that lists 192.168.40.7. That server is configured to forward lab.quarry.test back to Cloud DNS. What is the most likely symptom?
choices: Cloud DNS has lost the records, so every answer comes back empty right away without any delay at all
The VPC blocks all outbound UDP, so only domains with public records will resolve at all
The forwarding zone deletes itself after one failed query, which removes the entry from the network
The resolvers bounce the question between them until it times out, so lookups slow or fail
questions.why: Two resolvers forwarding the same domain to each other pass the question back and forth until it times out, making lookups slow or failing even though the records exist.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a forwarding zone in Cloud DNS and an inbound server policy, and name one limit or tradeoff of sending DNS queries to your own servers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A forwarding zone lives in Cloud DNS and handles lookups from the cloud side. It names one domain, such as corp.example, and lists target servers in the data centre. When a cloud machine asks for a name in that domain, the query is passed to those servers instead of being answered locally. An inbound server policy works the other way. It is set on the VPC network and creates an inbound forwarding endpoint, an address inside the VPC that on-premises resolvers can query to reach Cloud DNS private zones. The tradeoff is dependency. Every forwarded lookup now depends on the on-premises servers and on the VPN or interconnect path being up. If that path fails, names that could have been answered in the cloud start timing out, so you should keep forwarding targets redundant and check that the path is open for DNS traffic.
rubricPoints: A forwarding zone sends lookups for one domain from the cloud side to named target servers.
An inbound server policy exposes an address in the VPC so on-premises resolvers can query Cloud DNS private zones.
Forwarding depends on network reachability, such as VPN or interconnect, so a failed path breaks lookups.
Targets should be redundant, and forwarding loops between resolvers must be avoided.

suggested.rationale: A hybrid naming situation with competing resolver choices is best reasoned through as an exam-style scenario, since no current mission covers DNS.

lessons.plain: The domain name system, or DNS, is the internet's address book: it turns a readable name like shop.example.com into the number address a computer connects to. A DNS zone is a container of records for one domain that a DNS service answers for. A public zone answers questions from anyone on the internet. A private zone answers only for requests coming from networks you have attached to it, such as your own cloud network, so internal names stay hidden from outsiders. Split-horizon DNS means keeping both zones for the same name, so the same name gives different answers depending on who is asking. Insiders and outsiders can then each reach the right server using the same name.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's customers reach shop.example.com over the internet, and its staff inside the company cloud network also need to reach shop.example.com, but should land on an internal server instead. Should one name ever return different addresses, and how would you let both groups use the same name?
lessons.teach:
A DNS zone is the set of records a DNS service answers for one domain, such as example.com. A record is one entry, such as a name pointing to an IP address. A public zone is visible to the whole internet: any resolver, which is the server that answers a client's name question, can ask it. A private zone is visible only to the cloud networks you attach to it, so a request from outside those networks never reaches it. Attachment means the resolvers inside that network consult the private zone before anything else for the names it holds.

Split-horizon DNS means the same name gets different answers depending on where the question comes from. It works because the two zones are separate and the asking network decides which one answers.

Worked example. The company has a public zone for example.com with a record saying shop.example.com points to 203.0.113.10, a public load balancer. It also has a private zone for example.com, attached to its VPC, with a record saying shop.example.com points to 10.0.0.5, an internal load balancer.

Step 1: A customer asks for shop.example.com from the internet. That network is not attached to the private zone, so the public zone answers 203.0.113.10.

Step 2: A backend machine inside the VPC asks for the same name. Its network is attached to the private zone, so that zone answers first with 10.0.0.5.

Step 3: The backend connects to the internal address and its traffic never leaves the network.

Common mistake: creating a private zone for example.com but leaving out a record that internal clients still need, such as mail.example.com. Inside the VPC the private zone answers for the whole domain, so mail.example.com returns nothing rather than falling back to the public zone. In a running system, internal services that depend on that name fail to resolve even though the public records are fine.

The rule to remember: for any name, the zone attached to the asking network decides the answer, so every name internal clients need must exist in the private zone.

questions.prompt:
Lakeside Labs runs a public zone for lakeside-labs.io and a private zone for the same domain, attached only to the VPC named batch-vpc. The public zone has a record saying reports.lakeside-labs.io points to 198.51.100.44, a public load balancer. The private zone has a record saying reports.lakeside-labs.io points to 10.20.0.8, an internal load balancer.

Step 1: A partner on the internet asks for reports.lakeside-labs.io. Its network is not attached to the private zone, so the public zone answers 198.51.100.44.

Step 2: A nightly job running inside batch-vpc asks for reports.lakeside-labs.io. Fill in what happens at this step.

Step 3: The job connects to 10.20.0.8, so its traffic stays inside the network.
choices: The public zone answers first with 198.51.100.44, and the job sends its traffic out over the internet to the public load balancer.
Both zones answer, and the resolver picks whichever record has the lower time-to-live value.
The private zone, because batch-vpc is attached to it, answers first with 10.20.0.8 before the public zone is consulted.
The job receives no answer at all, because a private zone cannot hold a record for a name that also exists publicly.
questions.why: Because batch-vpc is attached to the private zone, its resolvers consult that zone first for names it holds, so the internal address 10.20.0.8 is returned.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines a private zone in cloud DNS?
choices: A zone that stores records for internal IP addresses and automatically publishes them to every project in the organisation.
A zone that any resolver on the internet can query, but which holds only internal-use records.
A zone whose records are visible only to the cloud networks attached to it, so requests from outside those networks never reach it.
A zone that serves as a backup copy of the public zone and answers only when the public zone is unreachable.
questions.why: A private zone is visible only to the networks attached to it, and requests from elsewhere never reach it, which is the definition given in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A team creates a private zone for corp-tools.net and attaches it to their VPC. The private zone holds one record, api.corp-tools.net. The public zone for corp-tools.net also holds mail.corp-tools.net. A virtual machine inside the VPC asks for mail.corp-tools.net. What happens?
choices: The private zone passes the question to the public zone, which returns the mail address.
The virtual machine receives the public address for mail because internal lookups always prefer public records.
The attached private zone answers for the whole domain and has no mail record, so the lookup returns nothing and does not fall back to the public zone.
The lookup is queued until a mail record is added to the private zone, then answered automatically.
questions.why: For a name in an attached network, the private zone answers for the whole domain, so a missing internal record returns nothing rather than falling back to the public zone.

questions.prompt: A company wants the name status.harbor-foods.com to reach a public load balancer for customers on the internet and an internal load balancer for servers in its VPC. Which setup achieves this?
choices: A single public zone for harbor-foods.com with the internal address, because internet customers can reach private addresses through the VPC.
Two private zones for harbor-foods.com, one attached to the VPC and one attached to a second VPC, each holding the public address.
A public zone for harbor-foods.com with the public address only, and a rule that rewrites the answer for VPC clients at query time.
A public zone for harbor-foods.com with the public address, plus a private zone for harbor-foods.com attached to the VPC with the internal address.
