questions.why: Split-horizon DNS needs two separate zones for the same name, a public one answering internet clients and an attached private one answering the VPC, so each asker gets the right address.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a public zone and a private zone can both hold shop.example.com and still work correctly, and name one limit or risk of split-horizon DNS that you would watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both zones can hold the same name because they answer different askers. The public zone is reachable from the internet and gives customers the public load balancer address. The private zone is attached only to our VPC, so resolvers inside the network check it first and get the internal address. Which zone answers depends on which network the query comes from, not on the name itself. The main risk is that a private zone takes over the whole domain for the networks attached to it. Any name missing from the private zone, such as an internal mail host, stops resolving inside the VPC even though it still works from the internet. So before attaching a private zone, I would confirm that every record internal clients need exists in it, and I would test resolution from inside the network as well as from outside.
rubricPoints: Explains that a public zone answers any internet asker while a private zone answers only attached networks.
Explains that the asking network determines which zone answers, so one name can return different addresses.
Names the risk that a private zone shadows the whole domain, so missing records stop resolving inside the network.
Recommends checking that all internally needed records exist and testing resolution from inside and outside.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style split-horizon scenario about which zone answers which asker adds the most, and no listed mission or engine covers DNS directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine several separate office buildings, each with its own internal phone directory that only staff inside can use. Sometimes a team in one building needs to look up names kept in another building's directory, without moving that directory. DNS cross-project binding and DNS peering are two ways Google Cloud lets a private name lookup reach across network boundaries that belong to different projects. Your job is to know which one fits a given setup, and what each one costs in terms of ownership and trust.
lessons.guessPrompt: If two separate networks in different projects both need to resolve the same private hostname, what do you think has to be true about who controls the records and where the lookup is answered?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A DNS zone is a set of names, such as app.internal.example, and the answers for them. A private zone answers only queries that come from networks you attach to it. A VPC network is a virtual network, and a project is the container that owns resources, permissions and billing. Cross-project binding means a private zone owned in one project is attached to a VPC network that lives in a different project, so that network's machines can resolve the zone's records. The zone owner keeps control of the records, but the network's project must also allow the attachment, which takes permissions in both projects. DNS peering means a network that does not own a zone forwards lookups for that zone's names to another network, called the producer. The producer answers from its own private zones. The consumer keeps no copy of the records.

Why it works: a machine sends its lookup to the resolver of its network. That resolver checks the zones bound to the network. With peering, a matching name is handed to the producer network's resolver, which applies its own bindings, so the answer reflects the producer's view.

Worked example: a payments service on network B needs db.internal.example, which lives in a private zone bound to network A in project one. Step 1: the zone owner also binds network B, which is cross-project binding, so B's resolver answers directly. Step 2: as an alternative, B creates a peering zone for internal.example that targets network A. A lookup from B is forwarded to A's resolver, which answers from A's bindings.

Common mistake: assuming peering copies records into the consumer, or that binding gives the other project the right to edit the zone. Neither is true. A peered network sees whatever the producer sees, and only the zone owner edits records.

Consequence: if the producer's resolver cannot answer, lookups from every consumer that peers to it fail too, so one producer outage can break many dependent networks at once.

questions.prompt: A retail company has a private zone named orders.corp.test in project shop-core, bound to a VPC network called edge-vpc. The analytics team runs reporting machines on a network called reporting-vpc in project analytics-prod, and those machines need the orders names. The analytics team chooses peering. Step 1: in analytics-prod, they create a peering zone for orders.corp.test that targets edge-vpc. Step 2: a reporting machine looks up orders.corp.test. Missing step: ??? Step 3: the reporting machine receives the record and the lookup succeeds.
choices: The query is sent to the shop-core owner's console, which must approve each lookup before an answer is returned.
The reporting network's resolver copies the record from edge-vpc into a local zone and answers from that copy.
The reporting network's resolver ignores the peering zone and answers from whatever zones are bound to reporting-vpc.
The query is forwarded to edge-vpc's resolver, which answers from the private zones bound to edge-vpc.
questions.why: With peering, the consumer hands the matching name to the producer network's resolver, and that resolver answers using its own bindings, not a copy or an approval step.

questions.prompt: A retail team in project store-web owns a private zone cart.internal.shop bound to front-vpc. A batch job in project etl-jobs runs on batch-vpc and needs those names resolved. Which action makes batch-vpc's machines able to resolve cart.internal.shop through the zone?
choices: Exporting the zone's records to a file and loading them into a new zone in etl-jobs.
Creating a single A record in batch-vpc that points to the front-vpc address.
Nothing; only the store-web owner can answer for the zone, so the batch project must wait.
Binding the zone to batch-vpc, which needs permission in both projects for the attachment.
questions.why: Cross-project binding attaches the owner's zone to the other project's network, and the attachment requires permissions in both projects.

questions.prompt: Five consumer networks peer to a producer network P for the zone corp.example. P's resolver becomes unavailable. What happens to lookups from the consumers for corp.example names?
choices: Only the zone owner loses the ability to edit the records until P recovers.
Every consumer that forwards corp.example lookups to P fails, because P is the only place those names are answered.
Nothing fails, because each consumer keeps its own copy of the records from when peering was set up.
Only the newest consumer network fails, because the others already have records stored.
questions.why: Peered consumers keep no copy of the records, so when the producer's resolver cannot answer, all dependent lookups fail together.

questions.prompt: A developer says: we peered our network to the producer's zone, so we can now add and change records in that zone from our own project. Which statement is correct?
choices: That is correct, because peering gives the consumer's project edit rights over the producer's zone.
That is incorrect, because peering does not grant edit rights and the consumer can only copy records into its own zone to change them.
That is correct only for records whose names end with the consumer project's own name.
That is incorrect, because peering gives read access only, and the consumer's project still cannot edit the zone through the producer's owner.
questions.why: Peering lets a consumer's lookups be answered by the producer, but only the zone owner edits records, and the consumer keeps no copy to edit.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between cross-project binding and DNS peering for a private zone, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing peering over binding.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cross-project binding attaches the existing private zone directly to a network in another project, so that network's resolver answers from the zone itself. The zone owner still controls every record, and the network's project must allow the attachment. DNS peering works differently: the consumer network creates its own zone that points lookups for those names at a producer network, and the producer's resolver answers. The consumer never holds a copy of the records. The tradeoff with peering is dependency. Every lookup now passes through the producer's resolver, so if that producer has a problem or its bindings change, the consumer's answers change or fail with it. Binding avoids that forwarding step but spreads the zone across more attached networks, which needs careful permission management.
rubricPoints: Cross-project binding attaches the owner's private zone directly to a network in another project.
DNS peering forwards matching lookups to a producer network, which answers from its own zones.
Neither approach copies records; the zone owner or producer keeps control of the data.
A named tradeoff, such as the consumer depending on the producer's resolver availability.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration facts and the distinction between two setups, which a reading lesson covers well with no existing mission or planned engine targeting DNS.

lessons.plain: Cloud DNS is Google Cloud's hosted service for the phone book of the internet. It turns a human name like shop.example.com into the numeric address a computer connects to. You keep your names in a managed zone, a container for every record under one domain, and each record is one entry such as 'this name points to this address'. On Kubernetes, services get new addresses as they are rebuilt, so keeping names current by hand does not scale. The external-dns operator is a small program running inside the cluster that watches for services wanting a public name and writes the matching record into Cloud DNS for you.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a web service's public IP address changes after its server is replaced, what would have to happen so that users typing the same domain name still reach it, and what should make that change?
lessons.teach:
DNS, the Domain Name System, is the lookup service that maps names to addresses. A resolver asks a chain of servers for the record for a name, and each answer carries a TTL, the time-to-live in seconds that tells caches how long they may keep it. Cloud DNS is Google Cloud's hosted DNS. Its key objects are the managed zone, which holds all records for one domain such as example.com, and the record set, which groups records of one name and type, such as an A record that maps a name to an IPv4 address.

Why it works: a name in a zone is just data, so changing an address means changing one record, and every client picks up the new answer once its cached copy expires. The hard part on Kubernetes is that addresses are assigned by the platform and change when load balancers are recreated. External-dns is an open-source controller you run inside the cluster. It watches Kubernetes objects that carry a hostname, reads the address the platform assigned, and creates or updates the matching record in the Cloud DNS zone. It also writes an ownership TXT record next to each entry, so it only deletes records it created itself.

Worked example. A Service exposes a load balancer and carries an annotation asking for api.example.com. Step 1: the load balancer gets external IP 203.0.113.10. Step 2: external-dns sees the Service and the address. Step 3: it calls Cloud DNS, which holds the zone example.com, and writes an A record for api.example.com pointing to 203.0.113.10 with a 300 second TTL. Step 4: a client resolves the name and gets that address, cached for up to five minutes.

Common mistake: deploying the controller without giving its identity permission to edit the zone, or creating a zone for a subdomain without delegating it from the parent zone. The controller then logs errors and no record appears, while the Service looks healthy.

Consequence: if the Service is recreated with a new IP, clients keep reaching the old address until the cached TTL expires, so records that move need short TTLs.

questions.prompt: A platform team at a different company, Northwind, hosts its public names in a Cloud DNS project. They create a new managed zone named payments.northwind.test for a subdomain of northwind.test. Their external-dns controller has the right permissions, and a Service annotated with pay.payments.northwind.test gets external IP 198.51.100.91. The trace is: Step 1: the team creates the managed zone payments.northwind.test. Step 2: external-dns sees the Service annotation and the address 198.51.100.91. Step 3: this step is missing from the trace. Step 4: external-dns writes an A record for pay.payments.northwind.test pointing to 198.51.100.91 with a 120 second TTL inside the new zone. Which missing step makes the record resolvable from the public internet?
choices: Lower the TTL on the parent zone's apex record to 60 seconds
Add NS records in the parent zone northwind.test that delegate payments.northwind.test to the new zone's name servers
Give the Service a second annotation with the same hostname
Copy the A record from the new zone into the parent zone by hand
questions.why: A subdomain zone is only reached once the parent zone delegates it with NS records pointing to the new zone's name servers, and without that the record written in step 4 is never queried.

questions.prompt: In external-dns, what is the purpose of the ownership TXT record written next to each entry?
choices: It tells Cloud DNS which load balancer the address belongs to
It marks the record as created by external-dns so the controller only deletes records it made itself
It stores the Service's external IP so clients can read it
It sets the TTL that caches may use for the entry
questions.why: The ownership TXT record lets the controller tell its own entries apart from others, so it only deletes records it created.

questions.prompt: A Service's external IP changes from 203.0.113.40 to 203.0.113.62. The A record for its hostname has a TTL of 3600 seconds, and a client resolved the name one minute before the change. What is the longest that client can keep using the old address?
choices: Up to 3600 seconds after it last fetched the record, the cached TTL
Up to 60 seconds, the time since the change was made
Indefinitely, because cached answers never expire on their own
Immediately, because external-dns clears caches when a Service changes
questions.why: A cached answer may be kept for the TTL it was issued with, so the client can hold the old address for up to 3600 seconds from its last lookup.

questions.prompt: A team sees that its Service has a healthy external IP, but no A record appears in Cloud DNS for the hostname in the annotation, and the controller logs show permission errors. What is the most likely cause and first check?
choices: The hostname should be a CNAME pointing at the Service name instead of an A record
The controller's identity may lack permission to edit the managed zone, so check its logs and grant that access
The TTL on the zone is too high, so the record is hidden until it expires
The zone should be recreated as a subdomain zone, which fixes permission scope
questions.why: Healthy Service with no record and permission errors in the controller logs points to the controller's identity lacking edit rights on the zone, which is the common mistake described.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Kubernetes service's public hostname gets into Cloud DNS when external-dns is used, and name one limit or tradeoff of that setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Service gets an external address from the load balancer the platform creates for it. External-dns, running as a controller in the cluster, watches Services and Ingresses that carry a hostname annotation. When it sees one with an address, it writes an A record for that hostname into the matching Cloud DNS managed zone, and it also writes a TXT ownership record so it knows which entries it owns. The controller's identity needs permission to edit that zone, or nothing gets written. The tradeoff is timing: the record only follows the address after the controller's next sync, and resolvers keep serving the old answer until its TTL runs out. So a replaced load balancer can leave users on an old address for minutes. Shorter TTLs reduce that window, but they mean more lookups and more load on the DNS service.
rubricPoints: Explains that external-dns watches the cluster objects carrying a hostname and reads the address the platform assigned
Says the controller writes an A record into the matching Cloud DNS managed zone, with a TXT record marking ownership
Notes that the controller needs permission on the zone for any record to appear
Names a tradeoff such as cached answers lingering until the TTL expires, or the sync delay

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine exercises DNS zones, records, or controllers, so this is best learned from the product material and console steps.

lessons.plain: Dedicated Interconnect is a private, physical link that your company runs from its own network into a building where Google's network already sits. Traffic between your data center and your cloud networks travels over that link instead of the public internet. Once the link exists, you divide it into logical lanes called VLAN attachments, one for each network path you need, and each lane has its own routing session. Think of the physical link as a highway and each VLAN attachment as a lane with its own signposts that tell traffic where to go.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an office sends a large amount of data to a cloud provider every day, why might a private cable into the provider's building be preferred over sending the same data across the public internet? Give one reason based on your own intuition.
lessons.teach:
Dedicated Interconnect is a direct private physical link between your on-premises network and Google's network. It is made at a colocation facility, which is a shared data center building where many networks meet. You order the connection, Google provisions it, and your router is joined to Google's equipment in that building with a physical cross-connect cable. A connection is made of one or more physical circuits, commonly 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps each, bundled together.

A VLAN attachment is a logical circuit that rides on that physical connection. It is tagged with a VLAN ID, a number that keeps traffic on a shared link separated into isolated channels. Each attachment is tied to one Cloud Router in one region and one VPC network, and you choose its bandwidth. A Cloud Router is the Google Cloud service that learns and advertises routes using BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, which is the standard way networks tell each other which address ranges they can reach. Each attachment carries a BGP session between the Cloud Router and your on-premises router, addressed with a small pair of link-local addresses.

Worked example: you have a connection in one metro and need a path to a production VPC in europe-west1. You create a VLAN attachment in europe-west1 using VLAN ID 100 at 1 Gbps. Google gives the attachment its addresses. You configure the matching VLAN ID and BGP peer addresses on your router. The BGP session comes up, the Cloud Router learns your office ranges, and it advertises the VPC subnet ranges back to you. Traffic for those subnets now uses the private path.

Common mistake: creating the attachment but leaving the VLAN ID or BGP peer addresses on your router mismatched. The session stays down, no routes are exchanged, and traffic that should use the link has no valid route.

In a running system, a single connection with a single attachment is a single point of failure. Redundant designs use more attachments and connections across facilities, and the availability you get depends on that topology.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a warehouse network and needs a private path to its VPC named ledger-prod in asia-southeast1. The engineer creates a VLAN attachment in asia-southeast1 with VLAN ID 214 and 2 Gbps of bandwidth, tied to a Cloud Router in that region. Google assigns the attachment its link-local BGP peer addresses. Next, the engineer configures the warehouse router with VLAN ID 214 and those peer addresses. Step 3 is missing from the sequence: the BGP session is then established, the Cloud Router learns the warehouse ranges, and it advertises the ledger-prod subnet ranges back. What is the missing step 3?
choices: Change the attachment's bandwidth to match the router's physical port speed
Make sure the router's BGP session is configured with the peer addresses and the router's own link-local address on the VLAN 214 sub-interface, so the session can start
Add a static route in ledger-prod for the warehouse ranges so traffic can leave the VPC
Create a second attachment in a different region so the session has redundancy
questions.why: The BGP session can only come up once the router is set to the same VLAN ID and peer addresses as the attachment, which is the step that connects the two ends.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the VLAN ID on a VLAN attachment do?
choices: It sets the speed of the physical cross-connect cable in the colocation facility
It names the Cloud Router that learns routes for the attachment
It keeps traffic on a shared physical link separated into isolated channels
It tells Google which VPC network the attachment belongs to
questions.why: A VLAN ID is a tag that separates traffic on a shared link into isolated channels, as the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A team creates a VLAN attachment and sets the VLAN ID correctly on its router, but types one wrong BGP peer address into the router. What is the most likely result?
choices: The BGP session stays down, no routes are exchanged, and traffic that should use the link has no valid route
The BGP session comes up, but the router sends no traffic because bandwidth is too low
The cross-connect cable is disabled by Google until the address is fixed
The attachment automatically corrects the address and routes are exchanged within seconds
questions.why: A mismatched peer address keeps the BGP session down, so no routes are learned or advertised and traffic has no valid path over the link.

questions.prompt: A company wants a single VLAN attachment to connect its on-premises network to two different VPC networks, one in us-east4 and one in europe-west2. Based on how attachments are defined, which statement is correct?
choices: Not possible: each attachment is tied to one Cloud Router in one region and one VPC network
It works, provided the two VPCs are peered with each other
It works if both VPCs use the same subnet ranges
It works if the Cloud Router is set to a global region
questions.why: Each VLAN attachment is tied to exactly one Cloud Router in one region and one VPC network, so a second VPC or region needs its own attachment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a Dedicated Interconnect connection and a VLAN attachment, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a single connection.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Dedicated Interconnect connection is the physical link: a private cable from our data center into a colocation facility where Google's network is. We order it, Google provisions it, and it is made of one or more bundled circuits. A VLAN attachment is a logical lane on that connection. It has a VLAN ID, a bandwidth we choose, and it is tied to one Cloud Router in one region and one VPC. Each attachment runs a BGP session with our router so routes can be exchanged. The main tradeoff is that one connection in one facility is a single point of failure: if the cable, the facility, or our router fails, the path is down. Better availability needs redundant connections and attachments in more than one place. Physical provisioning also takes lead time, so this is not a quick change.
rubricPoints: A Dedicated Interconnect connection is the physical private link at a colocation facility.
A VLAN attachment is a logical lane on the connection, tied to a VLAN ID, bandwidth, one Cloud Router, one region, and one VPC.
Each attachment needs a BGP session between the Cloud Router and the on-premises router to exchange routes.
A single connection or attachment is a single point of failure, so redundancy is needed for higher availability.
Physical provisioning takes lead time and is not an instant change.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers physical interconnect ordering, VLAN attachments, or BGP setup, so reading the product facts and console steps is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Partner Interconnect is a way to link your own office or data centre network to a Google Cloud network through a service provider you already buy connectivity from, when you cannot or do not want to place your own router inside a Google facility. You ask the provider for a private slice of their network, called a VLAN attachment, that leads into Google Cloud. The main design choice is how much of the stack the provider handles. Some providers only carry raw Ethernet frames at layer 2, while others also take part in exchanging routing information with you at layer 3.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a provider hands you a private link that carries raw Ethernet frames and nothing more, who do you think must run the routing protocol that tells each side which network address ranges live where: your router, or the provider's router?
lessons.teach:
Layer 2 means the data link layer. Here the provider moves Ethernet frames between your equipment and Google's edge, and does not take part in IP routing. Layer 3 means the network layer, where the provider also participates in routing, usually by exchanging routes with you over BGP, the border gateway protocol that lets networks announce which address ranges they can reach. A VLAN is a virtual LAN, a tag on frames that keeps one customer's traffic separate on a shared link. In Google Cloud, a VLAN attachment is the resource that represents one such logical connection, and Cloud Router is the managed router that speaks BGP for it. A pairing key is a one-time code you generate for the attachment and give to your provider so they can claim and activate it.

Why it works: the layer decides who owns the routing configuration. With Layer 2, you still run BGP between your router and Cloud Router across the attachment, so you configure the routing yourself. With Layer 3, the provider's router takes part in the routing exchange and passes your prefixes along.

Worked example. Atlas Freight has an on-premises router that serves 10.20.0.0/16, and wants its VPC subnet 10.0.0.0/16 to reach it. First, Atlas creates a Layer 2 partner VLAN attachment and receives a pairing key. Second, Atlas gives the key to its provider, who activates the attachment on VLAN 101. Third, Atlas configures a BGP session between its router and Cloud Router over VLAN 101. Fourth, Atlas's router announces 10.20.0.0/16 and Cloud Router announces 10.0.0.0/16. Packets now flow in both directions.

Common mistake: treating a created attachment as working. An attachment that exists but has not been activated by the provider, or a BGP session that is down, carries no traffic.

Consequence in a running system: if the BGP session is missing, instances send packets to 10.20.x.x, the VPC has no route for that range, and the calls time out with little clear error on the application side.

So when you choose a partner interconnect, first decide which layer the provider carries, because that decides which side owns the routing configuration you must get right.

questions.prompt: Ferrum Labs uses a Layer 3 Partner Interconnect. Layer 3 means the provider takes part in IP routing, usually by exchanging routes over BGP (the border gateway protocol, which announces which address ranges each side can reach). Ferrum's on-premises network is 10.60.0.0/16 and its VPC subnet is 10.70.0.0/18. Step 1: Ferrum creates a Layer 3 VLAN attachment (the Google Cloud resource for one logical connection) and receives a pairing key (a one-time code given to the provider to claim the attachment). Step 2: the provider claims the key and activates the attachment on VLAN 417. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: Cloud Router announces 10.70.0.0/18 to the provider, and the provider passes Ferrum's 10.60.0.0/16 to Cloud Router. Which choice correctly fills step 3?
choices: The provider's router establishes a BGP session with Cloud Router over VLAN 417 and exchanges Ferrum's prefixes
Ferrum adds a static route for 10.60.0.0/16 in the VPC and skips BGP entirely
Ferrum configures its own router to run a BGP session directly with Cloud Router over VLAN 417
Ferrum creates a second Layer 2 attachment so that BGP can be configured on its own router
questions.why: At Layer 3 the provider's router takes part in the routing exchange, so the BGP session runs between the provider and Cloud Router and carries Ferrum's prefixes.

questions.prompt: In a Layer 2 partner attachment, which party runs the BGP session that exchanges routes with Cloud Router? BGP is the border gateway protocol used to announce reachable address ranges.
choices: Your own router, because the provider only moves Ethernet frames at Layer 2
Nobody; routes must be fixed statically in the VPC
Google's edge equipment, which replaces Cloud Router for this link
The provider's router, which then passes your prefixes along
questions.why: At Layer 2 the provider only carries Ethernet frames, so you still run BGP between your router and Cloud Router across the attachment.

questions.prompt: A team creates a Layer 2 VLAN attachment and sees it listed in the console. Instances in 10.0.0.0/16 time out when calling hosts in 10.44.0.0/16 on-premises. Which explanation best fits?
choices: The pairing key was copied correctly, so the fault is probably the on-premises DNS server resolving the hostnames
The subnet 10.0.0.0/16 is too large for a VPC subnet, so instances cannot send packets
A Layer 2 attachment cannot carry IP traffic at all, so it should be deleted and recreated
The provider has not activated the attachment, or BGP is down, so the VPC lacks a route to 10.44.0.0/16
questions.why: A listed attachment that is not activated, or a BGP session that is down, leaves no route for the on-premises range, so packets have nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: Mira Foods wants its provider's router, not its own router, to take part in the routing exchange with Cloud Router, so it does not want to run a BGP session on its own equipment. Which option fits this requirement?
choices: A static route on the on-premises router, with no attachment at all
A VLAN attachment created with no pairing key, so no provider is involved
A Layer 2 partner attachment, where Mira Foods runs BGP on its own router
A Layer 3 partner attachment, where the provider's router handles the routing exchange
questions.why: A Layer 3 attachment makes the provider part of the routing exchange, which matches a requirement to keep BGP off the customer's own router.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says Partner Interconnect Layer 2 and Layer 3 are just two names for the same thing. Explain to them, in your own words, how the two differ in who takes part in routing, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing Layer 2.
lessons.modelAnswer: They are not the same, and the difference is who takes part in routing. With a Layer 2 partner attachment, the provider only carries Ethernet frames on a VLAN, so our own router and Cloud Router must run a BGP session across it, and we own that configuration. With Layer 3, the provider's router exchanges routes with us and with Google, so the provider is part of the routing path. The tradeoff of Layer 2 is control versus burden: we set BGP details and peering ourselves, but we must get ASNs, VLAN IDs and BGP settings right, and a mismatch shows up as missing routes rather than a clear error. Layer 3 hands more routing responsibility to the provider but gives us less direct control. Either way, the pairing key and provider activation must happen before any traffic can flow.
rubricPoints: Layer 2 means the provider carries only frames, so the customer runs BGP with Cloud Router.
Layer 3 means the provider takes part in routing and exchanges routes.
A pairing key and provider activation are needed before the attachment carries traffic.
A stated limit: Layer 2 gives control but places configuration burden and silent route failures on the customer.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining who owns routing at each layer and its tradeoffs, which is best practised by explaining it back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Cross-Cloud Interconnect is a private, dedicated link that a company buys so its Google Cloud network can talk directly to another cloud provider's network, such as Azure or AWS, without sending traffic over the public internet. Think of it as a leased private road between two cities rather than driving on public streets. The connection is the underlying dedicated link itself. VLAN attachments are separate logical lanes carried on that link, each one plugged into a router on the Google Cloud side that tells the other side which address ranges are reachable. This lesson covers how you set up both pieces and why you usually set up more than one.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you have one dedicated link between Google Cloud and another cloud provider, and that link goes down, what do you think happens to traffic between the two clouds, and what would you add to prevent that outage?
lessons.teach:
A Cross-Cloud Interconnect connection is a dedicated link between a Google Cloud edge location and a partner location in another cloud provider's network. You choose its bandwidth and the metro where it lands, and the other cloud side must accept it before it becomes usable. A VLAN attachment is a logical circuit that rides on a connection. VLAN is a tag that separates traffic sharing one physical link into isolated channels. Each VLAN attachment is tied to a Cloud Router, a managed router that speaks BGP, the protocol routers use to announce which IP address ranges they can reach. The BGP session is the peering between the Cloud Router and the router at the far end of that attachment.

Why it works: traffic follows routes. The Cloud Router learns the other cloud's address ranges over BGP and advertises your VPC subnets, so packets leave on whichever attachment holds the best route. Because the link is private, its latency and bandwidth are more predictable than a path over the internet.

Worked example: your application in one metro must reach a database in another cloud's network in the same metro. Step 1: order two 10 Gbps connections in separate facilities in that metro. Step 2: once each connection is active, create VLAN attachment A on the first connection with its own VLAN ID and a Cloud Router in your VPC region. Step 3: create VLAN attachment B on the second connection with a different VLAN ID and a second Cloud Router. Step 4: confirm both BGP sessions establish and that the database subnet appears in the learned routes.

Common mistake: creating attachments before the connection is active, or assuming two attachments on one connection are redundant. They share one physical link, so one facility failure removes both. High availability needs separate connections.

Consequence: when a BGP session drops, its routes are withdrawn and traffic to the other cloud fails rather than slowing down. Check learned routes and session state before blaming the application.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain in Denver needs its pricing service to reach an inventory database in another cloud's network in the same metro. Their steps so far: (1) order one 5 Gbps Cross-Cloud Interconnect connection, which is a dedicated link between a Google Cloud edge location and a partner location in another cloud, in a Denver facility; (2) wait until the partner side has accepted it and the connection shows as active; (3) MISSING STEP; (4) confirm the BGP session, the peering between the Cloud Router and the far-end router, is established and the inventory subnet appears in the learned routes. Which action completes step 3?
choices: Enable an internet VPN tunnel as the path to the database while the interconnect is built
Advertise the inventory subnet as a static route on the grocery chain's own routers
Order a second connection in the same Denver facility so the design is redundant
Create a VLAN attachment on the active connection with its own VLAN ID, tied to a Cloud Router in the VPC region
questions.why: The VLAN attachment is the logical circuit that rides on the connection and carries the BGP session, so it must exist before step 4 can check the session and learned routes.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a VLAN ID do on a Cross-Cloud Interconnect connection?
choices: It separates traffic sharing one physical link into isolated channels
It announces the VPC subnets to the far-end router over BGP
It tells the partner which metro the connection lands in
It sets the bandwidth available to the attachment on that link
questions.why: A VLAN is a tag that keeps traffic sharing one physical link separated into isolated channels, as the teaching text defines it.

questions.prompt: A team creates two VLAN attachments on one 10 Gbps connection and assumes a single facility outage cannot take both down. What is wrong with that assumption?
choices: The bandwidth is split so neither attachment can carry production traffic
Both attachments must use the same VLAN ID, which causes a conflict
Both attachments ride one physical link, so one failure removes both; redundancy needs separate connections
Two attachments always need two Cloud Routers, so the design fails at setup
questions.why: Attachments on one connection share one physical link, so high availability requires separate connections, not extra attachments on the same one.

questions.prompt: A BGP session on one VLAN attachment drops. What happens to traffic headed for the other cloud's network?
choices: The Cloud Router keeps the old routes and continues forwarding indefinitely
Its routes are withdrawn and the traffic to the other cloud fails
It slows down while the link renegotiates its path
Traffic automatically moves to the internet with no configuration needed
questions.why: When a BGP session drops, the routes it carried are withdrawn, so traffic to the other cloud fails outright rather than slowing down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a Cross-Cloud Interconnect connection and a VLAN attachment, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a single connection.
lessons.modelAnswer: The connection is the dedicated physical or provider-managed link between Google Cloud and another cloud provider's network, and we pay for its bandwidth in a chosen metro. A VLAN attachment is a logical lane on that connection. Each attachment is tied to a Cloud Router that uses BGP to exchange routes with the other side, so an attachment only carries traffic once its BGP session is established and the expected prefixes are learned. The main tradeoff of a single connection is that it is a single point of failure: a facility outage or a fiber cut takes down every attachment on it, so the availability target depends on having a second connection in a separate facility. Two attachments on one connection add isolation between workloads but not physical redundancy.
rubricPoints: Connection is the dedicated link to the other cloud, with chosen bandwidth and metro
VLAN attachment is a logical circuit on a connection, tied to a Cloud Router
BGP session must establish and routes must be learned before traffic flows
A single connection is a single point of failure; redundancy needs separate connections

suggested.rationale: Console setup steps and product facts are best looked up, and no listed mission or planned engine covers cloud network provisioning.

lessons.plain: Google Cloud Interconnect is a private physical link from your own data center or a partner facility into Google's network, so traffic does not cross the public internet. HA VPN is a pair of encrypted tunnels built with IPsec, a standard that scrambles traffic so only the two ends can read it. HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect means running those encrypted tunnels inside the private link. You keep the dedicated path and add encryption on top, which is useful when rules or auditors require data to be encrypted in transit even on a link you already own.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company connects its office network to Google Cloud over a private Interconnect link, but a compliance auditor asks that all traffic be encrypted in transit on that link. Would you rely on the private link alone, add an encrypted VPN running over it, or switch to the public internet with a VPN?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Interconnect is a private connection into Google's network. Dedicated Interconnect is a physical link you order directly, and Partner Interconnect uses a service provider. Either one carries traffic over a VLAN attachment, a logical connection that tells Google which VPC network and Cloud Router the traffic belongs to. A Cloud Router is a managed component that exchanges routes with your other network using BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol. HA VPN is a VPN gateway with two interfaces, and each interface builds an IPsec tunnel. IPsec encrypts the packets and authenticates both ends.

Why this works: the interconnect provides a private path, and the tunnels add encryption and authentication. The tunnels are carried over VLAN attachments, so the interconnect becomes the underlay for the VPN.

Worked example: a company has a Dedicated Interconnect with two VLAN attachments in different zones. Step 1: create an HA VPN gateway in the VPC. Step 2: attach each VLAN attachment to a Cloud Router. Step 3: create one tunnel from each HA VPN interface over a VLAN attachment. Step 4: set up BGP sessions over those tunnels so the on-premises router learns VPC routes and the reverse. Step 5: traffic now flows through the interconnect inside encrypted IPsec tunnels.

Common mistake: assuming the Interconnect itself encrypts traffic. It does not. Another mistake is building only one VLAN attachment or one tunnel and expecting the high availability SLA to apply.

Consequence: if a VLAN attachment or its tunnel fails, BGP drops the routes that depended on it, so traffic must fail over to the other path. Your SLA depends on the topology you build, so check Google's current published terms for the exact figure.

questions.prompt: Tidewater Logistics is building HA VPN over a Partner Interconnect that has two VLAN attachments, one in zone a and one in zone b. Their runbook lists the steps in this order. Step 1: create an HA VPN gateway in the VPC named vpc-east. Step 2: create tunnel t1 from the gateway's first interface over VLAN attachment zone-a, and start a BGP session on t1. Step 3: this step is missing from the runbook and is the one you must fill in. Step 4: attach both VLAN attachments to the Cloud Router, so that BGP sessions carry routes for both paths. Which step belongs in the gap at Step 3 so the setup has redundant paths?
choices: Replace the HA VPN gateway with a single classic VPN tunnel so that only one tunnel needs to stay up
Create tunnel t2 from the gateway's second interface over VLAN attachment zone-b, and start a BGP session on t2
Turn on IPsec encryption directly on the zone-a VLAN attachment so the Partner Interconnect carries encrypted traffic
Add a static default route on the warehouse router pointing at the zone-a VLAN attachment
questions.why: Each HA VPN interface builds its own IPsec tunnel over a VLAN attachment, so the second interface needs its own tunnel over the second attachment to give the redundant path the runbook is aiming for.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a VLAN attachment do in a Cloud Interconnect setup?
choices: It tells Google which VPC network and Cloud Router an interconnect's traffic belongs to
It sets the uptime percentage that applies to the interconnect
It is the BGP session that learns routes from the on-premises router
It encrypts every packet so that the interconnect link does not need IPsec
questions.why: The teaching text defines a VLAN attachment as the logical connection that links traffic on the interconnect to a specific VPC network and Cloud Router, and it does not handle encryption, routing exchange, or SLA terms.

questions.prompt: A company already has a Dedicated Interconnect and wants the traffic on it to be encrypted. A junior engineer proposes enabling encryption on the Interconnect itself. What is the correct approach?
choices: Enable encryption on the Cloud Router, since it sits between the interconnect and the VPC
Rely on the Partner Interconnect provider, which encrypts traffic on its own network
Build HA VPN tunnels over the VLAN attachments, because the tunnels add IPsec encryption and authentication while the interconnect provides the private path
Use the Interconnect's built-in encryption setting, which is applied per VLAN attachment
questions.why: The teaching text says the Interconnect does not encrypt traffic, so encryption comes from IPsec tunnels built over the VLAN attachments by the HA VPN gateway.

questions.prompt: An HA VPN design runs over two VLAN attachments in different zones, with one tunnel per gateway interface. The VLAN attachment for one tunnel fails. What happens to the routes that depended on it?
choices: All traffic on the interconnect stops until an administrator creates a new Cloud Router
The routes stay in the VPC because the other tunnel keeps them alive without BGP
BGP drops the routes that depended on the failed tunnel, and traffic must fail over to the other path
The Cloud Router rebuilds the failed VLAN attachment automatically and no routes change
questions.why: The teaching text says that when a VLAN attachment or its tunnel fails, BGP drops the routes that depended on it and traffic has to fail over to the other path.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect gives you that a plain Interconnect does not, when you would choose it, and one limit or tradeoff you would weigh before recommending it.
lessons.modelAnswer: HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect adds IPsec encryption to a private Interconnect link. The Interconnect gives a dedicated path into Google's network, but it does not encrypt traffic by itself. The VPN tunnels run over VLAN attachments, and BGP through Cloud Router exchanges routes across them. You would choose this when policy requires encryption in transit on a link you already own. The main tradeoff is overhead: encryption adds CPU cost and per-tunnel throughput limits, so high-bandwidth workloads may need planning. Also, the availability figure depends on the topology, including how many VLAN attachments and tunnels you build, so you should check the current published SLA for the exact design before promising it.
rubricPoints: Cloud Interconnect provides a private path but does not encrypt traffic by itself
HA VPN adds IPsec encryption by running tunnels over VLAN attachments
BGP through Cloud Router exchanges routes across the tunnels
Tradeoffs include encryption overhead and per-tunnel throughput limits
The SLA depends on topology, so it must be checked against current published terms

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right mechanism and SLA for a scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission covers this directly.

lessons.plain: A service level agreement, or SLA, is the uptime promise a provider puts in writing. A 99.9 percent promise allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime in a month, and 99.99 percent allows about 4 minutes. A link between your office or data centre and a cloud network only meets such a promise if it is built in a particular way: enough separate physical connections, placed in the right locations. This lesson covers those layouts, which are called topologies, and why a single link is never enough for a high promise.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office reaches the cloud over one physical cable. If you add a second identical cable, but both run into the same building, why might you still fall short of a 99.99 percent uptime promise?
lessons.teach:
An SLA is the availability percentage a provider commits to, where availability means the share of time a service is reachable. Google's interconnect SLAs depend on topology, meaning how many connections you have and where they sit. A metro is a city-level area where the provider has facilities. An edge availability domain is an independent failure zone inside a metro, with its own power and equipment. Dedicated Interconnect links your own cable to the provider at an edge facility. Partner Interconnect reaches the cloud through a service provider. Both attach to a Cloud Router, the routing component that exchanges routes with your side, through VLAN attachments, which are logical circuits carried on a physical connection.

Why it works: an availability promise covers the whole path, and failures are usually local, such as a card, a building, or a power feed. A second connection in a different domain keeps the path up when one domain fails. Two connections in one metro, each in a different edge availability domain, match the 99.9 percent topology. Four connections across two metros, two in each metro with each pair split across domains, match the 99.99 percent topology.

Worked example for a 99.99 percent target. Step 1: count connections and note that you need four. Step 2: choose two metros, A and B. Step 3: in metro A, place one connection in domain 1 and one in domain 2, then repeat in metro B. Step 4: give each connection its own VLAN attachment on a Cloud Router. Step 5: check that your on-premises routers also have redundant paths, so failover actually works.

Common mistake: buying four connections in one building. This looks redundant but shares one metro and often one failure domain, so it does not meet the 99.99 percent topology.

Consequence: if the topology is wrong, one facility outage can take the whole link down, and an SLA credit afterwards does not restore the lost service. The layout is what the promise depends on.

questions.prompt: A payments firm needs a 99.99 percent interconnect topology and has chosen two metros, Denver and Phoenix. Step 1: it plans four connections in total. Step 2: in Denver, it places one connection in edge availability domain 1 and one in domain 2, so the Denver pair is split across domains. Step 3: in Phoenix, both connections are placed in domain 1 of the same facility. Step 4: each connection gets its own VLAN attachment on a Cloud Router. What completes the plan so the Phoenix side matches the 99.99 percent topology?
choices: Add a fifth connection in Denver so the total outweighs the Phoenix risk.
Replace the Cloud Router with a static route so the Phoenix pair needs no routing component.
Keep both Phoenix connections in domain 1 but give them separate VLAN attachments.
Move one Phoenix connection into domain 2 so that each metro's pair is split across two domains.
questions.why: Each metro's pair must be split across two independent edge availability domains, so moving one Phoenix connection to domain 2 is the only option that fixes the shared failure zone without changing the rest of the layout.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants a 99.9 percent interconnect topology. It has two connections in one metro, both in edge availability domain 1. Which change makes its design match the 99.9 percent topology?
choices: Move one connection into a different edge availability domain in the same metro.
Move one connection to a second metro and leave both in domain 1.
Add a third connection in the same domain 1 so one spare exists.
Replace both connections with a Partner Interconnect in the same domain.
questions.why: The 99.9 percent topology needs two connections in one metro, each in a different edge availability domain, so moving one connection to another domain in the same metro is the required change.

questions.prompt: A team with four connections, all in one edge availability domain inside one metro, says its design meets the 99.99 percent topology because it has four links. What is the main problem with this claim?
choices: The team must use a VPN instead, because interconnects cannot meet any 99.99 percent target.
Four links is too few, and the topology needs at least eight connections.
The connections all share one metro and one failure domain, so one local failure can take them all down.
Dedicated Interconnect cannot be used at more than one edge facility in a metro.
questions.why: Counting links is not enough; the 99.99 percent topology needs connections spread across two metros with splits across domains, because a shared metro and domain can fail together.

questions.prompt: In the context of an interconnect SLA, what does availability mean, and why does an SLA credit received after an outage not solve the problem?
choices: Availability is the number of cables installed, and a credit adds cables after the fact.
Availability is the speed of the link, and a credit increases bandwidth for the next month.
Availability is the number of routes in Cloud Router, and a credit removes routes that caused the outage.
Availability is the share of time the service is reachable, and a credit pays money back but does not restore the service that was lost during the outage.
questions.why: Availability means the share of time a service is reachable, and a credit compensates after the fact but cannot bring back the time the service was down, which is why the topology must be right beforehand.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a 99.9 percent and a 99.99 percent interconnect layout, and name one limit or tradeoff of the higher option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the availability target and the downtime it allows. 99.9 percent is about 43 minutes a month and is met by two connections in one metro, each in a different edge availability domain, so the loss of one domain is survivable. 99.99 percent is about 4 minutes a month and needs four connections across two metros, two per metro, split across domains, so losing a whole metro is also survivable. The main tradeoff of the higher option is cost and complexity: four circuits, two sites, more VLAN attachments and Cloud Routers, and more on-premises routing to configure and test. So I would choose 99.99 only if the business impact justifies that cost. I would also remind the team that the SLA covers the provider side, so our own routers and failover design still need careful work.
rubricPoints: States the downtime allowed by 99.9 percent and 99.99 percent in plain terms
Describes the 99.9 layout: two connections in one metro, in different edge availability domains
Describes the 99.99 layout: four connections across two metros, split across domains
Names a real tradeoff of the higher option, such as cost, complexity, or on-premises redundancy

suggested.rationale: The topology rules and SLA figures are reference facts, and no listed mission or planned engine covers interconnect layouts.

lessons.plain: HA VPN is a way to connect your Google Cloud network to your own office or data center over the public internet, using an encrypted tunnel. Think of it as joining two buildings with two guarded corridors instead of one, so that if one corridor is blocked, traffic keeps flowing through the other. Your on-premises side has a VPN device that terminates the tunnels, and the two sides automatically exchange lists of the address ranges they host, so each knows where to send traffic. This objective is about setting up that pairing so it survives a single failure.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your office has one VPN device, and you build one encrypted tunnel from it to the cloud. If that tunnel or that device fails, what happens to cloud servers that need data from the office, and what would you add to keep that traffic flowing?
lessons.teach:
An HA VPN gateway is the Google Cloud side of a site-to-site VPN. It has two interfaces, and each interface has its own public IP address. A tunnel is one encrypted IPsec connection between one gateway interface and one interface on your side. A peer VPN gateway is a resource in Google Cloud that describes your on-premises device, including its public IP addresses. Cloud Router is the component that runs BGP, a routing protocol in which each side announces the address ranges it can reach over a given path. An ASN is the autonomous system number that identifies each side in BGP. Why it works: when one tunnel dies, its BGP session drops, the routes learned through it disappear, and traffic moves to the surviving tunnel without a human changing anything.

Worked example: the cloud VPC uses 10.10.0.0/16 and the office uses 10.20.0.0/16. Step 1: create an HA VPN gateway with two interfaces. Step 2: create a peer gateway that lists your device's public IPs. Step 3: create two tunnels, one per gateway interface, each paired with a different peer interface. Step 4: attach a Cloud Router with one BGP session per tunnel. Step 5: the cloud announces 10.10.0.0/16 and the office announces 10.20.0.0/16 over both tunnels. If tunnel 1 fails, its BGP routes are withdrawn and office-bound traffic uses tunnel 2.

Common mistake: building one tunnel and calling the link highly available. Google publishes a 99.99% availability target for HA VPN, but only when both gateway interfaces, both tunnels, and BGP are configured, and the on-premises side also needs redundant devices or paths. A single tunnel carries a lower target and a single point of failure.

In a running system, a lone tunnel means a single fault cuts every hybrid service until someone notices and rebuilds the link. Two tunnels with BGP turn that into an automatic reroute.

questions.prompt: A logistics company, Harbor Foods, wants its cloud network to reach its regional depot. The cloud network is a VPC (virtual private cloud, a private network you define inside Google Cloud) using 172.31.0.0/20. The depot uses 192.168.40.0/24 and has two routers with public IPs 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.11. The engineer follows these steps. Step 1: create an HA VPN gateway with two interfaces, each with its own public IP. Step 2: create a peer VPN gateway listing 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.11. Step 3: create two tunnels, one from each gateway interface, each paired with a different depot router. Step 4 is missing and must be filled in: ______. Which completion correctly finishes the setup so that traffic can fail over between tunnels?
choices: Create a third tunnel on the first gateway interface so that one interface carries two encrypted connections for extra capacity.
Add a static route to 192.168.40.0/24 pointing at one tunnel only, and skip BGP, since static routes are simpler to maintain.
Assign both depot routers the same ASN in the peer gateway so that BGP treats them as a single neighbor and avoids duplicate routes.
Attach a Cloud Router with one BGP session per tunnel, so the cloud announces 172.31.0.0/20 and the depot announces 192.168.40.0/24 over both tunnels and routes disappear when one tunnel drops.
questions.why: Cloud Router runs BGP, and one BGP session per tunnel lets each side announce its ranges over both paths, so a failed tunnel's routes are withdrawn and traffic shifts automatically.

questions.prompt: In this context, what does a peer VPN gateway resource describe?
choices: The on-premises device, including its public IP addresses, so Google Cloud knows where to send the tunnels.
The autonomous system number that identifies your network in BGP routing.
The Google Cloud side of the site-to-site VPN, including its two interfaces and their public IPs.
The encrypted IPsec connection that carries traffic between one gateway interface and one interface on your side.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the peer VPN gateway as the Google Cloud resource that describes your on-premises device and its public IP addresses.

questions.prompt: A team builds one IPsec tunnel between an HA VPN gateway and its office router, then describes the link as highly available. Which statement correctly explains why this is a mistake?
choices: One tunnel is a single point of failure and carries a lower availability target; the 99.99% target requires both gateway interfaces, both tunnels, and BGP, plus redundant on-premises devices or paths.
One tunnel is fine because BGP alone provides the full 99.99% availability target regardless of how many tunnels exist.
One tunnel is acceptable as long as the on-premises router has two public IP addresses, since the gateway interfaces are then redundant.
One tunnel is fully redundant because IPsec automatically creates a second encrypted connection when the first one fails.
questions.why: The teaching text says the 99.99% target applies only when the full redundant set is in place, and a single tunnel has a lower target and a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: A hybrid link has two tunnels, each with its own BGP session. Tunnel 1 fails. What happens to the routes learned through tunnel 1, and how does traffic respond?
choices: All routes on both tunnels are deleted, so the hybrid link stays down until the tunnels are rebuilt.
The ASN on the surviving tunnel changes to match the failed one, which then reroutes traffic after a manual restart.
The routes stay in place and traffic keeps trying tunnel 1 until an engineer manually removes them from the Cloud Router.
The routes learned through tunnel 1 are withdrawn when its BGP session drops, and office-bound traffic moves to the surviving tunnel without anyone changing configuration.
questions.why: When a tunnel dies, its BGP session drops and the routes learned through it disappear, so traffic uses the surviving tunnel automatically.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our office link is highly available because we have a VPN tunnel to the cloud. Explain to them what HA VPN actually requires, which availability target it is designed to meet, and one limit or tradeoff of using it instead of a dedicated private link.
lessons.modelAnswer: HA VPN is only highly available if it is built as a pair: two gateway interfaces on the Google Cloud side, two tunnels, and a Cloud Router running BGP with a session on each tunnel. The on-premises side needs matching redundancy too, such as two devices or two uplinks, or the office becomes the single point of failure. When everything is in place, Google's stated target is 99.99 percent for the cloud side. One tunnel alone gets a lower target and cannot reroute, so it is not HA. The tradeoff is that VPN runs over the public internet, so bandwidth and latency vary and are capped per tunnel, while a dedicated interconnect offers private, more predictable paths at higher cost and setup effort.
rubricPoints: HA VPN needs two gateway interfaces, two tunnels, and BGP sessions through Cloud Router to be highly available.
The published 99.99 percent target applies only to the full redundant topology, and the on-premises side must also be redundant.
A single tunnel has a lower target and no automatic failover.
VPN runs over the public internet, so throughput and latency are less predictable than a dedicated private link.

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly facts about gateway, tunnel, and SLA topology that are best learned from the reading, and no listed mission or planned engine covers VPN setup.

lessons.plain: Imagine two office buildings that need a private, encrypted hallway between them rather than using the public street. In Google Cloud, each private network (called a VPC) is like one building. HA VPN is a way to build that encrypted link between two VPC networks over the public internet, using two tunnels instead of one so traffic keeps flowing if one link drops. Each side has a gateway, and a router on each side learns the routes automatically. The two networks can sit in the same project, in different projects, or in different regions.
lessons.guessPrompt: If two cloud networks each use the same private address range, such as 10.0.0.0/24, and you want instances in one to reach instances in the other privately, what do you expect will go wrong?
lessons.teach:
HA VPN, short for High Availability Virtual Private Network, is a regional gateway that carries encrypted IP traffic over the public internet. A VPC-to-VPC setup means both ends are Google Cloud networks, so you create an HA VPN gateway in each VPC and join the two. Each HA VPN gateway has two interfaces, and each interface has its own public address and can host a tunnel. A tunnel is one encrypted IPsec connection. The two sides agree on encryption keys using IKE, and you supply a shared secret, called a pre-shared key, that both sides must match exactly. Cloud Router is a managed service that exchanges routes over BGP, the protocol that tells each network which destination ranges are reachable through which tunnel. Each tunnel carries its own BGP session, addressed with link-local addresses, and each side needs an autonomous system number, or ASN, which is a unique number identifying its routing domain.

Worked example: VPC A uses 10.1.0.0/16 and VPC B uses 10.2.0.0/16. Step 1: create an HA VPN gateway in each VPC in the same region. Step 2: create two tunnels on each side, one per interface, and pair each tunnel with its peer on the other side. Step 3: create a Cloud Router on each side with a different ASN, for example 64514 and 64515. Step 4: set up a BGP session on each tunnel. Step 5: the routers advertise 10.1.0.0/16 to VPC B and 10.2.0.0/16 to VPC A, so traffic between the ranges now crosses the encrypted tunnels.

Common mistake: overlapping subnet ranges. If both VPCs use 10.0.0.0/24, the routers cannot tell which network a destination belongs to, so the tunnel is useless for those addresses. Plan non-overlapping ranges before you build anything.

Consequence in a running system: when one tunnel fails, its BGP session drops, its routes are withdrawn, and traffic shifts to the surviving tunnel. That failover is the reason for the redundant design. A single-tunnel setup has no such protection and goes dark when that tunnel fails.

questions.prompt: A retail company has an orders VPC using 10.50.0.0/18 and a reporting VPC using 10.60.0.0/18, both in the same region. An engineer connects them with HA VPN, a regional gateway that carries encrypted traffic over the public internet. The steps so far: Step 1: create an HA VPN gateway in each VPC. Step 2: create two tunnels on each side, one per interface, and pair each tunnel with its peer on the other side. Step 3: [MISSING]. Step 4: create a Cloud Router on each side with ASNs 65010 and 65020, and start a BGP session on each tunnel. Step 5: each router advertises its own VPC range to the other side. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: Create a second HA VPN gateway in a different region for each VPC
Give both VPCs the same ASN so the BGP sessions match
Change the reporting VPC range to 10.50.0.0/18 so the ranges overlap and routes are shared
Set the same pre-shared key on both ends of each tunnel pair
questions.why: Each tunnel pair must use a pre-shared key, the shared secret that both sides must match exactly, before IKE can agree on keys and bring the tunnel up.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the job of the BGP session that runs on each HA VPN tunnel?
choices: It encrypts the packets so that the public internet cannot read them
It assigns each VPC its public address on the gateway interface
It stores the pre-shared key that both sides must match
It tells each network which destination ranges are reachable through that tunnel
questions.why: The teaching text says BGP, run by Cloud Router, exchanges routes so each network knows which destination ranges sit behind which tunnel.

questions.prompt: A team builds a single HA VPN tunnel between two VPCs and no second tunnel. The tunnel later fails. What happens to traffic between the two VPCs?
choices: It continues over the same tunnel once the BGP session reconnects on its own
It is dropped with no alternate path, because there is no surviving tunnel to fail over to
It is split across the two VPCs' Cloud Routers until the tunnel is repaired
It shifts automatically to the public internet through the gateway's second interface
questions.why: The text explains that failover depends on a surviving tunnel, so a single-tunnel setup goes dark when that tunnel fails.

questions.prompt: Two VPCs both use 192.168.4.0/22 as their subnet range. An engineer wants them joined with HA VPN. What should they do before building anything, and why?
choices: Pick a larger ASN for each Cloud Router so the routers can tell the networks apart
Add a second pre-shared key so the tunnels can distinguish the two address spaces
Plan non-overlapping ranges first, because overlapping ranges make the routers unable to tell which network a destination belongs to
Turn off BGP so that the routers stop trying to advertise the duplicate ranges
questions.why: The teaching text names overlapping subnet ranges as the common mistake and says to plan non-overlapping ranges before building the tunnels.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would connect two VPC networks with HA VPN, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create an HA VPN gateway in each VPC in the regions we need, then build two tunnels per side, one on each gateway interface, so one tunnel failing does not cut the link. Each side gets a Cloud Router with a distinct private ASN, and BGP sessions on each tunnel exchange the subnet routes automatically. Before building, I would confirm the two VPCs use non-overlapping ranges, because overlapping ranges make routing ambiguous. The main tradeoff is that the traffic still rides the public internet inside encrypted tunnels, so throughput is capped per tunnel and latency varies with the internet path. Dedicated or partner links avoid that, but cost more and take longer to set up. I would also note that the redundant design is what the availability promise depends on, so a single-tunnel shortcut would quietly remove it.
rubricPoints: HA VPN uses two tunnels across two gateway interfaces for redundancy
Cloud Router with distinct ASNs exchanges subnet routes over BGP
The two VPC subnet ranges must not overlap
Traffic crosses the public internet, so throughput and latency are limits to name

suggested.rationale: The core facts are gateway, tunnel, router, and addressing configuration best absorbed from explanation and console-level reading, and no listed mission or planned engine targets hybrid VPN setup.

lessons.plain: A VPN tunnel is a private, encrypted pipe carried over the public internet that links your office network to your cloud network. Classic VPN is Google Cloud's older gateway for building these pipes. The key design question is how the cloud side decides which packets should enter the pipe. A route-based VPN lets the routing table make that decision, so any traffic a route points at the tunnel uses it. A policy-based VPN instead lists, in advance, the exact address ranges allowed through the tunnel, and only matching pairs are carried. Choosing the wrong style can leave some networks silently unreachable even when the tunnel itself reports healthy.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two engineers describe the same office-to-cloud link. One says send all traffic for the office range down the tunnel, based on routes. The other says only send these exact source and destination range pairs down the tunnel, written into the tunnel settings. Which description is route-based and which is policy-based, and how could a tunnel show as up while some subnets still fail?
lessons.teach:
A VPN tunnel is an encrypted connection between two gateways, here your on-premises router and a Google Cloud VPN gateway. Traffic is encrypted with IPsec, a standard suite for protecting IP packets. A gateway is the endpoint device that sends and receives tunnel traffic. Classic VPN is the older Google Cloud gateway type, and its published availability target is 99.9 percent. Routing decides which next hop a packet is sent to. A static route is a fixed entry you type in. Dynamic routing uses BGP, a protocol routers use to exchange route information automatically through Cloud Router. A traffic selector is a pair of IP ranges, one local and one remote, that a policy-based tunnel uses to decide which packets it accepts.

Why it works: a route-based tunnel treats the tunnel as a next hop. Any packet whose destination matches a route toward the tunnel is encrypted and sent. A policy-based tunnel ignores the route table for admission and checks each packet against its selectors instead.

Worked example. The office uses 10.0.0.0/16. The cloud VPC subnet is 10.20.1.0/24. Route-based: add a cloud route for 10.0.0.0/16 whose next hop is the tunnel, and a matching route on the office side for 10.20.0.0/16. A packet from 10.20.1.5 to 10.0.4.9 hits the cloud route, is encrypted, and is delivered. Policy-based: configure the tunnel with local selector 10.20.1.0/24 and remote selector 10.0.0.0/16. The same packet matches the selectors and passes. Now a host in 10.20.2.0/24 sends to 10.0.4.9. It has no selector match, so the tunnel drops it even if some route points there.

Common mistake: adding a new cloud subnet, creating its route, and forgetting to add it to the policy selectors. The tunnel stays Established, monitoring looks green, and only that subnet fails.

In a running system this means you must check the tunnel's selectors or routes after every subnet change, not just the tunnel status.

questions.prompt: A clinic has an on-premises range of 172.16.0.0/20 and a Google Cloud VPC subnet of 192.168.40.0/24. It builds a route-based Classic VPN tunnel. Steps so far: 1) The tunnel status shows Established. 2) A cloud route for 172.16.0.0/20 with the tunnel as next hop is added. 3) [step missing from this list]. 4) A ping from 192.168.40.7 to 172.16.3.20 succeeds. Which item fills step 3?
choices: Lower the tunnel's availability target to 99.9 percent so the status refreshes
Add a route on the clinic's router for 192.168.40.0/24 whose next hop is the tunnel
Add a second cloud route for 172.16.0.0/20 with the default internet gateway as next hop
Change the tunnel to policy-based so each packet is checked against selectors
questions.why: A route-based tunnel needs a route in each direction, so the on-premises router must send the cloud subnet's range into the tunnel for the return path to work.

questions.prompt: Which pair best describes a traffic selector?
choices: A list of BGP peers exchanged automatically by Cloud Router
One local IP range and one remote IP range that a policy-based tunnel uses to decide which packets it accepts
A fixed static route with a metric value
A single gateway address and a port number
questions.why: A traffic selector is defined as a pair of IP ranges, one local and one remote, used by a policy-based tunnel to admit packets.

questions.prompt: A policy-based Classic VPN tunnel has local selector 10.50.4.0/23 and remote selector 10.7.0.0/16. A host at 10.50.6.12 sends a packet to 10.7.2.2, and a route pointing 10.7.0.0/16 toward the tunnel exists. What happens to the packet?
choices: It is dropped, because 10.50.6.12 falls outside the local selector
It is sent unencrypted through the default internet route
It is accepted, because the tunnel status shows Established
It is encrypted and delivered, because a route toward the tunnel exists
questions.why: A policy-based tunnel checks each packet against its selectors rather than the route table, and 10.50.6.12 is not inside 10.50.4.0/23, so the packet is dropped.

questions.prompt: A Google Cloud VPC subnet is 10.90.0.0/24 and the on-premises network is 10.40.0.0/16. A route-based Classic VPN tunnel is Established, and the cloud side has a route for 10.40.0.0/16 with the tunnel as next hop. The on-premises router has no route for 10.90.0.0/24 toward the tunnel. What is the likely result for a host at 10.40.3.8 reaching 10.90.0.5?
choices: It fails because Classic VPN cannot carry traffic to private IP ranges
It fails because the tunnel must be policy-based before any route can be used
It works, because one cloud-side route covers traffic in both directions
It fails in the on-premises to cloud direction, because the on-premises router never sends 10.90.0.0/24 into the tunnel
questions.why: Each direction of a route-based tunnel depends on its own router having a route pointing into the tunnel, so the missing on-premises route blocks traffic from 10.40.3.8 even though the tunnel is Established.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between route-based and policy-based Classic VPN, and name one limit or tradeoff of each when a new subnet is added to the cloud side later.
lessons.modelAnswer: Route-based means the tunnel is just a next hop in the routing table. If a route points a destination at the tunnel, the traffic is encrypted and sent, so adding a subnet usually means adding a route on both sides, and BGP can advertise that automatically. The limit is that routes decide everything, so an overly broad route can send more traffic through the tunnel than intended. Policy-based means the tunnel carries only traffic that matches its configured local and remote ranges. Its tradeoff is that every new subnet needs a matching selector pair, or traffic is dropped while the tunnel still looks up. It also typically relies on static routing, so you lose automatic route exchange. Before any subnet change I would check both the routes and the selectors.
rubricPoints: Route-based VPN uses the routing table, so a route pointing at the tunnel decides what gets sent through it.
Policy-based VPN admits only traffic matching configured local and remote selector ranges.
A new subnet in a policy-based setup needs a matching selector, or traffic is dropped even though the tunnel is up.
Route-based setups depend on correct routes, and a broad route can send unintended traffic through the tunnel.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers VPN design, so explaining the selector-versus-route distinction back to a teammate is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: When your company network and Google Cloud exchange route information automatically, a small set of settings tells each side who it is, which path it prefers, and how it trusts the other side. Think of two border offices passing around a directory of addresses they can reach. Each office has an official number identifying its organisation, a preference score saying which doorway people should use when more than one exists, a tiny private address on the single cable that connects them, and a shared password that proves the other office is genuine. Get any of these wrong and the directory either never arrives or sends traffic the long way round.
