lessons.guessPrompt: If your office has two cables to the same cloud network and both can reach the same server subnet, which single setting would you change to make one cable the preferred route, and why might you not want both cables set to equal preference?
lessons.teach: A Cloud Router is the Google Cloud component that speaks BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the standard way networks tell each other which address ranges they can reach). Four settings shape that conversation. The ASN (autonomous system number) is the number that identifies a network in BGP; your Cloud Router has one, and the on-premises router must have a different one for an external BGP session. The MED (multi-exit discriminator) is a priority value sent with each advertised route; when two paths reach the same range, the lower MED wins and the higher one is kept as backup. Each BGP session runs over one link and uses a pair of link-local addresses, small addresses from the 169.254.0.0/16 range that exist only on that cable, one for each router. Authentication means both ends share a secret key (BGP MD5) that signs each session message; a mismatch stops the session from forming. Worked example: on-premises advertises 10.20.0.0/16 on link A with MED 100 and on link B with MED 200. Step 1, the Cloud Router receives both paths. Step 2, it compares the MED values. Step 3, 100 is lower, so link A is selected and link B is held in reserve. Step 4, if link A fails, its session drops and the route learned over link B takes over. Common mistake: giving both links the same MED when the design needed one primary, which makes them share traffic evenly, or reusing the same ASN on both sides. Consequence: a wrong key, ASN, or link-local pair keeps the session down, its routes disappear, and traffic falls back to whatever path remains or stops entirely.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm connects its Cloud Router to on-premises over two links. Session P carries 192.168.40.0/24 with MED 60, and session Q carries the same range with MED 30. Step 1: the Cloud Router receives both paths. Step 2: it compares the MED values and finds 30 is lower, so the path learned on session Q is selected. Step 3: session Q goes down. Step 4 (to complete): what happens to traffic bound for 192.168.40.0/24?
choices: The route learned over session P becomes the active path, because it is the only remaining route to that range.
The Cloud Router raises the MED of session P to 30 so the two match.
Both paths are used equally, since the MED values no longer matter once one session is down.
Traffic to the range stops until an engineer changes the MED values by hand.
questions.why: When session Q drops, its route is withdrawn, and the route still learned over session P is the only path left, so it takes over.

questions.prompt: In the BGP setup described in the teaching text, what is a MED?
choices: A priority value on each route; lower is preferred.
A shared secret key that signs each session message between the routers.
The number that identifies a network in BGP and must differ across the two sides.
Two small link-local addresses that exist only on the cable.
questions.why: The MED is a priority value sent with each route, and when two paths reach the same range the lower value wins.

questions.prompt: A new link is set up with Cloud Router link-local address 169.254.20.1, while the on-premises router on the same cable uses 169.254.21.2. The BGP session never comes up. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The session needs a higher route priority before it can form.
The MED on the on-premises side is set too high.
The two link-local addresses do not form a matching pair on that cable, so the routers cannot reach each other on the session.
The Cloud Router's ASN is lower than the on-premises ASN.
questions.why: Each session needs its pair of link-local addresses to belong to the same link, and these two sit in different ranges, so the session cannot form.

questions.prompt: A team has two links to the same on-premises range, both advertised with MED 100, and wants one link to be primary. Which change achieves that?
choices: Lower the MED on the backup link below the primary so the backup wins.
Give the backup link a higher MED than the primary, for example 200 against the primary's 100.
Remove the link-local addresses from the backup session.
Keep both at 100, because equal MED always sends traffic over the first link learned.
questions.why: A lower MED is preferred, so the intended primary keeps the lower value and the backup gets the higher one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Cloud Router decides which of two links to use for the same on-premises range, naming the setting that controls it and one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The Cloud Router receives the same on-premises range over two BGP sessions. Each advertised path carries a MED, and the router prefers the lower value, so we set the primary link to a lower MED than the backup, for example 100 against 200. Both sessions stay up, so the backup is ready the moment the primary session drops. The limit is that MED only affects how Google Cloud picks among paths it has received; it does not change which path the on-premises side prefers for traffic going the other way, so that needs configuration on our side. Equal MEDs mean both links carry traffic, which may not be what we want. Before going live we confirm both sessions are established, check that the learned routes show the expected priority, and test failover by bringing the primary link down. Authentication keys and link-local addresses must match on each session or the backup never comes up.
rubricPoints: The MED is a priority value where the lower number is preferred between paths to the same range.
Both sessions should stay established so the backup is ready for failover.
A limit: MED only controls the cloud side's choice, not the on-premises side's preference for return traffic.
Equal MEDs cause traffic to be shared across links, which may not match the design.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which path the network actually selects when two links advertise the same range makes the effect of MED concrete.

lessons.plain: When two networks are joined by a link, such as an office and a cloud network, each side needs to notice quickly when the other side has gone silent. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection is a small, fast check in which two directly connected devices send each other tiny messages many times per second. If those messages stop arriving, both sides conclude the path is broken within a fraction of a second. Routing protocols can then move traffic to a backup path right away instead of waiting for their own slower timers to expire. BFD is a helper for a routing protocol, not a routing protocol itself.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a routing session only declares its neighbor dead after 60 seconds of silence. Roughly how long could traffic keep flowing into a dead link before anything reacts, and what would you change to shorten that wait?
lessons.teach:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, or BFD, is a lightweight protocol that two directly connected devices use to check that the path between them still forwards traffic. Each side sends a small control packet at a fixed rate, called the transmit interval. If a side receives no packet for a set period, it declares the path down. That period is the transmit interval multiplied by the detection multiplier, which is the number of missed intervals tolerated before failure is declared. BFD only watches the link; it does not choose routes. Its job is to tell a routing protocol such as BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol that exchanges routes between networks, that a neighbor is gone, so BGP can drop those routes immediately.

Why it works: BGP's own keepalive and hold timers are designed for stability and are often measured in tens of seconds. BFD runs on a much faster clock, so failure is noticed in well under a second.

Worked example: the transmit interval is 300 ms and the multiplier is 3, so the detection time is 900 ms. The last packet arrives at 600 ms. No packet arrives at 900 ms or 1200 ms, and by 1500 ms, 900 ms after the last packet, the path is declared down. BGP then withdraws the routes that used this link and traffic shifts to the backup path.

Common mistake: enabling BFD on one end only, or with mismatched timers, so the session flaps or never detects anything. Both ends must agree on the settings.

Consequence: without BFD, a cut link can keep receiving traffic that goes nowhere for tens of seconds. With BFD configured on both ends, the outage window shrinks to about the detection time.

questions.prompt: A freight company runs BGP with a port partner over a leased fiber link, and BFD is enabled on both routers. Their transmit interval is 200 ms and the detection multiplier is 4. Step 1: detection time = 200 ms x 4 = 800 ms. Step 2: the last BFD packet arrived at the 1000 ms mark, when the fiber began failing. Step 3 is missing. Work out the time at which the path is declared down, and state what BGP does with the routes that used this link at that moment.
choices: At 1800 ms; BGP withdraws the routes that used this link
At 1800 ms; BFD itself moves the traffic onto the backup link
At 1000 ms; BGP keeps the routes until its own hold timer expires
At 800 ms; BFD selects a new path for the traffic
questions.why: The path is declared down once no packet has arrived for the 800 ms detection time, which is 1000 ms plus 800 ms, and BFD then tells BGP, which withdraws the routes that depended on the failed link, since BFD only watches the link and does not choose routes.

questions.prompt: In one sentence, what is the job of BFD in a network that also runs BGP?
choices: To choose the best route to each destination network and install it in the routing table
To exchange full routing tables between autonomous networks at a fixed interval
To encrypt the control packets sent between two routers over a leased line
To check that a directly connected neighbor still forwards traffic and tell BGP quickly when it does not
questions.why: BFD is a lightweight liveness check on a direct link; it signals failure to a routing protocol such as BGP but does not pick routes, exchange full tables, or encrypt traffic.

questions.prompt: A team enables BFD on the router in its office but not on the matching router at the far end of a hybrid link to a data center. What is the most likely result?
choices: BGP automatically turns BFD on at the far end, so the link is protected
Nothing changes, because BFD only matters on the side that sends the routes
The session can flap or never detect a real failure, because both ends must run BFD with agreed settings
The far end detects the failure in half the time because it is the only one checking
questions.why: BFD works as a pair, so enabling it on one end only or with mismatched timers leads to unstable sessions or missed failures, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A link runs BFD with a transmit interval of 150 ms and a detection multiplier of 5. How long after the last received packet is the path declared down?
choices: 150 ms, which is the transmit interval alone
155 ms, which is the interval plus the multiplier
1.5 seconds, which is the interval multiplied by 10
750 ms, which is the interval multiplied by the multiplier
questions.why: The detection time is the transmit interval multiplied by the detection multiplier, so 150 ms x 5 = 750 ms, and the path is declared down when no packet arrives for that long.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we enable BFD on a BGP session over a hybrid link, and name one limit or tradeoff of making the BFD timers very aggressive.
lessons.modelAnswer: BGP alone takes a long time to notice that a link is dead, because its keepalive and hold timers are tuned for stability. Traffic can keep flowing into a broken path for tens of seconds. BFD sends tiny packets at a fast rate between the two directly connected routers, so it detects a failed path in roughly a second and tells BGP right away, which withdraws the routes and moves traffic to the backup. The limit is that BFD only checks the link between two neighbors. It does not see problems further along the path. The tradeoff with very aggressive timers is false alarms: a busy or briefly congested link can drop a few packets, and very short detection times can make the session flap, which causes route churn. Both ends must also use matching settings, so the timers should be chosen with the link's real behavior in mind.
rubricPoints: BFD is a fast link-liveness check between directly connected peers, not a routing protocol.
Detection time equals the transmit interval times the detection multiplier.
BFD tells BGP about a failure quickly so routes are withdrawn and traffic fails over.
Aggressive timers risk false failures and flapping, and both ends must match.

suggested.rationale: BFD is a mechanism whose key facts are timers and settings, and no listed OpsForge mission or planned engine covers it directly, so reading the teaching is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Think of two offices that need to tell each other which addresses they can reach. A router that speaks a routing protocol can hand a neighbour a list of the networks it can reach, and it can also take in the list the neighbour sends back. In Google Cloud, Cloud Router is the managed service that trades those lists with your on-premises routers over BGP, a routing protocol. Custom advertised and custom learned routes are the settings that let you decide, instead of accepting defaults, which networks you send out and which ones you accept in.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your cloud network has three subnets, but your office should only learn about two of them. Before reading, what would you expect to control which subnets your office hears about, and why might sending everything be a problem?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Router is a managed Google Cloud service that runs BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, with a peer on your side of a hybrid link such as an Interconnect or an HA VPN tunnel. BGP is how two routers exchange lists of IP prefixes, which are address ranges written like 10.0.0.0/24. A prefix you advertise tells the peer to send traffic for that range to you. A prefix you learn is one the peer advertised to you, which your VPC can then use as a route.

Advertisement has two modes. In default mode, Cloud Router advertises the subnets of the network it serves. In custom mode, you choose the list yourself: specific subnet ranges, or custom prefixes that are not subnets, such as a summary range covering several subnets. Check which mode a router is in before you change it, because the default list is replaced once you switch.

Learning works the same way on the way in. Routes learned from the peer are installed into the VPC routing table only if they are accepted. Custom learned route filtering lets you accept or reject particular prefixes, so an unexpected default route or an overlapping range from the office cannot quietly capture traffic.

Worked example: the cloud VPC has subnets 10.10.1.0/24, 10.10.2.0/24 and 10.10.9.0/24, and the office should reach only the first two. Step one: set Cloud Router to custom advertisement and list 10.10.1.0/24 and 10.10.2.0/24. Step two: the router builds its outgoing list from that set, so 10.10.9.0/24 is never announced. Step three: if the office advertises 0.0.0.0/0, a learned-route filter that rejects it stops the cloud from sending all internet-bound traffic toward the office.

Common mistake: assuming custom mode means only what you remember to type. Forgetting a subnet leaves the office unable to reach it, and the symptom looks like a firewall fault even though no packet was ever routed to it.

Consequence: a route change reaches the peer once the BGP session updates, so a wrong filter can black-hole production traffic until it is corrected. Custom routing is a precise tool that rewards checking the advertised and learned lists after every change.

questions.prompt: Lumen Dental runs a Cloud Router in custom advertisement mode over an HA VPN tunnel. Its VPC has subnets 172.16.4.0/24, 172.16.5.0/24 and 172.16.8.0/24 (a lab subnet). The goal is for the office to reach the first two subnets through one summary range. Step one: add the custom prefix 172.16.4.0/23 to the advertised list. Step two: the router's outgoing list now holds only 172.16.4.0/23, so 172.16.8.0/24 is never announced. Step three is missing. Which step completes the plan?
choices: Leave learned routes unfiltered, because the office's 172.16.0.0/20 range is only learned and cannot affect where traffic goes
Switch the router back to default mode so the lab subnet 172.16.8.0/24 is advertised automatically
Advertise 172.16.8.0/24 as well, because a summary range never covers the subnets inside it
Add a learned-route filter that rejects the office's overlapping 172.16.0.0/20 range so it cannot capture traffic meant for the cloud subnets
questions.why: An overlapping range learned from the office can capture cloud-bound traffic, so a learned-route filter that rejects it is the missing step that keeps the summary plan safe.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean when a Cloud Router advertises a prefix to its BGP peer?
choices: It blocks the peer from sending any traffic to the prefix until the filter is removed
It creates a firewall rule that allows the peer to open connections into the range
It copies the prefix from the peer into the VPC routing table as an accepted route
It tells the peer that traffic for that address range should be sent to this side
questions.why: Advertising a prefix is how a router tells its peer which address range it can receive traffic for, which is the definition given in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A team switches a Cloud Router from default to custom advertisement mode and adds only 192.168.20.0/24. Afterwards, the on-premises team reports that the subnet 192.168.30.0/24 is unreachable, even though its firewall rules allow the traffic. What best explains this?
choices: The firewall rules must be reset whenever the router changes mode, so the traffic is being blocked there
The BGP session has failed and must be restarted before any prefix can be learned by the peer
The on-premises routers have a static route pointing at a different gateway for the subnet
Switching to custom mode replaced the default list, and 192.168.30.0/24 was never added, so the peer was never told about it
questions.why: Custom mode replaces the default advertised list with only what you type, so an omitted subnet is never announced and the symptom looks like a firewall fault.

questions.prompt: An on-premises router advertises 172.17.0.0/16, which contains a cloud subnet 172.17.3.0/24 that is meant to be reached only locally. Which control prevents this learned prefix from being installed into the VPC routing table and capturing traffic?
choices: Changing the Cloud Router back to default advertisement mode
Creating a firewall rule that denies inbound traffic from 172.17.0.0/16
Setting a custom learned-route filter that rejects the 172.17.0.0/16 prefix
Adding 172.17.3.0/24 to the custom advertised list on the Cloud Router
questions.why: Learned-route filtering decides which prefixes the peer sends are accepted into the VPC routing table, so rejecting the overlapping range stops it from capturing traffic, while the other options control outgoing advertisements or firewalling instead.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we set Cloud Router to custom advertisement instead of leaving the default. Explain to them what custom advertised and custom learned routes do, and name one limit or tradeoff of filtering routes by hand.
lessons.modelAnswer: Default advertisement sends the subnets automatically, which is easy but may expose networks the office should not see. Custom advertisement lets us name exactly which prefixes Cloud Router announces to the on-premises peer, including summary ranges that are not subnets. Custom learned route filtering works on the way in: we accept only the prefixes we want from the office, so a stray default route or an overlapping range cannot take over traffic. The tradeoff is maintenance. Every new subnet or office range needs a matching change to the lists, or traffic silently fails with no error on the route itself. We should review the advertised and learned lists after every change and treat them as part of the network design, not a one-time setup.
rubricPoints: Custom advertisement chooses exactly which prefixes Cloud Router announces, replacing the default subnet list
Custom learned route filtering controls which prefixes from the peer are accepted into the VPC
A named limit: manual lists must be updated when subnets change, or traffic fails silently
Routes take effect on the peer after the BGP session updates, so changes need checking

suggested.rationale: Tracing which prefixes reach which network segment in a planned path tracer would let the learner see the effect of advertised and learned route lists on real paths.

lessons.plain: When a cloud network can reach the same destination through more than one route, something has to pick one. This objective is about choosing which rule set the network uses for that choice. Think of a delivery company with two roads to the same town: it needs a consistent method for deciding which road trucks take, and changing that method can send trucks down a different road tomorrow. Knowing which method your network uses, and why, lets you predict where traffic goes before something breaks.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a cloud network learns two different routes to the same address range, and both look equally good at first glance, what would you expect the network to do, and what could go wrong if that choice changed without anyone noticing?
lessons.teach:
A route is a rule that tells a network where to send traffic for a destination range. In Google Cloud, a VPC network is a virtual network that holds these routes. Cloud Router is the component that learns routes from an on-premises or other-cloud peer using BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, which is the standard way networks exchange reachability information. When BGP offers more than one path to the same destination, the VPC runs best path selection: a fixed sequence of comparisons that keeps one winner and discards the rest. Google Cloud offers two such sequences at the VPC level, called legacy and standard. They differ in which attributes they compare and in what order. The choice is a network-wide setting, so it affects every router in that network.

Why it works: the algorithm compares candidate routes attribute by attribute. The first attribute where the candidates differ decides the winner, and later attributes are ignored. That makes the outcome predictable, but it also means a small change in one attribute can flip the whole result.

Worked example. Two candidate routes to 10.20.0.0/16 arrive, one from a router in region A and one from a router in region B. Step 1: list both candidates with their attributes. Step 2: compare the first attribute in the chosen algorithm's order. Suppose they tie. Step 3: move to the next attribute. The region A route wins on it. Step 4: the losing route stays in the table only as a backup, and only if its priority allows it. Check the current vendor documentation for the exact attribute order of each algorithm.

Common mistake: treating the setting as cosmetic and changing it during a migration. Consequence: traffic can move to a different path mid-session. If a stateful firewall sees only one direction of a flow, the connection breaks.

The selection rule is part of the design, not an afterthought. Choose it on purpose, record it, and test traffic paths after any change.

questions.prompt: A team runs a VPC network, which is a virtual network that holds routes. Two candidate routes to 192.168.40.0/24 arrive by BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol that routers use to exchange reachability. One comes from a Cloud Router in europe-west1 and one from a Cloud Router in us-east4. Cloud Router is the component that learns BGP routes. Work through best path selection under the network's chosen algorithm. Step 1: list both candidates with their attributes. Step 2: compare the first attribute in that algorithm's order. The two candidates tie. Step 3: [missing]. Which completion correctly fills the missing step?
choices: Move to the next attribute in the chosen algorithm's order, and let the first attribute that differs decide the winner
Switch to the other algorithm and use whichever route it prefers
Keep the route from the region whose name comes first alphabetically
Declare both routes winners and split traffic between them evenly
questions.why: Best path selection keeps one winner, and the first attribute where the candidates differ decides the result, so the next attribute in order is compared when there is a tie.

questions.prompt: In a Google Cloud VPC network, what is the scope of the legacy or standard best path selection setting?
choices: Each subnet can use its own setting
Each Cloud Router can be set separately
Each region chooses one setting for its own traffic
The whole network: every router in that VPC follows the same setting
questions.why: The teaching text says the choice is a network-wide setting that affects every router in the network.

questions.prompt: Two candidate routes to 10.50.0.0/18 are compared under one best path algorithm. Route X differs from route Y first on an attribute where X is better. On every later attribute, Y is better. Which route wins?
choices: Route X, because the first attribute that differs decides and later attributes are ignored
Neither route wins, because a tie is required before any decision
Route Y, because it is better on more attributes
Both routes are kept as equal winners
questions.why: Each comparison is made in order, and the first attribute where the candidates differ decides the winner, so later attributes do not matter.

questions.prompt: A team changes the best path selection setting during a migration and does not test traffic afterward. A stateful firewall, which tracks connections and needs to see both directions of a session, is in the path. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Traffic can move to a different path mid-session, so the firewall may see only one direction and the connection breaks
The VPC rejects all BGP advertisements until the setting is reverted
Cloud Router permanently deletes all learned routes
Nothing changes, because the setting only affects routes that are never used
questions.why: The teaching text warns that changing the setting can move traffic to a different path mid-session, and a stateful firewall that sees only one direction of a flow can break the connection.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what best path selection does at a VPC, when you would choose legacy versus standard, and one limit or risk of changing the setting later.
lessons.modelAnswer: Best path selection is the step where the VPC picks one route when BGP offers several paths to the same destination. It works through a fixed list of attributes and stops at the first attribute that separates the candidates. Legacy and standard are two different lists, and the setting applies to the whole network, not one router. I would choose between them by checking which behavior matches the routing design we need, especially in a multi-region setup where paths come from different regions. The main limit is that the setting is global to the VPC, so changing it can shift traffic for every connected router at once. A change can move established flows onto a different path, and stateful firewalls may drop them if they only see one direction. So I would change it only in a planned window, test paths before and after, and keep a rollback plan.
rubricPoints: Best path selection picks one route when several paths to the same destination exist.
Legacy and standard are two different attribute orders, set at the VPC level.
The first differing attribute decides the winner, so small changes can flip the result.
Changing the setting can move live traffic and break flows, so it needs a planned change and testing.

suggested.rationale: A planned path tracer would let the learner see which of two routes wins under each setting, which is the core reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Network Connectivity Center is a way to connect several separate networks through one central hub, like a station where many roads meet. Your cloud network is one place, and your office or another cloud is another. A hybrid spoke is one road from that hub out to a place outside Google Cloud. This lesson covers two kinds: a VPN spoke, which is an encrypted link carried over the public internet, and a VLAN attachment spoke, which is a logical connection over a private physical link to Google. Creating a spoke means choosing the right kind and wiring it to the hub so routes can flow.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has an office network and a Google Cloud network. Without any notes, what would you expect a central hub with spokes to gain you compared with connecting every network directly to every other network?
lessons.teach:
Network Connectivity Center, shortened to NCC, is a hub resource in your project that joins otherwise separate networks. Each connection that plugs into the hub is called a spoke. A hybrid spoke reaches outside Google Cloud, to an on-premises site or another cloud. This objective covers two hybrid spoke types. A VPN spoke uses one or more VPN tunnels, which are encrypted connections over the public internet. A VLAN attachment spoke uses a VLAN attachment, the Google-side end of a logical circuit (a VLAN, or virtual LAN, is a separated slice of a private physical link) running over a Dedicated or Partner Interconnect.

Why it works: each hybrid spoke is tied to a Cloud Router, which uses BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the routing protocol networks use to tell each other which address ranges they can reach) to learn and advertise routes. Once routes are exchanged, the hub can carry traffic to and from that spoke, so one hybrid link serves many attached networks without a separate link for every pair.

Worked example: an office uses 10.20.0.0/16 and needs to reach a VPC. Step 1: create the hub. Step 2: create a VPN spoke with tunnels to the office gateway, backed by a Cloud Router. Step 3: the router learns 10.20.0.0/16 from the office over BGP. Step 4: the hub lists that route for the spoke, so traffic to 10.20.0.0/16 leaves through the tunnel.

Common mistake: creating the spoke without a working BGP session, then assuming the hub will route. The tunnel can show as up while no routes are exchanged, so traffic is silently dropped.

Consequence: a spoke with no learned routes looks connected in the console but carries no production traffic, so verify learned routes after every change. A spoke is only as useful as the routes it exchanges.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain has a warehouse at 192.168.40.0/24 and wants its Google Cloud VPC to reach it through a VLAN attachment spoke on a Dedicated Interconnect. Here is the setup so far. Step 1: create the NCC hub in the project. Step 2: create a VLAN attachment on the Dedicated Interconnect and attach it to a Cloud Router. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the hub lists 192.168.40.0/24 for the spoke, so traffic to the warehouse leaves through the attachment.
choices: Enable Private Google Access on the VPC subnet so the warehouse can reach Google APIs.
Raise the MTU on the VLAN attachment to 9000 so large packets can cross the link.
The on-premises router and the Cloud Router establish a BGP session, and the Cloud Router learns 192.168.40.0/24 from it.
Create a second NCC hub dedicated to the warehouse so its routes stay separate.
questions.why: Step 4 can only list the warehouse route if the Cloud Router has first learned it over a working BGP session, which is the missing step.

questions.prompt: In Network Connectivity Center, what is a spoke?
choices: A connection plugged into the hub that joins a network to it.
The routing protocol that tells networks which address ranges they can reach.
The encrypted tunnel that carries traffic over the public internet.
The Cloud Router that advertises routes to the on-premises site.
questions.why: A spoke is the name for each connection that plugs into an NCC hub, while the Cloud Router, tunnel, and BGP are parts that support a spoke rather than being the spoke itself.

questions.prompt: A team creates a VPN spoke to a partner's gateway. The tunnel shows as up in the console, but production traffic to the partner's address range is dropped. Which check is most likely to find the cause?
choices: Confirm the hub was created in a different region from the Cloud Router.
Confirm the tunnel's shared secret is longer than twenty characters.
Confirm the VLAN attachment has the correct VLAN ID for the partner circuit.
Confirm the BGP session is established and that the partner's address range appears as a learned route for the spoke.
questions.why: A tunnel can be up while no routes are exchanged, so the spoke carries no traffic until BGP has learned the partner's range, which is why verifying learned routes is the right check.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts the two hybrid spoke types covered in this objective?
choices: A VPN spoke uses encrypted tunnels over the public internet, while a VLAN attachment spoke uses a VLAN attachment over a Dedicated or Partner Interconnect.
A VLAN attachment spoke runs over the public internet, and a VPN spoke runs over a private physical link.
A VPN spoke does not need a Cloud Router, because the tunnel itself exchanges routes.
Both spoke types require a Partner Interconnect, and they differ only in the name of their Cloud Router.
questions.why: The VPN spoke relies on encrypted tunnels across the internet, and the VLAN attachment spoke relies on a VLAN attachment carried by an Interconnect, and both are tied to a Cloud Router that exchanges routes over BGP.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would create a VPN-based hybrid spoke in Network Connectivity Center instead of a VLAN attachment spoke, and name one limit or tradeoff of the VPN choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a VPN spoke when the on-premises site needs a quick, encrypted link and a dedicated private circuit is not yet ordered or not justified by the traffic. The spoke rides tunnels over the public internet, so the speed and latency depend on internet paths and can vary, unlike a private interconnect. Each spoke still needs a Cloud Router with a working BGP session, because the hub only knows routes that the router has learned. Before go-live I would confirm learned and advertised routes, not just that the tunnel is up. If the workload later needs steadier throughput or private connectivity, I would plan a move to a VLAN attachment spoke over an interconnect.
rubricPoints: A hybrid spoke is a connection from the NCC hub to a network outside Google Cloud.
VPN spokes use encrypted tunnels over the internet, with variable performance.
VLAN attachment spokes ride a private interconnect and are chosen for steadier, private links.
Each hybrid spoke depends on a Cloud Router with BGP routes; a tunnel that is up alone does not prove routing works.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a VPN spoke and a VLAN attachment spoke in a realistic scenario builds the decision skill this objective tests, and no listed mission covers hybrid network connectivity directly.

lessons.plain: Picture two offices, each with its own private network, that need to share files. Normally their traffic would have to cross the public internet, which is slow and unpredictable. Site-to-site data transfer lets a cloud provider's own private backbone act as the middle road. Each office connects into the cloud network once, and the cloud carries traffic between the offices. The offices talk to each other without touching the public internet, and the cloud handles the routing between them. Think of it as a private highway linking two buildings, with the cloud as the highway operator.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two branch offices each connect to the same cloud network through their own VPN tunnel. Without any extra feature turned on, can a server in branch A reach a server in branch B through the cloud, and why might it fail by default?
lessons.teach:
Site-to-site data transfer means letting two on-premises sites, which are physical locations such as a head office or a factory with their own networks, exchange data with each other through a cloud provider's network. Each site first links to the cloud through a hybrid spoke, meaning a connection attachment such as a VPN tunnel or a VLAN attachment on a dedicated interconnect. A hub is the central cloud resource that collects those spokes. When site-to-site data transfer is enabled on the hub, the hub forwards traffic between spokes, so site A can reach site B across the provider's backbone, which is the private high-capacity network inside the provider's facilities.

Why it works: by default the cloud usually routes between each site and the cloud network, not from one site to another. Enabling the feature tells the hub to carry spoke-to-spoke traffic. Routing exchange using BGP, the protocol routers use to announce which address ranges they can reach, tells each site which ranges sit behind the other.

Worked example: the head office uses range 10.1.0.0/16 and the factory uses 10.2.0.0/16. Step 1: each site has a hybrid spoke to the hub. Step 2: each site announces its range to the hub over BGP. Step 3: the hub learns 10.1.0.0/16 from one spoke and 10.2.0.0/16 from the other. Step 4: with data transfer enabled, the hub forwards a packet from 10.1.0.5 to 10.2.0.9 out the factory spoke, and the packet never crosses the public internet.

Common mistake: assuming two sites can talk just because both have working tunnels into the cloud. If the feature is off, or the two sites use overlapping address ranges, traffic fails or is misrouted.

Consequence in a running system: if a site changes its announced ranges and the hub's learned routes are not updated, traffic can be dropped or sent the wrong way, so you verify the learned routes, not only the tunnel status. Site-to-site data transfer moves data over the provider's network, and that usage can carry charges, so check pricing before you enable it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a warehouse at 192.168.10.0/24 and a depot at 192.168.20.0/24. Each site has a VPN tunnel to the same cloud hub. Step 1: each site has a hybrid spoke to the hub. Step 2: each site announces its range to the hub over BGP. Step 3: the hub learns 192.168.10.0/24 from the warehouse spoke and 192.168.20.0/24 from the depot spoke. Step 4 is missing. A warehouse host at 192.168.10.40 now needs to send a packet to 192.168.20.15 at the depot. Which missing step makes that work?
choices: Renumber the depot to a range that starts with 10. so the hub accepts it.
Check that the depot tunnel shows as up in the console, since a working tunnel is enough for the two sites to talk.
Enable site-to-site data transfer on the hub so it forwards traffic between the warehouse and depot spokes.
Add a default route on the warehouse router that sends all traffic to the public internet.
questions.why: Spoke-to-spoke forwarding only happens when site-to-site data transfer is enabled on the hub, because by default the hub carries traffic between each site and the cloud, not between sites.

questions.prompt: When site-to-site data transfer is turned off on a hub, which traffic does the hub still carry?
choices: Only traffic between the hub and cloud resources inside the same project.
Traffic between two sites, sent over the public internet instead of the provider network.
Traffic from each site to the cloud network, but not traffic from one site to another.
No traffic at all, because the hub drops every packet not addressed to the cloud.
questions.why: By default the hub routes between each site and the cloud network; carrying site-to-site traffic requires the feature to be enabled.

questions.prompt: A clinic and a lab both announce 172.16.5.0/24 over BGP to the same hub, and both tunnels are up. Clinic-to-lab traffic fails. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The tunnels are too slow, so the hub needs a larger VLAN attachment.
The lab must be moved to a dedicated interconnect before it can reach the clinic.
The two sites use overlapping address ranges, so the hub cannot route between them reliably.
BGP cannot carry any address ranges that start with 172.
questions.why: Overlapping announced ranges make the hub unable to tell which spoke a destination belongs to, so traffic is misrouted or dropped even when every tunnel is up.

questions.prompt: A factory changes the range it announces from 10.2.0.0/16 to 10.3.0.0/16, but the hub still shows the old route. Which check best catches this problem?
choices: Compare the routes the hub has learned against the ranges the factory now announces.
Restart the head office VPN tunnel so the hub clears its address table.
Confirm the factory tunnel is still up, since tunnel status shows which routes were learned.
Check the billing report for site-to-site traffic from the factory.
questions.why: Tunnel status only shows whether the link is up, so the learned routes must be compared directly with what each site currently announces to catch stale routes.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why two branch offices cannot just talk to each other directly when each already has a VPN to the cloud. Explain what site-to-site data transfer adds, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each branch VPN only connects that branch to the cloud network. By default the cloud routes traffic between a branch and the cloud, not from one branch to another, so the two offices cannot reach each other just because both have tunnels. Site-to-site data transfer, enabled on the hub that both branch connections attach to, tells the cloud to carry traffic between those connections across the provider's backbone instead of the public internet. The branches exchange routes through BGP, so each learns the other's address ranges. The tradeoff is that traffic now passes through a shared cloud hub, so it can carry data transfer charges and depends on that hub's routing. Overlapping address ranges between the offices would also break it, so the ranges must be unique before you turn it on.
rubricPoints: Explains that by default the cloud routes between each site and the cloud, not between sites
Describes the hub forwarding spoke-to-spoke traffic over the provider backbone once the feature is enabled
Notes that BGP route exchange must tell each site the other's address ranges
Names a limit such as data transfer charges, dependence on the hub, or overlapping address ranges

suggested.rationale: Tracing which path a packet takes between two sites through a hub matches what this engine plans to teach, though no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A router appliance is a virtual machine you run inside your cloud network that does routing work, usually with routing software from a networking vendor. Think of it as a dedicated gatekeeper at the edge of your cloud network. It tells the rest of the cloud which other networks it can reach, such as a branch office or another cloud, and it passes traffic along to them. This matters when you need a routing feature that the cloud's built-in router does not provide, or when you already run a trusted routing product and want to keep it. Learning this objective means knowing what the appliance does, how it shares its routes, and what breaks when it fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has a virtual machine in the cloud running a third-party routing product, and it sits between the cloud network and an office network. Without any reading, what do you think the cloud network needs to learn from that virtual machine before it can send traffic to the office, and what might go wrong if it learns nothing?
lessons.teach:
A router appliance is a virtual machine in your cloud network that runs routing software and forwards traffic for networks you cannot reach directly. A prefix is a block of IP addresses, written like 192.168.50.0/24. A next hop is the device a packet should be handed to next. BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is the standard way routers tell each other which prefixes they can reach. Cloud Router is the cloud's managed router that speaks BGP and keeps a table of learned routes. IP forwarding is the setting that lets a virtual machine pass packets that are not addressed to itself.

Why it works: the appliance opens a BGP session with Cloud Router and announces the office prefixes it can reach. Cloud Router installs those prefixes into the network's routing table, with the appliance as the next hop. Traffic to the office then flows to the appliance, which forwards it onward.

Worked example: the office network is 192.168.50.0/24. Step 1: the appliance learns that prefix from its office-side link. Step 2: it announces 192.168.50.0/24 to Cloud Router over BGP. Step 3: Cloud Router adds the route with the appliance as next hop. Step 4: a cloud workload sends a packet to 192.168.50.10. Step 5: the route points at the appliance, which forwards the packet over its office-side link.

Common mistake: assuming the virtual machine is enough by itself. Without a working BGP session and IP forwarding on the appliance, no route is learned and traffic is dropped.

Consequence: if the appliance goes down, its BGP session ends and the routes it announced are withdrawn. Traffic to the office fails unless a second appliance announces the same prefix.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a router appliance, a virtual machine named edge-gw-2, to reach its depot network 172.20.16.0/22. Here is the trace. Step 1: edge-gw-2 has a BGP session up with Cloud Router and IP forwarding turned on. Step 2: edge-gw-2 learns 172.20.16.0/22 over its depot-side link and announces it to Cloud Router over BGP. Step 3: Cloud Router installs a route for 172.20.16.0/22 with edge-gw-2 as the next hop. Step 4: a cloud workload sends a packet to 172.20.17.40. Step 5 is missing. Which step completes the trace?
choices: The packet is delivered to the address of edge-gw-2 itself and never reaches the depot.
The workload drops the packet because a route with a next hop is never needed for traffic to leave the cloud.
Cloud Router sends the packet straight to the depot over the public internet, bypassing the appliance.
Edge-gw-2 passes the packet, which is not addressed to it, out its depot-side link toward 172.20.17.40.
questions.why: IP forwarding lets edge-gw-2 pass a packet addressed to another host, so it hands the packet onward over its depot-side link, which completes the path the route set up.

questions.prompt: In this teaching text, what is a prefix such as 10.8.0.0/16?
choices: A firewall rule that allows traffic from a given source.
A single host address assigned to one virtual machine.
A routing protocol that routers use to share their tables.
A block of IP addresses written in a compact form.
questions.why: A prefix is defined in the text as a block of IP addresses, and the slash number describes how large that block is.

questions.prompt: A team builds a router appliance VM for a branch network 10.60.0.0/20. The VM has its branch-side link working and IP forwarding turned off, and its BGP session with Cloud Router never comes up. A cloud workload then sends traffic toward the branch. What is the most likely result?
choices: The traffic reaches the branch directly because the VM's branch-side link is already working.
No branch prefix is learned, so no route with the appliance as next hop exists, and the traffic is dropped.
Cloud Router learns the branch prefix from the VM and routes traffic through it anyway.
Cloud Router sends the traffic to a default gateway that forwards it to the branch automatically.
questions.why: Without a working BGP session no route is learned, and without IP forwarding the VM will not pass packets not addressed to itself, so the traffic is dropped.

questions.prompt: A company runs two router appliances, each announcing the same branch prefix 10.60.0.0/20 to Cloud Router over BGP. One appliance goes down. What happens to traffic to the branch?
choices: Traffic to the branch continues, because the remaining appliance still announces the same prefix and the route is kept.
Cloud Router deletes the branch prefix from every network, including the healthy appliance's announcement.
Traffic to the branch is redirected to the failed appliance until it restarts.
Traffic to the branch fails for the whole period, because routes never move to another appliance.
questions.why: When an appliance fails its BGP session ends and its routes are withdrawn, but a second appliance announcing the same prefix keeps the branch reachable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a router appliance is in a Google Cloud network, how it shares routes with Cloud Router, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on one.
lessons.modelAnswer: A router appliance is a virtual machine we run in our cloud network with routing software, usually from a vendor, so it can handle routing that the cloud's built-in router does not do. It connects to Cloud Router over BGP, which is the standard protocol for exchanging routes. The appliance announces the prefixes it can reach, such as our office network, and Cloud Router installs those routes with the appliance as the next hop. Traffic to the office then goes through the appliance. The main tradeoff is that we own the appliance's uptime and configuration. If it fails, its BGP session drops and the routes it advertised disappear, so traffic to that network fails. To reduce that risk we would run a second appliance advertising the same prefix, and we would have to check that the route preference between the two behaves the way we expect.
rubricPoints: A router appliance is a virtual machine in the cloud network running routing software that forwards traffic
It exchanges routes with Cloud Router over a BGP session and is used as a next hop
Its routes disappear when the appliance or its BGP session fails
A second appliance advertising the same prefix is a common way to reduce that single point of failure

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and console configuration, which the planned engines do not directly cover, so reading the teaching text is the best fit for now.

lessons.plain: Transitivity means that if A is connected to B, and B is connected to C, then A can reach C by passing through B. In cloud networks this does not always hold. Some connection types pass traffic along through a middle network, and others deliberately refuse to. When a team expects traffic to hop through a middle network and it silently fails, the usual cause is that the connection type is not transitive. Solving it means knowing which links pass traffic along and designing the path so traffic really has a route.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose network X is peered with network Y, and network Y is peered with network Z. With nothing else added, can a server in X send packets directly to a server in Z by going through Y? Answer yes or no and give a reason.
lessons.teach: Transitivity is the idea that a relationship passes through a middle point. In networking, a route is transitive when traffic from network A can reach network C by passing through network B, even though A and C were never connected directly. Many people assume every link works this way. In Google Cloud, VPC Network Peering does not. A VPC network is an isolated virtual network inside a project, and peering is a private link that joins two of them directly. Peering only exposes the subnets of the two networks it joins. It does not forward traffic that arrived from a third peered network. The reason is control: if one peering quietly passed along every network behind it, a single link could grant access to many networks at once, and access would become hard to reason about. Connection designs that are built to carry traffic onward, such as a hub-based connectivity service, or a VPN or Interconnect whose learned routes are shared through a Cloud Router, are the ones that act as transit. Worked example: network HUB is peered with SPOKE-A and SPOKE-B. Step 1: a VM in SPOKE-A sends a packet to 10.2.0.5, which lives in SPOKE-B. Step 2: SPOKE-A's peering to HUB shares only HUB's subnets, so SPOKE-A has no route to SPOKE-B's subnet through that peering. Step 3: the packet has no matching route and is dropped. Step 4: the fix is a transit-capable design between SPOKE-A and SPOKE-B, not more peerings to HUB. Common mistake: assuming that because both spokes peer with the hub they can reach each other, then spending hours on firewall rules that were never the problem. Consequence in a running system: traffic between spokes fails while each spoke still reaches the hub, which makes the outage look intermittent and easy to misdiagnose.

questions.prompt: A company runs a VPC named ops-vpc with a VM at 10.40.1.9. It has a VPC Network Peering to payments-vpc, which has subnets 10.30.0.0/16 and 10.31.0.0/16. Separately, payments-vpc is peered to data-vpc, which holds a database subnet at 172.20.8.0/24. The ops VM tries to reach 172.20.8.14. Step 1: the packet leaves ops-vpc toward 172.20.8.14. Step 2: the peering between ops-vpc and payments-vpc shares only payments-vpc's own subnets, so ops-vpc gets no route to 172.20.8.0/24 through that peering. Step 3: [missing step]. Final result: the packet is dropped, and the database never receives it.
choices: The database firewall rule blocks the address 10.40.1.9, so the packet is rejected after it arrives
The packet has no matching route in ops-vpc, so it has nowhere to go and is discarded at the source
The packet reaches data-vpc but nothing listens on the database port, so the connection is refused
payments-vpc forwards the packet onward into data-vpc, because two peerings in a chain count as one continuous link
questions.why: Because ops-vpc has no route to 172.20.8.0/24, the packet has no matching route and is dropped before it leaves the network, which is what the missing step describes.

questions.prompt: In Google Cloud, which kind of connection design can carry traffic from one network through a middle network onward to a third one?
choices: A firewall rule that allows ingress from another project's internal range
A hub-based connectivity service, or a VPN or Interconnect whose learned routes are shared through a Cloud Router
A VPC Network Peering link between two VPC networks
A static route that points to a Google-managed API endpoint
questions.why: Only designs built to forward traffic onward, such as a hub-based service or a shared-route VPN or Interconnect through Cloud Router, act as transit; a plain peering does not.

questions.prompt: A team has analytics-vpc peered to lake-vpc, and lake-vpc peered to vendor-vpc. A VM in analytics-vpc cannot reach a subnet in vendor-vpc, and the firewall rules on every network allow the traffic. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Peered networks can only reach subnets in the same region, so the vendor subnet is out of reach
The vendor subnet overlaps with lake-vpc and the peering dropped the route
Peering between analytics-vpc and lake-vpc does not carry traffic on to vendor-vpc, so analytics-vpc has no route there
The firewall rules must be set on the peering link itself before any traffic can pass
questions.why: VPC Network Peering exposes only the subnets of the two networks it directly joins, so analytics-vpc has no route to vendor-vpc even though both chains are peered.

questions.prompt: Monitoring shows that a VM in app-east reaches shared-services-vpc without trouble, but cannot reach reporting-vpc. The reporting-vpc VM can reach shared-services-vpc. What is the best first check?
choices: Rewrite the firewall rules on reporting-vpc to allow every source range
Add a second peering from reporting-vpc to app-east and wait for it to activate
Restart the app-east VM so it picks up a fresh copy of the peering table
Confirm whether app-east has a route to reporting-vpc's subnets, since a peering to shared-services-vpc does not share reporting-vpc's subnets
questions.why: The symptom points to a missing route caused by peering not transiting traffic, so checking the route table before touching firewalls is the right first step.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our two application VPCs are both peered with the shared services VPC, so they should talk to each other automatically. Explain to them whether that is true, what the transitivity limit means here, and one way to fix it, naming the tradeoff of that fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: That is not true, because VPC Network Peering is not transitive. Each peering shares only the subnet routes of the two networks it directly joins. App-VPC-1 can reach shared services, and app-VPC-2 can reach shared services, but app-VPC-1 has no route to app-VPC-2 through shared services, so traffic between the apps is dropped. You can confirm this by checking the effective routes on a VM in app-VPC-1 for app-VPC-2's subnet; the route will be missing. One fix is a direct peering between the two app VPCs. That is simple, but it must be created for every pair and does not scale past a few networks. A better fix for many networks is a hub-based design, such as Network Connectivity Center or a routed VPN between the networks. That scales better but adds cost and configuration. The tradeoff is simplicity against scale and cost.
rubricPoints: States that VPC Network Peering is not transitive and only shares routes of the two directly joined networks.
Explains that the missing route is why traffic between the two app VPCs is dropped.
Gives one fix, such as direct peering or a transit-capable hub design.
Names the tradeoff of that fix, such as simplicity versus scale and cost.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which network segments carry a packet and where a route is missing is the hands-on practice this objective needs, and the planned path tracer would build exactly that.

lessons.plain: Networking parts of a cloud setup, such as tunnels, routers, firewalls, DNS and address translation, do their work without telling you much by default. Cloud Logging is the place where those parts can write short records of what happened: a tunnel came up, a packet was blocked, a DNS lookup was answered. Turning logging on for each component is a deliberate choice, and reviewing those records later is how you find out what the network actually did. Think of a building's visitor book: it is only useful if someone switched it on before the visitors arrived, and keeping every entry costs time and paper.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server in a private subnet suddenly cannot reach an outside API, and nobody remembers changing anything. Before reading anything here, which records would you want switched on in advance so you could tell whether a firewall, the address translation, or a VPN tunnel caused it, and why might you not want to record everything?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Logging is Google Cloud's central log store: components write structured records into it, and you read them with filters. Each networking component has its own switch. Cloud VPN writes tunnel status and negotiation events, which show whether the encrypted link to another site is up. Cloud Router exchanges routes with peers using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the protocol routers use to announce which address ranges they can reach), and it can log session changes and route updates per router. Cloud NAT (network address translation, which lets private machines reach outside services through a shared outside address) can log only translation errors or all translations, per gateway. VPC Flow Logs (sampled records of traffic between VM instances) are enabled per subnet and carry sampling and aggregation settings. Firewall rule logging records matches for each rule you mark. Cloud DNS query logging records lookups in zones where it is enabled. VPC Service Controls (a perimeter that blocks data access from outside trusted boundaries) writes violation records to audit logs. Network Connectivity Center (which manages hub-and-spoke connections) records configuration changes in audit logs. Logs exist only for what was switched on, and they are kept for the retention period of the log bucket they land in.

Worked example: NAT logging is set to errors only. A VM cannot reach the API. Step 1: confirm the NAT gateway has error logging on. Step 2: filter by the VM's internal address. Step 3: read the error type. If it reports port allocation failure, translation capacity is exhausted, not a firewall block. Step 4: act on that capacity.

Common mistake: enabling full flow logging on every subnet, then finding the bill and the noise are large, when sampling and filters would have answered the question. Consequence: if a log was never switched on, the incident has no evidence and you must reproduce it.

A switched-on log is a record of past behavior, not a live alarm, and its value depends on being enabled before the problem starts.

questions.prompt: Halvorsen Logistics runs a Cloud Router in us-east1 that holds a BGP session with an office router. Users report the session dropped at about 02:10, and the network team wants to know when the office router withdrew its routes. Step 1: confirm that logging is switched on for that Cloud Router. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: read the session-down event and its timestamp. Step 4: compare that timestamp with the office router's maintenance record. Which action is the missing Step 2?
choices: Restart the Cloud Router so the session re-establishes and writes fresh events.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the office subnet to capture the dropped packets.
Filter the Cloud Router's log entries by the router's name and a time window around 02:10.
Switch on Cloud NAT error logging so translation failures appear next to the BGP events.
questions.why: Filtering by the router and a time window around the drop isolates the session records from that period, which is the step that turns the switched-on log into usable evidence.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm has turned on VPC Flow Logs for one subnet that holds its reporting servers. Which description of what those records contain is accurate?
choices: A live alert that fires the moment a firewall rule denies a packet.
A record of each DNS lookup made by the reporting servers.
A complete packet capture of every byte the servers send to the internet.
Sampled records of traffic between VM instances in that subnet, with sampling and aggregation settings.
questions.why: VPC Flow Logs are sampled records of traffic between VM instances, enabled per subnet, with sampling and aggregation settings, and they are not full captures, alerts, or DNS logs.

questions.prompt: Last month a team never switched on Cloud Router session logging. This week a BGP session on that router flapped for four minutes. What can the team find in Cloud Logging about those four minutes?
choices: The session-change entries for those four minutes, which show the exact cause.
Nothing from Cloud Logging for those four minutes, so they must reproduce the flap to gather evidence.
Entries that appear once they enable logging now, because the history is backfilled.
Cloud VPN tunnel negotiation events replayed from the same period.
questions.why: Logs exist only for what was switched on before the problem, so with session logging off the incident has no recorded evidence and must be reproduced.

questions.prompt: A company restricts access to a storage bucket with a VPC Service Controls perimeter. A caller outside the trusted boundary was refused. The security engineer wants to see which caller was refused and when. Where should the engineer look?
choices: The Cloud Router route update log for the bucket's region.
The violation records written to audit logs for the perimeter.
The Cloud NAT translation logs for the caller's subnet.
The DNS query log for the bucket's hostname.
questions.why: VPC Service Controls writes violation records to audit logs, so those records show refused access attempts, while the other logs cover unrelated components.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who will own our network logs next week which networking components need logging switched on deliberately, what it costs to turn everything on, and one thing these logs cannot tell you.
lessons.modelAnswer: Most networking components only write logs after someone enables them, and each has its own switch. Cloud VPN and Cloud Router produce tunnel and BGP session events, Cloud NAT lets you choose errors only or all translations, and VPC Flow Logs are enabled per subnet with sampling and aggregation settings. Firewall rule logging is set per rule, while VPC Service Controls violations and Network Connectivity Center changes land in audit logs. The tradeoff is cost and volume: full flow logging on every subnet is expensive and noisy, so we enable what answers likely questions and use filters and exclusions to trim the rest. The limit is that logs record only what happened after logging was on, so an incident from before that has no evidence. Retention is set by the log bucket, so we check that too.
rubricPoints: Names that each networking component has its own logging switch, set per router, subnet, rule, gateway or zone
Explains the cost and noise tradeoff of logging everything and how sampling or filters reduce it
States that logs only exist from the time logging was enabled and cannot reconstruct earlier events
Mentions that retention is governed by the log bucket, so how long records survive needs checking

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly per-component settings, log locations and tradeoffs, which a short reading of the console and product options covers better than an existing mission.

lessons.plain: Monitoring network metrics means keeping a steady record of numbers that describe how network parts behave over time, such as how many bytes cross a connection, whether a link is up, or how many requests a load balancer rejected. Think of a building's electricity meter and a panel of warning lights: you do not wait for someone to report a blackout, you watch the numbers and get an alert when one drifts outside its normal range. This objective covers the main network pieces on Google Cloud: VPN tunnels, dedicated links to your data center, the routers that exchange routes, load balancers, a web application firewall service, and the NAT service that lets private machines reach the internet. Each of these publishes its own numbers that you can watch.
lessons.guessPrompt: A VPN tunnel to your office went down at 2am, but nobody noticed until 9am. What kind of signal could have caught it within minutes, and what single number would you have watched?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a numeric measurement recorded at regular intervals. It has a name and often labels that say which resource it came from, such as which tunnel or which load balancer. A time series is the sequence of values for one metric with one set of labels. Cloud Monitoring, part of Google Cloud Observability, stores these series, draws them on dashboards, and runs alert policies that fire when a value crosses a threshold for a set duration. It works because a failing network part usually changes a number before a person notices. A tunnel that drops shows its status fall. A NAT gateway that runs out of ports shows dropped outbound packets rise. A web firewall policy that starts blocking traffic shows its denied-request count climb.

Worked example: you watch the tunnel status metric for one Cloud VPN tunnel. Step 1: it reads 1 (up) all week. Step 2: at 02:10 it drops to 0. Step 3: an alert policy that says 'status is 0 for 5 minutes' fires at 02:15. Step 4: the traffic byte metric for that tunnel is flat from 02:10 onward, which confirms a real outage rather than a faulty sensor.

Common mistake: setting thresholds from one unusual day and never checking the normal range. Alerts then either fire constantly or never fire. Look at each metric's baseline first, then set the threshold above normal noise.

Consequence in a running system: when NAT runs out of ports, outbound calls from your servers fail intermittently, and the failures look like application bugs unless someone watches the NAT dropped-packet metric. Watching these numbers turns network trouble from a surprise into an early, measurable signal.

questions.prompt: A retail company watches the denied-request count for its web firewall policy. A metric is a number recorded at regular intervals, and this one counts requests the policy blocked. Step 1: on normal days the count stays between 20 and 40 per hour. Step 2: on Tuesday at 14:00 it jumps to 900 per hour. Step 3: the team wants an alert policy that fires only when the count stays high for 10 minutes, and they need to choose the threshold. Which threshold fits the baseline they recorded?
choices: 5000, which is so high the alert would never fire even during an attack
3, which is below normal so the alert fires constantly
35, which sits inside the normal range so the alert fires on ordinary days
200, which is above normal noise but below the Tuesday spike
questions.why: A threshold should sit above the normal noise seen in the baseline, so 200 avoids false alarms while still catching the 900 spike, whereas 3 and 35 cause constant firing and 5000 never fires.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a time series in Cloud Monitoring?
choices: A single reading of a metric taken once during an incident
A list of every alert policy that has fired across all projects in a month
The fixed threshold that a metric must cross before an alert is sent
The sequence of values for one metric with one set of labels, such as one specific tunnel
questions.why: The teaching text defines a time series as the sequence of values for one metric with one set of labels, so a single tunnel's status readings over time form one series.

questions.prompt: A team sees intermittent failures on outbound calls from their servers. Their NAT gateway's dropped-packet metric has been rising steadily for the past hour, while their application logs show no code changes. What does the rising metric most directly suggest?
choices: The sensor recording the metric is faulty and should be replaced
The alert threshold is too high and should be lowered to zero
The NAT gateway is dropping outbound packets, which fits running out of ports and would explain the intermittent failures
The application code has a bug unrelated to the network, so the metric can be ignored
questions.why: The teaching text says that when NAT runs out of ports, the dropped-packet metric rises and outbound calls fail intermittently, so a rising dropped-packet count points to the NAT gateway as the cause.

questions.prompt: An alert policy is set to fire when a Cloud VPN tunnel's status is 0 for 5 minutes. The status drops to 0 at 09:00 and returns to 1 at 09:03. Does the alert fire, and why?
choices: Yes, because the traffic byte metric also changed during those 3 minutes
No, because the status was 0 for only 3 minutes, which is less than the required 5-minute duration
Yes, because any drop to 0 fires an alert immediately regardless of duration
No, because alerts can only fire on values above the threshold, never below it
questions.why: An alert policy fires only when the value crosses the threshold for the set duration, and 3 minutes of status 0 does not meet the 5-minute requirement.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only watched application logs how you would choose which network metrics to watch for a setup that uses both a VPN and a dedicated interconnect. Name one limit of metrics compared with other diagnostic tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the path each piece of traffic takes. For the VPN, I would watch tunnel status and bytes sent and received, so I know whether the tunnel is up and carrying traffic. For the interconnect, I would watch the VLAN attachment's link state and throughput, and I would compare throughput to the provisioned capacity. The Cloud Router metrics tell me whether BGP sessions are up and how many routes are being learned, because a session can stay up while learning nothing useful. Then I would set alerts on the change, not just on the absolute value, and check each one against its normal range. The main limit of metrics is that they tell you that something changed and where, but not why. A flat byte count shows a problem; it does not show which packet was dropped or which firewall rule matched. For that, I would move to more detailed tools after the alert fires.
rubricPoints: Names specific metrics for VPN tunnels, interconnect attachments, and Cloud Router sessions
Explains that thresholds should be based on a normal baseline
States that metrics show that and where something changed, not the detailed cause
Mentions a more detailed tool as the next step after an alert

suggested.rationale: Building a metric alarm with a threshold and duration directly practises choosing and reading network metrics.

lessons.plain: Draining and redirecting traffic means moving users away from one part of a service without breaking the requests they already have in progress. Think of a busy shop that wants to close one checkout lane for cleaning. It stops sending new customers to that lane, lets the people already at it finish paying, and directs everyone else to the open lanes. A load balancer is the front door that spreads incoming requests across several servers. Using it this way lets you take a server out for maintenance or deployment with few or no visible failures for users.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you remove one of three servers from a pool while some users are halfway through a large download. What should happen to those downloads, and where should brand-new requests go?
lessons.teach:
Draining means letting a server finish the work it already holds while sending it no new work. Redirecting means changing where new requests are routed, often in steps. Both happen at the load balancer, the component that accepts user requests and forwards each one to a backend. A backend is a server or group of servers that does the actual work. In Google Cloud, an Application Load Balancer works at the level of web requests. Backends are grouped into a backend service, and a URL map decides which backend service handles a request, based on details such as host name or path.

Why it works: when a backend is taken out of rotation, the balancer stops choosing it for new requests, but connections already open to it are allowed to finish. A connection draining timeout sets how long the balancer waits for those old connections before cutting them off. Health checks are separate. They are periodic probes that decide whether a backend is fit to receive traffic at all.

Worked example: a backend service has two instance groups, A and B, each receiving half of the traffic. You need to update A. Step 1: set A's share to zero, or remove A from the backend service. Step 2: new requests now reach only B. Step 3: requests already running on A continue until they finish or the drain timeout, say 300 seconds, passes. Step 4: after A is updated and passes its health checks, return it to the service and raise its share gradually.

Common mistake: removing a backend and deleting its virtual machines in the same moment, or setting the drain timeout too short for long uploads, which cuts users off mid-request.

Consequence: when a deploy skips the drain step, error rates spike during the rollout, and the load balancer logs show failures on instances that were already gone.

questions.prompt: A media company, StreamHub, runs a backend service with three instance groups: X, Y and Z, each getting a third of traffic. They need to patch group Z. Step 1: set Z's share to zero so new requests stop going to it. Step 2: new requests now reach only X and Y. Step 3: requests already running on Z are allowed to finish, up to a drain timeout of 600 seconds. Step 4 is missing and is the one you must identify: what should happen to Z's virtual machines before they are deleted or patched?
choices: Raise Z's share back to one third so it receives new requests while it is being patched.
Lower the drain timeout to 10 seconds so the patch finishes faster.
Delete Z's virtual machines immediately so the freed capacity is available to X and Y.
Wait until the open connections finish or the 600-second drain timeout passes, then delete or patch Z's virtual machines.
questions.why: Deleting Z's machines before its open connections finish or the drain timeout passes repeats the common mistake, so the correct step is to wait for the drain to complete before removing the machines.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is connection draining in an Application Load Balancer, where a backend is a server or group of servers that does the work?
choices: Letting a backend finish the requests it already holds while sending it no new requests.
Permanently removing a backend from the backend service and deleting its records.
Splitting all incoming requests evenly across every backend in the backend service.
Checking each backend every few seconds to see whether it is fit to receive traffic.
questions.why: Draining is defined in the text as finishing work already held while receiving no new work, which is what the second choice states in plain words.

questions.prompt: A backend in a ticketing company's service has been failing its health checks for ten minutes. What does that failing result tell the load balancer, and what does it not tell it?
choices: It tells the balancer the backend is unfit to receive traffic, and it sets how long old connections may finish before being cut off.
It tells the balancer the backend is unfit to receive traffic, but it does not set how long old connections are allowed to finish.
It tells the balancer to delete the backend's virtual machines, but it does not affect new requests.
It tells the balancer to double the drain timeout, so old connections can run longer.
questions.why: Health checks are separate periodic probes that decide fitness to receive traffic, while the connection draining timeout is a different setting that governs old connections.

questions.prompt: A video platform sets the connection draining timeout on a backend to 120 seconds. A user has an upload that takes 40 minutes and is in progress on that backend when the backend is removed from rotation. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The upload continues for 40 minutes because the timeout only applies to idle connections.
The upload is cut off once the 120-second timeout passes, because the timeout is shorter than the upload.
The upload is held until the backend passes its health checks again.
The upload finishes normally because new requests are no longer sent to the backend.
questions.why: The drain timeout is the maximum wait for old connections, so a 40-minute upload with a 120-second timeout will be cut off mid-request.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would take one backend out of a load-balanced service for maintenance without dropping users, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose.
