choices: The last machine that will process the packet's data, which is always the destination address in the packet.
The next device that receives the packet on its way toward its destination, such as an internal load balancer here.
The public address that outside clients use to reach the load balancer over the internet.
The health check result that decides which appliance is allowed to receive traffic.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the next hop as the next device that receives the packet, which in this objective is an internal load balancer.

questions.prompt: A route points at an internal load balancer. Every appliance in its backend group fails its health check at the same moment. What happens to traffic that matches the route?
choices: The load balancer queues the packets until an appliance recovers, then delivers them in order.
The route falls back to the default internet gateway, so traffic continues over the public internet.
Traffic to that address range is dropped, because the route has no healthy target, and the outage sits in the network path.
The application servers detect the outage and reroute the packets themselves to another network.
questions.why: With no healthy appliance, the route has no valid target, so matching traffic is dropped and the fault appears in the network path rather than the application.

questions.prompt: A multi-NIC appliance VM has one interface in each of two networks, but its IP forwarding setting is turned off. A client's packet arrives at the appliance addressed to a host in the other network. What is the most likely result?
choices: The packet is forwarded normally, because the appliance already has an interface in both networks.
The appliance forwards the packet only if the client's route was set up as a static route.
The load balancer rewrites the address so the appliance accepts the packet as its own.
The packet is silently lost on the appliance, because the VM is not allowed to forward packets that are not addressed to itself.
questions.why: IP forwarding is the VM setting that allows it to pass on packets not addressed to itself, and without it the packets arrive and then disappear.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an internal load balancer used as a route's next hop gives high availability for a pool of multi-NIC appliances. Name one limit or tradeoff of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: A route in one network points its destination range at the forwarding rule of an internal load balancer, instead of at a single appliance. The load balancer spreads traffic across appliances in several zones and uses health checks to skip any that are down, so one failure does not stop the path. Each appliance has a second interface in the other network and must have IP forwarding enabled, otherwise packets it receives are dropped. A tradeoff to mention is that the load balancer sees traffic as passthrough, so the appliances need routes back that send replies through the same pool. If return traffic takes another path, the appliance never sees it, and stateful inspection breaks.
rubricPoints: A route's next hop is the internal load balancer forwarding rule, not a single VM.
Health checks remove failed appliances so traffic keeps flowing through healthy ones.
Appliances need a second interface in the other network and IP forwarding enabled.
Return traffic must also route through the same appliance pool to stay inspected.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the hop-by-hop path from a client through the route, load balancer and appliance would make the next-hop behaviour visible, though no listed mission covers it today.

lessons.plain: Normally a computer decides where to send a packet by looking only at its destination address, like a postal sorter who reads only the city. A policy-based route is a rule that looks at more than that: where the packet came from, what kind of traffic it is, and which protocol it uses. When a packet matches the rule, it is sent to a chosen helper device instead of the usual path. This matters when one machine has several network connections and you want certain traffic, such as traffic between two private networks, to pass through a security appliance that can inspect it, while everything else keeps its normal route. Done well, the setup also keeps working if one helper fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: A virtual machine has two network connections, one in each of two private networks. You want only traffic from one network to the other to be sent through a security appliance, while other traffic keeps its normal path. Before reading on, what would you add to the routing setup, and what would you match on besides the destination?
lessons.teach:
A route is a line in a routing table that says: for destinations in this range, send packets to this next hop, meaning the next device on the path. A policy-based route adds conditions. It can match on a source address range, a destination range, and a protocol. When a packet matches, that policy-based route's next hop takes precedence over the ordinary routes for that traffic. Traffic that matches no policy-based route follows normal routing as before. A multi-NIC virtual machine is a machine with more than one network interface, where each interface attaches to a different network, and it forwards packets between them. An internal passthrough load balancer is a private load balancer that forwards packets without changing them, and it can serve as a next hop. A health check is a periodic probe that decides whether a backend is still able to take traffic.

Why it works: the rule applies only to the flow you name, so you can steer one kind of traffic through an inspection appliance without moving everything else. Worked example: network A uses 10.1.0.0/24 and network B uses 10.2.0.0/24. Step 1: deploy two appliance VMs, each with one NIC in each network, in two zones. Step 2: place them behind an internal passthrough load balancer, whose forwarding rule becomes the next hop. Step 3: create a policy-based route in network A matching source 10.1.0.0/24 and destination 10.2.0.0/24, with that load balancer as next hop. Step 4: a packet from 10.1.0.5 to 10.2.0.7 matches, goes to the load balancer, which sends it to a healthy appliance. If one appliance fails its health check, new flows go to the other, which is the high-availability part.

Common mistake: forgetting return traffic. The reply from 10.2.0.7 must also pass through an appliance, so network B needs a matching policy-based route too. Otherwise a stateful inspector sees only half of the conversation and drops it.

Consequence: if the next hop has no healthy backend, matching traffic has nowhere to go and is dropped. A wrong rule can cut off a live path while the sending side shows no error.

questions.prompt: Harbor Foods has an app network at 192.168.20.0/24 and a payments network at 192.168.40.0/24. It deploys two inspection VMs, each with one NIC in each network, placed in two zones behind an internal passthrough load balancer. Step 1 is done: the two inspection VMs are running. Step 2 is done: the load balancer's forwarding rule is the candidate next hop. Step 3 is done: a policy-based route in the app network matches source 192.168.20.0/24 and destination 192.168.40.0/24 and uses the load balancer as next hop. Step 4 is missing, and it is the step that handles traffic coming back from payments to the app network. Which choice completes the setup?
choices: Add a mirrored policy-based route in the payments network: source 192.168.40.0/24, destination 192.168.20.0/24, next hop the same load balancer.
Shorten the load balancer's health check interval so replies are not dropped while probes run.
Add a firewall rule allowing replies from 192.168.40.0/24, because replies never need a route through the load balancer.
Point the policy route's next hop at one inspection VM's internal IP so replies skip the load balancer.
questions.why: Reply packets form a separate flow in the opposite direction, so they need their own policy-based route pointing at the same load balancer so a stateful appliance sees both halves of the conversation.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what a policy-based route adds beyond an ordinary route?
choices: It replaces the health check, so backends are probed less often and traffic is steered without probing.
It is a route that only works between two VMs in the same zone and ignores the routing table entirely.
It adds match conditions (source range, destination range, protocol), and its next hop wins for packets that match.
It moves traffic to a different region whenever the local path looks slow to the sender.
questions.why: A policy-based route adds conditions it can match on, and when a packet matches, its next hop takes precedence over ordinary routes for that traffic.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Logistics has a policy-based route matching source 172.20.5.0/24 and destination 172.21.0.0/20, with an internal passthrough load balancer as next hop. All of its inspection VMs behind that load balancer currently fail their health checks. What happens to a packet from 172.20.5.31 to 172.21.3.8?
choices: It follows the ordinary route for 172.21.0.0/20, because the policy route is skipped whenever its backends are unhealthy.
It is sent automatically to a healthy VM in another region that the team has not configured.
It is dropped, and the sending side usually sees no error from the route itself.
It is held in a queue until a health check passes, and then it is delivered in order.
questions.why: A matching packet is sent to the next hop, and if that next hop has no healthy backend the packet has nowhere to go and is dropped, with no error shown to the sender.

questions.prompt: Kestrel Media has a policy-based route whose match conditions are source 10.70.3.0/24, destination 10.80.0.0/16, and protocol TCP only, with a load balancer as next hop. A UDP packet is sent from 10.70.3.12 to 10.80.4.4. Which routing applies to that packet?
choices: Both routes at once, with the packet copied to the load balancer as well as the ordinary path.
Neither route, so the packet is rejected at the source VM before it leaves.
The policy route, because it still matches on the source and destination ranges.
The ordinary route, because the policy route requires a protocol match and this packet is UDP, not TCP.
questions.why: A policy-based route applies only when every condition it names matches, so a UDP packet fails the protocol condition and follows normal routing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a policy-based route does, how it differs from a normal route, and one limit or tradeoff of using it with a high-availability appliance pair.
lessons.modelAnswer: A normal route only looks at where a packet is going. A policy-based route also looks at where the packet came from and which protocol it uses, so we can send one specific flow to a chosen next hop, such as an inspection appliance, and leave everything else alone. The next hop here is an internal load balancer in front of two appliances in different zones, so if one fails its health check, new traffic goes to the other. The tradeoff is that we now have a second routing layer to reason about. The rule has to exist in both directions so replies pass through the same appliance, and if every backend fails, matching traffic is dropped rather than rerouted. We also have to check priorities so the policy-based route is the one that wins for that traffic.
rubricPoints: A policy-based route matches on more than destination, such as source and protocol, and its next hop applies to matching traffic only.
Traffic that matches no policy-based route keeps following normal routing.
The next hop is often an internal load balancer, which uses health checks to spread traffic across appliances in several zones.
Return traffic needs its own matching rule in the other direction, or stateful inspection breaks.
If no healthy backend remains, matching traffic is dropped, so the rule is a risk as well as a benefit.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would let the learner watch which route and next hop a packet actually takes, which is the core skill this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Out-of-band security integration means connecting a security tool to your network by giving it a copy of the traffic to inspect, instead of placing it in the path where every packet must pass through it. Think of a camera watching a shop doorway on a monitor versus a guard standing in the doorway checking each person. The camera can spot trouble and raise an alarm, but it cannot stop anyone by itself. Choosing between the two is a strategy decision about how much delay you tolerate, how much risk you accept, and whether the tool must block traffic or only watch it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has a third-party intrusion detection tool. Should it sit where every packet must pass through it, or should it only receive copies of the traffic? What would you lose with each choice?
lessons.teach:
Inline inspection means the security appliance sits in the traffic path, so every packet passes through it. It can block, but a failure or slowdown in the appliance affects production. Out-of-band inspection means the appliance receives a copy of the traffic while the original flow continues untouched. It can detect and alert, but it cannot block on its own. In Google Cloud, Packet Mirroring is the feature that copies packets from selected VM instances in a VPC to a collector destination, usually reached through an internal load balancer in front of collector VMs. A mirror filter narrows which traffic is copied, by direction, protocol, or address range. A collector is the self-managed analysis tool that receives the copies.

Why it works: the copy is taken from the network, so the production path never waits on the tool. The collector sees what happened and can feed alerts or a log pipeline. The trade-off is that mirrored bytes consume bandwidth and collector capacity, and under heavy load copies can be dropped, so the mirror is not a complete audit record.

Worked example: a web tier of three VMs needs port-scan detection with no added latency. Step 1: select the web-tier instances by network tag. Step 2: set the filter to inbound TCP. Step 3: the copies flow to a collector pool behind an internal load balancer. Step 4: the collector flags a scan pattern and raises an alert. Blocking happens only when the team adds or changes a firewall rule. The result is detection, with prevention handled elsewhere.

Common mistake: assuming a mirrored tool stops attacks, or mirroring every subnet in a busy VPC so the collectors saturate. In a running system, saturated collectors drop copies silently, and the team believes nothing happened when the tool simply never saw the traffic.

Out-of-band integration is a strategy for watching and alerting without taking on the delay and failure risk of sitting in the path.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs a checkout service on four VMs in its own VPC. The security lead wants out-of-band monitoring for data leaving that service. Her engineer completes these steps: (1) selects the four checkout VMs as mirror sources by network tag, (2) sets the mirror filter to outbound TCP traffic, and (4) configures the collector to flag transfers larger than 500 MB and open a ticket. Step 3 is missing. What is it?
choices: Turn on inline inspection so every packet passes through the collector before it leaves.
Add a deny firewall rule that cuts off any flow the collector flags.
Point the mirror at an internal load balancer that fronts the collector VMs, so the copied packets reach the analysis tool.
Move the checkout VMs into a separate subnet so their traffic bypasses the VPC.
questions.why: Mirrored copies need a collector destination, usually an internal load balancer in front of collector VMs, and the other three options either add blocking, which out-of-band inspection does not do by itself, or change the traffic path.

questions.prompt: A team wants a security tool to see a copy of traffic from its database VMs while the original flows continue untouched. Which description fits this strategy?
choices: Inline inspection, where the tool sits in the path and can block traffic.
A load balancer that spreads database queries across replica servers.
Out-of-band inspection, where the tool receives copies and can alert but cannot block on its own.
A firewall rule that denies traffic from unknown addresses.
questions.why: Out-of-band inspection receives a copy of traffic while the original flow continues, so it detects and alerts but does not block by itself.

questions.prompt: A team mirrors every subnet in a busy VPC to a collector pool of three small VMs. Weeks later an intrusion goes unreported. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The collector's firewall blocked the mirrored traffic before the tool could inspect it.
Out-of-band tools always see every intrusion, so the firewall rules must be at fault.
Packet Mirroring slowed production, so the platform turned the mirror off automatically.
The collectors were saturated and dropped copies silently, so the tool never saw the traffic.
questions.why: Under heavy load, copies can be dropped without notice, so mirroring every subnet into undersized collectors can leave the tool blind to real traffic.

questions.prompt: A team's mirror collector drops copies during peak hours. Which conclusion is the safest?
choices: The collector is deliberately blocking copies to protect the network.
The mirror is a complete audit record, so the gap means nothing happened.
Production traffic was not affected, so no review of the gap is needed.
The mirror is not a complete record, so the team should treat missing copies as a blind spot and plan for it.
questions.why: Mirrored copies can be dropped under load and are not a complete audit record, so the safe response is to treat gaps as blind spots rather than proof that nothing happened.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes putting a third-party inspection appliance inline for all traffic into our production VPC because we want to be safe. Explain in your own words when an out-of-band design is the better strategy, and name one limit or trade-off the team must accept with it.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would say the inline idea trades safety for risk. An inline appliance can block, but every packet depends on it, so a slowdown or failure hits production directly. An out-of-band design copies traffic to the tool, so the production path keeps running. It is the better strategy when the goal is detection, forensics, or alerting, and when the business cannot accept added latency or a new single point of failure. The limit is that the tool cannot block anything by itself. If we want prevention, we must pair it with firewall rules that the team changes after an alert, which adds response time. Mirrored copies also cost bandwidth and collector capacity, and under load some copies may be dropped, so we should not treat the mirror as a complete record. I would propose out-of-band first, measure what it misses, then decide whether any specific segment needs inline blocking.
rubricPoints: Defines inline as in-path (can block, adds a failure dependency) and out-of-band as a copy (detects, does not block)
Explains that out-of-band suits detection and alerting when latency or added failure risk is unacceptable
Names a real limit: out-of-band cannot block alone and needs firewall changes or other controls
Names a second trade-off: mirrored copies consume bandwidth and can be dropped under load

suggested.rationale: The objective is a design strategy, so being able to argue inline versus out-of-band in your own words is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Packet Mirroring is a way to send a copy of network traffic from chosen machines to a separate machine whose only job is to watch. Think of photocopying every letter a clerk handles and sending the copies to an auditor's desk, while the original letters keep moving normally. Engineers use this to investigate attacks, measure what is really happening, or feed an intrusion detection tool. The copies are made beside the real traffic rather than in its path, so a watching tool that fails does not break the application. This objective covers choosing which traffic gets copied and where the copies are delivered when the watcher is a machine you run yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you copy every packet from a busy web server to a monitoring machine, what would you expect to happen to the users' requests, and why might you still choose to copy only some of the packets?
lessons.teach:
Packet Mirroring is a Google Cloud feature that makes out-of-band copies of packets passing through selected virtual machines in a VPC network. A VPC network is your private virtual network in the cloud. Out-of-band means the copies are taken alongside the traffic instead of being inserted into it. The mirrored source is the set of instances, subnets, or network tags whose traffic you want copied. The collector is the machine or group of machines that receives the copies. In this objective the collector is self-managed, meaning you run the capture or analysis software yourself. A mirroring policy ties a source to a collector and can narrow the copies with filters on IP protocol, IP address range, and direction (ingress, egress, or both). Because the original packets are not redirected, they keep flowing to their real destination unchanged.

The collector is not addressed directly. You place collector instances behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer and point the mirroring policy at that load balancer's forwarding rule. This gives the collectors one stable address and spreads copies across them. The collectors must sit in the same region as the mirrored sources, and firewall rules must allow the mirrored copies to reach the collector's ports.

Worked example: a web subnet 10.10.1.0/24 holds three web servers. Step 1: create a policy with that subnet as the source. Step 2: filter to TCP, in both directions. Step 3: set the collector to an internal load balancer fronting two capture VMs, and allow the copies through the firewall to those VMs. A user request reaches a web server, which answers normally. A copy of each matching packet is sent to the load balancer, which forwards it to one capture VM, where your tool records it. The user never sees the copy.

Common mistake: pointing the policy at one collector VM's address instead of a load balancer, or forgetting the firewall rule, so copies silently never arrive. On a running system, mirroring adds load on the source VMs and on the collector path, and it adds cost. Copying everything from a busy tier can saturate the collectors and inflate the bill, which is why narrow filters matter.

questions.prompt: A payments team wants to copy packets from the subnet 172.20.5.0/24, which lives in europe-west1, to a self-managed intrusion analysis tool. Step 1: create a mirroring policy with 172.20.5.0/24 as the source. Step 2: filter to UDP only, ingress direction only. Step 3 is missing: the policy's collector destination must be set to the forwarding rule of an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer placed in europe-west1, and that load balancer fronts the analysis VMs. Step 4: add a firewall rule that allows the mirrored copies to reach the analysis VMs on their listening port. Which statement correctly completes the missing Step 3?
choices: Set the collector destination to an external load balancer in us-central1 so the analysis VMs can be placed anywhere.
Set the collector destination to the forwarding rule of the internal passthrough Network Load Balancer in europe-west1 that fronts the analysis VMs.
Set the collector destination to the private IP address of the first analysis VM so copies go straight to one host.
Leave the collector destination empty, because the policy sends copies to whichever VM the source subnet uses most.
questions.why: The policy must point at the forwarding rule of an internal passthrough load balancer in the same region as the source, because that gives the collectors one stable address and spreads copies across them.

questions.prompt: In Packet Mirroring, what does it mean that the copies are made out-of-band?
choices: The copies are taken alongside the traffic, so the original packets still reach their real destination unchanged.
The copies are delivered only after the destination host has acknowledged the original packet.
The copies are stored on the source VM's disk before any packet leaves the network.
The copies are sent along the original path and the original packets are rerouted to the collector.
questions.why: Out-of-band means the mirror is a side copy, so the original packets keep flowing to their real destination without being redirected or delayed.

questions.prompt: A team creates a mirroring policy for a busy tier in europe-west1, but places the self-managed collectors in us-central1 to save on capacity. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The mirrored copies will be duplicated and billed twice, but the collectors will still receive all traffic.
The source VMs will stop answering user requests until the collectors are moved into the same region.
Nothing is wrong, because collectors can be in any region once a load balancer is in front of them.
The collectors must be in the same region as the mirrored sources, so the copies will not be delivered as intended.
questions.why: The teaching text states that collectors must sit in the same region as the mirrored sources, so a cross-region placement breaks delivery of the copies.

questions.prompt: An analyst wants to capture only outbound TCP traffic leaving the instances tagged batch-workers in a VPC, and nothing else. Which combination of filters should the mirroring policy use?
choices: Direction set to egress, IP protocol set to TCP.
Direction set to egress, IP protocol set to all protocols.
Direction set to ingress, IP protocol set to UDP.
Direction set to both, IP protocol set to all protocols.
questions.why: Narrow filters on direction and IP protocol are what limit the copies to exactly the traffic wanted, here outbound TCP, which also keeps load and cost down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up Packet Mirroring so a self-managed capture tool sees traffic from one web tier, and name one limit or tradeoff you would warn them about.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the collector VMs behind an internal passthrough load balancer in the same region as the web tier, because the mirroring policy targets the load balancer's forwarding rule rather than an individual VM. Then I would create the policy with the web tier's subnet or network tag as the source, add filters so only the protocols and address ranges we need are copied, and check that firewall rules let the mirrored copies reach the capture ports. The tradeoff to warn about is that mirroring is a copy, so it adds load and cost on the source VMs and the collector path. If the filters are too broad, the collectors can fall behind or drop copies, and the capture becomes incomplete even though the production traffic is fine.
rubricPoints: Collector is reached through an internal passthrough load balancer forwarding rule, not a single VM address
Source is chosen by subnet, instance, or network tag, and filters narrow what is copied
Collectors must be in the same region and firewall rules must allow the copies
Mirroring is out-of-band, so production traffic is unaffected by the copy
Copying too much adds load, cost, and risk of incomplete captures

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console configuration and product facts, which reading and the official flow describe better than an existing OpsForge mission.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Logistics: planning a first cloud network for GKE and a managed database
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional freight company with one data centre that uses private addresses from 10.20.0.0/16 and a legacy range 10.40.0.0/14. It is moving its booking website into Google Cloud. The team plans a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster, which is a managed service that runs containers on groups of virtual machines called nodes. They also plan a managed MySQL database, which should be reachable only through private addresses. The company expects traffic to grow about tenfold within two years, and its customers are spread across Europe and North America. Two constraints matter: the cloud addresses must never overlap with the data centre ranges, because the two sides will be joined by a VPN tunnel, and the company has a limited regional quota for external IP addresses. A senior engineer asks you to write up a short design plan. The plan must name the specific Google Cloud constructs and the constraint that shapes each choice, in plain language that a new teammate could follow. Complete these sub-tasks: 1. Choose the network tier and the VPC type (standalone or Shared VPC) for this company, and explain which quota or scale constraint drives your choice. 2. Plan the GKE subnet with its primary range, pod secondary range and service secondary range, sizing each so the cluster can grow, and state how you avoid overlap with the data centre. 3. Explain how the GKE nodes and the database will reach Google services privately, and state the MTU value you would set for the VPN link and why it matters.
subParts: Network tier and VPC type choice with quota driver
GKE subnet and secondary range sizing without overlap
Private access to the database and MTU for the VPN link
modelAnswer: Premium Network Service Tier is the default tier that carries traffic over Google's global backbone for as much of the path as possible, while Standard tier uses the public internet for more of the path and is regional in scope. For a company with customers on two continents, Premium is the sound choice. A VPC, short for virtual private cloud, is your own isolated software network inside Google Cloud. A standalone VPC is owned and administered by one project. A Shared VPC lets a host project share its subnets with service projects, which suits a company with several teams and central network control. For a first build with one application team, a standalone VPC is simpler and avoids extra permission setup. The constraint that drives the decision is the regional external IP quota, a limit on how many public addresses one project can hold in a region. Keeping the GKE nodes private and using a load balancer for public traffic keeps the public address count low. Shared VPC becomes worth it later, when several projects must share one address plan and one set of firewall rules.

A subnet is a range of IP addresses inside a VPC tied to one region. GKE needs three ranges: a primary range for node addresses, a secondary range for pods, which are the groups of containers, and a secondary range for services, which are the stable virtual addresses that front pods. Pod and service ranges must be secondary ranges on the same subnet. Sizing for growth: a /16 leaves room for many nodes, so a primary range of 172.20.0.0/20 gives about 4,000 node addresses. The default pod setup gives each node a block of pod addresses; a secondary pod range of 172.24.0.0/16 supports many nodes at the usual per-node allocation. A service range of 172.28.0.0/20 supports thousands of services. These ranges come from 172.16.0.0/12, which does not overlap with 10.20.0.0/16 or 10.40.0.0/14. Overlap is the mistake to avoid: if cloud and data centre ranges collide, routing over the VPN becomes ambiguous and traffic can go to the wrong side. Check every range against the data centre list before you deploy, because a subnet's primary range cannot be changed later without rebuilding it.

Private Google Access lets VMs and nodes with only internal addresses reach Google APIs and services through internal routing. Private Services Access is a separate pattern: you reserve an internal address block in your VPC and create a peering link so a managed service such as Cloud SQL gets a private address inside that block. The database therefore uses a reserved range, for example 172.31.0.0/16, that must not overlap with the other ranges. Private Service Connect is an alternative that gives a private endpoint address inside your own subnet; it is useful when you want to avoid the reserved peering block. For the VPN link, MTU, the maximum transmission unit, is the largest packet size a link carries without splitting. A VPN tunnel adds encapsulation headers, so the VPC MTU is commonly kept at the default of 1460 bytes so packets fit after the extra header bytes are added. If the MTU is set too high, large packets are dropped or fragmented, which shows up as sessions that connect but stall when they send big payloads, such as file uploads on the booking site.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern warehouse subnet, sharing, and peering
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional company that runs a warehouse tracking app. Its network team uses a VPC (virtual private cloud, meaning a private network you define inside Google Cloud that holds subnets, which are smaller address blocks inside that network). The app runs in a subnet called inventory-subnet in region europe-west1 with the IPv4 range 10.10.0.0/24, and the team is almost out of addresses. Several changes must be made this week. Answer each numbered task.

1. The subnet needs more addresses. Name the operation to use, state which direction the prefix length may change (the prefix length is the number after the slash that sets how many addresses a range holds), and say what the team must not do to the existing range.

2. A separate service project called fulfilment-prod must launch VMs into inventory-subnet. That subnet lives in a host project using Shared VPC (a setup where one host project owns the network and service projects attach to it). Name the IAM role (IAM means Identity and Access Management, the permission system) and the level at which it must be granted. Explain what a broader grant at the project level would do.

3. The VMs have no external IP addresses but must call Cloud Storage APIs. Name the subnet setting to enable and explain what it allows. State one thing it does not provide.

4. A partner company's VPC using 10.20.0.0/16 will be connected to Harbor Lantern's VPC through VPC Network Peering (a connection where two VPC networks exchange traffic privately). Explain the address condition that must hold, and explain why a network the partner reaches through its own peering cannot be reached through this one.
subParts: Expand the subnet's IP range: name the operation, the allowed direction of the prefix change, and what must not be done to the existing range.
Grant subnet access to the service project: name the role and the grant level, and explain the effect of a project-level grant.
Reach Google APIs without external IPs: name the subnet setting and what it does not provide.
Peer with the partner VPC: state the address condition and explain why peering is not transitive.
modelAnswer: Use the expand-IP-range operation on the existing subnet (in the console or command line tools). The prefix length can only be made smaller, for example changing /24 to /23, which doubles the addresses. A prefix length can never be increased through this operation, so /23 cannot be shrunk back to /24. The team must not delete and recreate the subnet or move VMs to a new range, because expansion keeps existing addresses valid and the VMs keep running. The new, larger range must still avoid overlapping other subnets and any peered or connected address ranges.

Grant the Compute Network User role (roles/compute.networkUser) on the specific inventory-subnet, not on the whole host project, to the users, groups, or service accounts in fulfilment-prod that create VMs. The service project's Compute service agent also needs this role on that subnet so VM creation can attach to it. A project-level grant on the host project would give access to every subnet there, which is broader than the task needs. Granting a powerful admin role such as Compute Admin on the host project would be a common mistake that gives control over the shared network itself.

Enable Private Google Access on inventory-subnet, which is a subnet-level setting. It lets VMs with only internal addresses reach Google APIs and many Google-managed services through Google's network instead of the public internet. It does not give those VMs general internet access, does not give them an external IP, and does not make on-premises networks reachable.

The two address ranges must not overlap. 10.10.0.0/24 and 10.20.0.0/16 do not overlap, so this peering is allowed. Peering is not transitive, meaning that if the partner is peered with a third network, Harbor Lantern does not gain a route to that third network through the partner. Traffic that depends on passing through the partner's peering is dropped because the peering only carries traffic between its two directly connected networks. A reachable path would need its own peering, or a hub design such as Network Connectivity Center.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Tickets: global web entry point, CDN caching, and DNS failover
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Tickets is a fictional company that sells concert tickets online. Its website runs on virtual machines in two Google Cloud regions. Each region uses a managed instance group, which is a set of identical virtual machines created from one template, where Google Cloud can add or replace machines automatically as load changes. Customers reach the site at www.brightwater-example.com over HTTPS, which is encrypted web traffic. The team wants one global public entry point so that a visitor in Europe and a visitor in the United States both reach the nearest healthy region. Requests whose path starts with /api/ must go to the application servers, while requests under /static/ must be served from a Cloud Storage bucket. Cloud Storage is object storage, meaning files are kept as named objects rather than on a disk. Product photos and stylesheets live in that bucket, and the team wants them copied to edge locations near customers with Cloud CDN, a content delivery network that keeps copies of popular responses so they do not travel back to the origin each time. Each cached copy stays until its time-to-live (TTL, the number of seconds a copy may be reused) runs out. A separate backup stack, with its own load balancer and its own IP address, runs in a second project. If the primary load balancer stops passing its health checks (automated probes that test whether a target still answers), the team wants the domain name to point to the backup stack. Please answer the following: 1. Name the load balancer type you would choose for this public, global, HTTPS traffic with path-based routing, and explain in one or two sentences why it fits better than a regional or passthrough option. 2. A designer replaces a product photo in the bucket, but customers still see the old photo an hour later. Explain why this happens, and name the fix that removes the old cached copy without changing the file name. 3. Describe the Cloud DNS setting that sends traffic to the backup stack only when the primary's health check fails, and name the DNS record type the team should use for the domain pointing at each load balancer IP address.
subParts: Choose the global external Application Load Balancer and justify it
Explain the stale photo and name the cache invalidation fix
Describe the DNS failover routing policy and the A record type
modelAnswer: Choose a global external Application Load Balancer. It is a proxy-based, Layer 7 load balancer, meaning it reads HTTP paths and hostnames, so it can send /api/ and /static/ to different backends from one URL map (the set of rules that matches request paths to backend services). It is external, so it accepts traffic from the public internet, and global, so one anycast IP address (one address advertised from many locations so the nearest location answers) serves users worldwide and sends each user to a healthy region. A regional load balancer would only serve one region, and a passthrough load balancer forwards packets without reading paths, so it cannot split /api/ from /static/.

The old photo is still in the edge cache. Cloud CDN keeps a copy of each object until its TTL expires, and replacing the file in the bucket does not automatically remove copies already stored at edge locations. The fix is to invalidate the cached path, for example /static/product/photo.jpg, using a cache invalidation request, which tells the edge locations to drop that copy so the next request fetches the new version from the bucket. Another valid option is to upload the new photo under a new file name, since a new path has no old cached copy. Clearing the browser cache on one computer does not help, because the stale copy is stored in Google's edge locations for every visitor.

Use a Cloud DNS routing policy of the failover type on the record for www.brightwater-example.com. The primary record points to the primary load balancer IP address and is linked to a health check that probes that address. The backup record points to the backup stack's IP address. While the health check passes, Cloud DNS answers with the primary address. When the health check fails, Cloud DNS answers with the backup address. The domain entries for each load balancer IP are A records, which map a hostname to an IPv4 address. A failover policy without a linked health check never switches, so the outage would continue while users still receive the failing address.

scenarios.title: Brackwater Freight's Hybrid Link Upgrade
scenarios.scenario: Brackwater Freight Ltd is a fictional company that runs its warehouse inventory database in an on-premises data center in one city and is moving its order-processing web tier to Google Cloud. The two sides must talk privately, not over the public internet. A dedicated interconnect is a physical fiber link you lease from a colocation or carrier location straight into Google's network edge, so traffic between your data center and your cloud VPC (virtual private cloud, a private network you define in the cloud) never crosses the public internet. A VLAN attachment is the logical circuit on that physical link that ties one cloud VPC region to the interconnect, and it uses a VLAN ID (a numeric tag that separates traffic on a shared link). Cloud Router is a managed Google Cloud service that exchanges routes with your on-premises routers using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the standard protocol that announces which IP address ranges are reachable through which path). Each Cloud Router and each on-premises router has an ASN (autonomous system number, a unique number identifying a routing domain). Brackwater's network team wants the order tier to stay reachable if one physical link or one whole city site fails. Their order database cannot tolerate more than a few minutes of downtime per year, so they plan a 99.99 percent SLA (service level agreement, the uptime Google commits to in writing) topology. They also plan to make one path the preferred one using the MED (multi-exit discriminator, a BGP value where a lower number is preferred for routes advertised to a neighbor) and to advertise only the 10.40.0.0/16 subnet to on-premises rather than every route in the VPC. Answer these three sub-tasks: 1. Name the dedicated interconnect topology that meets a 99.99 percent SLA, and state how many connections and how many metros it requires. 2. Explain which value the team should lower on the preferred Cloud Router path to make it win, and what happens to traffic if the preferred link fails. 3. Describe how the team would use custom advertised routes so that only the 10.40.0.0/16 range is announced on-premises, and state one reason BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, a fast liveness check between two routers) helps detect the failure quickly.
modelAnswer: A 99.99 percent SLA for Dedicated Interconnect requires four connections spread across two metros (two separate metropolitan areas), with two connections in each metro, and each pair placed in different edge availability domains (separate failure zones at Google's edge within a metro). Two connections in one metro in two edge availability domains only reach the 99.9 percent tier, so the team must add a second metro to reach 99.99.

The team should lower the MED on the routes advertised from the preferred Cloud Router path, because a lower MED value is preferred by the neighbor. If the preferred link fails, BGP sessions on that path go down, the routes learned through it are withdrawn, and traffic moves to the remaining path that still has its routes, at the higher MED, so the order tier stays reachable, though perhaps on a less preferred path.

The team would configure the Cloud Router to use custom advertised routes, which means turning off the default of advertising all subnets and instead listing only 10.40.0.0/16 as a custom prefix to advertise to on-premises. BFD helps because it sends very frequent short check messages between the two routers, so a failed link is detected in well under a second rather than waiting for slower BGP hold timers, which lets routing switch over sooner.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Dental Supply: Intermittent Office Link and Blocked Database Access
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Dental Supply is a fictional company that runs its order system on Google Cloud. Its head office connects to the cloud through an HA Cloud VPN tunnel pair, and Cloud Router exchanges routes with the office router using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol, the protocol routers use to tell each other which address ranges they can reach). Over the past two days, the warehouse team reported that the office link drops for about two minutes every few hours. Separately, a new application VM in subnet app-prod can no longer reach the orders database on TCP port 5432 after a firewall change made yesterday by a colleague. You are the on-call network engineer. Work through the following: 1. Name the specific Google Cloud tool or log source you would check first to confirm whether the VPN tunnels and the BGP session are actually going down and coming back, and explain what each one tells you. 2. Name the tool you would use to test whether the app VM can reach the database without sending real traffic first, state which two kinds of configuration it checks, and explain how you would use its result to decide whether the problem is in routing or in firewall rules. 3. Name the tool that lists warnings about firewall rules that are shadowed, unused, or overly broad, and say whether it would have flagged yesterday's change, and explain how you would confirm which rule actually matched the blocked traffic.
subParts: Name the tool or log source to confirm VPN tunnel and BGP session drops, and what each reveals
Name the connectivity diagnosis tool, the two configuration types it checks, and how to interpret its result
Name the firewall-rule analysis tool and the way to confirm which rule matched blocked traffic
modelAnswer: Check Cloud Logging for the Cloud VPN tunnel and Cloud Router logs, and review the Cloud Monitoring metrics for the VPN tunnel status and the Cloud Router BGP session state. Cloud Logging stores the timestamped events, so you can see each tunnel going down, the IKE (Internet Key Exchange, the handshake that sets up an encrypted VPN tunnel) negotiation, and the BGP session moving to a not-established state and back. Monitoring metrics show the same events as graphs, so you can line up the drops against the two-minute outages and spot whether the tunnel and the BGP session fall at the same moment. If the tunnel drops first, the cause is usually on the VPN path; if the BGP session drops while the tunnel stays up, the cause is usually in the routing exchange, such as a peer timer or a missing route advertisement.

Use Connectivity Tests. This tool builds a model of the network path from the app VM to the database IP and checks two kinds of configuration: routes, meaning whether a route exists that sends the traffic toward the database and that the destination is reachable from that route, and firewall rules, meaning whether an ingress or egress rule allows TCP port 5432 for that source and destination. The test returns the result of the analysis without relying on live traffic, so it is safe to run in production. If the result shows a valid route but a firewall rule that denies the traffic, the fault is in firewall configuration. If the route is missing or points to the wrong next hop, the fault is in routing.

Use Firewall Insights, which reports on firewall rules by showing shadowed rules (rules that never take effect because a higher-priority rule already matches), unused rules, and rules that allow more than they need. It would flag yesterday's change if the new rule was shadowed or unused, but it will not show a live match on its own. To confirm which rule actually matched the blocked traffic, turn on firewall rule logging for the relevant rule, or check the firewall logs in Cloud Logging, which record the rule name and the allow or deny action for each connection. The rule named in the log entry is the one that acted on the traffic. Common mistake: assuming a rule with the right ports is the one in effect when a higher-priority deny rule is matching first.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Shop: Protecting the Storefront, Its Login, and Its Database
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lantern is a fictional online lantern retailer. Its storefront runs on Compute Engine virtual machines behind an external Application Load Balancer, which is Google Cloud's public entry point that spreads incoming web requests across backend machines. The team wants to attach a Cloud Armor security policy to that load balancer. Cloud Armor is Google Cloud's service for filtering web and network traffic with ordered rules, and a security policy is the named set of those rules. Its web application firewall (WAF) rules inspect each HTTP request for known attack patterns. SQL injection is an attack where someone types database commands into a form or URL so the database runs them. Rate limiting means counting requests from one client over a time window and slowing or blocking that client when the count passes a threshold. Recently the security log shows about 900 login attempts per minute from a small set of addresses, and some URLs contain the text 'UNION SELECT', a common SQL injection pattern. The database runs in a private subnet and should accept traffic only from the web tier on TCP port 3306. The company's folder has a hierarchical firewall policy, which is a rule set attached above the project level and evaluated before project rules, and that policy has a deny rule that also matches traffic from the web tier to the database on port 3306. Complete the following:
1. Name the Cloud Armor WAF rule type you would use to block the 'UNION SELECT' requests, and state the action you would set on the matching rule.
2. Describe how you would rate limit the login path to stop the 900-per-minute burst while keeping normal shoppers unaffected, including the threshold action you would choose.
3. Explain which firewall decision takes effect for web tier to database traffic on port 3306 when both the folder-level deny rule and a project-level VPC allow rule match, and what you would check first when troubleshooting.
modelAnswer: Use a preconfigured WAF rule for SQL injection (the sqli rule family) in the Cloud Armor security policy, or a custom rule that matches the 'UNION SELECT' text in the request path, query string, or body. Set the action to deny with an error status such as 403, so the request is refused before it reaches a backend. Preview mode can be used first to see matches in logs without blocking anything. Mention that the policy must be attached to the backend service of the load balancer for the rule to take effect on those requests.

Create a rate limiting rule scoped to the login path, matching requests to that URL. Count requests per client IP address over a short window, and set the threshold to a level above normal human behavior, such as the expected peak per address per minute. Use a throttle or rate-based ban action: throttle slows or limits requests above the threshold, and rate-based ban blocks the client for a set period after the threshold is crossed. Keep the rule scoped to the login path so ordinary browsing is not counted against the limit. Review the logs in preview mode before enforcing, so you can confirm that real shoppers stay under the threshold.

The deny decision wins. Hierarchical firewall policies are evaluated before VPC firewall rules, so a matching deny at the folder level blocks the traffic even though a project-level allow rule also matches. Troubleshooting starts by checking the effective firewall rules or firewall rule logs for the database instance to see which rule matched and at what level. The fix is made in the hierarchical policy, for example by narrowing its scope or adding a higher-priority allow for the web tier to port 3306, not by editing the VPC allow rule, because that rule cannot override a higher-level deny.
